Vehicle and Bicycle Parking Requirements 
The following uses shall be required for the project as currently contemplated and in 
any future iteration thereof as governed by this Development Plan: 
 
Vehicle Parking Maximums 
 
Vehicle Parking shall be provided subject to the maximums below based on proposed 
use: 
 
● 0.6 spaces per 1,000 sf of office/research laboratory (including start-up business 
and Affordable Cultural Space) or retail/restaurant/service. 
● 0.5 spaces per unit for rental residential, or 0.75 spaces per unit of condo 
residential 
 
Electric Vehicle Readiness 
 
No less than 25 percent of all vehicle parking provided shall be EV-installed and the 
remaining 75 percent shall be EV-ready. 
 
● EV-Ready: EV-Ready shall mean providing raceway to every parking space, 
adequate space in the electrical panel and space for additional transformer 
capacity to accommodate the future installation of the transformer, if necessary, 
and the associated Level 2 EVSE. The City approved EV Requirement Equivalent 
Calculator must be used if chargers other than Level 2 Chargers are planned to be 
installed in the future to meet with EV-Ready Requirements. 
● EVSE-Installed: “EVSE-Installed” shall mean an installed Level 2 EVSE. The 
City approved EV Requirement Equivalent Calculator must be used if chargers 
other than Level 2 Chargers are installed to meet the EVSE-Installed 
Requirement. 
 
Bicycle Parking Requirements 
 
Bicycle Parking shall be provided subject to the minimums below based on proposed 
use: 
 
Long-term secure bike parking 
 
● 1 space per 2,500 sf of office/life science (including start-up business and 
Affordable Cultural Space 
● 1 space per 3,000 sf of retail/restaurant/service 
● 1 space per 1 unit of residential

At least 25% of required spaces must be on-ground and secured with post-and-ring or 
inverted U racks. At least 5% of required spaces (no less than two) must be both on-
ground and extra-wide. Each post-and-ring or inverted U rack provides 2 bike parking 
spaces. All other spaces may be secured via two-tier racks, which provide a variable 
number of spaces. 
 
Short-term visitor bike parking 
 
● 1 space per 20,000 sf of office/life science (including start-up business and 
Affordable Cultural Space) 
● 1 space per 5,000 sf of retail/restaurant/service 
● 1 space per 5 units of residential 
 
Provision of Showers and Lockers 
 
● 1 shower per 60,000 sf of office/life science and 1 locker per 6,000 sf of retail

RE: Support for 1033-1055 Washington Street
Dear Members of the BPDA Board,
I am writing in support of the proposed project at 1033-1055 Washington Street, which will
construct two buildings for life science and office uses of approximately 150 feet tall. The buildings
will be linked by an above grade connection, and will include ground-floor retail space, as well as
community space. There will be an underground two level parking garage with up to 353
accessory vehicle parking space, and approximately 266 bicycle parking spaces for building tenants
and visitors. The project will also include public realm improvements, which include new street
trees, a pedestrian plaza, and improvements to sidewalks.
The current site is an underutilized parcel of land located near public transportation and surrounded
by a vibrant residential and commercial community. The proposed project will activate this area,
and the mixed use characteristics of the buildings will be fitting for the area. The proponent has
gone through the community process and was willing to listen to concerns from neighbors, and
worked to address issues that were brought up during the Article 80 process. This project will
provide $6.3 million in Neighborhood Housing Trust payments and $1.1 million in Neighborhoods
Jobs Trust payments.
I hope that the BPDA will approve this project. Should you have any questions, please feel free to
contact me at 617-635-3203, or at Ed.Flynn@Boston.gov.
Sincerely,
Ed Flynn
Boston City Councilor, District 2

Re: Neighborhood Input for 1033-1055 Washington Street
Dear Chief Jemison and members of the BPDA Board,
I am writing in regards to the proposed project at 1033-1055 Washington Street, and call
attention to community input from abutters relating to open space, traffic, and other aspects of
the project. As the 1033-1055 Washington Street project will have a critical impact on the
neighborhood, I hope that the BPDA will take these comments into serious consideration, and
work with residents to ensure that this development is one that will reflect input from the
community.
In particular, neighbors have expressed the following recommendations and suggestions on the
project:
●
Adjacent BPDA-owned parcel to be made into park: There is a BPDA-owned parcel
that is between the south side of The Lucas Condominiums (140 Shawmut Ave) and the
project, which sits vacant for years. The developer of the 1033-1055 Washington St is
willing to fund and provide for the landscaping and perpetual maintenance of a park for
South End community residents with this vacant parcel, and residents are requesting that
this parcel be be preserved for the community and the city grant the necessary
permissions to the Druker Washington Street Project to landscape and maintain the park
as part of their overall proposal.
●
No additional curb cuts on Shawmut Avenue: Residents have noted that there are
many families and elderly that use Shawmut Ave, and substantially increased traffic on
Shawmut Ave will pose risks to residents and pedestrians. They are requesting that there
be no further curb cuts on Shawmut Avenue or any changes to traffic direction that would
eliminate or reduce public parking on both sides of Shawmut Avenue.

●
Parking allocation: Residents request that the project provide and maintain public access
to parking for residents residing in the area.
●
Building height and shadowing: The project building height is 150 feet. However, there
is an additional allocation of 20 feet to accommodate the mechanicals. As this may
impact the buildings with lower heights in the area, residents are recommending to push
all mechanical equipment on the North Building back approximately 20 feet from the
perimeter to reduce shadowing and noise impacts.
●
The Lucas Condominiums’s foundation stability: Seismic measures and strict
protocols need to be undertaken to ensure that foundation stability of The Lucas, most
critically along the east side of the building that will abut the excavation for the garage
under the project.
●
Project timing and sidewalk closures: Residents request to know the specific number of
construction days once approval has been given. They would also like to understand
if/when and for how long sidewalk areas would be impacted along Shawmut Avenue.
I hope that the BPDA will take these recommendations into consideration as it works with the
developer and neighbors as this project undergoes its community process. Should you have any
questions, please feel free to contact me at 617-635-3203, or at Ed.Flynn@Boston.gov.
Sincerely,

Project Notification Form 
I have reviewed the Project Notification Form (the “PNF”) dated February 7, 2023, and 
submit the following comments for the Environmental Protection component. The 
Drucker Company, Ltd. (the “Proponent”) proposes to demolish the existing one-story 
vacant warehouse and construct two life science/office buildings (the “Proposed 
Project”). 
 
Wind 
 
The Proponent shall be required to conduct a qualitative analysis of the level wind 
impacts. The analysis shall determine the potential pedestrian level winds adjacent to and 
in the vicinity of the Proposed Project and identify where wind velocities are expected to 
exceed acceptable levels, including the Boston Planning & Development Agency’s (the 
“BPDA”) guideline of an effective gust velocity of 31 miles per hour (mph) not to be 
exceeded more than 1% of the time. 
 
Particular attention shall be given to public and other areas of pedestrian use, including, 
but not limited to, entrances to the Proposed Project and existing and proposed buildings 
in the vicinity of the Proposed Project, on the existing and proposed open spaces, 
dedicated public parklands and publicly accessible open spaces, public plazas, as well as 
sidewalks and pedestrian walkways adjacent to and in the vicinity of the Proposed 
Project. 
 
The Proponent shall be required to evaluate the following conditions: 
 
1. No-Build: Existing conditions of the site and the environs to establish the 
baseline (including projects under construction). 
2. Build-Existing condition of the site together with the Proposed Project. 
3. Full Build-The Proposed Project and the BPDA Board approved projects, not 
yet under construction. 
 
The Proponent shall be required to submit a list of the BPDA Board approved projects, 
not yet under construction, proposed to be included in the Full Build condition. 
 
The BPDA will review the results of the qualitative analysis and will work with the 
Proponent to generate a wind sensor plan to be used for the quantitative (wind tunnel) 
		

analysis. The Proponent will be asked to evaluate the same three conditions (described 
above) for the quantitative analysis. 
 
Shadow 
 
The results of the shadow analysis demonstrate that the Proposed Project is not 
anticipated to create an adverse impact, thus no additional study shall be required. 
 
Solar Glare 
 
The Proponent shall not be required to conduct a solar glare analysis at this time, as the 
Proponent has stated that the Proposed Project design does not include the use of highly 
reflective materials. However, should the design change and incorporate highly 
reflective materials, the Proponent shall be required to measure potential reflective glare 
from the Proposed Project onto potentially affected streets and public open spaces as well 
as the sidewalk areas, to determine the likelihood of visual impairment or discomfort due 
to reflective spot glare. 
 
Daylight 
 
The Proponent shall be required to perform a daylight analysis and evaluate the following 
conditions: 
1. No-Build: Existing conditions, including all projects currently under 
construction. 
2. Build: Existing conditions, all buildings under construction and the Proposed 
Project. 
3. Full Build: Existing conditions, all buildings under construction, the Proposed 
Project and all BPDA Board approved projects not yet under construction (the 
Proponent shall be required to submit a list of BPDA Board approved projects 
in advance for review and approval). 
 
The Proponent shall be required to measure the percentage of skydome that is anticipated 
to be obstructed by the Proposed Project. The analysis shall include each major building 
façade fronting public ways or passages. The daylight analysis shall be conducted by use 
of the “BRADA” computer program, or a similar program to be approved by the BPDA 
in advance. 
 
Air Quality 
 
The Proponent has demonstrated that the Proposed Project will comply with the 
Massachusetts and National Ambient Air Quality Standards. 
 
Noise 
 
The Proponent shall be required to conduct a noise analysis of the potential impacts from 
the Proposed Project, including rooftop mechanical equipment and other noise sources 
		

(e.g., emergency generators) to demonstrate that the Proposed Project is designed to 
attenuate noise to meet the “Regulations for the Control of Noise in the City of Boston”, 
MassDEP noise limits and federal regulations and guidelines. 
 
Solid and Hazardous Wastes 
 
Any known or potential hazardous wastes or contaminants on the Proposed Project site 
must be described, together with a description of remediation measures to ensure their 
safe removal and disposal, pursuant to M.G.L. Chapter 21E and the Massachusetts 
Contingency Plan. Any potential hazardous wastes to be generated by the Proposed 
Project must be identified. The existence of underground storage tanks (UST) and above 
ground storage tanks (AST) on the Proposed Project site must be identified. Potential 
waste generation must be estimated and plans for disposal indicated.

Dear Ms. Black,
The City of Boston’s Age Strong Commission is submitting the following comments on the
PNF for the 1033-1035 Washington St project currently proposed by The Druker Company.
Age Strong supports this project’s signiﬁcant contribution to public realm improvements.
The pedestrian plaza creates a safe through-block connection while promoting
neighborhood connectivity by routing pedestrians through 18/7 retail activity, outdoor cafe
seating, and engagement with neighbors sharing the space. Additionally, the internalization
of loading and parking promotes pedestrian safety beyond the development. The potential
green space in the pedestrian plaza and surrounding neighborhood maximizes the
opportunity for climate change mitigation and adaptation. The developers should maximize
these green spaces and climate mitigation/adaptation features. We request the proponent
consider the following recommendations as the design progresses.
A. Community and Retail Space
Please consider older adults’ needs when seeking tenants for the community and
retail spaces. Everyday amenities that are walkable for older adults in the
neighborhood support the ability to age in place. For example, convenience stores,
pharmacies, and cafes or restaurants address older adults' functional needs.
Community spaces geared toward social connection fulﬁll older adults’ social needs.
B. Open Space
The open spaces have strong potential to support community connection and
physical and mental health. We encourage thoughtful consideration of elements that
invite older adults into the space.
a.
Weather
Design for year-round usage by planning for various types of weather. For
example, the installation of awnings and electrical hookups to maintain use in
both hot and cold weather.
b.
Seating
Places to rest allow older adults to enjoy the outdoor space. Incorporate
age-friendly seating along pedestrian paths, corridors, and open spaces.
Age-friendly seating includes armrests for ease of access and vertical
backrests for support. When citing benches, place them under an overhang,

ﬂexible seating arrangements.
c.
Trees
Trees are essential for physical and mental health. Older adults are more
vulnerable to the adverse effects of high heat. We would like to see details
about the design of tree pits, which should maintain accessibility while
preserving the health of the tree. Provide maintenance plans for plantings to
ensure the health of the trees and the surrounding area is safe and
accessible.
d.
Restrooms
Include public restrooms easily accessible from the open spaces. Ensure
there is wayﬁnding signage, they are marked open for public use and
unlocked. Site restrooms near entrances.
C. Pedestrian Pickup/Dropoff
Many older adults need rides because of mobility challenges. Locate the passenger
pickup/dropoff site close to building entrances. This increases safety and minimizes
potential conﬂict with other transportation modes. If passengers will need to cross
a bike lane to enter/exit the vehicle, provide a buffer (painted or island) with enough
space to check for oncoming bikes before crossing and to load/unload mobility aids.
D. Parking Entrance/Exit
Design clear lines of sight for safe entrance and exit of the parking garages. We
recommend yellow detectable warning strips and the installation of audio warning
cues in front of parking entrances for the safety of low-vision pedestrians. The
design should prioritize the responsibility of drivers to check for pedestrians.
E. Wayﬁnding and Dementia Friendly Features
We recommend wayﬁnding signs that include both words and universal icons
directing users within the site and to streets on either side of the through-block
connection. The placement of signs should be eye-level, in clear contrast to the
white or light background, and resistant to glare. Include signs to exits and
entrances, restrooms, parking, and other public spaces. Install visual landmarks at
important intersections and complex junctions. Ensure these areas are well-lit.
Avoid using black designs on concrete as black paint on the ground can create an
illusion of a black hole for someone living with dementia or cognitive impairment.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments and recommendations.

Dear Sarah: 
 
The MBTA appreciates the opportunity to provide initial comments on the 1033-1055 Washington 
Street project which is adjacent to MBTA property (Shawmut Substation). The MBTA is supportive 
of projects such as 1033-1055 Washington Street, which leverage the MBTA’s transit network and 
increases transit ridership through dense, mixed-use developments. 
The 1033-1055 Washington Street project includes the construction of two life science / office 
buildings approximately 150 ft in height with an aggregate gross floor area of approximately 
588,000 square feet. The project is sited on the MBTA Silver Line corridor and will bring a 
considerable number of new workers and visitors, many of whom will make use of the available 
MBTA transportation network along Washington Street daily. This project is also within close 
proximity to the MBTA Shawmut Substation, a key piece of MBTA infrastructure. 
With regard to the proposed project and its potential impacts to the Shawmut Substation, as well 
as the ridership in the immediate area, the MBTA makes the following preliminary comments as 
part of the initial PNF submission. 
 
MBTA Comments: 
Zoning and Planning: 
The 1033-1055 Washington Street project is located in the Harrison-Albany Corridor Strategic 
Plan’s sub-area. “The sub-area should emphasize its location as the vital physical and economic 
link between the City's downtown, Chinatown, and South End neighborhoods with convenient 
access to South Boston and the regional roadway system.” The Plan states: “Future development 
should provide exciting new 18-hour uses within a pedestrian-friendly public realm that includes a 
finer grain of city blocks that allow for enhanced transportation access and circulation.” The Plan 
also emphasizes maintaining “bus only” lanes for the Silver Line from Herald Street to East 
		

Berkeley Street and “maintaining the current curb-to-curb width without interruption to the 
exclusive Silver Line bus lanes.” Due to the increased vehicle trips of the project, the MBTA asks 
the Proponent to eliminate the proposed curb cuts on Washington Street and consolidate the curb 
cuts to Shawmut Avenue to maintain Washington Street’s public transit use as the priority. 
Additionally, the MBTA notes that throughout the design and construction process for this 
development, access to the MBTA Shawmut Substation must be maintained at all times. 
 
Transit Impacts: 
The MBTA studied the Proponent’s transit impacts analysis and considered these figures in 
conversation with existing ridership and the broader context of development in the South End / 
Herald Street Station Area. The Proponent estimates that a significant portion of new trips from 
their development will use transit—nearly 7 new riders from each thousand square feet added, 
compared to a median rate in the City of Boston of 4.32. This results in an anticipated 4,085 
people who are expected to use transit to get to and from 1033-1055 Washington St. 
These new riders (primarily from the Office and Life Science aspects of the project buildings) will 
presumably use the adjacent Herald Street and East Berkeley Street Silver Line stations, the 
closest rapid transit stops within a ¼ mile radius. These stations saw a combined weekday average 
of 1,419 riders in 2019. If most the Proponent’s 4,085 projected riders use the Silver Line here, it 
will nearly triple the existing ridership. 
Put into context, the project represents a considerable contribution to new weekday ridership in 
this corner of the South End. These new, added riders would represent nearly half of the total 
riders added from development either planned, completed, or under construction in this area of 
the South End. Looking solely at the future project pipeline, 1033-1055 Washington St is expected 
to contribute nearly ninety percent of future riders here. The chart below illustrates the project’s 
role in producing new ridership in this area.

this corridor, and suggests that commensurate mitigation from the Proponent could help to offset 
this substantial passenger influx. 
Bus Access, Circulation, and Traffic Improvements: 
The MBTA looks forward to working with the Proponent, to prioritize transit as a first choice in the 
area. Bus priority in the area should be carefully considered, especially as the Bus Network 
Redesign process continues. The Harrison-Albany Corridor area is well-served by the Silver Line 4 
and 5 as well as Route 9, 11, and 39. With that said, we recommend further study with regards to 
potential bus lanes on Herald St and/or potential routing changes for Route 9 in order to improve 
efficiency. The project should contribute to improving bus access and circulation around the 
Harrison-Albany Corridor area. The MBTA also requests consultation as the Proponent develops 
any concepts or designs for streets in the area, as bus stop location is a key part of that design. 
The MBTA looks forward to working with the City of Boston and MassDOT to identify solutions to 
address this through upcoming area studies. 
Parking Supply and Management: 
The Proponent proposes that “the vehicle parking needs of the Project will be accommodated by 
approximately 371 on-site parking spaces (303 net-new parking spaces on site), or at a rate of 
approximately 0.63 parking spaces/1,000 SF.” Due to the transit-oriented nature of the project, 
the MBTA asks the Proponent to commit to supporting transit as part of the parking strategy. The 
focus of the project’s parking strategy needs to be an effort to minimize supply as a means of 
reducing automobile dependence in favor of transit and other active transportation means. 
 
The MBTA is supportive of this sustainability-minded focus on reducing automobile use in favor of 
transit and active transportation. The MBTA looks forward to continuing to work with the 
Proponent to understand the impacts of the resulting transportation demand on facilities and 
service networks and identify ways for the project to address these impacts. 
 
Proposed Transportation and Asset Mitigation:

In light of the above review of the proposed 1033-1055 Washington Street project’s projected 
increase in ridership demand on the various bus networks that serve the development area, as 
well as its proximity to the Shawmut Substation, the MBTA proposes the following would be

1. Conduct a study of the potential benefits for a bus lane on Herald Street and/or potential

2. Eliminate the proposed curb cuts on Washington Street and consolidate the curb cuts to

1033-1055 Washington Street - Boston Public Works Department Comments 
 
Included here are Boston Public Works Department comments for the 1033-1055 Washington Street Draft Project 
Impact Report. 
 
Project Specific Scope Considerations: 
The developer should coordinate with BTD and PWD to develop safety and accessibility improvements for 
pedestrians and cyclists in the area that will be impacted by the development. The developer should coordinate 
with BTD & PWD to propose traffic signal and pedestrian improvements at Shawmut Avenue and E. Berkeley 
Street intersection. The developer should also consider using the same building material as the other side of 
Washington Street, when improving the pedestrian. 
 
Site Plan: 
The developer must provide an engineer’s site plan at an appropriate engineering scale that shows curb 
functionality on both sides of all streets that abut the property. 
 
Construction Within The Public Right-of-Way (ROW): 
All proposed design and construction within the Public ROW shall conform to PWD Design Standards 
(https://www.boston.gov/departments/public-works/public-works-design-standards). Any non-standard materials 
(i.e. pavers, landscaping, bike racks, etc.) proposed within the Public ROW will require approval through the Public 
Improvement Commission (PIC) process and a fully executed License, Maintenance and Indemnification (LM&I) 
Agreement with the PIC. Please note that the comments below are specific to proposed work within the Public 
ROW. 
 
Sidewalks: 
The developer is responsible for the reconstruction of the sidewalks abutting the project and, wherever possible, to 
extend the limits to the nearest intersection to encourage and compliment pedestrian improvements and travel 
along all sidewalks within the ROW within and beyond the project limits. The reconstruction effort also must meet 
current Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)/Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (AAB) guidelines, 
including the installation of new or reconstruction of existing pedestrian ramps at all corners of all intersections 
abutting the project site if not already constructed to ADA/AAB compliance per Code of Massachusetts Regulations 
Title 521, Section 21 (https://www.mass.gov/regulations/521-CMR-21-curb-cuts). This includes converting apex 
ramps to perpendicular ramps at intersection corners and constructing or reconstructing reciprocal pedestrian 
ramps where applicable. Plans showing the extents of the proposed sidewalk improvements associated with this 
project must be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval. Changes to any curb 
geometry will need to be reviewed and approved through the PIC. 
 
Please note that at signalized intersections, any alteration to pedestrian ramps may also require upgrading the 
traffic signal equipment to ensure that the signal post and pedestrian push button locations meet current ADA and

IQHQ-103 Beacon, LLC (the “Proponent”) proposes the development of a mixed-
use/life science project with ground level retail amenity space which is intended to 
bring new vibrancy and activity to an existing underutilized site (the “Proposed 
Project”). The contemplated building program for the Proposed Project consists of 
approximately 241,000 square feet of gross floor area (“GFA”) of Core Shell lab-
ready space, approximately 4,000 GFA of retail space on the ground floor, 
approximately 5,000 square feet of secure bicycle room(s), two (2) levels of 
underground parking for approximately 196 vehicles and so-called “back of house” 
space to support these uses (the “Building”).

RESILIENCY AND SUSTAINABILITY 
Article 37: The Building is subject to Article 37 (Green Buildings) of the Code, 
pursuant to Section 80B Large Project Review. It will meet the requirements 
necessary to achieve at least a Gold-level certifiability using LEEDv4 rating system, 
which will exceed the City of Boston’s (the “City’s”) requirements under Article 37. It 
will be designed with energy-efficient HVAC and lighting equipment and systems 

and will incorporate other potential energy conservation measures, as reasonable 
and feasible. 
Smart Utilities: The Building will comply with the BPDA’s Smart Utilities Policy for 
Article 80 Development Review, as applicable. 
TRANSPORTATION 
The Project Site is in close proximity to several MBTA bus routes, and Commuter 
Rail lines, all of which provide easy access to the Project Site from the surrounding 
neighborhood and other areas of the City and beyond. The Proponent will enter 
into a Transportation Access Plan Agreement with the Boston Transportation 
Department in which it will commit to Transportation Demand Measures (TDMs) 
consistent with the City’s guidelines. 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
The Proposed Project sits within the Guest Street Local Industrial-2 (LI-2) Zoning 
Subdistrict which allows Research and Laboratory Uses. Planned Development Area 
(PDA) eligibility for sites over an acre within the Guest Street LI-2 subdistrict is 
established by Section 51-44 of the Boston Zoning Code. The Proposed Project is 
also located within the planning boundaries of the 2012 BPDA Board Approved 
Brighton/Guest Street Planning Study & Urban Design Guidelines (Plan). The Plan 
states, as specific developments for this area are proposed, the BRA’s Article 80 
process will involve review of project elements such as design, layout, and 
distribution of heights. The Plan creates a public realm context for underutilized 
industrial and commercial areas and requires the introduction of new streets for 
on-site circulation and servicing/loading. The Plan also requires the creation of 
urban blocks with complete streetscapes to create a context for development and a 
new mixed-use district. If aspects of a proposed development are inconsistent with 
this Plan’s guidelines, but provide significant public benefits, there is opportunity to 
be flexible. Mitigation and overall benefit, however, must be provided to 
accommodate exceptions as part of the Article 80 community review process. 
Additionally, the Proposed Project is covered under the two neighborhood wide 
planning studies, the Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan (2021) led by the BPDA and 
supported by the Transportation and Public Works Departments, and the Allston-
Brighton Arts, Culture, and Placekeeping Report (2021) led by the Mayor’s Office of 
Arts and Culture (MOAC). The Allston-Brighton Mobility Study seeks to advance the 
goals of Go Boston 2030 and focuses on increasing access and mobility choice for 
all road users. Specifically, the Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan advances projects and 

policies that provide comfortable and safe pedestrian improvements, and low-
stress bicycle facilities for North Beacon Street between Market Street and 
Cambridge Street. The Allston-Brighton Peacekeeping Report provides a catalog of 
existing art uses, art/cultural institutions, and cultural assets in the neighborhood 
as well as recommendations for preserving, relocating, and creating new art and 
cultural spaces. 
The Proposed Project does not comply with the dimensional and density 
recommendations within the Brighton Guest Planning Study Area, which proposes 
a FAR between 0.75 - 1.50 and maximum height limit up to 40 feet and/or up to 4 
stories along the North Beacon Street edge and a FAR between 1.25 - 3.25 and 
maximum height limit up to 110 feet and/or up to 12 stories in the northern portion 
of the site. The Proposed Project exceeds heights in both zones and density across 
the site with a building height of approximately 92 feet and 6 stories across the site, 
with an additional approximately 30 feet for mechanical screening, and excluding 
stepbacks at an approximate FAR of 3.7. Stepbacks include approximately 15 feet at 
48 feet of height along North Beacon Street and Arthur Street and a second 
stepback along North Beacon Street of approximately 20 feet at 92 feet of height 
above the highest occupiable floor. Additionally, the Proposed Project partially 
complies with the guideline of the Plan that throughout the Study Area, street walls 
should not exceed 40’ in height with stepbacks of 15’ at 40’ heights to ensure a 
human scale to the streets. However, the Proposed Project aligns in intent with 
select elements of the Plan in several ways. First, by creating an active edge on 
North Beacon Street through the creation of ground floor retail space, and sidewalk 
and multimodal street improvements. Second, by including two stepbacks along 
North Beacon Street with design elements such as large plantings that soften the 
visual impact of the building edge. Third, by creating active uses along Arthur Street 
that may include retail, restaurants, recreation, galleries, lobbies, lounges, places 
where people are actively working together, with frequent front doors and front 
gardens. Finally, by anchoring a mixed-use urban district and supporting a lively, 
diverse and 18-hour quality of life with enjoyable streetscapes. All these 
improvements are critical to the creation of new space at the corner of North 
Beacon Street and Arthur Street as a ceremonial gateway, giving the Study Area its 
own identity. Design review of this project focused on some of the unique features 
of large sites and lab buildings all with the overarching framework of this site as a 
gateway to the mixed-use district and along Arthur Street to the Boston Landing T 
Station. Design review included creating clear and accessible circulation pathways, 
consolidated vehicular entry points, enjoyable and sustainable streetscape 

experience, well detailed ground-level facades for the human scale, aligned building 
and street edges, and impactful views across and along Arthur Street. 
In summary, while the Proposed Project exceeds the recommendations in the Plan, 
it contributes community benefit through enhancing the public realm with ground 
floor retail on both North Beacon Street and Arthur Street as well as significant 
streetscape improvements on all edges, including consolidation to a single 
vehicular curb cut, a raised and overall safer crosswalks, creation of bicycle facilities 
along North Beacon Street and Arthur Street, and Boston Complete Streets 
compliant sidewalk elements with additional active zones along Arthur Street. 
Additionally, in bridging between two height and density zones described in the 
Plan, the Proposed Project introduces stepbacks and contributes to the creation of 
a gateway at Arthur Street, anchoring the future mixed-use district that is imagined 
in the Plan to the west of this unique site. 
The Proposed Project will require approval from the Boston Zoning Commission. 
ZONING & REGULATORY CONTEXT 
The Project Site is located within the Allston/Brighton Neighborhood District and 
the Guest Street Local Industrial-2 Zoning Subdistrict (the “Guest Street LI-2”) as 
shown on the Allston Brighton Neighborhood District Map 7A/7B/7C/7D, and as set 
forth in Article 51 of the Code. 
Pursuant to Sec. 51-44 of the Code, properties within the Guest Street LI-2 are 
eligible for Planned Development Area (“PDA”) designation to allow for variations 
from the underlying zoning requirements, including but not limited to maximum 
height and density, allowed uses, and number of parking spaces and amount and 
location of loading facilities. 
PROJECT BENEFITS AND MITIGATION 
As will be further defined in the Cooperation Agreement, the Proposed Project will 
provide the following benefits for the City and the neighborhood: 
a. Improvements to the Aesthetic Character of the Project Site: The
Proposed Project will replace the existing one-story brick block
commercial building primarily used for retail purposes and a significant
at-grade parking lot, unenclosed loading bays and loading areas
situated along Arthur Street that did not allow for open space or
landscaped areas, with a building that allows for the provision of

publicly accessible open space and a more generous streetscape that 
will visually activate and enliven the Project Site. 
b. Sustainability and Resiliency: The Proposed Project will incorporate
design elements to improve on-site stormwater management and
reduce the risk of precipitation-based flooding, such as reducing
impervious surfaces, increasing the amount of greenery and
incorporating green infrastructure. The Proposed Project is also
designed to reduce heat island impacts to the extent feasible and it will
exceed the requirements of Article 37 (Green Buildings) aiming to
achieve certifiability at least at a Gold level using the LEEDv4 rating
system. The Proponent is committed to utilizing energy-efficient HVAC
and lighting equipment and systems.
c. Social and Economic: The Proposed Project is expected to contain
approximately 245,000 sf of Development Impact Project uses, as the
term is defined in the Code (“DIP Uses”). Deducting the 100,000 s.f.
exemption under Section 80B-7.4 of the Code, there will be
approximately 141,000 sf of DIP Uses at the Proposed Project that will
be subject to DIP exactions. Pursuant to the provisions of Section 80B-
7 of the Code, the Proposed Project will provide estimated linkage
funds of approximately $2,231,550.00 in housing and jobs linkage
payments and will result in the creation of approximately 300
permanent on-site jobs and approximately 200 temporary construction
jobs. The Project is also expected to generate approximately $5 million
annually in new real estate tax revenues for the City, and significant
business tax revenues for the Commonwealth.
d. Transit Oriented Development: The Project Site is in close proximity to
several MBTA bus routes, and Commuter Rail lines, all of which provide
easy access to the Project Site from the surrounding neighborhood and
other areas of the City and beyond. The Proponent will enter into a
Transportation Access Plan Agreement with the Boston Transportation
Department in which it will commit to Transportation Demand
Measures (TDMs) consistent with the City’s guidelines.
e. Smart Utilities: The Building will comply with the BPDA’s Smart Utilities
Policy for Article 80 Development Review, as applicable.

Plan, the comment period was subsequently re-opened through December 18,

published in the Boston Herald.

BPDA, city, and state staff/departments on May 24, 2023, to review the PNF filing. A 
Meeting of the Impact Advisory Group (“IAG”) was held on June 14, 2023. A Public 
Meeting was held on June 7, 2023.

(“BCDC”) on August 1, 2023, with a Design Committee meeting on October 17, 2023.

DEVELOPMENT PLAN

103 NORTH BEACON STREET 
BOSTON, MASSACHUSETTS 
Dated: January 18, 2024 
1.
Development Plan: Pursuant to Section 3-1A.a and Article 80C of the Boston
Zoning Code (the “Code”), this plan constitutes the Planned Development Area Development Plan 
(the “Development Plan”) for a Planned Development Area Overlay District (the “PDA Overlay 
District”) containing approximately 67,586 square feet (1.55 acres) commonly referred to as 103 
North Beacon Street in the Brighton neighborhood (the “Site”). The Site is more particularly 
described in Section 3, below, and in Exhibit A and Exhibit B attached hereto. The Proponent (as 
defined below) proposes to redevelop the Site by demolishing the existing improvements and 
constructing an approximately 245,000 square-foot (“sf”) of gross floor area (“GFA”) mixed-use 
building with a below-grade parking garage (the “Project”). Collectively, the Site and the Project 
make up the “Planned Development Area” or “PDA” for which this Development Plan will 
constitute and provide the permanent zoning. 
This Development Plan sets forth the proposed location and appearance of structures, open 
spaces, uses, maximum densities and dimensions of structures, traffic circulation, parking and 
loading facilities, and other requirements applicable to the PDA. Capitalized terms used but not 
defined herein shall have the meanings assigned to such terms in the Code as in effect as of the 
date hereof, without giving effect to any subsequent amendments to the Code. 
This Development Plan consists of six (6) pages of text plus attachments designated 
Exhibits A through G. All references to this Development Plan contained herein shall pertain 
only to such pages and exhibits. This Development Plan shall constitute permanent zoning for the 
Site in accordance with Section 3-1A and Article 80C of the Code and is intended to address all 
requirements of the Code applicable to the Site and the Project. 
2.

3.
PDA Overlay District: The PDA Overlay District totals approximately 67,586 sf
(1.55 acres) and is located within the block bounded by North Beacon Street, Arthur Street, 
Herrick Street, and Hichborn Street. The Site is currently improved by a one-story commercial 
building at 103 North Beacon Street, surface parking and loading service on Arthur Street. 
As depicted on the draft PDA Overlay Plan, a copy of which is attached hereto as Exhibit 
C and is incorporated herein by reference, the PDA Overlay District is located in the 
Allston/Brighton Neighborhood District and the Guest Street Local Industrial-2 zoning subdistrict. 
4.
The Building: The Proponent proposes the development of a mixed-use/life
science development with ground level retail amenity space, as specified in Section 8 of this 
Development Plan, which is designed to bring new vibrancy and activity to an existing 
underutilized site. The contemplated building program consists of approximately 241,000 GFA of 
Core Shell lab-ready space with approximately 4,000 GFA of retail space within the ground floor, 
secure bicycle room, two (2) levels of underground accessory parking for no more than 196 
vehicles, and so-called “back of house” space to support these uses (the “Building”). 
5.
Proposed Location and Appearance of the Building: The proposed location of
the Project is shown on survey plan included as Exhibit B and the Draft PDA Overlay Plan 
included as Exhibit C. The various components of the Project are shown in the Conceptual Site 
Plan & Renderings included as Exhibit D, Massing Diagram of New Building included as Exhibit 
E, and Site Plan Open Space Diagram included as Exhibit F. 
The Site design focuses on creating a more generous and enlivened streetscape along North 
Beacon Street and Arthur Street through wider sidewalks, landscaping, and seating for the public. 
Envisioned as a conduit for activity, the Project has been oriented on the Site to allow for extra 
wide pedestrian sidewalks along both North Beacon and Arthur Street which afford room for 
sidewalk activation as well as facilitate Arthur Street becoming a connector between the nearby 
Boston Landing project and the North Beacon Street Corridor. 
6.
Proposed Density and Dimensions of Structures: The specific height (as
defined in the Zoning Code) for any building within the Site will be calculated from the average 
mean grade as defined in the Zoning Code (the “Code”). The maximum height of the Building, 
inclusive of all rooftop mechanical equipment, penthouses, structures, screens, and other 
projections, shall be 147 feet. The mechanical penthouse or mechanical screen rising above the 
roof of the Building shall not exceed 40 feet above the roof of the Building, and the rooftop 
exhaust related mechanical elements, such as, flues and exhaust vents shall not exceed 55 feet 
above the roof of the Building. The height of the mechanical screen, penthouse or elements shall 
be measured from the top of the flat roof of the Building to the highest point of the mechanical 
screen, penthouse, or element. 

3 
The Building will contain up to a total of 245,000 square feet of GFA1, which results in 
an FAR of up to 3.65 across the full PDA Overlay District. See Exhibit E for massing diagram. 
The maximum building height, FAR and GFA set out above will be the only dimensional 
requirements applicable to the PDA Overlay District. All other dimensional or design 
requirements of the Code shall not be applicable to the PDA Overlay District and are superseded 
by this Development Plan. The Project shall be subject to design, environmental and other 
development review by the BPDA, and aspects of the Project approved as part of such review 
shall be and hereby are deemed to be the dimensional and design requirements applicable to the 
Building and are hereby incorporated in this Development Plan. 
7.
Proposed Open Space and Landscaping: The Project will create approximately
10,800 square feet of new publicly accessible open space on the Site. This publicly accessible 
open space, coupled with approximately 4,000 GFA of retail space within the ground floor of the 
Building, will help to activate the Site and surrounding area. In addition, the public realm area 
along North Beacon Street and Arthur Street will be improved with the design and construction of 
low-stress bike lanes and extra wide pedestrian sidewalks which afford room for sidewalk 
activation as well as facilitate Arthur Street becoming a connector between the nearby Boston 
Landing project and the North Beacon Street Corridor. See Exhibit F for areas of open space as 
shown and defined. 
The Project’s design strategy focuses on creating a more generous and enlivened 
streetscape along North Beacon Street and Arthur Street through a wider sidewalk, landscaping, 
low-stress bike lane, and seating for the public. 
8.
Proposed Uses: The Building will be used primarily for office, laboratory,
research and development, retail and parking facilities (as accessory, ancillary, and principal uses). 
The Lab, Research Laboratory uses shall be limited to Biosafety Levels 1 and 2. In addition to the 
uses listed above, all of the uses listed in Exhibit G shall be permitted as of right on the PDA 
Overly District. 
9.
Proposed Traffic Circulation: The Site is currently accessed from two wide curb
cuts located, respectively, on Arthur Street and Hichborn Street. The Project will consolidate the 
curb-cuts and include one curb-cut on Herrick Street for access to both the parking garage and the 
loading service/area. The reduction in curb-cuts is designed to streamline vehicle movements. 
10.
Proposed Accessory Parking and Loading Facilities: The Project will include
two levels of below-grade accessory parking for no more than 196 vehicles. Non-accessory 
parking is not an allowed use. All loading and service activity will be actively managed by the 
building transportation coordinator, and the Project will meet the City’s Bike Parking Guidelines 
by providing a minimum of 147 secure indoor bicycle parking spaces and 14 publicly short-term 
accessible bicycle parking spaces. 

4 
11.
Access to Public Transportation: The Site located near the Massachusetts Bay
Transportation Authority (“MBTA”) Boston Landing Station which provides access to the 
Framingham/Worcester commuter rail, and is also located along MBTA bus routes 57, 64, 66, and 
86. 
12.
Signage: The signage program for the Project shall be subject to design,
environmental and other development review by the BPDA, and any sign approved as part of such 
review shall be deemed to be in compliance with the Development Plan. 
13.
Development Review Procedures: All aspects of the Building’s design will be
subject to ongoing development and design review and approval by the BPDA. 
14.
Green Building and Resiliency Measures: The Building is subject to Article 37
(Green Buildings) of the Code, pursuant to Section 80B Large Project Review. It will meet the 
requirements necessary to achieve at least a Gold-level certifiability using LEEDv4 rating system, 
which will exceed the City’s requirements under Article 37. It will be designed with energy-
efficient HVAC and lighting equipment and systems and will incorporate other potential energy 
conservation measures, as reasonable and feasible. 
15.
Public Benefits: The PDA will provide many public benefits to the Brighton
neighborhood and to the City of Boston, including the creation of job opportunities and training, 
significant landscaping improvements around the Site, and the generation of additional tax 
revenues: 
a.
Improvements to the Aesthetic Character of the Site: The Project will replace the
existing one-story brick block commercial building primarily used for retail
purposes and a significant at-grade parking lot, unenclosed loading bays and
loading areas situated along Arthur Street that did not allow for open space or
landscaped areas, with a new building that allows for the provision of publicly
accessible open space and a more generous streetscape that will visually activate
and enliven the Site.
b. Sustainability and Resiliency: The Project will incorporate design elements to
improve on-site stormwater management and reduce the risk of precipitation-based
flooding, such as reducing impervious surfaces, increasing the amount of greenery
and incorporating green infrastructure. The Project is also designed to reduce heat
island impacts to the extent feasible and it will exceed the requirements of Article
37 (Green Buildings) aiming to achieve certifiability at least at a Gold level using
the LEEDv4 rating system. The Proponent is committed to utilizing energy-
efficient HVAC and lighting equipment and systems.
c.
Social and Economic: The Project is expected to generate approximately
$2,169,990 million in housing and jobs linkage payments and will result in the
creation of approximately 300 permanent on-site jobs and approximately 200
temporary construction jobs. The Project is also expected to generate

5 
approximately $5 million annually in new real estate tax revenues for the City, and 
significant business tax revenues for the Commonwealth. 
d. Transit Oriented Development: The PDA is in close proximity to several MBTA
bus, and Commuter Rail lines, all of which provide easy access to the Site from
the surrounding neighborhood and other areas of the City and beyond. The
Proponent will enter into a Transportation Access Plan Agreement with the Boston
Transportation Department in which it will commit to Transportation Demand
Measures (TDMs) consistent with the City’s guidelines.
e.
Smart Utilities: The New Building will comply with the BPDA’s Smart Utilities
Policy for Article 80 Development Review, as applicable.
f.
Right-of-Way Improvements: In consultation with the BPDA, the Boston
Transportation Department (“BTD”), and via approval of the Public
Improvements Commission (“PIC”), the Proponent shall perform the following
in-kind transportation improvements prior to the issuance of Certificate of
Occupancy:
○
Design and install a permanent low-stress bike facility (e.g., a sidewalk
level bike lane or similar) along North Beacon Street from Arthur Street to
Herrick Street along the frontage of the Site. This design shall tie into
BTD’s proposed bikeway improvements to North Beacon Street.
○
Design and install a permanent low-stress bike facility (e.g., a sidewalk
level bike lane or similar) along Arthur Street from North Beacon Street
through the intersection of Hichborn Street along the frontage of the Site.
○
Design and install a raised crosswalk across the western leg of Hichborn
Street at the intersection of Hichborn Street and Arthur Street. This raised
crosswalk should include both the crosswalk and the bike crossing at
sidewalk level to ensure bicyclists safely transition from the existing low-
stress bikeway on Arthur Street north of Hichborn Street to the new low-
stress bikeway to be designed and installed by the Proponent on Arthur
Street south of Hichborn Street.
○
Align the pedestrian receiving ramp located on the north side of North
Beacon Street at the intersection of North Beacon Street and Arthur Street
with the existing crosswalk.
○
Improve the crosswalk running from east to west on Arthur Street at the
intersection of North Beacon Street and Arthur Street to be consistent with
the permanent low-stress bike facility (e.g., a sidewalk level bike lane or
similar) being designed and installed by the Proponent along the frontage of
the Site.
16.
Boston Civic Design Commission: The Buildings will require Schematic Design
Approval by the Boston Civic Design Commission (“BCDC”) pursuant to Article 28 of the Code. 
17.
Applicability: In accordance with Section 80C-9 of the Code, consistency the
Building with this Development Plan shall constitute compliance with the dimensional, use, and 
all other requirements of the Code, to the extent such requirements have been addressed in the 

6 
Development Plan. Issuance of a Certification of Consistency for the Building will constitute 
compliance with all applicable provisions of the Code with respect to Planned Development Areas. 
18.
Minor Modification to Plans: This Development Plan sets forth the dimensional,
use, and other zoning requirements for the PDA Overlay District, to the extent such requirements 
have been addressed in this Development Plan. Upon approval of this Development Plan, final 
plans and specifications for the Building will be submitted to the BPDA pursuant to Section 3-1A, 
Article 80B, and Article 80C of the Code for final design review approval and certification as to 
consistency with this Development Plan, and to other governmental agencies for final approval. 
Subject to consistency with the dimensional regulations set forth in this Development Plan, minor 
changes may occur to the Building’s design described in this Development Plan without requiring 
an amendment to this Development Plan, as determined by the Director of the BPDA in accordance 
with Section 80A-6 of the Code, and subject to the use and dimensional requirements set forth in 
this Development Plan. No changes to the public benefits arising from the community driven 
Article 80B process shall require an amendment to this Development Plan, provided that the 
mitigation and/or community benefits as required under this Development Plan are not modified 
unless approved by the BPDA during Article 80B Review. 
19.
Development Schedule: The Proponent estimates that construction of the Project
will take approximately 32 months. 
20.
Proponent’s Obligation to Proceed with the Project: Notwithstanding anything
set forth herein to the contrary, under no circumstances shall the Proponent be obligated to proceed 
with any Building, or all or any portion of the Project.

deems appropriate and necessary in connection with the Proposed Project.

Project Site consists of 3,598 square feet of land area on a single parcel at the corner of 
Canal Street and Anthony “Rip” Valenti Way in the Bulfinch Triangle District, a section of 
Boston’s West End neighborhood.

THE ORIGINALLY APPROVED PROJECT 
 
On September 12, 2014, Somnath Living, LLC (the “Proponent”) submitted a Small Project 
Review Application (“SPRA”) with the BPDA seeking to develop the Project Site and 
construct a hotel building (the “Proposed Project”). On October 16, 2014, the BRA Board 
voted to approve the 104 Canal Street Hotel Development project (the “Originally Approved 
Project”). 
 
The Originally Approved Project consisted of the construction of a fifteen (15) story, 
approximately 47,355 GSF structure to be used as a 90-guestroom, overnight-stay hotel. 
The building would have had one additional story below grade and a mechanical 
penthouse occupying a portion of the roof level. The hotel was designed to have a ground 
floor lobby, cafe and amenity space opening directly onto Canal Street, and was to replace 
an existing one-story building previously used as a banking branch facility, and unoccupied 
then, and still today. No accessory parking was proposed. 
 
In addition to the 90 planned guestrooms, the Originally Approved Project included 
amenity spaces, including a lobby, fitness area, and cafe with outdoor seating. 
 
THE REVISED PLAN FOR 104 CANAL STREET 
 
Zoning relief for the Originally Approved Project was originally obtained from the Boston 
Board of Appeal (the “Board of Appeal”), under a decision dated April 21, 2015. However, 
the project did not proceed at that time, and it was later frustrated by the devastating 
effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the hospitality industry. After a string of extensions 
granted by the Board of Appeal, the zoning relief lapsed on February 24, 2022. 

 
 
 
On September 23, 2022, the Proponent submitted a letter with supporting drawings to the 
BPDA, to apprise the BPDA of changes to the Originally Approved Project, and to request a 
Certification of Approval. 
 
The following changes have been proposed to the Originally Approved Project (the 
“Proposed Project”): 
1. An increase in the expected number of guestrooms from 90 to 98; 
2. Removal of the originally proposed café, which is replaced by a smaller café for the 
guests; and 
3. Refinements to the facades made in consultation with BPDA Urban Design staff. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On September 23, 2022, the Proponent filed a letter with supporting drawings with the 
BPDA for the Proposed Project. The BPDA sponsored a public meeting on October 20, 2022 
via Zoom. The meeting was advertised in the relevant neighborhood newspaper, the 
Boston Guardian. The public meeting was posted on the BPDA website, a notification was 
posted to the BPDA website, and a notification was emailed to all subscribers of the BPDA’s 
West End neighborhood update list. The BPDA comment period ended on October 28, 
2022. 
 
Outside of the BPDA sponsored public meeting, the Proponent has met with the 
Downtown North Association, the West End Civic Association, and the Mayor’s Office of 
Neighborhood Services, and has been in contact with the office of City Councilor Ed Flynn. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT AND CITY STAFF REVIEW 
The Small Project Change for the previously approved project located at 104 Canal Street in 
the Bulfinch Triangle District is not subject to any recent plans adopted by the Boston 
Planning & Development Agency. The Proposal, however, is subject to Article 46 of the 
Boston Zoning Code. Section 46-8 of the zoning code outlines the design guidelines and 
requirements for projects within the Bulfinch Triangle District. 
 
The proposed Small Project Change is limited to the number of guestrooms, increasing 
from 90 to 98 guestrooms, and changes to the facades. No changes are proposed to the 
footprint, height, or square footage of the project. Planning and urban design staff 
reviewed the project given its context within the Bulfinch Triangle District and have 
determined that these proposed changes do not negatively impact the neighborhood. 
 
Architecturally the proposed masonry building will present a base, middle, and top with 
cornice that respects the architectural precedent of this architectural context. 
 
 

 
 
ZONING 
The property at 104 Canal Street is located within the General Area of the Bulfinch Triangle 
District, regulated under Article 46 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”). The property is 
also in a Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (“GCOD”) and the Restricted Parking 
District. 
The Proposed Project is anticipated to need relief from the Zoning Board of Appeals as 
follows: 
● 
Conditional Use Permit for GCOD compliance; 
● 
Variance for Floor Area Ratio; and 
● 
Variance for Building Height. 
 
MITIGATION & COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
The Proponent has maintained its commitment to the community benefits that were 
included with the Originally Approved Project, providing a number of public benefits to the 
West End neighborhood and the City of Boston as a whole: 
 
● 
The proposed Project will create a new hotel destination in the Bulfinch Triangle 
that will generate construction and service jobs and stimulate the local economy. 
● 
Somanth Hospitality anticipates the completed hotel will add approximately 25 full 
and part time permanent positions in hotel operations. 
● 
The Proposed Project strives to embrace design and construction principles that 
utilize a sustainable design approach which will create a pedestrian friendly 
development that encourages the use of public transportation. 
● 
Redeveloping an under-utilized property whose current scale is not in line with the 
surrounding urban environment. 
● 
Bring hotel patrons to the neighborhood who will frequent the local cultural and 
entertainment venues, contributing new revenue to the surrounding business 
community. 
● 
Contribute a direct economic benefit including the purchase of local resources 
(labor, goods, and services) for both initial construction and daily hotel operations. 
● 
Create a new attractive outdoor seating area which will enhance the vibrancy of the 
area and contribute to the Canal Street pedestrian experience. 
● 
Create a prominent public art element at adjacent infill space to further benefit the 
urban streetscape experience. 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
The Proposed Project complies with the requirements set forth in Section 80E of the Code 
for Small Project Review. Therefore, the BRA staff recommends that the Director be 
authorized to: (1) issue a Certification of Approval for the Proposed Project, in accordance 

 
 
with Article 80E, Small Project Review of the Code; and (2) execute any and all agreements 
and documents that the Director deems appropriate and necessary. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized on behalf of the Boston 
Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) to issue a Certification of Approval 
pursuant to Section 80E-6 of the Boston Zoning Code (the "Code"), approving 
Somnath Hospitality, LLC consisting of a fifteen-story hotel building with 
approximately 47,355 gross square feet and comprised of ninety-eight (98) 
guestrooms at 104 Canal Street in the West End neighborhood of Boston (the 
“Proposed Project”) in accordance with the requirements of Small Project 
Review, Article 80E, of the Code, subject to continuing design review; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to execute and deliver any 
other agreements and documents that the Director deems appropriate and 
necessary in connection with the Proposed Project.

PLANNING AND ZONING 
 
 The Proposed Project at 10 Malcolm X Boulevard is located in a Three-Family 
Residential (3F-4000) Subdistrict in the Roxbury Neighborhood District. 
 
The Proposed Project is located within the Highland Park Architectural Conservation 
District, designated in 2022, to preserve the architectural character of the Highland 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
25 
 
 
 
Park neighborhood, including signiﬁcant examples of late 18th, 19th, and early 20th 
century architectural styles. In the Highland Park Architectural Conservation District 
Report, the protection and retention of healthy trees, and the preservation of stone 
outcroppings, stone walls, and stone gate posts where possible are highlighted goals. 
The report also suggests that generally, the height of new construction shall respect certain 
standards of scale in order to maintain the District’s special qualities including overall 
building height and massing. 
 
The Site is also located in the study area for the Roxbury Strategic Master Plan (RSMP). 
This Plan discourages surface parking in the neighborhood, and recommends that 
developments consolidate parking where possible. The Proposed Project initially 
reduced the number of proposed parking spaces from 78 to 59 per staﬀ 
recommendations. Further project review contributed to an additional reduction in 
parking to 52 total spaces, with 21 of those dedicated to the existing oﬃce building to 
remain. 
 
The RSMP supports the preservation and rehabilitation of existing historic buildings, 
through a reinforcement of the integrity of historic buildings and places in Roxbury. 
Through the use of public art, the proposed development project updates and 
celebrates the existing historic building on the site. With the incorporation of ground 
ﬂoor retail, the proposed development also responds to the goals of the RSMP to 
support diverse economic activity particularly in the area around Nubian Square. 
 
This planning context is further supported by PLAN: Nubian Square, a planning 
initiative centered around the Nubian Square neighborhood. The Plan identiﬁes the 
needs of the Nubian Square study area regarding housing, transportation, green and 
resilient design, and jobs and economic development opportunities. The proposed 
development responds to the framework of PLAN: Nubian Square through the 
development of new housing units. 
 
In support of the economic development goals of PLAN: Nubian Square, the Proposed 
Project locates residential units near transit options, providing direct access in and out 
of the neighborhood for commuters. This element of the proposal also supports the 
goals of Housing a Changing City: Boston 2030 and Go Boston 2030 to increase housing 
options density near transit centers. 
 
In coordination with the resilience eﬀorts set forth in PLAN: Nubian Square, the Urban 
Forest Plan, and the Climate Action Plan, Heat Resilience Solutions for Boston identiﬁes 
the Nubian Square area as experiencing higher than median daytime temperatures 
compared to the city as a whole. In particular, the report cites institutional areas like 
those around Madison Park High as a contributor to high levels of urban heat. As a

result, increased canopy coverage was suggested on the site to mitigate these eﬀects 
and increase levels of comfort for residents and pedestrians alike in the proposed 
development area. The Proponent was responsive to this request through proposed 
increases to planted open space on site. 
 
The Site is also located in the Boulevard Planning and Neighborhood Design Overlay 
Districts. Accordingly, staﬀ review incorporated the context of Malcolm X Boulevard as 
an entrance to the larger neighborhood, the Highland Park Architectural Conservation 
District, and an MHC Historic Inventory Area. Parks Commission design review will also 
be required, per City Ordinance 7-4.11, due to the project site’s proximity to public 
open space. 
 
The Planning Review team acknowledges changes that have been made to the project 
throughout the review to better respond to the zoning and planning contexts of the 
site. The Proponent has pushed back the new residential building from the existing 
nearby lower-scale residential buildings to reduce the contrast between the proposed 
development and existing neighborhood fabric. In keeping with the neighborhood 
context, the proposed building fronting on Malcolm X Boulevard has been lowered by 
one story. Further measures were taken at the submission of the PNF to better align 
with requests by staﬀ regarding sidewalk dimensions and parking ratios.

Dear Mr. Harvey: 
The Boston Water and Sewer Commission (Commission) has reviewed the Project 
Notification Form (PNF) for the proposed 10 Malcolm X Boulevard project located at 10 
Malcolm X Boulevard in the Roxbury neighborhood of Boston. 
The proposed project is located on an approximately 72,003 square foot (sf) (1.65 acre) site 
currently occupied by a commercial building and surface parking. The project proponent, 10 
MX Owner, LLC, proposes to preserve the existing commercial building and construct two 
new buildings: 
1. A. six ( 6) story, 111-unit residential building with ground floor retail space in 
approximately 105,000 gross square feet (gsf), and 
2. A four ( 4) story, 21-unit residential building in approximately 22,000 gsf. 
The project site is bounded by Malcolm X Boulevard to the northeast, Guild Row to the east, 
Dudley Street to the south, and residential buildings and vacant BPDA land to the west. 
There will be approximately 54 vehicle parking spaces. 
According to the PNF, the project's proposed water demand is approximately 22,968 gallons 
per day (gpd). The Commission owns and maintains a 12-inch Southern Low DICL water 
main installed in 1994 in Malcolm X Boulevard and a 12-inch Southern High PCI water main 
installed in 1907 and rehabilitated in 1988 and a 24-inch Southern Low PCI water main 
installed in 1871 and rehabilitated in 1976 in Dudley Street. 
According to the PNF, the proposed sewage generation is 23,505 gpd, an increase of 20,880 
gpd over existing conditions. For sewage and storm drainage service, the site is served by a 
39-inch by 26-inch combined sewer in Malcolm X Boulevard, a 72-inch storm drain in Guild 
Row and a 39-inch by 26-inch combined sewer in Dudley Street. 
The Commission has the following comments regarding the PNF: 

General 
1. 
Prior to the initial phase of the site plan development, 10 MX Owner, LLC should 
meet with the Commission's Design and Engineering Customer Services to review 
water main, sewer and storm drainage system availability and potential upgrades that 
could impact the development. 
2. 
All new or relocated water mains, sewers and storm drains must be designed and 
constructed at IO MX Owner, LLC's expense. They must be designed and 
constructed in conformance with the Commission's design standards, Water 
Distribution System and Sewer Use regulations, and Requirements for Site Plans. The 
site plan should include the locations of new, relocated and existing water mains, 
sewers and drains which serve the site, proposed service connections, water meter 
locations, as well as back flow prevention devices in the facilities that will require 
inspection. A General Service Application must also be submitted to the Commission 
with the site plan. 
3. 
The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), in cooperation with the 
Massachusetts Water Resources Authority and its member communities, is 
implementing a coordinated approach to flow control in the MWRA regional 
wastewater system, particularly the removal of extraneous.clean water (e.g., 
infiltration/inflow (I/I)) in the system. In April of 2014, the Massachusetts DEP 
promulgated new regulations regarding wastewater. The Commission has a National 
Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Permit for its combined sewer 
overflows and is subject to these new regulations [314 CMR 12.00, section 
12.04(2)(d)]. This section requires all new sewer connectio"ns with design flows 
exceeding 15,000 gpd to mitigate the impacts of the development by removing four 
gallons of infiltration and inflow (I/I) for each new gallon of wastewater flow. In this 
regard, any new connection or expansion of an existing connection that exceeds 
15,000 gallons per day of wastewater shall assist in the I/I reduction effort to ensure 
that the additional wastewater flows are offset by the removal of Ill. Currently, a 
minimum ratio of 4: 1 for I/I removal to new wastewater flow added is used. The 
Commission supports the policy and will require proponent to develop a consistent 
inflow reduction plan. The 4: 1 requirement should be addressed at least 90 days prior 
to activation of water service and will be based on the estimated sewage generation 
provided on the project site plan. 
4. 
The design of the project should comply with the City of Boston's Complete Streets 
Initiative, which requires incorporation of "green infrastructure" into street 
designs. Green infrastructure includes greenscapes, such as trees, shrubs, grasses and 
other landscape plantings, as well as rain gardens and vegetative swales, infiltration 
2 

basins, and paving materials and permeable surfaces. The proponent must develop a 
maintenance plan for the proposed green infrastructure. For more information on the 
Complete Streets Initiative see the City's website at http://bostoncompletestreets.org/
