1.0 Introduction 
In accordance with Sections 3-1A and 80C-3 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”), 
this plan constitutes the Master Plan for Planned Development Area No. 146 (the 
“Master PDA”) for the development of the parcels located at 35-45 Morrissey Boulevard, 55 
Morrissey Boulevard, and 75 Morrissey Boulevard in the Dorchester Neighborhood Zoning 
District (“Site”). As more particularly described below, the Master PDA contemplates the 
demolition of the three existing buildings on the Site, and the phased construction and 
redevelopment of multiple buildings and public realm (the “Proposed Project” and “Project”, 
a/k/a “Columbia Point Crossing”), which are currently expected to be built in three phases over 
an approximately 5-to-10-year period. The Master PDA encompasses approximately 8.9 acres of 
area of land referred to herein as the “Master PDA Area.” A figure depicting the location of the 
Master PDA Area is included as Exhibit A. The legal description and survey plan of the Master 
PDA Area are included as Exhibit B. 
 
The Master PDA Area, which is approximately one-tenth of a mile away from the JFK/UMass 
MBTA Station, is within the Columbia-Morrissey Community Commercial Subdistrict 
(“Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict”), which was recently established in order to allow the 
creation of PDAs. The Master PDA proposes (1) the development of research & development 
and office space that will lead to the creation of new, high quality jobs and training opportunities 
for neighborhood students, and (2) the addition of housing units, including affordable units, and 
public space where none had existed, the Master PDA will further the goals for which the 
Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict was created, which include the provision of “public benefits to 
the Dorchester community, including the creation of new job opportunities” and the 
“encourage[ment] of economic development.” Zoning Code § 65-28, as recently amended. 
Likewise, although the objectives for PDAs in the Dorchester Neighborhood District are written 
in the disjunctive, the Proposed Project will help realize each and every one of them – i.e., “(a) 
diversification and expansion of Dorchester's economy and job opportunities through economic 
activity, such as private investment in manufacturing, commercial uses, or research and 
development; (b) creation of new job opportunities and establishment of educational facilities, 
career counseling, or technical assistance providing instruction or technical assistance in fields 
related to such jobs; or (c) improvements to the urban design characteristics and aesthetic 
character of the development PDA Area and its surroundings, and the enhancement of existing 
open space or the creation of new open space.” Zoning Code § 65-31. 
 
The Master PDA sets forth a statement of the development concept for the Master PDA Area, 
including the planning objectives and character of the development, the proposed uses of the 
area, the range of dimensional requirements contemplated for the Proposed Project, and the 
proposed phasing of construction. 
 
The Master PDA consists of [25] pages of text plus attachments designated Exhibits A through 
H and Appendix A through B. All references to this PDA contained herein will pertain only to 
these [25] pages and Exhibits. This Master PDA shall be governed by the Zoning Code in effect 
as of the date hereof and unless otherwise set forth herein, and all references to terms defined by 
the Zoning Code will have the meanings set forth in Section 2 of the Zoning Code, as amended 
to the effective date hereof, and not as amended hereafter.

3.0 Master PDA Area Description 
 
The Master PDA Area encompasses approximately 8.9 acres. The northern tip of the Master 
PDA Area is approximately one-tenth of a mile to the south of the JFK/UMass MBTA Station. 
The Master PDA Area includes the following three properties (1) 35-45 Morrissey Boulevard, 
which is improved with a one-story brick commercial building that is occupied by a Star Market 
grocery store and a liquor store; (2) 55 Morrissey Boulevard, which is improved with a two-story 
brick building that is entirely occupied by The Record Company; and (3) 75 Morrissey 
Boulevard, which is improved with a one-story commercial office building that has been vacant 
for several years and a surface parking lot. The Master PDA Area is bounded to the south by the 
former Boston Globe headquarters (now Southline), to the west by the Southeast Expressway 
(Interstate 93), to the north by two residential buildings, and to the east by Morrissey Boulevard. 
The Proposed Project currently contemplates the demolition of the three existing buildings (each 

 
5 
 
 
an “Existing Building”) on the Site and the construction of seven new buildings and open spaces. 
The legal description and survey plan of the Master PDA Area are attached as Exhibit B. 
 
4.0 The Proposed Project 
 
The Proposed Project reimagines the Master PDA Area as a vibrant mixed-use neighborhood. As 
illustrated in the conceptual site plan at Exhibit C, this Master PDA proposes seven (7) new 
buildings on the Site, four of which will house research and development/life science uses and 
three of which will consist of multi-family housing units, with all building ground floors 
providing a mix of restaurant, retail and/or public space. The Proposed Project contemplates the 
creation of a new roadway network and new low-stress bicycle facilities and pedestrian pathways 
within the Master PDA Area; the development of other publicly available space, including four 
(4) outdoor ground-level community recreation spaces (totaling approximately 1.35 acres), with 
landscaping and seating for use by shoppers, area employees, and area residents; and below-
grade parking. Approximately 4.0 acres and 45% of the Master PDA Area includes publicly 
accessible open spaces, public realm, and public roadways. The Proposed Project also calls for 
building heights to be appropriately scaled, such that the tallest buildings will be closest to the 
JFK/UMass MBTA Station and the Southeastern Expressway.

The Project Site is located within the Community Commercial zoning subdistrict of the 
Dorchester Neighborhood District, governed by Article 65 of the Code. The entire Project Site is 
also located within the Restricted Parking Overlay District established pursuant to Article 3-
1A(c), and the Coastal Flood Resilience Flood Overlay District established pursuant to Article 
25A of the Code. Finally, eastern portions of the Site along Morrissey Boulevard are located 
within the Morrissey Boulevard Greenbelt Protection Overlay district, established pursuant to 
Section 65-34 of the Code.

of the Code, as well as the Planned Development Area goals set forth in Section 65-28 of the 
Code. Section 65-28 of the Code provides that the BPDA may approve the establishment of a 
Planned Development Area within the Columbia-Morrissey Community Commercial Subdistrict 
in order to provide for a more flexible zoning law; to provide benefits to the Dorchester 
community, including the creation of job opportunities; and to encourage economic 
development. The Project will address all of these goals, as discussed in this Master PDA and in 
subsequent Article 80B submissions to be filed with the BPDA.

5.0 Planning Objectives and Character of Redevelopment 
 
 
The Proposed Project’s design aims to create a vibrant nucleus of innovative workspace, active 
community amenities, and public realm in the Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict. The Proposed 
Project will reinvigorate a stale stretch of Morrissey Boulevard2 with vibrant life sciences 
offices, residential, retail, exterior public open space, streetscaping, and improved circulation for 
all modes of movement and circulation in the neighborhood. And, the Proposed Project will pair 
well with newly developed 135 Morrissey Boulevard; draw people onto, into, and through the 
Master PDA Area, forging a better connection with the surrounding neighborhood; capitalize on 
the nearby JFK/UMass MBTA station; and add more cohesiveness to the Master PDA Area and 
surrounding context. 
 
5.1 Urban Design 
 
Much of the Master PDA Area is currently private, set off from and disconnected with the 
surrounding community, and offers minimal opportunities for jobs or job training, no residential 
units, and no meaningful open space. The parcel at 35-45 Morrissey Boulevard is currently 
improved with a building occupied by a Star Market grocery store and a liquor store; these uses 
are intended to be relocated to a new building in Phase 2 of the Project and the existing building 
demolished; 55 Morrissey Boulevard is currently improved with a two-story brick building that 
is entirely occupied by The Record Company — this building will ultimately be demolished; and 
75 Morrissey Boulevard has a one-story commercial office building, which has been vacant for 
several years, and a surface parking lot. Overall, the approximately 8.9-acre Master PDA Area is 
highly underutilized, and does not provide the type of economic development, jobs, housing, 
retail, and publicly available spaces that it is capable of offering. The Proposed Project intends to 
convert this largely dormant area into a welcoming and inclusive public realm, a vibrant new 
workplace hub for the life sciences industry, additional housing, and much needed community 
spaces for the neighborhood. 
 
The Master PDA Area will be defined by the newly created street network. Main Street will 
serve as the primary artery running north/south through the Project Site and parallel to Morrissey 
Boulevard. Three (3) perpendicular streets will provide access points connecting back to 
Morrissey Boulevard and a service road along the western perimeter of the Site will interconnect 
all the new roadways creating an entirely new neighborhood grid. The newly created blocks will 
provide defined spaces for buildings as well as publicly accessible open space. Street widths will

be ample and define an appropriate scale and separation between buildings, giving appropriate

located on Main Street, drawing attention away from Morrissey Boulevard and providing a more 
insulated and welcoming front door to the new buildings and open spaces. 
 
The varying building use types will provide opportunities to create architectural diversity in the 
character of the buildings. Retail uses on the ground floor will draw visitors into the storefronts 
and activate the streetscapes throughout the Site. Building massing will utilize selective setbacks 
above podium levels along Main Street and Morrissey Boulevard, helping to further improve the 
primary view corridor and provide greater open sky visibility. Building heights will generally 
scale upwards towards the north end of the Site approaching the MBTA station and towards I-93 
in an effort to locate the greatest density adjacent to the highly proximate public transportation 
and away from surrounding neighborhoods. The massings of the buildings also take into 
consideration the effects of shadow and sunlight on the thermal comfort of the exterior spaces, 
promoting heartily designed landscapes and public realm that offer opportunities for use year-
round. The Project also intends to capitalize on the Site’s views towards Boston and Dorchester 
Bay, as well as the newly created on-site public open spaces, to provide outdoor private amenity 
spaces for building users, such as upper-floor roof decks and balconies. 
 
In addition to the roadways, four (4) new dedicated park spaces will be created to further define 
the urban landscape of Master PDA Area. Parks will be located throughout the development Site 
to ensure open space are delivered within each phase of construction. A compliment of 
hardscape and softscape elements will define the park spaces and provide opportunities for 
programing that will benefit the community. 
 
Parking entrances and loading will be relegated to the side streets and rear service road, limiting 
the amount of commercial traffic on the pedestrian-focused Main Street. No parking or loading 
access shall occur on Main Street. The new perpendicular streets will also align with proposed 
roadways as part of the Dorchester Bay City development on the east side of Morrissey Blvd. 
 
When complete, the development will form a key link from the Columbia/Savin Hill 
Neighborhood to UMass, Bay City, and waterfront areas.

Guidelines at Appendix B. 
 
5.2 Public Realm 
 
5.2.1 Open Space

A primary design goal of the Proposed Project is to maximize publicly accessible open space that 
will serve the community and help define the character of the newly created neighborhood. In

5.2.3 New Roadway Infrastructure (Streets, Sidewalks and Bicycle Lanes) 
 
The Master PDA Area is bounded to the west by the Southeast Expressway and to the east by 
Morrissey Boulevard. There are currently no publicly accessibly roadways, sidewalks or bike 
paths through or across the Master PDA Area. The Proposed Project contemplates the creation of 
an entirely new roadway infrastructure within the PDA Area to support vehicular, bike and 
pedestrian accessibility as well as the funding of contributions to improve infrastructure along 
Morrissey Boulevard, Kosciuszko Circle, and the JFK/UMass MBTA Station to further improve 

 
15 
 
 
transportation infrastructure in the surrounding community. Certain roadways will be public 
ways as they serve a critical transportation network purpose. Other roadways may be private 
ways open to public travel. Specific details of the newly created streets are further described 
below, though for any streets that include a “flexible zone” it is the intent that further 
development of the street design within the street widths set forth herein may occur during the 
Article 80B process: 
 
Main Street 
Main Street will be a public way, serving as the primary artery of the new development, 
bisecting much of the Master PDA Area and serving as frontage for a majority of the new 
buildings. It will run in a north/south orientation parallel to Morrissey Boulevard starting 
from the northern-most edge of the Master PDA Area, where it will become a 
continuation of the existing interior street dividing the Hub 25 Apartment buildings, and 
continue south to its terminus at the newly created A Street intersection. Main Street is 
designed to meet the Neighborhood Main street typology as defined in the Boston 
Complete Streets Design Guidelines published by the City of Boston in 2013 and will 
meet City of Boston roadway standards. The street will have an 80-foot overall right-of-
way and include two-way vehicular travel lanes, a flexible vehicular zone on one side for 
uses such as temporary loading/unloading and pickup/drop off, protected bike lanes with 
3-foot buffer zones, furniture zones on both sides of varying dimensions, 2-foot frontage 
zones, as well as generous pedestrian walking zones on both sides of the street. The 
majority of Main Street will be raised to elevation 21.5 feet Boston City Base (“BCB”) to 
meet the SLR-DFE recommendations. The northern-most portion of Main Street will 
gradually ramp downwards to meet the existing grade at the northern edge of the Site. No 
parking or loading access shall occur on Main Street. 
 
Main Street will serve as a vibrant and active thoroughfare providing frontage for the 
retail uses, building lobbies, primary pedestrian pathways, bicycle pathways, and 
activated public zones. Portions of Main Street will be constructed within each Phase of 
the development as further described in Section 4.6.

A Street will be a public way from its intersection with Morrissey Boulevard through its 
intersection with Main Street, will be the southernmost east/west cross street within the

The portion of A Street spanning from Main Street to Morrissey Boulevard is designed to

B Street serves as an east/west cross street on the Site and provides a secondary 
exit/entrance into the Site from Morrissey Blvd. 
 
The portion of B Street spanning from Main Street to Morrissey Boulevard is designed to 
meet the Complete Streets Neighborhood Connector Design Guidelines. B Street will 
have a 48-foot overall right-of-way and include two-way vehicular travel lanes, furniture 
zones on both sides, 2-foot frontage zones, as well as pedestrian walking zones on both 
sides of the street. The garage and loading entrances/exits for both Building D and 
Building F may be located on this portion of B Street. This section of B Street will 
gradually ramp upwards from the existing elevation at Morrisey Boulevard to match the 
21.5 feet BCB elevation at its intersection with Main Street. While this conceptual 
grading provides for a functional connection with the current conditions at Morrissey 
Boulevard, there exists flexibility within the design to readily adapt to changes in the 
condition of Morrissey Boulevard in the future. 
 
The portion of B Street spanning from Main Street to West Street (service road) has been 
designed to meet the Complete Streets Neighborhood Connector Design Guidelines. This 

 
17 
 
 
portion of B Street will have a 48-foot overall right-of-way and include two-way 
vehicular travel lanes, furniture zones on both sides, 2-foot frontage zones, as well as 
pedestrian walking zones on both sides of the street. A garage entrance/egress for 
Building C may be located on this portion of B Street. This section of B Street will 
gradually ramp downwards from the intersection with Main Street at elevation 21.5 feet 
BCB to meet the existing elevations along the western edge of the Site at West Street 
(service road). 
 
B Street will be completed as part of the Phase 2 of the Project construction. 
 
D Street 
D Street serves as the northernmost east/west cross street within the Master PDA Area 
and will align with the currently proposed Pivot Plaza as part of the Dorchester Bay City 
Development on the eastern side of Morrissey Boulevard. Approximately half of D Street 
is within the Master PDA Area, and the remaining half of D Street to the north is outside 
the Master PDA Area. 
 
D Street, spanning from Main Street to Morrissey Boulevard, will provide the 
northernmost access point from Morrissey Boulevard to the Site. The existing condition 
of “D Street” is made up of a private driveway outside of and adjacent to the Master PDA 
Area under separate ownership, and surface parking and circulation areas within the Site 
and within the Master PDA Area. As envisioned in the Master PDA, the new D Street 
will be transformed into a public way designed to meet the goals of the Complete Streets 
Neighborhood Connector Design Guidelines and City of Boston roadway standards. 
When constructed, D Street will be a public way with a minimum right-of-way width of 
40 feet, including two-way vehicular travel, a bike facility, and a clear pedestrian 
sidewalk. The portion of D Street within the Master PDA Area should seek to be 
designed along with the existing adjacent private driveway in order to create an overall 
larger 62-foot overall right-of-way. If this larger 62-foot right-of-way is ultimately 
achieved with the cooperation of the adjacent property owner, then it will be laid out to 
include two-way vehicular travel, protected bike lanes, a clear pedestrian walking zone, 
and a furniture/frontage zone where the future right-of-way directly abuts a structure. 
This section of D Street will maintain the existing elevations of the adjacent street. 
 
The portion of D Street within the Master PDA Area spanning from Main Street to West 
Street (service road) will provide service access to the Site, and the portion of D Street 
within the Master PDA Area has been designed to meet the goals of the Complete Streets 
Neighborhood Connector Design Guidelines. This portion of D Street will be part of a 
larger 48-foot overall right-of-way, and within the Master PDA Area will include a 
vehicular travel lane, a furniture zone, 2-foot frontage zone, as well as pedestrian walking 
zone. The loading for Building G may be located on this portion of D Street. 
 

 
18 
 
 
 
 
The portion of D Street within the Master PDA Area will be completed as part of the 
Phase 3 of the Project construction. 
 
West Street 
West Street (service road) will run along the western perimeter of the Site spanning 
between D Street and the southern edge of Building A. West Street will primarily act as a 
service road for the Project uses as well as a secondary north/south vehicular route. 
Loading and garage access for Building A, primary loading for the grocery store 
(Building C), and garage and loading access for Building E may occur along West Street. 
West Street will have a 33-foot overall right-of-way and may include two-way vehicular 
travel lanes as well as a furniture zone and pedestrian walking zone on one side of the 
street. 
 
Portions of West Street will be constructed within each Phase of the Project Construction. 
 
Further details concerning the New Roadway Infrastructure are included in Exhibit F. 
 
5.3 Resiliency 
 
The Master PDA Area is within the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District (“CFROD”), the 
requirements for which are set forth in Article 25A of the Zoning Code. The Proposed Project 
will comply with the Minimum Sea Level Rise-Design Flood Elevation set forth in Article 25A 
and any other requirements and limitations set forth therein. Lowest occupiable floor elevations 
of all buildings within the Master PDA Area have been set to 21.5 feet BCB to meet the SLR-
DFE recommendations and to provide two-feet of freeboard above the SLE-BFE. For parts of 
buildings located below 21.5 feet, BCB appropriate flood protection measures will be employed 
to mitigate flooding risk. 
 
Further, additional site resilience measures including permeable pavement, bioretention, 
extensive landscape areas and subgrade infiltration systems are contemplated to further mitigate 
the effects of sea level rise and climate change. The Project will comply with all applicable 
resilience requirements and City policies at the time of each building’s Article 80B Review. 
 
A site plan showing anticipated building and roadway elevations is included in Exhibit H. 
 
5.4 Sustainability 
 
To promote sustainable and carbon neutral development, the Proposed Project shall be designed 
to comply with the requirements of Article 37 (Green Buildings) of the Zoning Code to achieve 
the following: 

 
19 
 
 
● 
Satisfaction of a minimum of LEED Gold certifiable standards for all buildings within 
the Proposed Project; 
● 
Employ a carbon neutral framework for all buildings including: 
o Prioritizing a high-performance building envelope to reduce energy consumption 
o Efficient electrification of all building systems and for normal operation of 
commercial lab (high ventilation use occupancies) building systems, including the 
following space heating/cooling, and DHW heating systems: 
▪ 
Air source heat pumps 
▪ 
Exhaust source heat pumps 
▪ 
Ground source heat pumps; 
o Optimize all building designs for on-site renewable energy production and 
installation of systems; 
● 
High indoor air quality (IAQ) and daylit interior spaces; 
● 
Completion of a District Energy Feasibility Study in accordance with the City of Boston 
Smart Utilities plan, which shall include consideration of: 
o Geoexchange (“geothermal”) applications 
o Peak load shaving strategy 
o District energy loop; 
● 
Additional density within an urban core to reduce suburban sprawl; 
● 
Maximization of open space and an accessible public realm, both outdoors and indoors; 
● 
Enhanced access to existing neighborhood pedestrian and bicycle networks; 
● 
Outdoor space for building occupants; 
● 
Walkable retail options for residents and neighborhood visitors; 
● 
Enhanced access to nearby public transit infrastructure to reduce the trip generation of 
cars to the Master PDA Area; 
● 
On-site stormwater retention and groundwater recharge in accordance with City of 
Boston requirements. 
 
6.0 Community Benefits & Mitigation Framework 
 
The development of the Proposed Project contemplated by this Master PDA will provide a range 
of public benefits described below; certain benefits will be delivered directly to the community 
upon the approval of this Master PDA, and other benefits and mitigation will occur following 
Article 80B review as the Proposed Project is further developed and impacts can be better 
measured. The mitigation framework set forth below is intended to ensure that as the Proposed 
Project creates impacts on its community, and the City more generally, that those impacts are 
mitigated. Modifications to and further development of the proposed improvements, as 
requested by the BPDA or other City Agency, described below are expected during the more 
detailed design impact review under Article 80B for each phase of the Project. 
 
6.1 Community Benefits 
 

 
20

cycle of the Project to ensure that community impacts are mitigated – and community benefits 
are provided – in a meaningful manner. Community benefits will therefore be provided both 
when the Master PDA Article 80C approval process is final and complete, and at various stages 
of the phased approval and development of the Site and specific buildings as part of the Article 
80B Large Project review process.

BPDA Board approval.

● Community Benefits Provided Following Article 80B Approvals 
 
o The Project is committed to providing open space to the community, and will 
dedicate the approximately 1.35 acres of developed park areas proposed within

$15 million in present-day value. The nature of the protection of each open space

6.2 Mitigation Framework 
 
The Project will employ a series of mitigation strategies addressing different possible impact 
areas at each phase of the Project. Throughout the Article 80B Large Project Review Process the 
below listed mitigation strategies may be re-assessed and tailored to meet and address 
community needs at the time a phase of the Proposed Project moves forward, such that 
mitigation is appropriate when the impacts of the Project are experienced during, and at the 
completion of, construction. 
● Transportation

of $5 per sf of GFA to a Transportation Mitigation Bank to be established by the 
City Transportation agencies to support area infrastructure improvements, such as

Boulevard. The Project will also provide an additional $200,000 payment to the 
Transportation Mitigation Bank to further assist the City Transportation agencies 
with funding for important traffic and infrastructure studies to improve this area 
(collectively, the “Transportation Payments”). The Transportation Payment will 
be made at the delivery – certificate of occupancy – of any building with 
lab/office use, and will be no greater than $4,600,000 which is the amount of 
lab/office use currently envisioned in the Master PDA. The separate $200,000 
study contribution will be made at the first certificate of occupancy of any 
building with lab/office use, and the remaining Transportation Payments will 
depend on a calculation of $5/sf of lab/office GFA. The determination of final 
Transportation Mitigation investment will be determined through the individual 
Phased Development Plan review and approval process and may include 
investment(s) in Commonwealth of Massachusetts / MBTA.

advantage of the Site’s proximity to public transportation, the Proponent is

o The Project will maximize open space and an accessible public realm, both

neighborhood.

7.0 Technical Studies Performed in Support of Development of the Master PDA 
 
A transportation study has been developed to understand impacts associated with the Project and 
to help devise a comprehensive transportation mitigation and improvement plan in the vicinity of 
the Project that supports future operations of the Project and provides area-wide transportation 
improvements to the Columbia-Morrissey Subdistrict of Boston. A major emphasis of this 
proposed redevelopment effort focuses on area mobility, including improved access and 
circulation to support the Master PDA Area and abutting properties, access to key transit nodes 
(namely, the JFK/UMass MBTA Station), and the significant network of pedestrian and bicycle 
infrastructure improvements. These elements are at the forefront of the analysis and future 
planning. Within the Project boundary, all new public streets have been designed to meet Boston 
Complete Streets guidance and promote safe pedestrian, bicycle, and vehicular circulation. As 

 
24 
 
 
the site is located one-tenth of a mile from the JFK/UMass MBTA Station, an emphasis will be 
placed on encouraging the use of public transportation for employees, visitors, and residents. 
 
It is understood that significant infrastructure improvements are contemplated for Morrissey 
Boulevard which will significantly alter the existing infrastructure in an effort to improve traffic 
and mobility issues within the neighborhood as a result of current and future projects. The 
Proposed Project provides for ample flexibility in adapting to changing infrastructure 
components along Morrissey Boulevard, and there will be continued collaboration with the 
appropriate local and state authorities to provide input and resources as appropriate to facilitate 
these future improvements between the eastern edge of the Site property line and the 
westernmost curb line of Morrissey Boulevard directly abutting the Site. Further, the Project is 
committed to help fund future improvements to the infrastructure along Morrissey Boulevard, 
Kosciuszko Circle and at the JFK/UMass MBTA Station to mitigate the direct impacts of the 
Project. 
 
A more detailed analysis is included in the Transportation Study that is included as Appendix A. 
 
8.0 Effect of Master PDA 
 
8.1 Zoning 
As shown on the Survey, Exhibit B, the Master PDA Area contains more than 5 acres of land, 
making it eligible, pursuant to Article 3-1A.a of the Zoning Code, for Master PDA approval 
through this submission. 
 
This Master PDA sets forth the zoning regulations for all elements of the Proposed Project for 
the Master PDA Area. Upon approval by the Boston Planning & Development Agency and the 
Boston Zoning Commission, any Development Plans and Article 80B filing relating to a building 
or Project phase within the Master PDA Area that is consistent with this Master PDA will be 
deemed to be consistent with the Zoning Code. 
 
8.2 Parcels 
The Master PDA Area is an assemblage of various legal lots which are all owned in fee by the 
Proponent. In order to implement the Project, it is contemplated that new legal lots will be 
created and one or more may be leased or conveyed to third parties. This Master PDA 
constitutes approval for any such subdivision, re-subdivision, ground lease, sublease, and other 
transfer or condominium creation at the Project Site, with each such parcel or sub-area being 
referred to herein as a “Project Component”. 
 
Notwithstanding anything set forth herein or in the Code to the contrary, for purposes of this 
Master PDA, compliance of the Proposed Project with the requirements of this Master PDA will 
be determined as if the entire Site were one Lot, even if it is comprised at any time of more than 
one Lot, including Lots that have been subdivided, re-subdivided, ground leased, subleased or 
combined or submitted to a condominium regime or other form of ownership. This Master PDA 
approves any zoning nonconformity created or increased by the separation of ownership of 

 
25 
 
 
individual Project Components, or by the subdivision, re-subdivision, combination, or 
submission to condominium ownership or other forms of ownership of the Proposed Project, 
provided that (a) the use provisions of this Master PDA are not violated by the resulting Lot or 
Lots, (b) the Site-wide FAR (as defined above) does not exceed the maximum density permitted 
under this Master PDA for the Site as a whole, (c) the open space and parking requirements of 
this Master PDA are met with respect to the Site as a whole, and (d) the public benefit 
obligations set forth in this Master PDA are not decreased without the prior written consent of 
the Director of the BPDA, and the scope of the public benefit obligations set forth in this Master 
PDA are not diminished. The compliance or non-compliance of any one Project Component shall 
not affect the compliance of any other Project Component, and each Project Component shall be 
eligible to receive its own Certification of Consistency or Partial Certification of Consistency. 
 
Any owner of an individual Project Component may seek amendment of this Master PDA only 
as to such Project Component in accordance with the procedures proscribed by the Code without 
the consent of any other owner of a Project Component. In the event that any amendment to this 
Master PDA proposed by the owner of a Project Component is approved in conjunction with a 
Development Plan approval or Development Plan amendment for such Project Component, and 
such Master PDA amendment affects the overall compliance of the Project with this Master 
PDA, this Master PDA shall be deemed amended with respect to the Project as a whole to the 
extent necessary for the Project to comply with this Master PDA. 
 
8.3 Development Review 
Each Project Component of the Proposed Project within the Master PDA Area will be required to 
undergo design review subsequent to the submission of one or more Project Notification Forms 
for the Project (“80B Review), as well as the submission of an individual Development Plan. In 
addition, each Project Component shall be subject to design, environmental and other Article 80 
development review by the BPDA, taking into account any technical studies already performed. 
Aspects of each Project Component approved as part of such review shall be deemed to be the 
dimensional, design and environmental requirements applicable to the Development Plan upon 
issuance of a Certification of Compliance and Certification of Consistency (or a Partial 
Certification of Compliance and Partial Certification of Consistency for the applicable Project 
Component) and pursuant to Sections 80B-6 and 80C-8 of the Code, respectively. 
 
Each Project Component will also be subject to review under Zoning Code Articles 28 (Boston 
Civic Design Commission review), 37 (Green Buildings), and 25A (Resiliency Review) at the 
time of filing. 
8.4 No Obligation to Proceed with Project 
Notwithstanding anything set forth herein to the contrary, under no circumstances shall the 
Proponent or any other party be obligated to proceed with the development of all or any portion 
of the Project.

faciliƟes, loading, and site condiƟons. ExisƟng counts for vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians were

transportaƟon analysis conducted as part of this evaluaƟon. 
The future transportaƟon condiƟons analysis evaluates potenƟal transportaƟon impacts 
associated with the Project. The long-term transportaƟon impacts are evaluated for the year 
2029, based on a seven-year horizon from the year of the ﬁling of this traﬃc study. 
 The No-Build (2029) CondiƟon analysis includes traﬃc growth associated with speciﬁc

impacts to roadway, parking, transit, pedestrian, and bicycle accommodaƟons, as well as 
loading and service accommodaƟons. 
The ﬁnal part of the transportaƟon study idenƟﬁes measures to miƟgate Project-related impacts 
and to address any traﬃc, pedestrian, bicycle, transit, safety, or construcƟon-related issues that 
are necessary to accommodate the Project.

1.4.5 
Trip GeneraƟon Methodology 
Determining the future trip generaƟon of the Project is a complex, mulƟ-step process that 
produces an esƟmate of vehicle trips, transit trips, and walk/bicycle trips associated with a 
proposed development and a speciﬁc land use program. A project’s locaƟon and proximity to 
diﬀerent travel modes determines how people will travel to and from a site. 
To esƟmate the number of trips expected to be generated by the Project, data published by the 
InsƟtute of TransportaƟon Engineers (ITE) in the Trip GeneraƟon Manual1 were used. ITE 
provides data to esƟmate the total number of unadjusted vehicular trips associated with the 
Project. In an urban seƫng well-served by transit, adjustments are necessary to account for 
other travel modes such as walking, bicycling, and transit. 
To esƟmate the unadjusted number of vehicular trips for the Project, the following ITE land use 
codes (LUC) were used: 
Land Use Code 221 – MulƟfamily Housing Mid Rise. High-rise mulƟfamily housing includes 
apartments, townhouses, or condominiums that have between three and ten levels. They are 
likely to have one or more elevators. CalculaƟons of the number of trips uses ITE’s average rate 
per unit. 
Land Use Code 222 – MulƟfamily Housing High Rise. High-rise mulƟfamily housing includes 
apartments, townhouses, or condominiums that have more than 10 levels. They are likely to 
have one or more elevators. CalculaƟons of the number of trips uses ITE’s average rate per unit. 
Land Use Code 760 – Research & Development Center. Research and development centers are 
faciliƟes or groups of faciliƟes devoted to research and development acƟviƟes. The range of 
speciﬁc types of businesses contained in this land use varies signiﬁcantly. Research and 
development centers may contain oﬃces and light fabricaƟon areas. CalculaƟons of the number 
of trips use ITE’s average rate per 1,000 sf. 
Land Use Code 820 – Shopping Center. The Shopping Center land use code is deﬁned as an 
integrated group of commercial establishments that is planned, developed, owned, and 
managed as a unit. Shopping center trip generaƟon esƟmates are based on average vehicle 
rates per square footage of retail space. CalculaƟons of the number of trips use ITE’s average 
rate per 1,000 sf.

shop within that development, reducing the potenƟal for trips to be made throughout the 
surrounding roadway network. These internal trips are typically walk trips in urban areas. The

Vehicle OperaƟons Analysis 
The criterion for evaluaƟng vehicle operaƟons is level of service (LOS), which is determined by 
assessing average delay experienced by vehicles at intersecƟons and along intersecƟon 
approaches. Traﬃcware’s Synchro (version 11) soŌware package was used to calculate average 
delay and associated LOS at the study area intersecƟons. This soŌware is based on the vehicle 
operaƟonal analysis methodology of the TransportaƟon Research Board’s (TRB’s) 2000 Highway 
Capacity Manual (HCM). One of the study intersecƟons is a roundabout; therefore, that locaƟon 
was analyzed using the SIDRA soŌware package instead of Synchro. Field observaƟons were 
performed to collect intersecƟon geometry such as number of turning lanes, lane length, and 
lane width that were then incorporated into the operaƟons analysis. 
LOS designaƟons are based on average delay per vehicle for all vehicles entering an intersecƟon. 
Table 1-7 displays the intersecƟon LOS criteria. LOS A indicates the most favorable condiƟon, 
with minimum traﬃc delay, while LOS F represents the worst condiƟon, with signiﬁcant traﬃc 
delay. LOS D or beƩer is typically considered desirable during the peak hours of traﬃc in urban 
and suburban seƫngs. However, LOS E or F is oŌen typical for a stop-controlled minor street that 
intersects a major roadway and does not necessarily indicate that the operaƟons at the 
intersecƟon are poor or failing.

In addiƟon to delay and LOS, the operaƟonal capacity and vehicular queues are calculated and

calculated measures. 
The volume-to-capacity raƟo (v/c raƟo) is a measure of congesƟon at an intersecƟon approach. A 
v/c raƟo below one indicates that the intersecƟon approach has adequate capacity to process 
the arriving traﬃc volumes over the course of an hour. A v/c raƟo of one or greater indicates that 
the traﬃc volume on the intersecƟon approach exceeds capacity. 
The 50th percenƟle queue length, measured in feet, represents the maximum queue length 
during a cycle of the traﬃc signal with typical (or median) entering traﬃc volumes. 
The 95th percenƟle queue, measured in feet, represents the farthest extent of the vehicle queue 
(to the last stopped vehicle) upstream from the stop line. This maximum queue occurs ﬁve 
percent, or less, of the Ɵme during the peak hour, and typically does not develop during oﬀ-peak

Transit Capacity Analysis 
As presented in SecƟon 1.2.8, transit service in the area includes the MBTA Red Line, Route 8, 
Route 16, and Route 41 buses, and the Project-generated transit trips are expected to use these 
MBTA services. The associated transit capacity evaluaƟon presented below is focused on those 
routes. 
1.6.1 
Transit Analysis Methodology 
The V/C is the primary measurement to determine the impact to transit service from the Project. 
The V/C raƟo is a measurement of the number of passengers divided by the planning capacity. A 
V/C raƟo of 1.0 or higher means the transit service is at capacity and any addiƟonal passengers 
either cannot ﬁt or will cause delays to service as passengers try to crowd onto the train or bus. 
To calculate the V/C, ridership and capacity were determined for the ExisƟng CondiƟon to 
evaluate how the transit service operates today. Then, like the process of projecƟng vehicular 
traﬃc, the future ridership and capacity was developed both for the No-Build (2029) CondiƟon, 
without the Project, and the Build (2029) CondiƟon, with the Project. 
The MBTA deﬁnes their capacity standard as the planning capacity, which is the number of 
passengers that can comfortably ﬁt on a train or bus. As deﬁned in the MBTA’s Service and 
Delivery Policy, the planning capacity for a bus is calculated as 125 percent of the seated capacity 
during oﬀ-peak hours and 140 percent of the seated capacity during peak hours. Bus capacity 
was also compared to the MBTA bus proﬁle sheets created under the BeƩer Bus Project. A 
standard 40-foot bus, with 39 seats, has a planning capacity of 48 passengers per bus during oﬀ-
peak hours and 55 passengers per bus during peak hours. A typical Red Line train car with 62 
seats has a planning capacity of 92 passengers during oﬀ-peak hours and 161 passengers during 
peak hours.

The V/C raƟo is the primary measurement to determine the impact that the Project has on

NEIGHBORHOOD 
ARCHITECTURAL CHARACTER
* As a maritime-adjacent 
development, Architectural Design 
& Materiality should exhibit a 
Connection To Natural Themes 
and Materials. 
* Design Teams should consider 
a Lighter and/or Warmer Material 
Palette.
* Special Attention should be 
paid to ground level facades, 
accentuating a Detailed, Textured 
Pedestrian Experience
* Building Crowns & Penthouses 
should have details Harmonious 
With Primary Architectural 
Facades 
* Outdoor Terraces, Balconies and 
Green Spaces are encouraged.

DESIGN GUIDELINES
EASTERN EDGE MASSING
BUILDING MASSING AT 
MORRISSEY BLVD
* In order to create a consistent 
streetwall edge, At least 80% of 
Building frontage along Morrissey 
Blvd, should meet grade within 20' 
of Build-To Line.
* Building Frontage At Morrissey 
Blvd should include a 5' Minimum 
Massing Stepback between 20'-80' 
above the Ground Floor, applicable 
to a Minimum of 75% of building 
frontage.
* Any Building Setbacks, 
Stepbacks or Massing Articulation
noted in these Design Guidelines 
should be understood as a Starting 
Point. Additional strategies 
should be employed on a building-
by-building basis, with the goal 
of Minimizing Shadow & Wind 
Impacts & Maximizing Ground 
Level Pedestrian Comfort.

DESIGN GUIDELINES
MAIN STREET MASSING
BUILDING MASSING AT MAIN 
STREET
* In order to create a consistent 
streetwall edge, At least 80% of 
each building's frontage along 
Main Street should meet grade 
within 20' of Build-To Line.
Within this grade frontage Design 
Variation & Changes In Plane are 
encouraged to promote a textured, 
inviting pedestrian experience.
* Building Frontage At Main Street
should include a 5' Minimum 
Massing Stepback between 20'-65' 
above the Ground Floor, applicable 
to a Minimum of 75% of building 
frontage.
* Any Building Setbacks, 
Stepbacks or Massing Articulation
noted in these Design Guidelines 
should be understood as a Starting 
Point. Additional strategies should 
be employed on a building-by-
building basis, with the goal of 
a Minimizing Shadow & Wind 
Impacts & Maximizing Ground 
Level Pedestrian Comfort.

DESIGN GUIDELINES
WESTERN / SOUTHERN EDGE MASSING AND CHARACTER
BUILDING MASSING AT 
WESTERN/SOUTHERN EDGE
* Masterplan goals of Variety in 
Height & Massing, with a level 
of Design Differentiation are 
also intended for Buildings at 
the Western Edge, facing I-93 / 
Dorchester neighborhoods.
* Design Language, Character & 
Fenestration at the Western Edge 
should have a similar level of 
development as other facades. 
* Due to visibility from I-93 and 
points west, Unique and/or Easily 
Recognizable Design Features 
should be considered, with special 
attention given to approaching 
views from distance.
* Buildings abutting the Southern 
Property Edge should maintain a 
Minimum 5' Setback from property 
line, and include fenestration, 
avoiding unbroken expanses of 
opaque wall.

DESIGN GUIDELINES
BUILDING CHARACTER AT OPEN SPACES
BUILDING CHARACTER AT 
OPEN SPACES
* Building Facades Directly 
Abutting Civic, Community & 
Family Open Spaces should 
feature a High Degree of 
Architectural Character and visual 
interest. 
* A Deﬁ ned, Horizontal Datum 
or change in cladding language 
located above the First or Second 
Story line should be employed to 
accentuate a Pedestrian Scale
fronting the open spaces.
* Building Frontage Abutting 
Open Spaces should include a 
5' Minimum Massing Stepback 
between 20'-80' above the Ground 
Floor, applicable to a Minimum of 
75% of building frontage.
* At facades facing the Pocket 
Park, Building Podium Levels (up to 
80') should Respond To The Park 
Scale & Program, with Ground 
Level Active Uses and Massing 
Edges Sculpted to draw in users 
from Main Street.

DESIGN GUIDELINES
BUILDING MASSING, TERRACES & BALCONIES
BUILDING MASSING AND 
SCULPTING AS RESPONSE TO 
ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS
* Design Teams will complete a 
Pedestrian Comfort Wind Study 
as part of Art 80B review. Building 
Massing Adjustments shall be

PROJECT SITE 
 
The Proposed Project is located at 75 Morrissey Boulevard, an approximately 2.24-
acre site (the “Phase 1 Project Site”) located within the Master Plan. The area of the 
Master Plan includes the parcels located at 35-45 Morrissey Boulevard, 55 
Morrissey Boulevard, and 75 Morrissey Boulevard in the Dorchester neighborhood 
of Boston (the “Master Plan Area”). The full Master Plan Area encompasses 
approximately 8.9 acres of land on Morrissey Boulevard, which area is generally 
bounded by Morrissey Boulevard to the east; the former Boston Globe site to the 
south (now Southline); the Southeast Expressway (Interstate Highway 93) to the 
west; and 25 Morrissey Boulevard to the north. The Master Plan Area is depicted on 
the plan attached to this Memorandum as Exhibit A. The Phase 1 Project Site is 
located within a short distance from the Massachusetts Bay Transportation 
Authority (“MBTA”) JFK/UMass subway station on the MBTA Red Line and commuter 
rail stop, and bus service on multiple MBTA bus routes. The Phase 1 Project Site is 
currently largely impervious and is improved with a long-vacant single-story 
commercial building constructed in the 1950s.

PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
The Phase 1 Project proposes redeveloping the underutilized, approximately 2.24- 
acre 75 Morrissey portion of the Master Plan with the development of two new 
residential buildings totaling approximately 754 residential units and approximately 
613,320 sf of gross floor area (respectively, “Building A” and “Building B”). The Phase 
1 Project will also include a mix of ground-floor retail uses, amenity, and 
community/civic spaces. The ground-level retail spaces will activate pedestrian 
activity along the building facades and streets, complemented by the 
community/civic spaces which will enhance the resident experience and diversity of 
programming opportunities offered by the Phase 1 Project. 
 
The Phase 1 Project also proposes an approximately 23,900 sf community park 
(“Community Park”), which will be public open space for the surrounding 
neighborhood, and which will be located centrally on the Phase 1 Project Site 
between Building A and Building B. The Community Park will serve as an open-air 
space for potential community gatherings and other cultural events envisioned 
within the context of the larger park space, including landscaped areas and 
meandering pathways. The Community Park will be an accessible public gathering 
space providing a strong visual and physical ADA-accessible connection to A Street 
and the northern courtyard at the adjoining Southline development, all in a manner 
that is intended to feel open and communicate permeability. 
 
Each building will also include three levels of subgrade parking. Both buildings 
collectively provide approximately 414 vehicular parking spaces below grade, and a 
total of approximately 760 bicycle parking spaces at- or above-grade. 
 
To support these new developments, the Phase 1 Project proposes new on- and 
off-site roadway improvements and infrastructure to support vehicular, bike, and

along the northern edge of the Project Site, will connect the Project Site to the main 
vehicular artery of Morrissey Boulevard. West Street, which runs along the western 
edge of the Phase 1 Project Site, is a service road which will connect to A Street, and 
will provide back-of-house services and connections for Building A. 
 
The Phase 1 Project will provide a significant number of income-restricted housing 
units and increase the available high-quality housing stock in the Dorchester and 
Columbia Point neighborhoods. 
 
The Proponent has designed the Phase 1 Project to fully align with the 
requirements set forth in the approved Master Plan.

PLANNING AND ZONING CONTEXT 
 
The proposed development at 75 Morrissey Boulevard (the “Project Site”) is located 
within the Dorchester Neighborhood Zoning District, within the Community 
Commercial (CC) Subdistrict, and is subject to multiple zoning overlays including the 
Greenbelt Protection Overlay District (GPOD), the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay 
District (CFROD), and the Restricted Parking District (RPD). 
 
The Master Plan Area encompasses approximately 8.9 acres across 35–45, 55, and 
75 Morrissey Boulevard. The Phase 1 Project covers the 2.24-acre site at 75 
Morrissey and serves as the first step in implementing the Master Plan. The 
Development Plan for this phase was submitted under Article 80C and Section 3-1A 
of the Boston Zoning Code. 
 
The approved Master Plan zoning allows for the construction of two new 18-story 
residential buildings—Building A and Building B—with a combined 754 residential 
units, approximately 613,320 gross square feet, and three levels of below-grade 
parking for 414 vehicles. Ground-floor commercial uses, civic/community spaces, 
and an approximately 23,900 square foot public Community Park are also included. 
The Master Plan permits maximum building heights of 204 feet for Building A and 
206 feet for Building B, with a sitewide FAR of up to 4.0 across the Master PDA area.

The Phase 1 Project proposes the demolition of the existing building at 75 
Morrissey and the construction of two new buildings. Building A and Building B will 
consist of residential uses with some commercial/retail uses at ground level. 
 
The site’s location within the GPOD, per Article 29, requires thoughtful integration 
of landscape, stormwater management, and open space to protect the 
environmental and scenic qualities of the Morrissey Boulevard corridor. Within the 
CFROD, new development must be designed to accommodate projected sea level 
rise and storm surge conditions for the year 2070, including the elevation of critical 
building systems and uses above the required Design Flood Elevation. 
 
URBAN DESIGN 
 
The proposed building massing responds to and enhances the surrounding 
context. Building A’s curved massing complements the similar curvature of 
Interstate 93’s roadway. The inside, east/south-facing portion of Building A follows a 
different curve to access views towards Quincy Bay. Building B’s massing is oriented 
to follow Morrissey Boulevard on its eastern face and defines an edge of the 
community park, establishing the orientation of the park’s main axis. 
To provide appropriate scaling, both Phase 1 Project buildings employ a two-story 
podium along the majority of the facades. Aside from the advantages in wind 
protection it provides, the podium massing creates smaller scale articulation closer 
to the ground floor. The podium houses the public uses, namely the retail spaces, 
community/civic spaces, and residential amenities and main-building entrances. 
Entrance locations, setbacks, and the programming of the ground floor spaces 
support the use and enjoyment of the community park and the surrounding 
sidewalks.

The Proponent submitted to the BPDA a Project Notification Form (“PNF”) on 
February 28, 2025, and a Development Plan for the Project on June 20, 2025, each 
initiating a 45-day comment period. A Community Advisory Committee meeting was 
held on March 24, 2025, with a community meeting on March 26, 
2025, each for review and discussion of the PNF. A subsequent Community 
Advisory Committee and community meeting was held on July 30, 2025.

the proposed site and building designs. Based on the final design presentation, the 
Boston Civic Design Commission voted to recommend the Project on July 1, 2025. 
 
The virtual public meetings were advertised in the relevant neighborhood 
newspapers and posted to the BPDA’s website and a calendar notification as sent 
to all subscribers of the BPDA’s Dorchester neighborhood updates. Local city and 
state elected officials received notification of the public meeting via email. The 
presentations and recordings of the virtual public meetings were published to the 
35-75 Morrissey Boulevard Phase 1 Project webpage on the BPDA website. 
 
The Phase 1 Project is subject to further review, including ongoing design review, 
other applicable City departments, and Commission Review.

Office of Housing (“MOH”) staff and outlined in an ARHAR for each building, and 
rental prices and income limits will be adjusted according to BPDA published 
maximum rental prices and income limits, as based on HUD AMIs, available at the

time of the initial rental of the IDP Units of each building. IDP Units must be 
comparable in size, design, and quality to the market-rate units in the Phase 1 
Project, cannot be stacked or concentrated on the same floors, and must be 
consistent in bedroom count with the entire Phase 1 Project. 
 
The ARHAR for each building must be executed along with, or prior to, the issuance 
of the Certification of Compliance for the Phase 1 Project. The Proponent must also 
register the Phase 1 Project with the Boston Fair Housing Commission (“BFHC”) 
upon issuance of the building permit. The IDP Units will not be marketed prior to 
the submission and approval of an Affirmative Marketing Plan to the BFHC and the 
BPDA. Preference will be given to applicants who meet the following criteria, 
weighted in the order below: 
• Boston resident; and 
• Household size (a minimum of one (1) person per bedroom 
 
Where a unit is built out for a specific disability (e.g., mobility or sensory), a 
preference will also be available to households with a person whose need matches 
the build out of the unit. The City of Boston Disabilities Commission may assist the 
BPDA in determining eligibility for such a preference. 
 
An affordability covenant will be placed on the IDP Units in each building to 
maintain affordability for a total period of fifty (50) years (this includes thirty (30) 
years with an option to extend for an additional period of twenty (20) years). The 
household income of the renter and the rent of any subsequent rental of the IDP 
Units during this fifty (50) year period must fall within the applicable income and 
rent limits for each IDP Unit. IDP Units may not be rented out by the developer 
prior to rental to an income-eligible household, and the BPDA or its assigns or 
successors will monitor the ongoing affordability of the IDP Units. 
 
MITIGATION & COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
The Proposed Project will provide community benefits for the Dorchester 
neighborhood and the City of Boston. The Proponent has made the following 
commitments: 
 
● The Proponent will be designing and constructing A Street, an entirely new 
off-site roadway of approximately 15,000 sf, including locations for new city 
utilities, that will be paid for by the Proponent at an estimated value/cost of 
approximately $5 million. 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
18 
 
 
DOCUMENT NO. 8239 
 
15 
 
● The Proposed Project will accommodate, as may be applicable in 
coordination with the BPDA and as set forth in the Master PDA, one on-site 
bikeshare station for year-round public use with a minimum of 19-docks. The 
Proponent will work with the BTD and BPDA to site the bike share station. 
The Proposed Project will also provide a total of approximately 760 bicycle 
parking spaces. 
● Prior to issuance of the Certificate of Occupancy for Building A the Proponent 
shall make an approximately $108,725 contribution to the Boston 
Transportation Department to support the bike share system. 
● Prior to issuance of the Certificate of Occupancy for Building B the Proponent 
shall make an approximately $101,030 contribution to the Boston 
Transportation Department to support the bike share system. 
● Consistent with the Master PDA, the Project will exceed the City's applicable 
Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”) policy by providing 20 percent 
affordable units (approximately 151 units). 
● The Project will provide approximately 7,450 sf of ground floor space for 
community/civic space-oriented uses. The Proponent will also partner with 
local organizations and institutions like the Mayor’s Office of Arts and Culture 
(“MOAC”), to sponsor permanent and rotating/short-term art installations on 
the Project Site by a diverse range of artists. The Proponent will partner with 
MOAC to create a public arts plan. 
● The Project also transforms a site largely covered by impervious asphalt 
surface parking and replaces it with an approximately 23,900 sf Community 
Park that will be dedicated to the public, allowing community members an 
entirely new space within the Columbia Point neighborhood. 
● To mitigate against impacts from additional residents and their use of 
existing public parks/open space, the Project will contribute $1 per sf of GFA 
of residential space to the City of Boston Parks Department, to be delivered 
in lump sum within thirty (30) days after issuance of each applicable 
occupancy permit for each residential building, and to be utilized for the 
ongoing maintenance of Moakley Park. 
● The Proponent is also committed to increasing the total tree canopy 
coverage on the Project Site, upon full maturity of the new tree plantings, by 
replacing large areas of asphalt-covered surface parking with thoughtfully 
designed and landscaped open space and a Complete Streets Compliant 
streetscape on the new “A Street.” West Street will be designed with a 6-foot 
sidewalk and a 4-foot planting zone. The Project will install approximately 
qty. 17 new sidewalk trees (cumulatively) on A Street and West Streets,

a minimum qty. 30 new site trees across the site. 
● Proponent will enter into a Transportation Access Plan Agreement (“TAPA”) 
with BTD in which it will commit to Transportation Demand Measures 
(“TDMs”) consistent with applicable City Guidelines. 
● The Proponent will coordinate with DCR, either an interim or permanent 
landscape resolution for the Project Site abutting Morrissey Boulevard. The 
landscape will include, without limitation, some combination of site trees, 
street trees, paving, planting, and possibly irrigation. The schedule of the 
Morrissey Blvd. Reconstruction Project does not have a known

● The Project will comply with the Smart Utility Policy for Article 80 
Development Review, as applicable. Additionally, in accordance with Boston’s 
Electric Vehicle (“EV”) Readiness Policy, 25 percent of the net new parking 
spaces in the Proposed Project’s below-grade garage will be equipped with 
EV supply equipment, and the remaining 75 percent of the parking spaces 
will be EV-ready for future installation. 
 
SUSTAINABLE AND RESILIENT DEVELOPMENT 
 
The Proponent is committed to supporting Boston’s sustainability and resiliency 
goals, including the following commitments: 
 
● The Proponent will design the Proposed Project buildings to be certifiable 
under LEED v4 BD&C New Construction Gold, with a target of at least 62 
points, and Passive House PHIUS 2024 standards. 
● Building A has a preliminary modeled pCEI of 0.63 kg CO2e/sf-yr. 
● Building B has a preliminary modeled pCEI of 0.64 kg CO2e/sf-yr 
● Both buildings will utilize all-efficient-electric space and DHW heating 
systems and will be fossil fuel free. 
● As the design progresses, the Proponent will analyze the feasibility of 
installing rooftop solar PV system(s). The buildings and rooftops will be 
designed to optimize solar PV generation and will be solar PV ready. 
● The Proposed Project will employ energy- and water-efficient features for 
mechanical, electrical, architectural, and structural systems, as well as 
materials, where feasible. Sustainable design elements relating to building 
energy management systems, lighting, recycling, conservation measures, 
local building materials, and clean construction vehicles will also be included, 
to the greatest extent practicable.

● To reduce embodied carbon emissions the Proponent will assess the 
feasibility of using mass timber or similar low carbon structure and enclosure 
construction materials and practices. 
● To mitigate the urban heat island effect, the Project will incorporate multiple 
strategies, including increased landscaping, the use of hardscape materials 
with low solar reflectance, and high-albedo roofing materials. 
● To further reduce carbon emissions, the Project team and the Proponent will 
evaluate the feasibility of purchasing renewable electricity including Boston’s 
Community Choice’s ‘Green 100’, entering into a Power Purchase Agreement, 
Virtual Power Purchase Agreement, or purchasing Massachusetts Class I 
Renewable Energy Credits. 
 
SMART UTILITIES 
 
The Proposed Project will comply with the Smart Utilities requirements found in 
Article 80B of the Code. Each of the buildings within the Proposed Project shall also 
meet or exceed the 1.25” of stormwater infiltration from the impervious areas of 
the Project Site standard, and the Proponent will incorporate several green 
infrastructure standards, including utilization of permeable pavers in the frontage 
zone and installation of rain gardens, vegetative swales, and native planting in the 
landscape design. The Proponent will make improvements to street lighting where 
necessary as part of the Project’s enhanced streetscapes. The Proposed Project will 
also adhere to the City of Boston’s EV readiness program; 25 percent of the net new 
parking spaces in the Proposed Project’s below-grade garages will be equipped with 
EV supply equipment, and the remaining 75 percent of the parking spaces will be 
EV-ready for future installation. The Proponent will complete the Smart Utilities 
review prior to obtaining a Certificate of Occupancy for the Proposed Project.

The Proposed Project at 358 Chestnut Hill Avenue is located in the Allston-Brighton 
Neighborhood Zoning District’s Neighborhood Shopping (NS-1) Subdistrict. It is also 
located within the study area of the Allston-Brighton Needs Assessment, which was 
adopted by the BPDA Board in January 2024. This planning process did not yield 
updated zoning, but provided staff with insight relevant to the review of this 
Proposal. The Allston-Brighton Needs Assessment focused on assessing the 
community’s assets and needs. A central finding of the report noted the need for 
housing that is both accessible and affordable. This project meets the community 
needs identified in the report by providing transit-oriented housing including four 
income-restricted units. 
 
While Historic Districts, designated by the Landmarks Commission, lie outside of 
zoning, the Proposed Project also sits in the Aberdeen Architectural Conservation 
District. This district helps protect the unique character of the romantic turn of the 
century style homes that are located in the area. During staff review of the project, 
input from the Aberdeen Architectural Conservation District Commission, informed 
a reduction of the height of the building from 7 to 6 stories. Due to the adjacent 
public park, the Proposed Project is also subject to a Parks Design Review as per

BPDA’s Brighton neighborhood update list. The public comment period ended on

PLANNING AND ZONING CONTEXT 
The Proposed Project is located within the Mission Hill Neighborhood District, in a 
Three-Family Residential (3F-2000) subdistrict, pursuant to Article 59 of the Boston 
Zoning Code. The Project Site at 36 Parker Hill Avenue, also known as 200 Hillside 
Street has been combined with the parcel containing the existing developments at 
40 Parker Hill Avenue and 44 Parker Hill Avenue. The usable open space, parking, 
and tenant amenities provided by each of the two existing buildings will continue to 
be shared among those two buildings. The amenities proposed for the new building 
are intended to be shared among the residents of all three buildings. The proposed 
courtyard area is also accessible by the existing building at 198 Hillside Street, in 
shared ownership, to the rear. The Proposed Project has been reviewed with 
respect to this context. 
The Mission Hill neighborhood is identified by Imagine Boston 2030 as an Enhanced 
Neighborhood, calling for contextually sensitive development to improve urban 
vitality and affirm neighborhood identity. In the Go Boston 2030 plan, Mission Hill is 
envisioned as a neighborhood with walkable and bicycle-friendly main streets. The 
location of additional housing units within a residential area so close to transit 
opportunities aligns with the goals of both Imagine Boston and Go Boston. This 
project has the potential to further contribute to the number of residents 
employing transit options in lieu of single occupancy vehicles to travel to work for a 
neighborhood where as of 2017, only 18.4% of commuters traveled in single 
occupancy vehicles. 
While Multi-Family Residential is a forbidden use, Section 59-7 - Use Regulations 
Applicable in Residential Subdistricts - provides Special Provisions for Residential 
Development in Three-Family Residential Subdistricts, which intends to support the 
development of residential units within the neighborhood through the allowance of 
multifamily residential buildings on lots of sufficient size, given that the character of 
the development respects the character of the neighborhood as a whole. As the 
dimensional regulations from the zoning code anticipate the development of a 
three-family residential building, some of the regulations may not be relevant to a 
multi-family residential building, such as FAR.

PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The proposed project is located in Grove Hall on Blue Hill Avenue, a major City 
thoroughfare serving several key bus routes, which includes the 45 bus that 
connects the project site north to Nubian Square and Ruggles station and south to 
Franklin Park at Columbia Road. This section of Blue Hill Avenue is characterized by 
3-4 story blocks, which are primarily residential with ground floor retailers. These 
include bakeries, bodegas, salons, and banks. There are also several religious 
institutional buildings in the area, including a Haitian church across the street from 
the project site and a mosque directly to the rear of the project site. 
 
The Proposed Project is located within the boundaries of the Roxbury Strategic 
Master Plan, adopted in 2004, with the goal to guide development for the next 10-
20 years in the Roxbury neighborhood. Key elements of this Plan include the 
enhancement of the civic and cultural environment, promoting a diverse economy 
and range of housing options, creating safer transportation connections and a lively 
public realm. Providing accessible, affordable housing is particularly critical to 
achieve housing stability within the Roxbury community, as well as mitigate rising 
citywide housing costs. 
 
The proposed project contributes to housing stability in the Roxbury community 
with the provision of 18 income-restricted units, which fills in a currently missing 
tooth in the built fabric. This building will mitigate the presence of several vacant 
lots and empty storefronts in the vicinity, improving street level activity and public

floor uses.

the placement and activation of the proposed community room. In addition, there

BPDA recommendations.

PLANNING CONTEXT 
Given its urban, transit-rich context, the extant surface parking that comprises most 
of the Proposed Project site is a highly inappropriate land use. In contrast, the 
proposed residential use is consistent with both city-wide planning goals for 
housing production, as well as the predominant land use of the surrounding area. 
 
No recent neighborhood plans or zoning updates have been conducted for this site. 
The Proposed Project is located across the street from Turnpike Air Rights Parcel 
12, which is guided by the Civic Vision for Turnpike Air Rights in Boston (2000) plan. 
However, because the findings and recommendations of this document are 
specifically tailored to the unique context of air-rights development over highway 
infrastructure, they are not relevant to 415 Newbury Street. 
 
The Proposed Project straddles two zoning districts: the General Business District 
(B-8-120b) at the easterly portion of the site, and the Apartment Residential District 
(H-3-65) at the westerly portion of the site. In this location, the 1855 Back Bay street 
network collides with the 1881 Fenway network, creating a series of acute angles 
where Massachusetts Avenue meets east-west cross streets, including Newbury 
Street. As a result, the General Business District, which follows the alignment of 
Massachusetts Avenue, bisects the site which follows the alignment of Newbury 
Street. 
 
BPDA staff recommended a massing approach aligned with both the underlying 
zoning, and the existing context of lower heights on the westerly portion of the site 
and greater heights on the easterly portion of the site. In the westerly Residential 
District, zoning allows up to 65 feet in height, with adjacent buildings ranging in 
height from 5 to 9 stories. The proposed westerly building height is 36 feet and 3 
stories. In the easterly Business District, zoning allows up to 120 feet in height, with 
abutting buildings ranging in height from 4 to 8 stories. The proposed easterly 
building, located in both zoning districts, is 120 feet and 11 stories. Accordingly, the 
overall Proposed Project is of appropriate overall density and adequate massing.

Boston Zoning Code and Map 1. The westerly portion of the Project Site located 
within the H-3-65 (Apartment Residential) district and the easterly portion is located

DEVELOPMENT PLAN FOR PLANNED DEVELOPMENT AREA NO. 145 
415 NEWBURY STREET, BACK BAY 
 
 
1. Board Action 
The Proponent (as defined below) is requesting approval of this Development Plan for 
Planned Development Area No. 145 from the Boston Redevelopment Authority d/b/a 
Boston Planning & Development Agency. 
2. Proponent 
Trinity Back Bay Development LLC with an address c/o Trinity Financial, 75 Federal 
Street, 4th Floor, Boston, MA 02110 
3. Project Location 
Planned Development Area No. 145 encompasses an approximately 48,161 square foot 
(1.1 acre) contiguous area of land (the “Project Site”) comprised of 374 Commonwealth 
Avenue containing the existing Harvard Club of Boston building (the “Clubhouse”), 415 
Newbury Street, and a portion of 380 Commonwealth Avenue, bounded to the north by 
Commonwealth Avenue and a private alley with abutting residential properties further 
north, to the south by Newbury Street, and to the east and west by commercial properties. 
4. Project Description 
The development program contemplates the construction of two new buildings containing 
approximately 133 residential units, residential amenities, and new Harvard Club of Boston 
facilities within approximately 157,000 square feet of Gross Floor Area (GFA) of new 
building space, together with up to 125 off-street vehicle parking spaces and related site 
and public realm improvements (the “Project”). Approximately 64,000 square feet of 
existing Clubhouse GFA will remain. The Project contemplates at least 133 indoor or 
covered bicycle parking spaces, and approximately 18 short-term bicycle racks (each with 
capacity for 2 bicycles) on Newbury Street and at the existing Clubhouse rear entrance. 
5. Public Benefits 
The Project includes streetscape improvements to Newbury Street westward past 
Massachusetts Avenue along the Project Site frontage and mixed-income housing that 
will exceed the applicable 13% income-restricted requirement of the City of Boston’s 
Inclusionary Development Policy under the Mayor’s Order Relative to Inclusionary 
Development dated December 9, 2015. The new construction will seek LEED Platinum 
Certification and will be all electric. The Project contemplates construction of an 
accessible, lit waiting area on site for the public when using MBTA’s The RIDE service 
or ridesharing services. Anticipated monetary contributions include amounts for a 
neighborhood housing Acquisition Opportunity Program, enhancement of neighborhood 
open space through the Parks and Recreation Department, and a new BlueBike station. 

 
 
 
6. Project Zoning 
The Project Site is located entirely within Boston proper, governed by the base Boston 
Zoning Code and Map 1. The westerly portion of the Project Site located within the H-3-
65 (Apartment Residential) district and the easterly portion is located within the B-8-
120b (General Business) district. The Project Site also is within the Restricted Parking 
Overlay District (RPOD) and the Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (GCOD). 
The Project Site is eligible for Planned Development Area designation. Approval of this 
Development Plan would provide the zoning relief required for the proposed 
development program.

Re: 415 Newbury St
Dear Chair Rojas and Members of the Board,
I write to you today in support of the proposal at 415 Newbury St. My support is based on two
major components of the project: housing affordability in the Back Bay and significant
contributions to the public realm.
The proposed development will include a portion of affordable homeownership units, which
will help to address the complete lack of affordable homeownership opportunities in the Back
Bay. It is good to see that as a result of neighborhood feedback, the proponents have made the
adjustment to keep all the affordable units on-site. I believe this shows a good-faith effort by
the proponent to improve the diversity of income-levels that can call Back Bay home.
The proposal also makes serious improvements to the public realm of not just the immediate
area, but projects important to the Back Bay. The developer has proposed to include a number
of public amenities in the project. The first of said improvements will include the beautification
of the end of Newbury St west of Massachusetts Avenue. This will turn a currently underutilized
and unappealing street into an activated, greener space by planting many trees and using
permeable pavers. Improvements also include a community contribution to improve the
connection at Charlesgate, which will hope to recapture the lost link in Frederick Law Olmsted’s
Emerald Necklace.
I concur with my neighbors’ concerns that the PDA does present a potentially precarious
precedent. My support for this proposal is dependent on the understanding that further PDAs in
the historic district should be put on pause indefinitely. This of course would not extend to air
rights projects which are appropriate considering the complexity of those projects. I fully
understand that the BPDA has agreed to study standards and conditions determining which
areas of the city are PDA-eligible. There is work being done on the Article 80 modernization
project and my hope is that as part of that, consideration for PDAs in the Back Bay Architectural
District are kept in mind throughout.

This firm represents the Windsor Place Condominium Trust, which is the duly elected 
and acting organization of unit owners for the Windsor Place Condominium, consisting of 92 
residential and 14 commercial units, located at 390 Commonwealth Avenue. Windsor Place, its 
owners and residents are direct abutters to the 415 Newbury Street Project. We write to express 
our strong support for the approval of the Project by the Boston Planning and Development 
Agency Board. Additionally, Windsor Place supports the utilization of a Planned Development 
Area (PDA) as the zoning mechanism for approval. 
 
Windsor Place has engaged in extensive discussions with the project proponent, Trinity. 
Trinity has been understanding of the impacts on neighboring properties and very willing to 
listen to, work with and understand the concerns of the Windsor Place residents and owners. The 
originally proposed project consisted of a ten (10) story hotel, with a roof top bar and lounge on 
the Harvard Club parking lot parcel. Windsor Place residents expressed major concerns 
regarding the initial iteration which included shadows cast by the proposed structure, loss of 
privacy, exposure to noise and other nuisance. The Windsor Place Condominium is unique in 
that it has an outdoor swimming pool and lounge area located on the 3rd floor rear of the 
building, abutting the Harvard Club parking lot. The construction of a ten or even five story 
building adjacent to that swimming pool, as originally proposed, would eliminate all privacy, 
inhibit sunlight, and arguably render this unique common area feature of a residential building 
useless. 
 
As such, and as evidence of their responsiveness to community concerns, Trinity 
amended their proposal. As a result, the current Project, consisting of a 3-story building on the 
parking lot abutting Windsor Place, and an 11-story building where the Harvard Club is located 
at 374 Commonwealth Ave, is one that respects the existing residents and improves the
