6.0 
Technical Studies in Support of Development of the PDA 
6.1 
Traffic 
This section provides a preliminary summary of the access and circulation characteristics of the 
PDA Master Plan Project and an overview of key impact analyses that will be conducted in 
forthcoming studies to be completed and included in connection with future City of Boston 
Article 80B & C permitting activities. 
The PDA Master Plan contemplates adherence to key City of Boston mobility initiatives, 
including compliance with prevailing Complete Street Guidelines, PLAN: Charlestown, 

 
22 
 
Vehicle Parking Guidelines, EV Parking Initiatives, Bicycle Parking Guidelines, Bluebike 
Parking Guidelines requirements, and the TDM Points System. Further, the Proposed Project 
looks to study, develop, and commit to robust and comprehensive transportation mitigation 
actions that are aimed to exceed BPDA and BTD requirements and will serve as exceptional 
public benefits. 
 
6.1.1 Bicycle Access and Infrastructure 
The Project will comply with the City of Boston Bicycle Parking Guidelines, providing secure, 
indoor bicycle storage for building occupants, as well as outdoor bicycle racks for visitor and 
public use. The bike rack location, type, and total number of spaces will conform to the latest 
City of Boston Bike Parking Guidelines at the time of each Development Plan filing. 
The Project will accommodate the planned Charlestown Community Path along the southern 
portion of the Site, which will provide a key connection between Charlestown, the Site, and the 
Harborwalk. 
 
6.1.2 Vehicle Parking 
Parking on the Site will be provided in accordance with Section 3.5.1 above. The Project will 
conform to the Electric Vehicle Readiness Policy at the time of each Development Plan filing. 
Current Electric Vehicle Readiness Policy requires new developments to equip 25% of their 
parking spaces to be EVSE installed and the remaining 75% to be EV-ready. The exact 
location, quantities, and type of EV-installed parking will be coordinated with the BTD and the 
BPDA as project planning evolves. 
 
 
6.1.3 Transportation Demand Management 
The Proposed Project will incorporate a robust and comprehensive program of TDM strategies to 
take full advantage of multiple mobility options. The Project’s goal will be to develop a broad set 
of alternatives for residents and employees of the Project so they will not be as dependent on 
personal vehicles. An important component of the TDM plan will be the incorporation of 
appropriate bicycle accommodations throughout and around the Site, including secure bike 
parking for residents, employees, and visitors to the Site. As mentioned previously, the 
Proponent will adhere to BTD guidelines for on-site long-term and short-term bike parking on a 
phase-by-phase basis to encourage the use of bicycles. The Proponent will also evaluate the 
incorporation of car sharing service(s) within the development if there is demand for it. The 
Proponent will contribute to the establishment and ongoing operations of the Charlestown Link 
shuttle service for as long as such service is operational and serves the Site. 
The Proponent will require all tenants to implement proactive TDM plans in accordance with the 
agreed upon Transportation Access Plan Agreement (“TAPA”) with the City of Boston for the 
Project. The Proposed Project will make use of and fulfill its TDM requirements by complying 
with and exceeding the City of Boston’s new TDM Points System. 
6.1.4 Transportation Studies Supporting Future Article 80 Permitting 
The future study of transportation in connection with the assessment of the Proposed Project will 
include detailed evaluation and summary of the existing and future transportation conditions 

 
23 
 
within the defined PDA Area associated with each future Development Plan and phase of the 
Project. These transportation studies will be developed to understand and mitigate the 
transportation impacts associated with the Project and to devise a comprehensive transportation 
mitigation and improvement plan in the vicinity of the Project that supports future operations of 
the Project and provides area-wide transportation improvements to the Charlestown area. 
The purpose of these analyses will be to: 
● Define and quantify existing transportation conditions for pedestrians, bicyclists, transit 
users, and motorists in the PDA Area; 
● Estimate the transportation impacts that will be generated under future conditions based 
on the anticipated program, provided parking, and phasing for the PDA Master 
Plan Project; 
● Develop a set of mitigation strategies and improvement measures which will help lessen 
the transportation demand effects of the Project, including potential off-site mitigation 
measures. Such strategies will be codified in TAPAs that will be developed with and 
approved by BTD; 
● Demonstrate that these improvement measures and transportation mitigation efforts will 
meet or exceed BPDA and BTD requirements and will serve as exceptional public 
benefits; and 
● Illustrate the Project’s prioritization of pedestrian and bicycle modes as part of the overall 
TDM strategy and commitment to modern mobility. 
 
Recognizing that transportation is a key policy priority at both city and state levels, these studies 
will be conducted in conformance with both BTD and MassDOT guidelines and use standard 
methodologies, including prevailing City of Boston standards for pedestrian, bicycle, transit, and 
vehicle analyses, and incorporating local travel characteristics as defined in Access Boston 2000-
2010, the Go Boston 2030 Action Plan, and PLAN: Charlestown. 
6.2 
Replacement Parking Spaces 
To ensure that the Replacement Parking will not be used for the benefit of the occupants of the 
Proposed Project pursuant to Section 3.5.1 above, Replacement Parking spaces will only be 
accessible to employees, clients, visitors, lessees, permittees, and authorized users of 465 
Medford Street and 529 Medford Street (“Authorized Parking Users”). The Replacement 
Parking spaces will be physically separated from any other Project parking spaces and will only 
be accessible to Authorized Parking Users via key code, card, remote-controlled opener, or other 
similar means of controlling access to Authorized Parking Users. 
The City of Boston Inspectional Services Department (“ISD”) or its designee shall have access to 
the Replacement Parking at any time while the Parking Garage is open for the sole purpose of 
reviewing use of the Replacement Parking to ensure that it is being used solely for Authorized 
Parking Users. If at any time ISD has reason to believe there are any non-Authorized Parking 
Users parking in the Replacement Parking spaces or that that any non-Authorized Parking Users 
have been parking in the Replacement Parking spaces, ISD or its designee may commence an 
enforcement proceeding by issuing a Notice of Probable Violation (“NOPV”) to the Proponent. 
The NOPV shall (i) state the factual basis for the allegation of the violation and the proposed 
remedial action to be taken by the Proponent, (ii) state that the Proponent must reply in writing to 
the NOPV within thirty (30) days from the date of the NOPV, and (iii) state that the Proponent 

 
24 
 
must appear before an informal conference with ISD on a designated date which must be at least 
thirty (30) days from the date of the NOPV. 
The Proponent, or its designee’s or representative’s written reply, must be filed with ISD and 
include a complete statement of all relevant facts and authority, and a full description of the 
reasons that the Proponent disputes the violation(s) alleged in the NOPV. If the Proponent or its 
representative fails to file a written reply and fails to appear at the informal conference, the 
Proponent shall be deemed to have admitted the accuracy of the factual allegations and legal 
conclusions stated in the NOPV, and the Proponent shall be subject to the written enforcement 
action set forth at the informal conference. 
A hearing officer designated by ISD shall conduct an informal review of the violation which shall 
consist of the informal conference and an analysis of the Proponent’s written reply. At any 
informal conference, the Proponent shall have the right to be represented by an attorney or other 
person, and shall have the right to present relevant documents to the hearing officer. The hearing 
officer shall make available to the Proponent any evidence in the Commission’s possession which 
indicates that the Proponent may have committed a violation, and the Proponent or its 
representative shall have the opportunity to rebut this evidence. However, this informal 
conference shall not be construed to be an adjudicatory proceeding as defined in M.G.L. Chapter 
30A. The hearing officer shall make a decision in writing. If the Proponent is not satisfied with 
the decision, the Proponent may request a hearing by ISD, provided that the Proponent makes 
such a request in writing within seven (7) calendar days of the date the decision is issued. 
If ISD finds that the Proponent has committed a violation, it may take appropriate enforcement 
action of issuing a fine or initiating an enforcement proceeding in a court of competent 
jurisdiction. If ISD or its designee undertakes enforcement proceedings and issues a fine, such 
fines may be as follows: 
• for the first offense, by a fine of not less than one thousand ($1,000) nor more than five 
thousand dollars ($5,000), and 
• for a subsequent offense, by a fine of not less than five thousand ($5,000) nor more than 
ten thousand dollars ($10,000). 
For the purpose of this Section, each day and part thereof on which a violation of such an order, 
rule, or regulation occurs, whether such violation be continuous or intermittent, shall be construed 
as a separate and succeeding offense. Additionally, for the purpose of this Section, each Parking 
Space in violation of such an order, rule, or regulation, whether such violation be continuous or 
intermittent, shall be construed as a separate and succeeding offense. 
To aid in the initial compliance review of the Replacement Parking Spaces, the Proponent shall 
bear the sole cost and expense of engaging a third-party independent auditor (the “Parking 
Auditor”) to complete a review and written report provided directly to ISD regarding the use of 
the Replacement Parking, which shall include any instances of use of the Replacement Parking 
by non-Authorized Parking Users (the “Parking Report”). The Parking Report may serve as the 
sole basis for the issuance of an NOPV by ISD, and ISD may engage directly with the Parking 
Auditor regarding any such Parking Report. From the date of the issuance of the first final 
certificate of occupancy for the Proposed Project (the “Parking Date”) up and through the third 
anniversary of the Parking Date, the Proponent shall cause to be provided a Parking Report no 
less than two times per calendar year at such times as may be directed by ISD, and from the third 
anniversary of the Parking Date through the tenth anniversary of the Parking Date, the Proponent 

 
25 
 
shall cause to be provided a Parking Report once per calendar year at such times as may be 
directed by ISD.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this PDA Master Plan or in the Zoning Code to the

Components, (ii) the subdivision or combination of the parcels that compose the Site, and/or (iii) 
the submission of one or more buildings or Project Components to a condominium regime; 
provided that: (a) the use provisions of this Development Plan are not violated by the resulting 
Project Component, (b) the Proposed Project’s Site-wide FAR (as defined above) does not 
exceed the maximum density permitted under this PDA Master Plan for the PDA Area as a 
whole, (c) the Open Space and parking requirements of this PDA Master Plan are met with 
respect to the Site as a whole, (d) the public benefit obligations set forth in this Development 
Plan are not decreased without the prior written consent of the Director of the BPDA, and the 
scope of the public benefit obligations set forth in this PDA Master Plan are not diminished, and 

 
26 
 
(e) the sequencing of such open space, public realm, and public benefits obligations set forth in 
this PDA Master Plan are met.

submission of one or more Development Plans for the Project. Review of environmental impacts 
will be studied during the Article 80B Large Project Review process, taking into account any 
technical studies already performed. Buildings will also be subject to review under Articles 25A 
(Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District), 28 (Boston Civic Design Commission review) and 
37 (Green Buildings) of the Zoning Code. 
7.4 
No Obligation to Proceed with Proposed Project 
 
Notwithstanding anything set forth herein to the contrary, under no circumstances shall the 
Proponent or any other party be obligated to proceed with the development of all or any portion 
of the Proposed Project.

maximize ground floor visibility of active and semi-active 
programming, such as lobby/building entry, tenant amenity

425 Medford Street in Charlestown; Master Plan for Planned Development Area 
 
Dear Ms. Polhemus; 
 
The Boston Parks and Recreation Department (BPRD) has reviewed the Article 80C Master Plan 
for Planned Development Area (PDA) at 425 Medford Street in Charlestown. BPRD has also 
reviewed the presentation that was made at a public meeting on April 13, 2022; and the 
presentation that was made to the Boston Civic Design Commission on May 3, 2022. 
 
The plans in the April and May presentations are different than those that were submitted in the 
PDA Master Plan. BPRD understands that the PDA Master Plan will continue to be refined until 
the BPDA Board votes on it. Once the dimensional limitations are set in the PDA Master Plan, 
the proponent will file a Project Notification Form and Development Plan for each phase and 
will present detailed information on a design that conforms to the PDA Master Plan. This letter 
comments on both the PDA Master Plan and the plans in the April and May presentations. 
 
Project Site The site at 425 Medford Street is approximately 20.5 acres. The proponent also 
owns the adjacent sites at 465 Medford Street and 529 Main Street. Five acres will be subdivided 
from those two properties and included in the PDA Master Plan Area (including what appears to 
be water sheet in front of 529 Main Street). This will allow the proponent to create a sea-level-
rise barrier which will protect all three of its properties from flooding (46 acres total). 
 
John J. Doherty Playground 
The John J. Doherty Playground is across the street from 
the project site, on the north side of Bunker Hill overlooking the Mystic River (a.k.a. 
Charlestown Heights). The park was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and is listed on 
the National Register of Historic Places. 
 
The City acquired an estate of 10.5 acres on both sides of Medford Street in 1891. The City used 
3.8 acres on Bunker Hill to create the park. Another 6.2 acres of flats on the Mystic River were 
transformed into Dewey Beach (now incorporated into the project site at 425 Medford Street). 
Another .5 acres along the Boston & Lowell Railroad separated the two public open spaces. 
 
Olmsted designed Charlestown Heights to take advantage of the steep hillside in order to capture 
the views and breezes from the Mystic River. The park opened in 1895 and included multiple 
terraces; walkways around a central open space; promenades; a scenic overlook; and perimeter 
landscaping that screened the surrounding neighborhood. Much of this design remains intact. 
City of Boston 
Parks and Recreation 
Mayor Michelle Wu 

2 
 
The connection to the river was further made through the creation of Dewey Beach at the bottom 
of the hill. An underpass was built at Medford Street to connect the park and the waterfront. The 
beach was built in 1898 with bathhouses and promenade piers. Dewey Beach was later polluted 
by land use and coal barges and sold to industrial interests. Only the stone terraces survive. 
 
Charlestown Heights is the best remaining example of five small City parks that Olmsted sited 
along river or ocean banks to provide refreshing breezes and distant views, and to incorporate 
public bathing or swimming. Frederick Law Olmsted, Jr. described the design intent as follows: 
 
“The feature of Charlestown Heights is a grand sweeping view over the marshes of the 
Mystic, as yet almost untouched, by the growth of the city, to the distant suburbs of Malden 
and Everett, with the permanently forested hills of the Middlesex Fells in the distance 
beyond. The design in this case takes the peculiar advantage of the location as its controlling 
motive throughout, and attempts to make the most of it.” (Harper's Weekly, 1897) 
 
The "grand sweeping view over the marshes" diminished due to landfill and industrial 
degradation. However, the park retains much of its original design intent. The proposed 
development should not impact the views of water and sky or the breezes from the Mystic River. 
 
John J. Ryan Playground 
The project will connect to John J. Ryan Playground - a 9 acre 
open space on the Mystic River that was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and built in 1891. 
Ryan Playground is a primary active recreational open space for the neighborhood and beyond. 
 
BPRD is planning significant capital improvements to make Ryan Playground more functional, 
more resilient and to maximize the value of the open space. Even with the improvements, this 
playground will be burdened by the number of new users from the project at 425 Medford Street. 
 
Project Buildout 
Apparently the project is evolving even as it goes through the PDA Master 
Plan review. The PDA Master Plan includes eight buildings with 1.8 million gsf of mixed use: 
residential (1,050,000 sf – a unit count is not readily provided but using the estimates in the 
April/May presentations, this will be about 1050 units); office/lab (575,000 sf); hotel (115,000 
sf); retail and restaurant (90,000 sf); a community center (6500 sf) and 1200 parking spaces. 
 
The April and May presentations included changes to the site design, heights, footprints and 
massing; and removed a building. However, the project retained about 1.8 million gsf of mixed 
use, reconfigured as follows: residential (562,000 sf with +/- 560 units); office/lab (988,000 sf); 
hotel (173,000 sf); retail and restaurant (60,000 sf); and community space (6000 sf). 
 
Grading 
The existing elevation of the site is not readily provided. BPRD has estimated it to 
be 7’ at the waterline and 13’ at the rail corridor at Medford Street. The site will be raised to 22’ 
BCB to protect the property from flooding. However, the information provided in the PDA 
Master Plan is not clear or consistent. The narrative says that the elevation will be increased to 
22’ BCB along the waterfront, but the sections appear to show a level grade across the entire site. 
 
It is not clear from what base elevation the building heights are being measured. 
 
 

3 
 
It is not clear how the elevated grade will meet its adjacencies. The plans show the site as level to 
the elevation of the rail corridor and Medford Street, when in fact an elevation of 22’ BCB could 
be 9’-10’ above the elevation at this point. 
 
The plans, renderings and cross sections are not clear or consistent in presenting the current or 
proposed grade, particularly in relation to adjacencies. It is not clear how the grade on site will 
interface with the existing grade at the rail corridor or the public realm at Medford Street. It is 
not clear from what grade the building heights are being measured. This clarity is needed in 
order to assess the impacts on Doherty Park, particularly the height of Buildings D, F, G, and H. 
 
Chapter 91 Height 
Chapter 91 restricts the heights of buildings to 55’ if they are within 100’ 
of the shoreline. The height may increase by 1 foot for every 2 feet further inland it is located. It 
is unclear if the heights in the PDA Master Plan conform to the height restrictions of Chapter 91. 
 
The west side of the site is Commonwealth Tidelands (Buildings D, F, G and H). The height of 
these buildings will particularly impact the views and user experience from Doherty Park. 
 
It should be clarified whether the PDA Master Plan meets the Chapter 91 height restrictions. 
 
Zoning Height 
The proposed project is located within the Harborpark: Charlestown 
Waterfront zoning district and the Charlestown Maritime Economy Reserve and the Mystic River 
Waterfront Manufacturing sub-districts. This underlying zoning is governed by Article 42B of 
the Zoning Code. The proposed project is also in the Coastal Zoning Overlay District which 
includes Charlestown’s waterfront along the Mystic River and the Schrafft’s City Center. 
 
The Charlestown Maritime Economy Reserve Subdistrict and the Mystic River Waterfront 
Manufacturing Subdistrict have a maximum building height of 55’ and a maximum FAR of 
2.0. The Coastal Zoning Overlay District allows heights to be measured from two feet above 
the Sea Level Rise Base Flood Elevation, rather than at grade as current zoning requires. It also 
makes allowances in setbacks, open space, etc. for vertical circulation and mechanical systems. 
 
PDA Master Plan Height 
The PDA Master Plan significantly exceeds the maximum height 
of 55’ under current zoning. Six buildings are double to quadruple the height allowed under 
zoning. This has a significant impact on the views and user experience from Doherty Park. 
 
The PDA Master Plan states that the buildings will step back along Medford Street as a scale-
reducing device toward the neighborhood. However, the tallest buildings are Building D (198’) 
and Building H (228’). These buildings are sited directly in front of Doherty Park which was 
specifically designed in relation to the Mystic River by Frederick Law Olmsted.

Massing 
The plans in the PDA Master Plan and the April and May presentations remained 
consistent at approximately 1.8 million gsf. But the massing and footprints changed in the April 
and May presentations. The footprints of Buildings E, G and H have increased. The footprints of 
Buildings D and F have decreased. 
 
Buildings B, C, E and F appear to have footprints of about 160’ x 250’. Building D has a 
footprint of about 160’ x 160’. Buildings G and H appear to have footprints of about 120’ x 250’. 
 
The PDA Master Plan states that individual buildings may exceed the overall FAR limit, but the 
overall FAR will be at or below 2.0. Approximately five acres will be subdivided from the 
adjacent properties at 465 Medford Street and 529 Main Street and incorporated into the project 
site (this appears to include the water sheet in front of 529 Main Street). 
 
The incorporation of the waterfront area and water sheet will allow the project to maintain an 
FAR of 1.68, while significantly exceeding the heights required under current zoning. 
 
The BPDA should consider whether the addition of open space that is currently part of the 
adjacent property can be used to calculate the FAR on the subject property. Further, it should be 
determined whether the water sheet at 529 Main Street can be counted toward the FAR. 
 
 

5 
 
View Corridors 
Frederick Law Olmsted designed Doherty Park specifically to capture the 
views of and breezes from the Mystic River. The connection to the water was completed with the 
creation of Dewey Beach on the park property at the bottom of the hill. The PDA Master Plan 
notes that the project is designed around three view corridors oriented north-south from the 
Charlestown hillside, across Medford Street, through the development, to the Mystic River. 
 
The April and May presentations made changes to the footprints in the PDA Master Plan. These 
changes created spaces in between the buildings that are more aligned and uniform. The April 
and May presentations show Olmsted Way as a pedestrian street that is 65’ wide, though sections 
show it as 65’-90’. Industrial Way is a pedestrian street that is 40’ wide. Central Drive is a 
vehicular street that is 50’ - 60’ wide. Cove Way is a vehicular street that is 50’ wide. 
 
Bunker Hill is 111’ at the top. The PDA Master Plan proposes buildings that are up to 220’. The 
project’s height, massing and siting will significantly impact the experience from Doherty Park. 
It will also break the sense of connection between the neighborhood and the waterfront. The 
project will block the water and the sky and will capture the amenity that the waterfront offers. 
 
Slide 46 of the April presentation includes one section that shows a cut through Doherty 
Playground along Buildings D and F. A cut through Buildings G and H should be provided. This 
section should also be provided for the heights in the PDA Master Plan. 
 
Slide 47 includes the heights of existing waterfront buildings. A version of this slide with the 
current buildings on the 425 Medford Street site should be shown for comparison. 
 
A model view should be created from each terrace of Doherty Park, through the proposed PDA 
Master Plan to the Mystic River. The key sight lines to the water should be retained. 
 
Designated Port Area 
A portion of the waterfront on the west side of the site is 
Designated Port Area (DPA). There is also a DPA area adjacent to the northeast site of the site. 
The plans are not consistent in showing how required vehicular access will be provided through 
the site to the DPA areas, including the DPA area that is shown as open space. 
 
It should be clarified if the DPA area is being counted as open space in exchange for 
development rights mitigated through the PDA. The required vehicular access to the PDA areas 
through the site should also be clarified, as it will impact the use of area shown as open space. 
 
Chapter 91 Open Space: 
Chapter 91 requires at least fifty percent of a project site to be 
dedicated to open space. The west side of the site is Commonwealth Tidelands (Buildings D, F, 
G and H). Open space in Commonwealth Tidelands must be accessible to and usable by the 
public 24 hours a day. No gates, fences, or barriers may be placed in a manner that impedes the 
free flow of pedestrian movement. All pedestrian access facilities shall be accessible to 
physically handicapped persons. Maintaining, cleaning, landscaping, and managing the open 
space and pedestrian access facilities shall be the responsibility of the Chapter 91 licensee. 
 
The proponent should explain how it is meeting the Chapter 91 open space requirements, as 
these requirements are separate from but directly related to the PDA Master Plan. 

6 
 
Resilient Waterfront The project site is a breach point for flooding during storm events. The 
project will include a 1.5 mile sea-level-rise barrier that will be integrated into five acres of 
waterfront open space across three separate sites. The grade at the water’s edge will be raised to 
an elevation of 22’ BCB (it is not clear if this elevation is maintained across the site). 
 
This elevation will protect the three contiguous sites owned by the proponent at 425 Medford 
Street, 465 Medford Street and 529 Main Street. The PDA Master Plan notes that the barrier will 
also protect 220 acres in Charlestown and hundreds of acres in Somerville and Cambridge. 
 
Project Open Space The PDA Master Plan states that the 25 acre site includes 13 acres of open 
space (58% of the total acreage). The open space is not clearly quantified in the PDA Master 
Plan - the plans are conceptual, the narrative is visionary and the renderings are illustrative. 
 
Five acres of resilient waterfront flood barrier will include the Harborwalk that will connect the 
project to Ryan Playground. Eight acres of open space will include a central pedestrian spine 
140’ wide to connect Medford Street to the river (it is not clear where this is on the plan); a 
stormwater channel; a dog park; passive and active recreation areas and seating; multiple look-
out areas; floodable steps; a public boat and kayak launch. A 2000’ segment of the Charlestown 
Community Path will be constructed across the three properties owned by the proponent. 
 
The PDA states that the project is also designed to provide approximately 6.65 acres of 
additional open and public gathering spaces including activated ground floor retail throughout. 
 
The April and May presentations include modifications to the open space plan. Building A has 
been removed from the Medford Street Community Path – this area is 60’ wide and includes a 
dog park. A plaza area within a hotel drop off (about 60’ x 120’) has been added between 
Buildings D and F. The waterfront open space at 425 Medford Street (which includes Designated 
Port Area) is a more uniform width of about 140’ from the top of grade (22’ BCB) at the water’s 
edge to the building façade. Two pocket parks of 1000 sf each are shown at Buildings G and H. 
The open space in front of Building B is not qualified or quantified so it is unclear how it will be 
used. Some of the plans in the April presentation show a significant amount of green roofs. 
 
BPRD has found it challenging to review the open space needed to serve a project with the 
significant dimensional limits requested in the PDA Master Plan. Many variables have not been 
included and only conceptual open space plans, narratives and renderings have been provided. 
 
The PDA Master Plan states that 13 acres or 58% of the site will be open space. This should be 
quantified and delineated prior to approval of the master plan. It should be clarified whether the 
calculations include public realm such as streets and sidewalks; water sheet acreage; designated 
port areas; activated ground floor retail; green roofs; the Community Path easement; etc. 
 
It is not clear how the 6.65 acres of “additional open space and public gathering spaces 
including activated ground floor retail” is being counted, or whether the activated ground floor 
retail is included in the calculation of 13 acres open space on site. 
 
 

7 
 
The open space needs should be assessed and the impacts mitigated prior to the approval of the 
PDA Master Plan. It is critical that the PDA Master Plan accommodate its open space needs 
onsite or mitigate them offsite. This should be confirmed prior to the approval of the PDA. 
 
The proposed height, massing and siting will impact Doherty Park. The density will impact both 
Doherty Park and Ryan Playground - already heavily utilized public open spaces. This should be 
mitigated through modifications to the project program, building design and offsite measures. 
 
Open spaces should be surveyed during the MEPA and BPDA approval process so that they are 
not diminished with subsequent amendments to the plan. 
 
Needs Analysis 
The PDA Master Plan does not readily provide the expected number of 
residents, visitors and other users or assess their open space and recreational needs. 
 
An open space needs analysis should be completed based on the projected users of open space. 
This analysis should estimate the demand for active recreational needs, the ability to 
accommodate those needs onsite, and/or the reliance on existing public open space. 
 
Impact Assessment The PDA Master Plan will add 1.8 million sf of development with 1050 
units. The users of the project will impact heavily used public parks for active recreation needs. 
 
The project should expect to meet the open space needs of its users within the project limits. It is 
critical that the project provide adequate active recreational open space onsite to meet the needs 
of its residents and reduce the burden on Doherty Park and Ryan Playground. 
 
Required Open Space 
The information below should be provided for further evaluation 
prior to the approval of the PDA Master Plan. The goal is to ensure that the open space is 
quantified and designed in a manner that meets the needs of the users and the neighborhood. 
Open space negotiated under the PDA or required by MEPA should not also count as a public 
benefit. Offsite mitigation should augment insufficient onsite open space. Open space negotiated 
in the PDA Master Plan or required by MEPA should be permanently protected in perpetuity.

Mitigation for impacts to adjacent open space and contributions to open space amenities. 

8 
 
Protection in Perpetuity 
Open space that is negotiated in exchange for PDA development 
rights; required by Chapter 91; or approved by the EOEEA Secretary as a Public Benefit should 
be transferred in fee to BPRD so that it is protected in perpetuity. It may be privately managed. 
 
Project Mitigation 
The height, massing, siting, density, scale and proximity of the project will 
significantly impact Doherty Park and Ryan Playground which are amenities to the project. 
 
The development program and buildings should be modified to eliminate impacts to the adjacent 
public parks. Impact mitigation in the form of a monetary contribution to the Fund for Parks 
should be provided at a scale commensurate with the scale and impacts of the development.

Dear Ms. Black,
The City of Boston’s Age Strong Commission is submitting the following comments on the
PDA Master Plan for the 425 Medford Street project currently proposed by The Flatley
Company.
1.
Pedestrian safety
We appreciate the attention to pedestrian experience, multiple modes of transit,
and recreational opportunities to make this space interactive and usable for all
visitors and passersby. We have some concerns about potential points of conflict
between users, especially older adult pedestrians who may react more slowly to
changes in their surroundings or have other sensory, cognitive, and functional
impairments that affect awareness of their surroundings.
a.
Pedestrian and bike points of conflict
We support the bike path that will enable active transportation, recreation,
and contribute to a more liveable city for all. However, we want to make sure
that attention is given to potential points of conflict between pedestrians and
bike riders. How will pedestrians, especially those coming from the dog park,
community plaza, or amphitheater, safely cross the bike path to access the
rest of the space?
b.
Active and distracted users
We support the recreational open and green spaces proposed for this project.
We believe that playgrounds, interactive water features, and sports courts
create space for community connections and intergenerational interactions.
We foresee potential points of conflict between distracted users of these
ACE+ 
City of Boston 
Age Strong Commission 
Mayor Michelle Wu 

spaces (children playing in water or on playgrounds, stray basketballs and
players chasing them). We would like to learn more about your plans to
contain these activities to the designated sites or otherwise buffer
pedestrian traffic around the sites to prevent potential conflicts.
c.
Wet surfaces
We would like to know how the site plans to address fall hazards around
water features, including the fountains, mist area, and floodable seats. We
commend the attention to climate resilient seating so that users of all ages
can enjoy this space for generations to come. We would like to know about
your plans to safely accommodate users when these features do become wet
from flooding. Will the cantilever steps be off limits until a certain time
period after a flooding event to allow them to dry fully, or are the steps
designed to safely accommodate users immediately after flooding has
receded?
2.
All age inclusion
We support the emphasis on community, play, and sports in this proposal. We are
excited about the variable uses and opportunity for outdoor activity and community
connections. We hope you will take steps to ensure that all members and all ages of
the community are invited into these spaces.
a.
Community plaza
At the BPDA scoping session, we heard some discussion about who will
manage the community plaza. We recommend that whoever manages this
building will provide programming for all ages. We also recommend paying
special attention to the design of this building so that it is not only accessible
but physically welcoming to community members of all ages and abilities.
b.
Sports court
We are excited that the sports court plans to include pickleball, which is
popular among older adults. We would like to learn more about who will
manage this court and how they will administer usage. Will the court be open
to the public? Will users be able to reserve the court? We hope that all
community members will be able to take advantage of the sports court
equally.
c.
Playground
We did not see detailed plans for the playground, but we do want to suggest
an age inclusive element. We recommend including outdoor exercise
equipment and/or adult playground equipment. This will create use
opportunities for all ages to exercise and interact with the site, as well as
spark intergenerational interactions and encourage a healthy community.

3.
Access to site
We appreciate the plans to connect this site to the larger community, especially by
extending the community bike path. We recognize that older adults should be able
to choose the mode of transportation that best suits their needs and abilities:
driving, walking, biking, or transit. We strongly support connections for active
transportation to encourage recreation and exercise, as well as accessible parking
and pickup and drop off prioritized for older adults to make the site accessible to all.
a.
Passenger pickup/drop off
We would like to learn more about plans for passenger pick up/dropoff. It is
important that this occurs away from potential points of conflict, such as
high vehicle traffic areas or the bike path, and as close as possible to building
entrances. We recommend adding this space on the road inside of the project
site for a centralized pickup/drop off point that allows those passengers to
access all parts of the site with less walking. A covered structure with
age-friendly seating (seat back and arm rests) would be ideal.
b.
Parking
We would like to learn more about the parking plan, particularly the plan for
accessible parking. Will some or all of the street parking be removed for this
project? We noticed that the existing street parking is reserved for
Charlestown residents for most of the week. Will this regulation stay in
place? We strongly encourage prioritizing some non-handicap parking
spaces for older adults?
4.
Usability
We want to ensure that this space is utilized as fully as possible, which means
anticipating needs by users of all ages. Older adults prefer to recreate in places
where they know they will be able to rest and use the bathroom as needed.
a.
Benches
We recommended adding benches at regular intervals along pedestrian paths
and corridors, as well as any lookout areas. Age friendly benches should have
a back as well as armrests that help older adults lift and lower themselves
onto the benches.
b.
Bathrooms
We recommend adding public bathrooms outside of the buildings so users
feel welcome to use the outdoor space without the confusion of finding an
indoor restroom or needing a reason to be in any of the indoor spaces.
5.
Accessibility
a.
Cantilever steps
The cantilever steps should be designed to include users who struggle to
navigate steps. The rendering does appear to include a ramp near the boat
launch, although this is unclear.

i.
Railings/grab bars
We recommend adding at least one railing with grab bars along the
steps at water’s edge. This railing would help users navigate safely
down the steps, with grab bars on the outside to help themselves lift
or lower onto the steps for seating. Even one or two railings at
different points along the steps would help make this area welcoming
to all.
ii.
Seating on the periphery or bridge
We also recommend seating that allows users to interact with the
waterfront without needing to navigate the steps. This could include
benches at the edge of the pedestrian way before the steps begin
and/or benches on the overhanging boardwalk.
b.
Canopy coverage
There are multiple mature trees along Medford Street and in the vicinity of
the new community center. We strongly support the preservation and
addition of trees to this space for the mental and physical health benefits of
green space, as well as air quality and heat protection provided by tree
canopy. We encourage tree pits that prevent sidewalk heaving and tree pit
covers that do not impede pedestrians, especially those using mobility aids.
6.
Weather
a.
We encourage the use of permeable pavement to reduce pooling from rain
and the buildup of ice. Minimizing the effects of precipitation on walking
surfaces makes travel safer. Safer travel encourages older adults to get out in
the winter, and therefore reduces social isolation.
b.
The COVID-19 pandemic ushered in an unprecedented interest in outdoor
spaces for gathering, even during adverse weather. We encourage you to
consider how the outdoor space in this plan can be utilized in all weather,
particularly a mixed use and recreational district with an emphasis on
interaction with the natural elements of the waterfront. We are interested to
see other plans that preserve the use of open spaces in variable weather
conditions, possibly including awnings, space and electrical hookup capacity
for outdoor heaters, seating options during wet conditions, and further plans
to minimize the effect of snow and ice buildup, particularly at curb cuts.
7.
Dementia friendly
We recommend the inclusion of wayfinding signage that includes both words and
universal icons. Provide signage with both large graphics and symbols at eye-level in
clear color contrast to the background and glare-resistant. Include signs to exits
and entrances, restrooms, community plaza, sports court, playground and other
public-use buildings/spaces. Install visual landmarks at important intersections and
complex junctions to assist wayfinding. Ensure these areas are well-lit. Avoid using

black when creating checkerboard designs on concrete. Black paint on the ground
creates an illusion of a black hole for someone with dementia or similar cognitive
issues.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments and recommendations.

Dear Director Golden: 
On behalf of the Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport), I appreciate the opportunity to submit the enclosed 
comments regarding The Flatley Company's (Proponent) Proposed PDA Master Plan (the Plan) for their property 
located at 425 Medford Street in Charlestown (the Site). The Plan is of particular interest to Massport given its 
adjacency to Massport's Medford Street Terminal and Autoport properties and the Mystic River Designated Port 
Area (DPA). 
Designated Port Area 
Massport emphasizes the importance of protecting the DPA area within the Plan's boundaries and minimizing 
conflicts with adjacent DPA areas. On the Site, it is important to establish and maintain a vehicular connection from 
Medford Street to the DPA that can be easily navigated by trucks. The western part of DPA square footage within 
the current Plan is shown as being used for proposed shoreline resiliency infrastructure, which will not be available 
to support maritime industrial use. Massport has asked the Proponent to consider reconfiguring the DPA area on 
the Site (with no change in total DPA square footage) to maximize its utility and improve its access to the adjacent 
slip. Additionally, the Proponent's development/design efforts should continue to consider nearby DPA uses, 
including the Autoport's operations at the Medford Street Terminal. Massport appreciates that the Plan as 
proposed does not contemplate any residential uses in the buildings on the eastern side of the Plan area, adjacent 
to the Medford Street Terminal. Future tenant agreements should acknowledge and seek to buffer and protect the 
maritime industrial uses in the Mystic River DPA. 
Transportation 
The proposed Plan will have a transformational effect on the Charlestown neighborhood with nearly 1.84 million 
square feet of proposed new development with a mix of commercial, research and development/lab, residential, 
and hotel space. The Proponent must take steps to minimize traffic impacts from this development on key 
transportation routes in the area, particularly Medford Street, as well as Terminal Street and Chelsea Street, a 
federally designated freight corridor, which serve as primary truck routes to the Autoport. 
Building Heights 
Massport has developed the Logan Airspace Map (Airspace Map) that defines the critical airspace around Logan 
Airport. The Airspace Map was created with input from airlines, pilots, city officials, and the Federal Aviation 
Administration (FAA) to protect the flight corridors in and out of the airport and to help guide developers and 
regulatory authorities on building heights. The Airspace Map aids developers in their planning and informs the FAA 
approval process of individual projects to determine if they present a potential hazard to air navigation.

It appears that the proposed heights included in the PDA Master Plan are consistent with the Airspace Map limits.

that proposed buildings do not exceed the airspace limit as defined by the Airspace Map (see 
http://www.massport.com/media/1545/boston-logan-airspace-map.pdf). The Airspace Map is based on the NAVO 
88 Datum as required by the FAA. To calculate the actual allowable building height, the site elevation, also based 
on NAVO 88, needs to be subtracted from the Airspace Limit at that location. Please note that the height of the 
structure is derived from the tallest building elements, such as rooftop utilities, elevator overrides, antennae, and 
any architectural design features. 
Coastal Resiliency 
The Plan's proposed investments in coastal resiliency are significant and commendable. Given the Site's waterfront 
location on the Mystic River, it is uniquely positioned to address coastal flooding and protect inland neighborhoods 
in Boston and other adjacent municipalities. It will be important for the Proponent to consider how the increased 
elevation along the perimeter of the Site connects to Medford Street, the existing rail corridor, and the Medford 
Street Terminal area to the east. In particular, in its design and planning efforts, the Proponent must consider 
Massport's existing rail easement along the rail corridor parallel to Medford Street, and ensure that a future 
reactivation of the rail is not precluded by any of the resiliency improvements. Similarly, such resiliency 
improvements, including raised ground elevations near the water's edge, should not preclude future use of the DPA 
area within the Plan. Massport requests that the Proponent coordinate with Massport to review how the resiliency 
improvements will fit into the larger context of the neighborhood and the Mystic River DPA. 
Public Access/Community Path 
The Proponent has been actively working with Massport and the BPDA to improve public access in the area, 
specifically advancing the Charlestown Community Path along the southern portion of the Site. Mass port looks 
forward to continuing the good collaboration on this important project, which will be a valuable community 
amenity and important connection for pedestrians and bicyclists. All public access plans, including the Charlestown 
Community Path, must consider Mass port's existing rail easement, and the potential reactivation of the rail in the

PROJECT SITE 
 
The Proposed Project is located on an approximately 11,762 square foot parcel of land 
located at 43 Preble Street in the Andrew Square neighborhood of South Boston (the 
“Project Site”). The Project Site is currently occupied by a single-story concrete block 
building used as an auto repair shop, with the vast majority of the site being used for 
surface vehicle storage. 43 Preble Street is located within a two-minute walk of the MBTA’s 
Andrew Station Red Line rapid transit and bus station.

PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
Thomas J. Noto (the “Proponent”) seeks to demolish the existing commercial auto repair 
structure occupying the Project Site and construct a four (4) story, approximately 40,242 
gross square foot residential building that will contain thirty (30) homeownership dwelling 
units, including five (5) income-restricted units, approximately 783 square feet of ground-
floor commercial space, and up to eighteen (18) off-street vehicle parking spaces (the 
“Proposed Project”). One (1) of the vehicle parking spaces will be dedicated to commercial 
uses, and the remaining will be dedicated to residential uses. The Proposed Project will also 
include an interior bicycle storage room with space for thirty-two (32) bicycles for residents 
and eight (8) exterior bicycle storage spaces for the public, consistent with the City of 
Boston Transportation Department (“BTD”) Bike Parking Guidelines. The residential 
homeownership units include approximately thirteen (13) one-bedroom units, sixteen (16) 
two-bedroom units, and one (1) three-bedroom unit. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The Project Site is located in the South Boston neighborhood district, within an L-5 Local 
Business subdistrict, pursuant to the Underlying Zoning articles of the Zoning Code. 
Dimensional regulations within the L-5 subdistrict reference those in the nearest H, R, or S 
subdistrict to the proposed development site. To the south of the relevant subdistrict, 
bounded to the north by Devine Way is a large H-1, Apartment Residential subdistrict. The 
Project Site is also located within the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District (CFROD), 
which would require any new construction to meet resilient design standards. These 
standards include elevating the ground floor of the building above Base Flood Elevation 
(“BFE”) for the year 2070, and limiting the uses that can be located below the Design Flood 
Elevation (“DFE”). The BFE for the Project Site is 19.5’. The required freeboard for this type 
of development is 1 foot, requiring a 20.5’ DFE. 
 
The Project Site is located at the southern edge of the PLAN: South Boston Dorchester 
Avenue (‘‘PLAN: Dot Ave’’) study area. The Plan: Dot Ave sets forth guidelines for building

dimension and use, derived from community input. Suggested heights are maximized 
nearest to the Andrew MBTA Station and to the west of Dorchester Avenue within the study 
area, topping out at 300’. East of Dorchester Avenue, along Preble Street, the Plan: Dot Ave 
recommends buildings with heights up to 60’. PLAN: Dot Ave was not codified into zoning, 
but it was adopted by the BPDA Board in December 2016. 
 
The Project Site is included within the proposed Use Zone 3: Residential + select 1st Floor 
Retail, demonstrating further alignment with PLAN: Dot Ave. The Plan: Dot Ave envisions 
this area as a buffer/transition zone between the commercial centers along Dorchester 
Avenue, the residential uses south of the study area, and the open space to the east in 
Moakley Park. Greenspace along Preble Street is only proposed in PLAN: Dot Ave through 
the addition of a continuous line of street trees along the sidewalks, which has been 
included in this proposed development scheme. Three street trees, evenly spaced, are 
proposed along the Preble Street frontage of the building, with an additional three to be 
added along Rogers Street, and four along Wendeller Street. 
 
While the existing zoning was compared to the proposed development site, more relevant 
to the site is the proposed zoning as per PLAN: Dot Ave. The PLAN: Dot Ave calls for up to 
60’ in height at the proposed site and increased density, relegating the zoning FAR, height, 
and setbacks suitable for zoning relief.

BPDA for the Proposed Project, pursuant to Article 80E of the Code. The BPDA sponsored 
and held virtual public meetings via Zoom on January 29, 2024, November 18, 2024 and 
August 18, 2025. The meetings was advertised in the local newspapers, posted on the 
BPDA website and a notification was emailed to all subscribers of the BPDA’s South Boston 
neighborhood update list. The public comment period ended on February 9, 2024.

Brighton is located at the corner of Leo M. Birmingham Parkway and Lothrop Street

The proposed redevelopment of the Project Site calls for the construction of a six 
(6)-story, approximately 39,505 gross square foot, residential multi-family building 
(the “Proposed Project”). The Proposed Project is contemplated to include 
approximately thirty-eight (38) residential rental units, approximately 2,315 SF of 
lobby and amenity space, including a sixth-floor outdoor patio for tenants, thirteen 
(13) accessory off-street parking spaces, and sixty (60) bike storage spaces. The 
Project will utilize alternative transit options, including a shared electric vehicle 
available to tenants to reduce vehicular traffic. The Project will also have solar PV on

On February 8, 2022, the Proponent filed a Small Project Review Application 
(“SPRA”) with the BPDA for the Proposed Project, pursuant to Article 80E of the 
Code. A Virtual Public Meeting to discuss the Proposed Project was held on April 13,

the public comment period in connection with the SPRA submission was extended 
by request of the Proponent, concluding on April 27, 2022, in order to allow the 
Proponent more time to engage directly with the neighborhood.

of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”). The Project Site is also located within a 
Greenbelt Protection Overlay District (“GPOD”), which is governed by Article 29 of 
the Code.

1. Insufficient Off-Street Parking 
2. Excessive Floor Area Ratio (“FAR”)

The project is located directly south of the study area for the Western Avenue 
Corridor Rezoning Study (WACRZ), currently in its final stages of refinements 
through an extensive community process. The WACRZ process has identified that 
multi-family residential development with active ground floor uses is a priority for 
this portion of the Western Avenue Corridor and area of Allston-Brighton in order 
to provide needed housing along a multi-modal retail corridor. 
 
During review, the team focused on securing safe vehicular access to the site and 
the design and location of usable open space and landscaping. Most importantly, 
the project’s mitigation advances the long-term plans for Leo Birmingham Parkway 
that the BPDA and the City worked with DCR on in 2017 as part of the Western 
Avenue at Leo M. Birmingham Parkway and Arsenal Street Intersection & Corridor

December 10, 2015 (the “IDP”) and is located within Zone B, as defined by the IDP.

designated as IDP units, and the WACRZ further recommends 19% of residential 
unit square footage as IDP units restricted at an average of 60% of Area Median 
Income (“AMI”). In this case, the Proposed Project has committed to providing seven

annually by the BPDA and based upon data from the United States Department of 
Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”), with the remaining one (1) unit made 
affordable to households earning not more than 100% of AMI.

SUMMARY: 
 
 
 
This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment 
Authority d/b/a/ Boston Planning & Development Agency (the 
“BPDA”): (1) approve the Third Amendment to Second Amended 
and Restated Development Plan for 49, 51 and 63 Melcher Street, 
within Planned Development Area No. 69, South Boston/The 100 
Acres (the “Development Plan”), in connection with the Proposed 
Project; (2) authorize the Director to petition the Boston Zoning 
Commission for approval of the Development Plan pursuant to 
Section 80C-7 of the Code; (3) authorize the Director to issue a 
Scoping Determination waiving the requirement of further review 
pursuant to Section 80B-5.3(d) of the Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Code”) for the proposed conversion of the building located at 51 
Melcher Street Boston, Massachusetts from office to life science 
laboratory with supporting office and accessory uses (the 
“Proposed Project”); (4) authorize the Director to issue a 
Certification of Compliance or Partial Certification of Compliance for 
the Proposed Project pursuant to Section 80B-6 of the Code, upon 
successful completion of the Article 80 Large Project Review 
process; (5) authorize the Director to issue a Certification of 
Consistency or Partial Certification of Consistency for the Proposed 
Project pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Code, upon successful 

 
 
completion of the Article 80C Planned Development Area Review 
process; and (6) authorize the Director to execute and deliver any 
and all documents, or amendments thereto, as the Director deems 
appropriate and necessary in connection with the Proposed Project 
and the Development Plan. 
 
 
PROJECT SITE 
 
The Proposed Project is bounded by Melcher Street to the North, Necco Court to 
the south, 49 Melcher Street to the west and 63 Melcher to the east (the “Project 
Site”). The approximately 13,927 square foot Project Site is composed of one parcel 
owned by GI ETS Fort Point I, LLC (the “Proponent”). The existing building on the 
Project Site, built in 1915, is nine stories tall with approximately 97,000 sf of office 
space.

PDA BACKGROUND 
 
On December 4, 2008, in accordance with that certain Master Plan (as amended 
through the Fifth Amendment dated October 21, 2020) for Planned Development 
Area No. 69 (The Hundred Acres), the BPDA approved a Development Plan for 49, 
51 and 63 Melcher (as modified as described below, the "Original Development 
Plan"). The Original Development Plan proposed a rehabilitation and expansion of 
the existing commonly-owned buildings at the Site (as defined in the Original 
Development Plan) into a single integrated office building with first-level 
retail/service space (as modified as described below, the "Original Project"). On 
February 4, 2009, the Boston Zoning Commission (the "Commission") approved the 
Original Development Plan, which became effective on February 5, 2009. 
 
On April 14, 2011, the BPDA approved a First Amended and Restated Development 
Plan, which the Commission approved on May 4, 2011, and became effective on 
May 6, 2011, and on February 16, 2012, the BPDA approved a Second Amended and 
Restated Development Plan, which the Commission approved on March 14, 2012, 

 
 
and which became effective the same day, both of which allowed certain changes 
to the design, use and phasing of the Original Project. Specifically, the Second 
Amended and Restated Development Plan separated the Original Project into three 
phases, to be developed by separate owners: "Phase I" at 63 Melcher Street; "Phase 
II" at the Project Site; and "Phase III" at 49 Melcher Street. On June 13, 2013, the 
BPDA approved a First Amendment to the Second Amended and Restated 
Development Plan revising the amount of Gross Floor Area (as defined in the Code) 
permitted in Phase II, which the Commission approved on July 10, 2013, and which 
became effective the same day. On February 16, 2012, the BPDA approved a 
Second Amendment to the Second Amended and Restated Development Plan 
revising the amount of Gross Floor Area permitted in Phase III, which the 
Commission approved on March 14, 2012, and which became effective the same 
day. Construction of Phases I, II and III of the Original Project is now complete. The 
Proposed Project results in a change in use of the Phase II portion of the Original 
Project. 
 
PROPOSED PROJECT DESCRIPTION 
 
The Proponent proposes to change the building use from office to life science 
laboratory with supporting office and accessory uses, including certain associated 
exterior building upgrades. The Development Plan, filed with the BPDA on March 3, 
2022, seeks to (i) establish the means through which the Proponent will 
demonstrate compliance of the Proposed Project with groundwater conservation 
and coastal flood resilience requirements of the Code, (ii) clarify the permitted uses 
at the Project Site (including by limiting any new laboratory space to biosafety levels 
1 and 2), and (iii) provide cross-default protections customarily applied to multi-
phased projects anticipated to be developed by separate owners. The Development 
Plan will have no effect on any area within the Develop Plan or the Master Plan for 
Planned Development Area No. 69, South Boston/The 100 Acres, as amended (the 
"Master Plan”), other than the Project Site. 
 
The Proponent has committed to meet the following design and operational 
standards intended to address concerns with the impacts of lab use raised by 
residential abutters: 
• All vivariums must be designed by qualified designers and consultants 
experienced in vivarium design; 
• The Proponent will engage an outside 3rd party company to review the 
design and operation of any vivarium to ensure that it complies with all 

 
 
applicable federal, state and local regulations and will not otherwise create a 
hazard to the neighborhood; 
• All vivariums must be self-contained and located near the core of the 
building, not along the perimeter walls of the building; and 
• The Project may not have more than (2) vivariums, and each such vivarium 
may not exceed 3,500 sf. 
• All chemical storage rooms must be self-contained and located near the core 
of the building, not along the perimeter walls of the building; 
• The Property Manager for the entirety of 51 Melcher will oversee chemical 
storage, permitting and compliance for all tenants; and 
• The Proponent will work with neighbors to establish a detailed community 
communications plan for public safety operations in the event a reportable 
incident occurs which may materially impact the neighboring buildings. 
 
Further, the Proponent has committed to install STC55-rated walls at all party walls 
prior to construction and during operation to limit construction impacts on 
adjacent residential uses. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT AND CITY STAFF REVIEW 
 
The Proposed Project is not located within the boundaries of a recent planning 
initiative. Instead, Planning Division staff considered the neighborhood context, 
adopted citywide plans including Imagine Boston 2030 and Go Boston 2030, 
Climate Ready Boston, the Zoning Code, and public feedback to review the 
Proposed Project. The key considerations of BPDA staff during review of the 
Proposed Project were: the project’s size and scale; proposed use and program 
within the existing envelope of the building; safe and convenient pedestrian and 
bicycle access and mobility; and climate resiliency. BPDA Planning Division staff met 
with the Proponent to address these considerations. 
 
ARTICLE 80 AND PUBLIC REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On November 1, 2021, the Proponent filed a Letter of Intent (the “LOI”) with the 
BPDA for the Proposed Project. On December 2, 2021, the Proponent filed a Project 
Notification Form (the ”PNF”) with the BPDA. The BPDA formed an Impact Advisory 
Group (“IAG”) on January 18, 2022, and held a Scoping Session on January 31, 2022. 
On March 3, 2022, the Proponent filed the Development Plan with the BPDA. Two 
IAG meetings were held virtually on March 8, 2022 and May 31, 2022, and two 
publicly advertised virtual public meetings were held regarding the PNF and 

 
 
Development Plan, on March 16, 2022 April 18, 2022. The public comment period 
for the PDA Amendment closed on April 17, 2022 and for the PNF on May 3, 2022. 
In addition to the above-mentioned meetings, the Proponent also conducted 
community outreach and attended a series of meetings before and during the 
Article 80 review process with abutters, local elected officials, local non-profit 
organizations, and nearby neighborhood civic associations to discuss the Proposed 
Project and solicit feedback. 
Sustainability 
 
● The building will be designed and constructed to meet LEED v4 BD+C Core 
and Shell Gold performance with 65 points and (presently) has a Building 2035 
pCEI 6.20 kg CO2e/sf-yr. 
● The building design will prioritize efficiency and electrification strategies to 
target a 97% reduction in fossil fuel consumption. Prior to the execution of a 
Cooperation Agreement for the Project, the Proponent and the IGBC will 
determine the appropriate means of achieving such reduction, which will be 
memorialized in the Cooperation Agreement. 
● The Cooperation Agreement will contain details on the Proponent’s 
obligations with respect to coordinating building planning and design to 
optimize solar renewable energy output and providing a preliminary system(s) 
design including system size, layout, and output in the Article 37 Design Filing. 
To the extent feasible, the Proponent shall support the installation of the system 
prior to final occupancy. 
● The proponent will complete and provide updated performance modeling 
prior to starting Design Development and providing Article 37 Design and 
Construction Filings 
Smart Utilities 
The Proponent agrees to complete the Smart Utilities review prior to obtaining a 
Certificate of Compliance. The items to be reviewed include: 
● Proposed transformer location lies within an Electrical Rm with access from 
Melcher St. Proponent will continue coordinating with Eversource, Public 
Improvement Commission (PIC) and BPDA design review staff to confirm 
● On-going review of Stormwater retention and/or management of 1.25 inches 
over the impervious area and confirmed on updated USP as it relates to car 
stacking system and associated infrastructure. 
● Proponent will coordinate conduit to support the Smart Streetlight 
requirement, running along the street light conduit and shadow under the 
sidewalks on Melcher Street., as applicable based on scope of sidewalk 

 
 
reconstruction (to be reviewed as part of on-going review processes with 
Urban Design and PIC). 
● A plan to address relevant conflicts reported through COBUCS if/as relevant. 
 
PUBLIC BENEFITS 
 
The Proposed Project will provide a number of public benefits to the immediate 
Fort Point neighborhood and the City of Boston as a whole. Through discussions 
with the IAG, the Boston Transportation Department (“BTD”) and members of the 
general public, the Proponent has committed up to $450,000 in support of public 
amenities and benefits, to be completed prior to the issuance of the Certificate of 
Occupancy by ISD for the Proposed Project, including the following: 
● Substantial Investment in sidewalk and streetscape improvements to the 
surrounding area, the scope of which will be determined in consultation with 
BTD, in order to provide a more complete pedestrian solution for the street, 
including designing plans to bring Melcher Street into compliance with the 
Americans with Disabilities Act Standards for Accessible Design; 
● Repairs and improvements to the historic skybridge between the Proposed 
Project and the adjacent building located at 281 Summer Street, which is a 
character-defining component of the Fort Point Channel Landmarks District; 
● A $60,000 contribution to local scholarship fund(s) to support Boston high 
school students seeking degrees in science, technology, engineering, and 
math (STEM); and 
● A $45,000 contribution to local arts organization(s) to be used for public art 
installation(s) in the area. 
 
In addition, the Proposed Project will provide the following public benefits: 
 
● The Proponent will donate office furniture at the Project Site—worth up to an 
estimated $100,000—to The Furniture Trust, a local non-profit dedicated to 
distributing used office furniture to local schools, nonprofits and community 
organizations, providing environmentally sustainable positive community 
impacts. 
● Proposed Project will greatly reduce greenhouse gas emissions of the 
building as part of the design commitment to LEED Gold certifiability; 
● Installation of soundproof STC55-rated wall at party walls before 
construction and during operations; 
● Installation of window treatments to mitigate light, and occupancy sensors to 
turn off or reduce minimum lighting levels; 

 
 
● Flood resilience measures will be implemented in order to prepare the 
Project Site for the 1 percent annual chance flood risk in the year 2070 with 
40” of sea level rise; 
● Historic features and façade will remain unchanged to stay consistent with 
neighborhood context; 
● Garden-level conference room space will be made available during off-hours 
for community use; 
● Increased on-site bicycle storage and accessibility, and availability for 
bikeshare accommodations (subject to ongoing coordination with BTD), 
promoting non-vehicular commuting and further-alleviating traffic; 
● The creation of construction jobs and permanent jobs; 
● The creation of approximately 101 construction jobs and 304 permanent 
jobs; and 
● Building conversion will increase marketability of the Project Site to avoid 
vacancy and ensure vibrant and active tenants and additional property tax 
revenue for the City of Boston. 
 
In addition, the Proponent intends to be an active and engaged corporate citizen 
and member of the Fort Point community. 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, the BPDA staff recommends that the BPDA Board: (1) 
approve the Development Plan, in connection with the Proposed Project; (2) 
authorize the Director to petition the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of 
the Development Plan pursuant to Section 80C-7 of the Code; (3) authorize the 
Director to issue a Scoping Determination waiving the requirement of further 
review pursuant to Section 80B-5.3(d) of the Code for the Proposed Project; (4) 
authorize the Director to issue a Certification of Compliance or Partial Certification 
of Compliance for the Proposed Project pursuant to Section 80B-6 of the Code, 
upon successful completion of the Article 80 Large Project Review process; (5) 
authorize the Director to issue a Certification of Consistency or Partial Certification 
of Consistency for the Proposed Project pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Code, 
upon successful completion of the Article 80C Planned Development Area Review 
process; and (6) authorize the Director to execute and deliver any and all 
documents, or amendments thereto, as the Director deems appropriate and 
necessary in connection with the Proposed Project and the Development Plan.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
 
The Project Site was previously part of South Boston’s 20th Century industrial zone, 
which stretches along the western side of Dorchester Avenue, between the MBTA’s 
Andrew and Broadway Subway stations. Still part of the South Bay as late as 1903, 
from the 1940s through the early 2000s, the Site was used as an industrial scrap and 
salvage yard. Due to its prior use, the Site is under Federal and State regulatory 
oversight by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) and Massachusetts 
Department of Environmental Protection (“DEP”) and requires extensive 
environmental remediation. As such, it presents an enormous opportunity to 
transform a blighted, vacant brownfield into a part of a new active and pedestrian-
friendly, transit-oriented development. 
 
The Proposed Project calls for the construction of a new 237-unit market rate, 16-
story residential building and a new 7-story, 94-unit income-restricted midrise 
building for seniors joined by a shared podium. The Proposed Project will contain 
approximately 326,000 square feet of gross floor area, including approximately 
11,710 square feet of ground floor retail / commercial space and 88 below grade 
parking spaces. The senior midrise building will have dedicated amenities and 
services common to service-enriched senior housing as well as full access to shared 
amenities within the planned community such as a gym, social activities, retail 
services and newly created open space. The programming will include supportive 
services to enhance the resident experience and quality of life and to maintain

partner for the project and will bring their very thorough program of services 
coordination, dedicated, and community-based services to this senior community. 
 
The Proposed Project’s 94-unit senior housing community will be its own separate 
condominium program within the overall 495 Dorchester Avenue project, with 
restrictions and financing through the low-income housing tax credit (“LIHTC”) 
program using 4% tax credits through tax-exempt debt. Other capital financing 
includes Linkage / Housing Creation funding generated by Phase 1 of the Master Plan 
and developer financing for the Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”) contribution 
as prescribed by the permitting. The IDP contribution amount will be finalized upon 
the approval of Phase 1B of the Master Plan Project, which is currently undergoing 
review by the BPDA under Article 80B. The senior housing component represents the 
fulfillment of the IDP requirement for the 495 Dorchester Avenue project, with the 
inclusion of forty-three (43) designated IDP units located within the senior midrise 
building. 
 
The Proposed Project is a key component in realizing the vision for PLAN: South 
Boston Dorchester Avenue (“PLAN: Dot Ave”) and the PLAN: South Boston Dorchester 
Avenue Transportation Planning Study. It will transform this long-distressed Project 
Site into residential uses and ground floor retail and commercial space. 
 
The Proposed Project will provide a significant number of income-restricted housing 
units within the PDA Master Plan area and increase the available high-quality housing 
stock in South Boston and will offer ground floor retail space to allow for activation of 
the public realm. Since the filing of the Supplemental Information document on June 
30, 2023, the Proponent has refined the residential program to increase the amount 
of affordable housing by introducing a 100% affordable midrise senior housing

PLANNING CONTEXT 
The Project Project is located in the geography of PLAN: South Boston, Dorchester 
Avenue, adopted by the BPDA Board in December 2016. Planning staff incorporated 
recommendations from this plan, as well the PLAN: South Boston Dorchester Avenue 
Transportation Plan and the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District (Zoning Article 
25) which were both adopted in 2021. 
PLAN: South Boston, Dorchester Avenue established a framework for the area’s 
evolution from an industrial to mixed-use neighborhood. While this plan was not 
codified as an update to the underlying zoning, plan recommendations did shape the 
zoning overlay for Planned Development Area (PDA) Number 144, CORE on the Dot, 
approved by the Boston Zoning Commission in October 2023. The Proposed Project is 
described in the PDA Master Plan and conforms to the PDA Master Plan. 
PLAN: South Boston, Dorchester Avenue recommendations for use, height, lot 
coverage, and new and existing public right-of-way (ROW) dimensions guided the 
evolution of the Master Plan PDA. The Proposed Project reflects these 
recommendations as the first phase of a Master Plan that will preserve ROW 
dimensions to achieve Complete Streets standards, create, maintain, and protect 
publicly accessible open spaces, and achieve a minimum 35% residential square 
footage across the Master Plan site. 
 
URBAN DESIGN 
The massing of the project, following PLAN: Dot Ave, appropriately steps down along 
Dorchester Avenue to the lower scale neighborhood to the east. 
The ground floor is designed to bridge resilience requirements of a raised floor level 
while providing different types of access for different users. 
In addition to commercial space, outdoor space is provided for the senior housing 
component to help activate the Dorchester Avenue street front. 
The character of the high-rise and mid-rise sections of the project are different to 
provide visual variety while being related in material, color, and fenestration to 
provide continuity.

to households earning not less than 30% of Area Median Income (“AMI”), as based

(“HUD”) and to households earning not less than 50% AMI. 
Of the 94 income-restricted units, forty-three (43) will be designated as IDP units, with 
ten (10) units at 80% of AMI or below and thirty-three (33) units at 60% of AMI or 
below. Affordability within the senior building will range from extremely low-income 
(ELI) units to self-pay LIHTC rents. Ten (10) units will be ELI and homeless priority, and 
another ten (10) units to ELI residents. The Proponent is also requesting Section 8 
and MRVP vouchers from EOHLC and PBVs from the BHA. The goal is to include 51 
units assisted by various operating subsidy programs and available to low-income 
seniors. The remaining 43 units will be IDP units, most set at 60% AMI with rents 
lowered to below 50% AMI, and 10 units with 80% AMI limit and rents set around 70% 
AMI. The Proponent will seek 4% LIHTC for the senior housing component, which will 
apply to the IDP units, but no EOHLC or City affordable housing subsidies or funding 
sources will be applied to the IDP Units. In summary, the 94 income-restricted units 
will be offered at a mix of income levels, ranging from 30% AMI to 80% AMI.
