1. 
PLANNED DEVELOPMENT AREA DEVELOPMENT PLAN: On October 
12, 2023, the Boston Redevelopment Authority, doing business as the Boston Planning & 
Development Agency (the “Authority”) approved the Master Plan for Planned Development 
Area No. 144 (the “PDA Master Plan”) pursuant to Article 3, Section 3-1A and Article 80, 
Section 80C of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”) for the parcels of land along Dorchester 
Avenue in South Boston (the “Development”). Capitalized terms used herein without definition 
which are defined in the PDA Master Plan shall have the meanings ascribed to them therein. 
 
On December 13, 2023, the Boston Zoning Commission (the “Commission”), by the 
adoption of Map Amendment No. 144, approved the PDA Master Plan and amended the series of 
maps entitled “Zoning Districts City of Boston,” dated August 15, 1962, as amended, by adding 
a “D” designation, indicating a Planned Development Area overlay district, to the 495 Project 
Site. 
 
The PDA Master Plan contemplates that one or more PDA Development Plans for phases 
of the Development may be submitted either simultaneously with or subsequent to the 
submission of the PDA Master Plan. 
 
In accordance with Article 3, Section 3-1A of the Code and Article 80, Section 80C, this 
development plan sets forth information on the construction of Phase 1A of the Development 
comprising 495 Dorchester Avenue (the “495 Project”). The 495 Project is located on an 
approximately 53,791 sf portion (the “495 Project Site”) of the of the approximately 21 acre site 
described in the PDA Master Plan along Dorchester Avenue in the South Boston section of 
Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts. The 495 Project Site is currently vacant. It has long 
been used for industrial purposes and the 495 Project will entail substantial environmental 
remediation due to the prior industrial uses. 

 
 
 
This development plan includes the proposed location and appearance of structures, open 
spaces and landscaping, the proposed uses of the 495 Project, the proposed dimensions of the 
structures, the proposed densities, the proposed traffic circulation, parking and loading facilities, 
access to public transportation and other major elements of the 495 Project (the “Development 
Plan”). This Development Plan constitutes the permanent zoning for the 495 Project and 
supersedes any existing zoning requirements contained in the Code. 
 
2. 
DEVELOPER: The owners and developer of the 495 Project Site is On the Dot 
LLC and entities affiliated with Core Investments, Inc. (with their successors and assigns, the 
“Owner” or the “Developer”). 
 
3. 
LOCATION AND DESCRIPTION OF THE PROJECT SITE: The 495 
Project Site is the approximately 53,791 square foot portion of the land described as Phase 1A in 
the PDA Master Plan. As of the date of this Development Plan, the 495 Project Site has not been 
subdivided into separate lots for zoning purposes. The Developer shall have the right to so 
subdivide the 495 Project Site at any time, which subdivision shall not require amendment of this 
Development Plan. 
 
The 495 Project Site lies in the South Boston District and more particularly within the I-2 
zoning district in which Planned Development Areas are allowed (the “Zoning District”). 
 
4. 
PROPOSED LOCATION AND APPEARANCE OF STRUCTURES: The 
495 Project consists of the development of one new building along with new sidewalks leading 
from Dorchester Avenue and Alger Street. The 495 Project consists of the development of one 
(1) new building containing approximately 326,000 square feet with 237 market rate units, 94 
units of affordable housing for seniors that will serve very low-income seniors with supportive 
services, two ground floor retail and commercial spaces containing a total of approximately 
8,437 square feet. There will be up-to 88 parking spaces constructed beneath the structure in an 
underground garage that will be accessed from Alger Street. 
 
The 495 Project is consistent with the criteria specified in Section 80C-4 of the Code for 
the approval of planned development areas in that the underlying zoning does not prohibit 
planned development areas, and the 495 Project Site is not located in a residential zoning district. 
Further, this Development Plan generally conforms to the plan for this area, including without 
limitation, the BPDA PLAN: Dot Ave. and PLAN South Boston Dorchester Ave. Transportation 
Plan; and on balance, nothing in this Development Plan will be injurious to the neighborhood or 
otherwise detrimental to the public welfare. This Development Plan furthers the goals of the 
neighborhood to create a vibrant, mixed-use, transit oriented development. 
 
Plans showing the architectural elements of the building comprising the 495 Project 
entitled “On the Dot Residential Plans” prepared by Utile (collectively, the “Project Plans”) are 
attached hereto as Appendix A and incorporated herein by this reference. 
 
5. 
OPEN SPACES AND LANDSCAPING: The 495 Project includes new 
sidewalks, bike lanes, new curbing, and street trees on the immediately adjacent portions of 

 
 
Dorchester Avenue and Alger Street, as illustrated in the attached Site Plan as Appendix B. The 
open space totals approximately 16,123 sf of which approximately 11,192 sf will be for the use 
of the residents. The public East Open space identified in the PDA Master Plan will be located 
adjacent to the 495 Project and will be further described in the PDA Development Plan that will 
be filed for Phase 1B immediately following this Development Plan. 
 
6. 
PROPOSED USES OF THE PROJECT SITE AND STRUCTURES: In 
accordance with Article 80, Section 80C of the Code, the uses of the 495 Project and 495 Project 
Site may include the allowed and conditional uses set forth in the Code, including without 
limitation the uses set forth in the PDA Master Plan, and described by reference to the definitions 
set forth in Article 2 of the Code as in effect on the date of approval of the PDA Master Plan, 
except as otherwise noted, all of which uses, notwithstanding any classification to the contrary in 
the Code, are expressly allowed within the 495 Project Site. A description of the major use 
components for the 495 Project is set forth in Appendix D. 
 
 
 
7.

9. 
PROPOSED VEHICULAR AND PEDESTRIAN TRAFFIC 
CIRCULATION: 
 
Traffic Circulation: 
 
Currently, the 495 Project Site has access from Dorchester Avenue and Alger Street. 
Alger Street will be improved, as will the sidewalks on Dorchester Ave. 
 
 
Pedestrian Circulation: 
 
The new sidewalks will be constructed to be in compliance with the City of Boston 
Complete Streets guidelines, with trees, landscaping, crosswalks, signage and other pedestrian 
friendly facilities. The major pedestrian routes will be along Dorchester Avenue, Alger Street, 
and the future Ellery Street. The MBTA Andrew Square Red Line T stop is approximately 150 
feet to the south of the 495 Project Site and pedestrians will be able to easily access this major 
subway and bus facility from the 495 Project Site. 
 
 
10. 
PARKING AND LOADING FACILITIES: 
 
Parking facilities will be provided underground, beneath the building with a total of 
approximately 88 underground parking spaces. The loading areas for the 495 Project will be off 
Alger Street and the below-grade parking garage entrance will be off Alger Street. The garage 
parking spaces included in the 495 Project need not comply with any parking stall or 
maneuvering aisle dimensional requirements of the Code. 
 
 
The 495 Project’s parking and loading facilities shall be subject to review and approval 
by the BPDA in accordance with the requirements of Article 80. Upon the issuance by the 
BPDA of a Certification of Compliance and a Certification of Consistency (or Partial 
Certification of Compliance or Partial Certification of Consistency, if applicable), the parking 
and loading facilities for the 495 Project and for each component of the 495 Project shall be 
deemed to be in compliance with the requirements of the Restricted Parking Overlay District and 
all other parking and loading requirements set forth in the Code. 
 
11. 
ACCESS TO PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION: The 495 Project Site is located 
within convenient distance of the MBTA public transportation system. The Red Line Andrew 
Square Station is located to the south, at a 3-5 minute walking distance from the 495 Project Site. 
Andrew Square Station is also a major MBTA bus hub. Many bus routes go through the station 
and make regular stops along Dorchester Avenue. 
 
12. 
ARTICLE 80B, LARGE PROJECT REVIEW: The undertaking of the 
Development (including without limitation the 495 Project) has been subject to Large Project 

 
 
Review by the Authority. In accordance with the requirements set forth in Section 80B, the 
Developer caused to be filed a Project Notification Form for the Project dated June 10, 2021. On 
March 16, 2022, the Developer filed a Draft Project Impact Report, and a Supplemental 
Information filing was made on June 30, 2023. 
 
13. 
AFFORDABLE HOUSING: The 495 Project includes 331 housing units, of 
which 94 units will be used for affordable housing serving low and very low-income seniors, 
with significant amenities and supportive services, dedicated to enhancing resident quality of life 
and maintain independent living as the residents age. These units represent 28% of the units of 
the 495 Project, well in excess of the City of Boston Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”) 
requirements, and the requirements of the PDA Master Plan. 
 
The 495 Project will also be fully compliant with the City of Boston Affirmatively 
Furthering Fair Housing and Affirmatively Integrated Communities (“AFFH”) policies and 
requirements. The Developer has been working with the Boston Interagency Fair Housing 
Development Committee (“BIFDC”) on the AFFH policies and requirements and will continue 
to work with BIFDC during the ongoing review process for the 495 Project. 
 
 
14. 
PUBLIC BENEFITS: The 495 Project, as a part of the Development, will 
provide substantial public benefits to the City of Boston and the surrounding neighborhood. 
These benefits will include: 
 
 
• Provides much needed housing and elderly housing in South Boston. 
 
• Provide service enriched senior housing with programming and supportive services 
provided for elderly residents to maintain independent living while aging in place. 
 
• Increase the availability of high quality housing stock in addition to furthering IDP and 
AFFH goals and requirements. 
 
• Provide that the issuance of a certificate of occupancy for the residential units at 495 
Dorchester Avenue occur prior to the issuance of any certificate of occupancy for any 
non-residential building included as part of the Project, ensuring that residents are 
present to help activate the portion of the 495 Project Site along Dorchester Avenue. 
 
• Provide for linkage funding from remainder of Phase 1 of Master Plan PDA (i.e., Phase 
1B) to be used for assistance with the financing for the construction of the 495 Project, to 
be further provided for in the PDA Development Plan for such phase. 
 
• The 495 Project transforms a contaminated former industrial site to create a safe, 
multimodal district through robust pedestrian, bicycle, and vehicle infrastructure that 
complies with Complete Street guidelines. 
 
• Improves pedestrian safety with new wider sidewalks, crosswalks, curbs, bike lanes and 
street trees along Dorchester Avenue and Alger Street to comply with Complete Streets 

 
 
guidelines. 
 
• Leverages existing nearby transit and alternative transportation choices to establish a 
true, transit oriented, development. 
 
• Targets LEED Platinum, all-electric, and Passive House standards to foster 
sustainability. 
 
• Improves resiliency by raising 495 Project Site grades and complying with flood district 
requirements. 
 
• Enables extensive environmental stabilization and remediation of land that was utilized 
for decades as a metal scrap yard that is currently under regulatory oversight by the 
federal EPA and Mass. DEP. 
 
• Identifies ground floor active retail space to be subsidized for the build-out and ongoing 
operation costs and made available to community start-ups, artists needing maker and 
industrial arts workspaces, and similarly identified community groups and programming, 
in conformance with the goals of the BPDA PLAN: Dot Ave. 
 
• Greatly improve stormwater and sewer infrastructure. 
 
 
15. 
DEVELOPMENT REVIEW PROCEDURES: All design plans for the 495 
Project are subject to the on-going development review and approval of the Authority. Such 
review is to be conducted in accordance with Article 80 of the Code and the Authority’s 
Development Review Procedures, as they may from time to time be updated. Once this 
Development Plan is approved, the BPDA may approve minor changes to the plans for the 495 
Project without the need for an amendment to this Development Plan as part of its development 
review and approval. Major or material changes, determined in the discretion of the BPDA, shall 
be determined accordance with section 80A-6 of the Code. 
 
16. 
COASTAL FLOOD RESILIENCE OVERLAY DISTRICT: Portions of the 
495 Project Site along Alger Street are within the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District 
(“CFROD”) and are subject to the requirements of Article 25A of the Code. The portions of the 
495 Project Site governed by the requirements of the CFROD have been designed to comply 
with said requirements. 
 
 
17. 
CONSISTENCY WITH THE PDA MASTER PLAN: This Project described 
in this Development Plan is consistent with the overall planning objectives and character of the 
Development described in the PDA Master Plan. The dimensional provisions, allowed uses, 
landscape phasing, parking and loading provisions described in this Development Plan shall be 
controlling for the Project and are consistent with and in compliance with the provisions in PDA 
Master Plan No. 144. 
 

 
 
 
18. 
APPLICABILITY OF ZONING CODE: Upon the approval of this 
Development Plan, in the event that the 495 Project (or any portion of the Project) described 
herein conflicts with any provision of the Code, such requirements of the Code shall be deemed 
waived. In accordance with the provisions of Section 80C of the Code, the BPDA shall be 
required to issue a Certification of Consistency (or partial Certification of Consistency) for the 
Project or portion(s) thereof. Upon the issuance of a Certification of Consistency (or Partial 
Certification of Consistency, if applicable) such Project or portion thereof shall be deemed to 
comply with any use, dimensional or other requirements of the Code. 
 
19. 
OWNERSHIP OF PROJECT SITE AND PROJECT. Although the 495 
Project Site is currently a portion of a single lot, it is contemplated that the 495 Project may be 
separately owned and financed including, without limitation, by the creation of separate parcels, 
condominium ownership, ground leases, or otherwise. The compliance or non-compliance of 
any other project described in the PDA Master Plan shall not affect the compliance of the 495 
Project with the requirements of this Development Plan. The Project will be eligible to receive 
its own Certification of Consistency or Partial Certification of Consistency if, and only if, the 
Director of the Authority makes the findings set forth in Article 80C-8 of the Code. If the 
Project is separately owned, the owner of the Project may seek an amendment of this 
Development Plan as to the 495 Project, provided that such amendment does not change any 
obligation or requirement of the PDA Master Plan, or any other project built in accordance with 
a separate development plan pursuant to the PDA Master Plan. 
 
20.

_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency ("BPDA") authorize the 
Director to: (1) issue a Certification of Approval for the proposed 
development located at 4 Liberty Square (as defined below, the 
“Proposed Project”), in accordance with Article 80E, Small Project 
Review of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”); (2) execute and deliver 
an Affordable Rental Housing Agreement and Restriction (“ARHAR”) in 
connection with the Proposed Project; (3) accept a Quitclaim Deed 
conveying a temporary, limited interest in 4 Liberty Square; and (4) 
enter into a PILOT Agreement for the Proposed Project, and to take 
any other actions, and to execute any other agreements and 
documents that the Director deems appropriate and necessary in 
connection with the Proposed Project. 
 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
BACKGROUND ON PILOT PROGRAM 
 
On November 24th 2024, 4 Liberty Square LLC (the “Proponent”) applied to Mayor 
Wu’s and the Planning Departments' Downtown Residential Conversion Incentive 
PILOT Program (the “PILOT Program”). The PILOT Program was authorized by the 
BPDA Board on October 12th, 2023 (“October Board Vote”) and offers to approved 
applicants a tax abatement in exchange for converting their underutilized office 
building into multi-family residential rental units. The October Board Vote 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
14 
authorized the creation of a Demonstration Project Plan Area in Downtown Boston 
(the “Plan Area”) and the Plan Area establishes an area where the BPDA is able to 
act pursuant to Massachusetts General Law Chapter 121B (“Chapter 121B”) and 
provide a contract for payment in lieu of taxes (“PILOT Agreement”) pursuant to 
Chapter 121B. 
 
In order to qualify for the PILOT program, the proponent must meet the 2024 IZ 
standards, which require that Seventeen Percent (17%) of all newly created units 
must be deed restricted affordable restricted for households making up to Sixty 
Percent (60%) of the Area Median Income (“AMI”), and an additional 3% of units 
must be available at HUD Small Area Fair Market Rent and reserved for voucher 
holders. Applicants must also comply with current Green Energy Stretch Goals, 
where applicable. 
 
 
PROJECT SITE 
 
The Proposed Project is located on an approximately 3,800 square foot parcel of 
land in the Liberty Square pocket of Government Center/Markets District on the 
Corner of Water St & Batterymarch Street. The project site is currently occupied by 
an existing underutilized 7 Story mixed use retail and office building.

PROPOSED PROJECT 
 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
14 
The Proposed Project at 4 Liberty Square is part of the Planning Department’s 
Office to Residential Conversion Program. 
 
4 Liberty Square LCC (“The Proponent”) is proposing the renovation of the existing 
+-25,000 Square foot seven (7) story office building with restaurant space on the 
ground level which sits prominently on Liberty Square at the corner of 
Batterymarch & Water Street. The proposed plans call for the existing office space 
on floors 2-7 to be converted to apartments, restaurant or retail use would remain 
on the ground level. The conversion will result in a new net residential total of 
approximately 22,086 gross floor area (“the Proposed project”). The Proposed 
project will Include thirty-six residential rental units including: thirty (30) studios, 
one (1) 1-bedroom, five (5) 2-bedrooms. The Proposed Project will include 
approximately 17% of the units income-restricted as IZ units and 3% of the units 
will be income-restricted for households with mobile housing vouchers as per the 
Inclusionary Zoning (Article 79 of the Code) and Office to Residential Conversion 
Program standards. The Proposed Project will also include an interior subsurface 
bicycle storage room with thirty-six (36) resident bike parking spaces.

I

BOARD APPROVED

Launched in October 2023, the Downtown Residential Conversion Incentive PILOT 
Program “Downtown Conversion Program” aims to support owners and developers 
of older commercial office building space in converting to residential units. The 
PILOT Program was informed by both 1) the City of Boston’s October 2022 
Downtown 
Revitalization Report which analyzed and made recommendations for downtown 
economic revitalization, as well as 2) the PLAN: Downtown planning process which 
recommended a downtown office conversion program as a key strategy for 
achieving the PLAN goals. In order to encourage new use of underutilized office 
space, the Downtown Conversion Program offers a tax abatement and a 
streamlined approval process to applicants who meet affordability and 
sustainability requirements. Accordingly, the Proposed Project would advance key 
recommendations of both the 2022 Downtown Revitalization Report and PLAN: 
Downtown. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On December 9th, 2024 the Proponent filed an Application for Small Project Review 
with the BPDA for the Proposed Project, pursuant to Article 80E of the Boston 
Zoning Code (the “Code”). The Planning Department sponsored and held a virtual 
public meeting on January 7th, 2025 via Zoom for the Proposed Project. The meeting 
was advertised in the Boston Guardian, posted on the Planning Department 
website and a notification was emailed to all subscribers of the Planning 
Department’s Downtown neighborhood update list. The public comment period 
ended on January 13th, 2025. 
 
ZONING 
 
The Project Site is located in the Government Center/Market district governed by 
Article 45 of the Code 
 
The Project Site is also located in the Coastal Flood Resilience Overlay District 
(CFROD), Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (GCOD), and the Restricted 
Parking District. 
 
PEDESTRIAN EASEMENT: 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
14 
The proposed project has agreed to grant a pedestrian easement to the City for the 
portion of the parcel that is currently acting as the public sidewalk at the corner of 
Water and Batterymarch Streets. This would require an action through the Public 
Improvement Commission to create the pedestrian easement. The current 
sidewalk condition does not accommodate an accessible ramp at this corner, 
because the sidewalk falls outside of the public right-of-way. Granting this 
pedestrian easement will allow the City to construct a corner accessible ramp to 
receive the existing crosswalks that land at this location. 
 
MITIGATION AND COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
The Proposed Project will include mitigation measures and community benefits to 
the neighborhood and the City of Boston (the “City”), including: 
● Revitalizing the downtown neighborhood by converting underutilized office 
space to on-site housing, bringing foot traffic back to the neighborhood, 
generating a new customer base for restaurants and shops, and creating a 
more vibrant urban core. 
● Creating seven (7) on-site income-restricted units, including six (6) IZ units at 
60% AMI and one (1) unit reserved for households with housing vouchers. 
● Meeting, where applicable, C.O.B Green Energy “Stretch Goals”; as required 
by the BPDA office to residential conversion program 
● The re-use of a vast majority of existing building components in order to 
minimize demolition waste and promote construction sustainability 
 
 
The Proposed Project and any proposed improvements to the public realm are 
subject to continued Public Improvement Commision (PIC) and Planning 
Department Design Review and approval. 
 
INCLUSIONARY ZONING 
 
The Proposed Project is subject to Zoning Code Article 79 Inclusionary Zoning, 
dated October 1, 2024 (“IZ”) and is located within Zone A, as defined by the IZ. IZ 
requires that 17% of the total number of units or residential leasable square 
footage within Article 80E Small Project developments are designated as IZ units. 
The project is further subject to the affordability requirements of the BPDA’s 
Downtown Residential Conversion Incentive PILOT Program dated July 10, 2023, 
which requires that Article 80E Small Projects applying under the PILOT program, in 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
14 
addition to complying with the 2024 IZ requirements, also include 3% of units to be 
made available to households with mobile housing vouchers. In this case, seven (7) 
units or 19.4% of the total number of units within the conversion project must be 
designated as income restricted units, consisting of 17% of units (the “IZ Units”) 
made available to the general public at no more than 60% of the Area 
Median Income (“AMI”), and 3% of units reserved for households who qualify with 
mobile housing vouchers with incomes up to 110% of AMI (the “Voucher Units”). Six 
(6) of the income-restricted units will be made affordable to households earning 
not more than 60% of AMI, as based upon data from the United States Department 
of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”) and published by the BPDA as annual 
income and rent limits, and the one (1) Voucher Unit will be made available to 
households with mobile housing vouchers qualifying at or below 110% of the AMI, 
and rented at no higher than the Small Area Fair Market Rent (SAFMR) for Zip Code 
02109 as published and adjusted annually by the Mayor’s Office of Housing 
(“MOH”).

Boston resident;

Household size (a minimum of one (1) person per bedroom); and

Households who are directly displaced or severely rent-burdened (to be

Where a unit is built out for a specific disability (e.g., mobility or sensory), a 
preference will also be available to households with a person whose need matches 
the build out of the unit. The City of Boston Disabilities Commission may assist the

An affordability covenant will be placed on the IZ Units and Voucher Unit to 
maintain affordability for a total period of fifty (50) years (this includes thirty (30) 
years with a BPDA option to extend for an additional period of twenty (20) years). 
The household income of the renter and rent of any subsequent rental of the IZ 
Units and Voucher Unit during this fifty (50) year period must fall within the 
applicable income and rent limits for each IZ Unit and Voucher Unit. IZ Units and 
Voucher Units may not be rented out by the developer prior to rental to an income 
eligible household, and the BPDA or its assigns or successors will monitor the 
ongoing affordability of the IZ Units and Voucher Unit. 
 
TERMS OF PILOT AGREEMENT 
 
Based on BPDA staff review under Article 80 and review under the PILOT Program, 
the Proponent has been selected to receive a PILOT Agreement, based on the

PILOT Program criteria. The Proponent will, upon approval by the BPDA Board, 
enter into a PILOT Agreement among the City of Boston (the “City”) and the BPDA. If 
approved today, the City and the BPDA will provide the Proposed Project an 
average tax abatement of up-to seventy-five percent (75%) of the assessed 
residential value for a term of twenty-nine (29) years, terms which are consistent 
with the October Board Vote. 
 
DEED CONVEYNCE 
 
In order to comply with the rules and regulations of Massachusetts General Law 
Chapter 121B, Section 16, the BPDA must take an interest in the Project Site. To 
effectuate that, the BPDA and the Owner of the 4 Liberty Square will execute a 
Quitclaim Deed to convey a temporary, limited rights in the 4 Liberty Square 
property. Additionally, the Owner and the BPDA will enter into to an 
indemnification agreement to ensure the BPDA does not have liability on the 
property. 
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
The Proposed Project complies with the requirements set forth in Section 80E of 
the Code for Small Project Review. Therefore, BPDA staff recommends that the 
Director be authorized to: (1) issue a Certification of Approval for the Proposed 
Project; (2) execute and deliver an Affordable Rental Housing Agreement and 
Restriction (“ARHAR”) in connection with the Proposed Project; (3) accept a 
Quitclaim Deed conveying a temporary, limited interest in 4 Liberty Square; and (4) 
enter into a PILOT Agreement for the Proposed Project, and to take any other 
actions, and to execute any other agreements and documents that the Director 
deems appropriate and necessary in connection with the Proposed Project.

Dear Mr. Norris,
The City of Boston’s Age Strong Commission is submitting the following comments on the
Small Project Review Application (SPRA) for the 4 Liberty Square project proposal. We
welcome this conversion of vacant office space to residential as it will bring additional
market rate residential housing to downtown.
Commenting from the perspective of the Age Strong Commission, and knowing that the
older adult population is the fastest growing population in Boston, we encourage the
proponent to think of designing these spaces with an older adult in mind.
We support the mix of one and two bedroom apartments, with the majority of studio
apartments. These can be optimal for seniors. We commend the proponent for the
intention to do robust community outreach to the neighborhood to hear concerns and
suggestions from neighbors.
In designing the residential quarters, please consider referring to this universal design
guideline created by Age Strong. Universal Design is an accessible and equitable framework
to create environments to benefit people of all ages. It is usually more affordable to design
utilizing these guidelines rather than retrofitting later.
Please find our specific recommendations for this project, below.
Pickup/Drop-off
In terms of public transportation, the site’s proximity to various bus routes is advantageous.
Since there is no parking proposed in this conversion project, we suggest a clear plan for
resident pickup and drop off. Perhaps a 15 minute parking allowance in front of the
building. Some older adults require the use of mobility devices, and it is best to be as close
to the entrance as possible. A similar suggestion would be a designated parking space near
the site. This type of parking space is beneficial for older adults who use the services of
ONE CITY HALL SQUARE | BOSTON, MA 02201 | BOSTON.GOV

Age Strong Commission 

visiting home health aides or personal care attendants. These services are essential and are
in line with our anti-displacement goal for older adults.
Bicycle Storage
We are pleased your proposal creates ample bicycle storage. We suggest the proposed
storage space also includes bicycle placement that does not require overhead lifting of
bicycles, which some older adults might find too difficult. Alternatively, you could designate
some ground level bicycle spaces, “age-friendly.”
Outdoor Space/Trees/Benches
We recommend the consideration of an awning or overhang to provide protection from
precipitation and sun/heat, which can have adverse effects on older adults. Awnings are
beneficial for residents as they enter and exit the building, and wait for transportation
pick-up. Protection should be provided to individual units including awnings and
overhangs over windows, especially on the south facing side.
The addition of street trees may not be possible, but are always a welcome addition to a
residential area. We also suggest age-friendly seating in the form of benches with armrests
and backrests. Benches help promote comfort, respite and can allow for social interaction.
Community connection increases the health and well-being of older adults.
Indoor Space
Age Strong understands that the design is in early stages. With retail/restaurant on the
ground floor, it may not be possible to include a small community space for the building. If
space does allow, we recommend carving out a small space for residents to do things like
collect mail and congregate inside.
Thank you for your consideration of these comments and recommendations.

A Letter of Intent for the Proposed Project was filed on February 8, 2023, pursuant to the

(“IAG”) were held on April 25, 2023, and July 29, 2024. Public meetings were held on May 2,

The buildings and site plan will comply with the Smart Utilities requirements found in 
Article 80B of the Code. The Proposed Project shall meet or exceed the 1.25” of stormwater 
infiltration per square inch of impervious development standard and will incorporate best 
practice green infrastructure standards within the public realm, when applicable. These 
elements include but are not limited to porous curb extensions, bio-retention strategies 
and/or rain gardens. The Proposed Project will also include smart streetlights standards for 
new sidewalks, including city shadow conduit and dual handholes in accordance with PIC 
requirements for work within the City of Boston right-of-way. The Proposed Project will also 
adhere to the City of Boston’s EV readiness program and shall have 25% of parking spaces 
EVSE- Installed and the remaining 75% EV-Ready for future installation. Utilities in any City 
of Boston right of way will be designed to conform with City of Boston Public Works 
Department standards and will undergo further review to ensure they are not in conflict

technologies.

DEVELOPMENT PLAN FOR PLANNED DEVELOPMENT AREA NO. 93 
500 Huntington Avenue 
MISSION HILL, BOSTON 
(As Amended) 
Proponent: 
Huntington Development Group LLC (the “Proponent”). The Proponent is a 
50% minority-owned development joint venture among affiliates of the Owens 
Companies, Inc., the oldest minority-owned and operated company in New 
England, Waldwin Development Group LLC, a longtime Boston-based, 
minority-owned business, and The Fallon Company LLC, a multi-generational 
Boston-based real estate developer. 
Site: 
The Project Site is located at Huntington Avenue, Parker Street and Ruggles 
Street, Boston and contains approximately 132,130 square feet of land (3.033 
acres) as shown on the plan entitled “Compiled Plot Plan, Wentworth 
Sweeney Field, Huntington Avenue in Boston, MA” prepared by Feldman 
Professional Land Surveyors, dated February 1, 2013. 
Proposed Project: 
The Project Site is currently subject to PDA No. 93, which was approved in 
2013 following an in-depth public process undertaken by Wentworth Institute 
of Technology. PDA No. 93 permits development of 640,000 square feet of 
gross floor area on the Project Site, comprised of office/R&D space and other 
commercial uses with ground floor retail and below-grade parking. The 
Proponent proposes to amend PDA No. 93 to refine the design and scope of 
the Project to improve its overall feasibility. Notably, the Proposed Project is 
consistent with the height, density, and parking limitations set forth in the 
previously approved PDA No. 93. The Proposed Project consists of a total 
of up to 640,000 square feet of gross floor area, comprised of life 
sciences/office/research and development space and other commercial or 
activated uses, first floor retail/restaurant/commercial/activated space; and up 
to 381 parking spaces in a below-grade garage. It is currently anticipated 
that the Proposed Project will consist of two buildings built in one or more 
phases. 
Proposed Uses: 
Consistent with PDA No. 93, the Proposed Project is currently anticipated to 
contain life sciences/office/research and development space and other 
commercial uses, first floor retail/restaurant/commercial/activated space and 
parking. The Proposed Project removes certain uses specific to Wentworth 
Institute of Technology that were contemplated in the prior filing. 
Proposed Densities: 
PDA No. 93 provides for an overall maximum Floor Area Ratio of 5.0 and a 
maximum gross floor area of 640,000 square feet. The Proposed Project 
reduces the maximum Floor Area Ratio to 4.84. 
 
Height: 
PDA No. 93 provides that the height of the buildings will be a maximum of 
253 feet to the top of the roof and 280 feet to the top of the mechanical 
equipment screens. The Proposed Project complies with these requirements. 

 
 
Construction Timetable: 
The construction period for the first phase will be approximately 30 months 
following completion of the regulatory approvals process and commencement 
of construction. 
Public Benefits: 
The approval of the Proposed Project will result in expanded public benefits for 
the Project, including: 
 
♦ Prioritizes unique workforce development opportunities and career ladders for 
a variety of roles through innovative partnerships, most notably including with 
Wentworth, its students and the local community. 
♦ Introduces, by virtue of the Proponent, an innovative 50% minority-owned 
development partnership to the Boston development landscape. 
♦ Fills a key void on Huntington Avenue Corridor, a void that has long been 
contemplated for redevelopment with a project similar to the Project, as noted 
in the City’s Avenue of the Arts design guidelines and PDA No. 93. 
♦ Maximizes the public realm on a site that was previously fenced off to the 
public by providing approximately 70,000 sf of publicly-accessible open 
space, a significant increase from PDA No. 93. 
♦ Includes ground floor retail, restaurant, commercial space, or other activated 
uses, to activate the new publicly accessible open space and Huntington 
Avenue. 
♦ Creates new outdoor spaces for gatherings and place-making for 
neighborhood use. 
♦ Opens the Project to students in the Real Estate Entrepreneurship Youth 
Program founded by The Fallon Company and Street2Ivy, which seeks to 
equip community youth with the skills, knowledge, and mentors needed to 
participate in real estate investing, and set them on a path to help eliminate 
the income and wealth disparity in Boston. 
♦ Partners with Wentworth’s RAMP program, which provides unique solutions 
for closing the opportunity gap in the construction industry by engaging with 
Boston youth early and often throughout their educational journey. 
♦ Significantly enhances neighborhood pedestrian and bike connectivity by 
providing publicly accessible paths through and around the site, improving 
connection among the Ruggles and Museum of Fine Arts MBTA stations, the 
neighboring institutions, the Southwest Corridor, and the Emerald Necklace.

In accordance with Section 3-1A, Article 80C-3, and Section 59-29 of the Boston Zoning

No. 93 (this “Amendment”) sets forth information regarding a project located in the Mission Hill 
neighborhood of the City of Boston (the “Project”). Planned Development Area No. 93 and the 
Development Plan for Planned Development Area No. 93 were approved by the Boston 
Redevelopment Authority on September 12, 2013 and adopted by the Boston Zoning 
Commission on October 9, 2013 (collectively, the “Original Development Plan”). Upon approval 
of this Amendment, the Original Development Plan, together with this Amendment, shall 
constitute the Development Plan for Planned Development Area No. 93, and are collectively 
referred to herein as “Development Plan”. 
 
The Development Plan sets forth the zoning for the Project and certain information about 
the Project, including project area, the proposed location and appearance of the structures, open 
spaces and landscaping, the proposed uses of the area, the proposed density, the proposed traffic 
circulation, parking and loading facilities, access to public transportation, proposed dimensions, 
development impact exaction, development review procedures, proposed public benefits and

Project Review under Article 80 of the Code, was filed with the Boston Redevelopment 
Authority (doing business as the Boston Planning & Development Agency, the “BPDA”). The 
Project is presently undergoing review by the Boston Civic Design Commission (“BCDC”) in 
connection with Article 28 of the Code. Based upon that process and the approval of this

pursuant to Sections 80B and 80C of the Code for final design review approval and certification 
as to consistency with this Development Plan.

subject to design, environmental and other Article 80 development review by the BPDA and by 
other governmental agencies and authorities, and the Project as described in this Development

80C-3(3) and 80C-4 of the Code and all other applicable provisions of the Code applicable to the 
approval of a Development Plan for a Planned Development Area. This Development Plan shall 
constitute permanent zoning for the Project site in accordance with Section 3-1A and Article 80C 
of the Code and is intended to address all requirements of the Code applicable to the Project site

2. Location and Description of Site. The Project site has not changed from the Original 
Development Plan. In addition to being in the Wentworth Community Commercial CC-3 
Subdistrict District and the Groundwater Conservation Overlay District as referenced in the Original 
Development Plan, the Project is located in a Restricted Parking Overlay District. It is 
contemplated that portions of the Project Site and the buildings and other improvements located 
thereon from time to time may be reconfigured into a number of smaller parcels or sub-areas, 
including, without limitation, through one or more subdivisions, ground leases, subleases, 
condominium regimes, or otherwise, which parcels or sub-areas may be under common or 
separate ownership, developed sequentially or simultaneously, and/or separately developed 
and/or financed (each such parcel or sub-area is referred to herein as a “Project Component”). 
As of the date of this Amendment, the Project site is anticipated to be comprised of two Project 
Components as further described below. The Project Components may be combined, divided, or 
otherwise changed and additional Project Component(s) may be created within the Project Site, 
in a manner that is not inconsistent with this Development Plan. As currently contemplated, the 
location and appearance of the buildings and open space will be generally consistent with the 
plan attached hereto as Exhibit C. 
 
Notwithstanding anything set forth herein or in the Code to the contrary, for purposes of this 
Development Plan, compliance of the individual Project Components with the requirements of 
this Development Plan will be determined as if the entire Project site were one Lot, even if it is 
comprised at any time of more than one Lot, including Lots that have been subdivided, re-
subdivided or combined or submitted to a condominium regime or other form of ownership. The 
Development Plan approves any zoning nonconformity created or increased by the separation of 
ownership of individual Project Components, or by the subdivision, re-subdivision, combination, 
or submission to condominium ownership or other forms of ownership of Project Components, 
provided that (a) the use provisions of the Development Plan are not violated by the resulting Lot 

3 
 
 
or Lots, (b) the Project’s site-wide FAR and gross floor area does not exceed the maximum 
density permitted under the Development Plan for the Project site as a whole, (c) the open space, 
parking and loading space requirements of this Development Plan are met with respect to the 
Project Site as a whole, (d) the public benefit obligations set forth in this Development Plan are 
not decreased without the prior written consent of the Director of the BPDA, and the scope of the 
public benefit obligations set forth in this Development Plan are not diminished, and (e) the 
sequencing of such open space, public realm, and public benefits obligations set forth in this 
Development Plan are consistent with this Development Plan. The compliance or non-
compliance of any one Project Component shall not affect the compliance of any other Project 
Component. 
 
3. Proposed Location, Dimensions, and Appearance of Structures. The proposed Project is a 
mixed-use development described in detail in the Original Development Plan. This Amendment 
updates the proposed location and orientation of the buildings to be constructed at the Project, 
reallocates gross floor area between them, and incorporates the current site plan for the Project. 
The maximum height and density of, and maximum parking permitted at, the Project have not 
changed. The lot coverage has decreased and open space along Huntington Avenue has 
significantly increased as shown on Exhibit C. 
 
The proposed Project, as affected by this Amendment, includes Building One, currently 
anticipated to contain up to 306,000 square feet of gross floor area within a 14-story building at 
the north-east corner of the site with a lower element located on Huntington Avenue of up to 
seven stories, and Building Two, currently anticipated to contain up to 334,000 square feet of 
gross floor area within an 15-story building. Building Two has frontage on both Parker Street 
and Ruggles Street. The maximum aggregate density of the above-referenced structures will not, 
in any event, exceed the 4.84 FAR or 640,000 maximum square feet of gross floor area. The 
maximum height of the buildings will be up to 237 feet to the top of the roof and up to 264 feet 
to the top of the mechanical equipment screens for the higher elements of Building One and 
Building Two (with such mechanical equipment within the screened area covering all or a 
portion of the roof as is provided in connection with the Article 80B design review process). 
Building One and Building Two will be subject to the 45 foot setback from Ruggles Street as 
shown in the Project submittals. 
 
Accordingly, the Original Development Plan is hereby amended by deleting plans 
attached as Exhibit C to the Original Development Plan in their entirety and substituting Exhibit 
C attached to this Amendment in place thereof (the “Project Plans”) and the dimensional table 
contained in the Original Development Plan is deleted in its entirety and the table attached as 
Exhibit A to this Amendment is inserted in its place. The final size, allocation of gross floor area, 
location, and appearance of the buildings will be subject to ongoing development and design 
review approval by the BPDA through the Large Project Review Process, in accordance with 
Article 80B-3 of the Code and the BRA Development Review Guidelines, dated 2006. The 
dimensional and other requirements specified in the Development Plan shall supersede such 
requirements of the Code, and shall be the only zoning requirements applicable to the Project and 
the Project Site. However, the Project shall be subject to design, environmental and other Article 
80 development review by the BPDA, and the aspects of the Project approved as part of such 
review shall be deemed to be the dimensional, design and environmental requirements applicable 

4 
 
 
to the Project, and deemed to satisfy the design criteria for public realm and the buildings set 
forth in in the Original Development Plan, upon issuance of a Certification of Compliance and 
Certification of Consistency (or a Partial Certification of Compliance and Partial Certification of 
Consistency for the applicable Project Component) and pursuant to Sections 80B-6 and 80C-8 of 
the Code, respectively. 
 
4. 
Open Space and Landscaping. The amended Project shall contain approximately 
70,000 square feet of publicly-accessible open space. The Project’s open space shall be subject to 
design, environmental and other Article 80 development review by the BPDA, and any open 
space or landscaping approved as part of such review shall be deemed to be in compliance with 
the Development Plan upon the issuance of a Certification of Compliance and Certification of 
Consistency (or a Partial Certification of Compliance and Partial Certification of Consistency for 
the applicable Project Component) in accordance with Sections 80B-6 and 80C-8 of the Code, 
respectively. 
 
5. 
Proposed Uses. The reference in the Original Development Plan to 78,400 square feet of 
space to be used by Wentworth Institute of Technology, Inc. (“WIT”) for institutional uses is 
hereby deleted, as is the note (indicated by an asterisk) referencing Educational Uses, Office 
Uses and Research and Development Uses in Building One on Exhibit D to the Original 
Development Plan. Exhibit D to the Original Development Plan is hereby amended by inserting 
at the end the following additional permitted uses: Research Laboratory, Research and 
Development Uses use, whether as a primary or ancillary use and any other use now or hereafter 
permitted under underlying zoning. The various uses and distribution of floor area to such uses 
may change as the Project is further refined and implemented in accordance with and subject to 
further design, environmental and other development review by the BPDA. Without limiting the 
foregoing, the development of the Project in accordance with the foregoing program or as refined 
and implemented in accordance with such further review shall be deemed in compliance with 
this Development Plan upon the issuance of a Certification of Consistency (or Partial 
Certification of Consistency for the applicable Project Component) in accordance with Section 
80C-8 of the Code. 
 
6. 
Signage. The signage program for the Project shall be subject to design, environmental 
and other development review by the BPDA, and any “Sign” approved as part of such review 
shall be deemed to be in compliance with this Development Plan. 
 
7. 
Transportation. The Project will provide adequate multimodal access and mitigate 
anticipated street safety and operational impacts in accordance with City goals, policies, and 
standards, as generally described in the transportation demand management program prepared by 
the Proponent and the corresponding Transportation Access Plan Agreement entered into by the 
Proponent with the City of Boston Transportation Department. The Project Site is well-served by 
rapid transit, commuter rail, high-frequency buses, the regional shared-use path network, and 
bikeshare, providing convenient multimodal access to and from much of Greater Boston. The 
Boston Transportation Department (“BTD”) assigns the Project Site a Mobility Score of 0.91, 
which limits allowable new motor vehicle parking and requires the execution of a robust 
Transportation Demand Management (“TDM”) program. 
 

5 
 
 
The Project will provide on-site motor vehicle parking in a single below-grade garage 
that will be accessed via a new driveway at Parker Street. The garage will connect to and serve 
Building One and Building Two, and will include a maximum of 355 new on-site motor vehicle 
parking spaces (i.e., resulting in a ratio of approximately .55 spaces per 1,000 sf of approved 
Gross Floor Area) in a single below-grade garage that is expected to be constructed under the 
footprint of both buildings as part of phased construction. 
 
As a bridge from the Project’s proposed parking ratio to the future-oriented parking ratio 
envisioned by the City, the Proponent commits to reevaluate on-site parking supply and demand 
periodically following construction of the Project, as follows: 
 
• 
Commencing 36 months after completing full lease up of Building one and Building two 
and continuing annually thereafter for a period of ten (10) years, the Proponent will 
prepare and submit to BPDA and BTD an analysis of the on-site parking supply. 
 
• 
In addition, within 2 years of issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy for Building one or 
Building two and continuing every 2 years after (until the parking studies required above 
commence), the Proponent will study and share results of employee, visitor, and/or 
patron transportation habits/patterns, vehicle and bike parking demand and utilization, 
and the status of required TDM measures. 
 
Recognizing that parking demand and supply issues may change rapidly in the coming years, the 
Proponent and the Director of Planning may by agreement amend the foregoing parking 
provisions of this Development Plan from time to time, by way of a director’s determination that 
such amendment is reasonable and appropriate. 
 
Building One will include an on-site ground-floor loading and service area for use by 
both buildings. All loading and service maneuvers will be accommodated on site within this area. 
Vehicles will access the loading and service area via a new driveway at Parker Street. The 
Project will provide at least 256 indoor and secured bicycle parking spaces and shower and 
locker facilities for employees and at least 38 exterior bicycle parking spaces for visitors in 
accordance with the January 2021 Bike Parking Guidelines issued by BTD. The motor vehicle 
parking, bicycle parking, and loading facilities for the Project are subject to refinement as 
development review of the Project proceeds as set forth below. 
 
The BPDA has determined that the Project will enhance the overall safety of adjacent 
streets and increase walking, biking, and transit access to the Project Site with on- and off-site 
investments. These investments include: 
 
• Streetscape improvements to public rights-of-way along the Project Site, including 
upgraded curb ramps, new street trees, new visitor bike racks, a consistent 10’ 
minimum pedestrian zone along Huntington Avenue and Ruggles Street, a consistent 
8’ minimum pedestrian zone along Parker Street, and, subject to the cooperation of 
the MBTA, a new floating bus stop on the Project Site, including bus shelter and stop 
amenities, along Ruggles Street (this stop is anticipated to consolidate existing bus 
stops 1798 and 1799); 

6 
 
 
• Publicly accessible pedestrian pathways through the Project Site and new mid-block 
crosswalks on Ruggles Street and Parker Street connecting these pathways and 
pedestrian desire lines to and through adjacent parcels; 
• To facilitate the development of the proposed “Roxbury to Fenway Connector” 
envisioned by BTD and the BPDA (as further described below), as a condition to the 
issuance of a building permit for the first building, Proponent agrees to submit to the 
BPDA 100% design and construction drawings for a separated, low-stress bicycle 
connection between Leon Street at the Southwest Corridor’s Ruggles Station to 
Huntington Avenue (a portion of which will be located on the project site as proposed 
by the Proponent and the balance of which will be on public land). 
• Contemporaneously with the construction of the first building the Proponent will 
construct such Ruggles Station-to-Huntington portion of the bicycle connection, 
subject to a scope and contribution cap on the Leon-to-Parker portion of such 
connection, to be mutually agreed upon in the Transportation Access Plan 
Agreement. 
• Funding and on-site space for two (2) 19-dock bikeshare stations or one large station 
of equivalent capacity; and 
• Within five (5) business days after issuance of a building permit for vertical 
construction of the first building, the Proponent shall make a one-time “bikeshare” 
contribution of $180,100.00 to BTD per the City’s Bike Parking Guidelines. 
• Funding and construction for a new southbound left-turn lane on Parker Street 
approaching Ruggles Street to address safety concerns and enhance intersection 
operations, subject to City approvals (collectively, the foregoing bullet point items 
being referred to as the “Mitigation Measures”). 
 
Following Large Project Review approval, the Proponent will make good faith efforts to meet 
with (in cooperation with other abutters with similar obligations) appropriate stakeholders in 
order to allow for the development of design and construction plans for improvements to 
Ruggles Street, Louis Prang Street, and/or The Fenway that enable safe, comfortable, and 
accessible travel for pedestrians and bicyclists in separated facilities as described below. The 
configuration and scope will be determined in coordination with these agencies (taking into 
account interim and future configurations of the adjacent transportation corridors through the 
“Roxbury-Fenway Connector West” concept design process), requires interagency coordination, 
and is not yet fully defined. However, these improvements are anticipated to include, subject to 
final design, permitting, and costing: 
• A safe, dedicated, and continuous two-way bikeway on Ruggles Street, Louis Prang 
Street, and The Fenway between the Southwest Corridor at Ruggles Station and the Back 
Bay Fens shared-use path near the intersection of The Fenway and Park Drive as it 
crosses the Muddy River. This may be a combination of permanent (e.g., curb, concrete, 
landscaping, etc.) and “quick-build” (e.g., signs, pavement markings, flexposts, signal 
timing changes, etc.) improvements, as determined through the design process; 
• Reconstruction of the northern side of Ruggles Street between the Ruggles Station 
busway and the Project Site to separate pedestrians, bicyclists, and motor vehicles into 
safe, dedicated spaces, including maintenance of existing mature trees and, as needed, 

7 
 
 
related ADA-compliance, protected islands, and/or traffic signal modifications; 
• Integration of this bikeway into the Project Site between Parker Street and Huntington 
Avenue; 
• Modifications, as needed, to the Ruggles Street / Louis Prang Street / Huntington Avenue 
intersection and the Louis Prang Street / The Fenway / Evans Way intersection to legibly 
connect bicyclists between the Project Site and existing shared-use paths. 
For clarification, Proponent shall only be required to design and permit such 
improvements and implement such construction to the extent specifically provided in the 
Mitigation Measures. Other abutters to the proposed improvements or the City will be 
responsible for designing and/or implementing the remainder of such work. 
In the event that circumstances change regarding this mitigation, including that the applicable 
public agencies cannot agree on the appropriate design or necessary permits and approvals are 
not obtained by the date on which a building permit is issued for the first building of the 
Proposed Project, the Proponent will escrow an appropriate sum based on the proposal for design 
and construction costs obtained by the Proponent with the BPDA, or its successor, for the BPDA, 
or its successor, to use in the redesign and improvement of areas identified in the Fenway 
Transportation Action Plan, including the Roxbury-Fenway Connector West concept design 
process pursuant to a mutually acceptable escrow agreement with the BPDA or its successor, or 
subject to a mutually acceptable escrow or other agreement with Proponent’s lender or title 
company. Thereafter, such payment shall be deemed full satisfaction of the Proponent’s 
requirements hereunder. 
Potential impacts stemming from the above parking and loading facilities have been 
adequately studied by Planning and BTD in the course of Large Project Review for the Project. 
The Proponent will provide for the foregoing mitigation measures to address any such traffic and 
safety impacts in a manner consistent with a Transportation Access Plan Agreement (“TAPA”) 
to be entered into between the Proponent and BTD. Subject to the cooperation of the City and 
the MBTA, where applicable, the foregoing mitigation shall be completed in phases as will be 
further described in the TAPA and in any event prior to the issuance of the certificate of 
occupancy for the last Project Component. 
 
8. 
Green Buildings 
 
Sustainability and Resiliency 
• 
The buildings will each be, at a minimum, designed to be certifiable to LEED 
Gold standards. 
• 
Dedicate 25% of parking spaces to electric vehicles while also facilitating a future 
conversion to all-electric (100% of spaces will be EV-ready at the issuance of the

Generate electricity on-site through rooftop photovoltaic (PV) panels to be

building. 

8 
 
 
 
In addition, the Project will comply with the City of Boston’s Article 37 of the Code and 
the Smart Utilities obligations under Article 80 Large Project Review. 
 
9. Public Benefits 
 
The adoption of this Amendment will result in expanded public benefits for the Project, 
including: 
 
• 
Prioritizes unique workforce development opportunities and career ladders for a 
variety of roles through innovative partnerships, most notably including with 
Wentworth, its students and the local community. 
• Introduces, by virtue of the Proponent, an innovative 50% minority-owned 
development partnership to the Boston development landscape. 
• Fills a key void on Huntington Avenue Corridor, a void that has long been 
contemplated for redevelopment with a project similar to the Project, as noted in

• Partners with Wentworth’s RAMP program, which provides unique solutions for

• Significantly enhances neighborhood pedestrian, bike, and transit connectivity by

Amendment of Development Plan. Any owner or ground tenant of a Project 
Component may seek amendment of the Development Plan only as to such Project Component 

9 
 
 
without the consent of any other owner or ground tenant of another Project Component, in

Estimated Development Schedule. The Proponent anticipates that the Project will be

No Obligation to Proceed with Project. Nothing in this Development Plan shall be

To: Stephen Harvey
Project Manager
Boston Planning and Development Agency
Re: 500 Huntington Ave
Date: May 19, 2023
Dear Mr. Harvey,
The City of Boston’s Age Strong Commission is submitting the following comments on the
PNF for the 500 Huntington Ave project currently proposed by Huntington Development
Group. Age Strong supports the conversion of these private fields to a development that
includes over one acre of publicly accessible open and green space. We appreciate the
focus on pedestrian-friendly development, especially seating, lighting, and additional street
trees. We request the proponent consider the following recommendations as the design
progresses.
A. Pick Up/Drop Off
Many older adults need rides because of mobility challenges. Locate the passenger
pickup/dropoff site close to building entrances. This increases safety and minimizes
potential conflict with other transportation modes. If passengers will need to cross
a bike lane to enter/exit the vehicle, provide a buffer (painted or island) with enough
space to check for oncoming bikes before crossing and to load/unload mobility aids.
B. Parking Garage
Design clear lines of sight for safe entrance and exit of the parking garage. We
recommend yellow detectable warning strips and the installation of audio warning
cues in front of parking entrances for the safety of low-vision pedestrians. The
design should prioritize the responsibility of drivers to locate pedestrians.
C. Trees
Trees are essential for physical and mental health and older adults are more
vulnerable to the adverse effects of high heat. We are pleased with the plan to plant
an abundance of new trees. We would like to see details about the design of tree
pits, which should maintain accessibility while preserving the health of the tree.
Provide maintenance plans for plantings to ensure the health of the trees and the
surrounding area is safe and accessible.
D. Seating
Places to rest allow older adults to enjoy the outdoor space. Incorporate

PLANNING CONTEXT 
The Proposed Project will be located in the Economic Development Area North 
subdistrict of the South End Neighborhood zoning district. The site is also located in 
the Groundwater Conservation, Coastal Flood Resilience, and Planned 
Development Area #114 overlay districts. The local neighborhood plan, the 
Harrison-Albany Corridor Strategic Plan, was adopted by the BRA Board in 2011, 
and subsequently codified into zoning (Article 64 of the Code) by the Boston Zoning 
Commission in January 2012. 
The neighborhood plan was created to inform land use, building form, and public 
realm improvements. At the time the plan was created, the area was characterized 
by large parcels hosting primarily commercial, industrial, and surface parking uses. 
The plan sought to activate this portion of the South End with a balanced mix of 
active, commercial, and residential uses. The Proposed Project aligns with the 
Strategic Plan’s goals by promoting pedestrian activity through the introduction of 
residential and active ground floor uses. Additionally, new interstitial connections 
were proposed to break down the large scale of the blocks in the area and 
strengthen connections between the area, Downtown, and the nearby Chinatown 
neighborhood. 

 
4 
In its use and design, the Proposed Project is aligned with the provisions of Planned 
Development Area #114 (the “PDA”), which is also derived from the Harrison-Albany 
Corridor Strategic Plan. Of note, the provision of income-restricted housing furthers 
the goals of both Boston Housing Strategy 2025 and the Development Plan for the 
PDA (the “PDA”), to ensure the provision of housing that is income-restricted to 
households with a range of incomes. 
Planning Department staff have worked with the Proponent to ensure that the 
proposed public realm improvements will be consistent with Boston Complete 
Streets guidelines. The streetscape will be made more pedestrian-friendly by 
establishing a strong street edge, providing clear building entrances, and 
integrating service facilities for parking and loading, while maintaining vehicular 
access from adjacent Washington Street. The Proposed Project will encourage 
context-appropriate modes of transportation by incorporating on-site bicycle 
parking and minimizing on-site motor vehicle parking. Furthermore, the public 
realm will be significantly improved through thoughtful landscape design and 
streetscape enhancements along Herald Street and Washington Street, including 
the addition of wider, landscaped sidewalks and other upgrades to enhance the 
pedestrian experience.

Re: Letter of support for 50 Herald Street Affordable Housing 
 
Dear Members of the BPDA Board, 
 
I am writing in support of the 50 Herald Street Affordable Housing Project proposed by the Chinese 
Consolidated Benevolent Association of New England, Inc. (CCBA) and Beacon Communities LLC. 
 
50 Herald Street is the second phase of the Shawmut Avenue/Washington Street Block Planned 
Development Area (PDA) project, approved by the BPDA in 2018. Phase 1 of the project, 100-112 
Shawmut, was completed in 2021 by the Davis Companies. For Phase 2, CCBA and Beacon 
Communities are jointly proposing the development of a new mixed-use building at the approximately 
32,909 SF site of the existing C-Mart Asian supermarket. The new 7-story building will be 100% 
affordable and is anticipated to include 117 housing units and a new ground-floor Asian grocery store. 
The project will also meet Passive House certification and be LEED-certifiable, fulfilling the city’s 
sustainability guidelines. 
 
In addition to increasing the affordable housing supply in Boston, the project will strengthen the 
community by maintaining a local neighborhood amenity and job center, in the form of the proposed 
Asian grocery store, as well as providing public realm improvements, including new street trees, 
greenery, and sidewalk upgrades around the site. Located at the intersection of Herald Street and 
Washington Street along highway I-90, the project will create a more attractive South End gateway and 
connection between the South End and Chinatown. 
 
With our affordable housing crisis, and as Chinatown and the South End continue to evolve, it is critical 
to increase income restricted housing to retain working families and the cultural and economic diversity 
of the two neighborhoods. I hope that the Planning Department Board will vote in favor of this proposal. 
If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to reach out to me at 617-635-3202, or at 
Ed.Flynn@Boston.gov. Thank you for your consideration.

units.

Certification of Approval for the Proposed Project. The Proponent must also 
register the Proposed Project with the Boston Fair Housing Commission (“BFHC”) 
upon issuance of the building permit. The IDP Units will not be marketed prior to 
the submission and approval of an Affirmative Marketing Plan to the BFHC and 
the BPDA. Preference will be given to applicants who meet the following criteria, 
weighted in the order below: 
(1) Boston resident; and 
(2) Household size (a minimum of one (1) person per bedroom). 
 
An affordability covenant will be placed on the IDP Units to maintain affordability 
for a total period of fifty (50) years (this includes thirty (30) years with a BPDA 
option to extend for an additional period of twenty (20) years). The household 
income of the renter and rent of any subsequent rental of the IDP Units during 
this fifty (50) year period must fall within the applicable income and rent limits for 
each IDP Unit. IDP Units may not be rented out by the developer prior to rental to 
an income eligible household, and the BPDA or its assigns or successors will 
monitor the ongoing affordability of the IDP Units. 
 
In addition to the provision of two (2) IDP Units, the Proposed Project will make a 
partial unit contribution of $24,000 (0.08 x $ 300,000).

BACKGROUND 
 
On February 10, 2021, the Proponent filed a Letter of Intent (“LOI”) in accordance 
with the BPDA’s policy regarding Provision of Mitigation by Development Projects in 
Boston. The Proponent filed a Project Notification Form (“PNF”) on June 23, 2021, 
for sequential construction of a new mixed-use residential apartment development 
of approximately 68,136 gross square feet (“gsf”) of floor area, containing up to 
sixty-five (65) residential apartment units and twenty-four (24) first-floor garage 
parking spaces in a six (6) story building, including renovating the existing four (4) 
story building (“Fox Hall” and collectively, the “Approved Project”). The scope of 
work included restoration of Fox Hall, an existing mixed-use building, and 
construction of a new residential development on a vacant portion of the Project 

 
4 
 
Site to the rear of Fox Hall. The Approved Project was all affordable, deed-restricted 
with on-site parking for 24 vehicles and bicycle storage for each dwelling unit. 
 
The Approved Project retained and supported the existing ground floor retailers 
and upgraded the SRO program on the upper floors of the existing Fox Hall, while 
adding a new residential building component of approximately 68,136 square feet 
on the rear lot, bringing the total proposed floor area to 95,670 square feet, 
including the existing Fox Hall. 
 
On June 16, 2022, the BPDA approved the Approved Project. 
 
 
NOTICE OF PROJECT CHANGE 
 
On October 6, 2023, the Proponent submitted a Notice of Project Change (the 
“NPC”) to the BPDA pursuant to Article 80A-6 of the Code. 
 
The NPC Project still calls for the restoration of the existing mixed-use Fox Hall 
building, as well as introducing new senior multifamily residential development 
without parking on a vacant portion of the Site to the rear of Fox Hall. The NPC 
Project will also continue to retain and support the existing ground floor retailers, 
while adding a new five (5) story residential building on the rear lot, bringing the 
total proposed floor area to 72,087 square feet including the Fox Hall building 
renovations. The NPC Project also removes the parking program as previously 
included in the Approved Project and now instead provides a short-term drop-off 
space for the entire NPC Project. The new building addition and subsequent 
renovation of the existing building, the same as the Approved Project, will create a 
total of 65 deed-restricted multi-family residential units.

PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The Proposed Project is located within the Upham's Corner Arts and Innovation 
District. This district is the product of several planning processes, including the 
Upham’s Corner Implementation Process and the Upham’s Corner Station Area 
Plan of the Fairmount Indigo Planning Initiative. 
 
A primary goal of these planning processes is the promotion of economic 
development without displacement. While the Proposed Project is larger in scale 

 
6 
 
than the existing context in which it is located, Upham's Corner Arts and Innovation 
District plan does not provide dimensional guidelines for private land. The overall 
program that combines new investment while retaining existing income-restricted 
units is consistent with the primary planning goal of preventing residential 
displacement 
 
 
ZONING 
 
The Project Site is located within a Neighborhood Shopping (“NS”) Zoning 
Subdistrict of the Dorchester Neighborhood Zoning District and is therefore subject 
to Article 65 of the Zoning Code. The Project Site is also located within the Uphams 
Corner Neighborhood Design Overlay District (“NDOD”) and is subject to Article 65, 
Section 65-32 of the Zoning Code, as well as a Boston Massachusetts Historical 
Commission Historic Inventory Area. 
 
The NPC Project will not require any new zoning relief that is different than the 
Approved Project, including: Multifamily Residential Use Conditional in Basement 
and First Story; FAR Excessive; Building Height Excessive; and Usable Open Space 
Insufficient. As such, the Proponent shall file revised plans with the City of Boston 
Zoning Board of Appeal on Petition BOA#1433649 for confirmation of the same via 
Board Final Arbiter (“BFA”) and the zoning relief necessary to construct the NPC 
Project. 
 
The NPC Project will also be subject to continuing BPDA Design Review. 
 
 
MITIGATION & COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
The NPC Project will continue to provide mitigation and community benefits for the 
Dorchester neighborhood and the City as a whole, including: 
 
● Development of up to sixty-five (65) income-restricted affordable units 
(totaling the entirety of the NPC Project), to be designated between 
30% and 80% AMI. 
 
● If the NPC Project includes any artist live/work units or on-site artist 
space, the Proponent will work with the BPDA and the City to design 

 
7 
 
and program this component, prior to the issuance of a building 
permit. 
 
● Addition/upgrade of approximately 5,500 gross square feet of street 
level retail space along Columbia Road. 
 
● Construction of an energy efficient building that incorporates 
measures to reduce the NPC Project’s impacts on the environment, 
including a building envelope that minimizes the building’s energy 
needs and all electric mechanical systems. 
 
● Include site infrastructure improvements including stormwater 
management strategies that will significantly improve the quality and 
decrease the quantity of stormwater generated by the Project Site 
when compared with existing conditions. 
 
● Improve the safety and visual appearance of the Project Site and 
immediate area through improved landscaping and lighting. 
 
● The Proponent will preserve the existing Arion Street mural. 
 
● Funding the installation of a fifteen (15) –dock BlueBikes station at the 
Project Site or a mutually agreeable location with the Boston 
Transportation Department (“BTD”), at a cost of up to $49,000 due at 
Certificate of Compliance. 
 
● Installation of up to two (2) new street trees in and around the Project 
Site, including widened sidewalks and other streetscape amenities to 
improve and enhance the pedestrian landscape and experience. 
 
● In consultation with the BPDA, BTD and PIC, the Proponent shall 
design and implement daylighting improvements at the intersection 
Arion Street and Columbia Road, for a total monetary contribution not 
to exceed $40,000.00. Said improvements shall be designed to comply 
with City standards and completed by the issuance of a Certificate of 
Occupancy for the NPC Project. 
 

 
8 
 
● The NPC Project will be designed and constructed to meet the USGBC’s 
LEED BD&C v4 Gold standard for both buildings by achieving 60 points 
each. 
 
● In alignment with the city’s carbon neutral goals, the NPC project is 
designed to target 2035 pCEI value of 1.58 kg CO2e/sf-yr prioritizing 
high performance building enclosure solutions to meet Passive House 
standards for both buildings. The NPC Project will be designed with all-
efficient electric systems for HVAC and hot water needs for both 
buildings. The team will further pursue the ZNC goal of converting the 
existing restaurant’s gas usage to fully electric cooktop systems. 
 
● The design will be optimized for solar renewable energy output with 
an approximately 74.5 kW array modeled across the buildings. 
Modeled system locations and sizes will be finalized prior to Article 37 
approval with a goal on onsite installation during construction. 
 
● The buildings will purchase 100% renewable electricity for all common 
area loads and set up new residential unit meters subscribing to 
Boston Community Choice Electricity’s “Green 100” (100% renewable 
electricity) option AND new owners will be informed of the benefits of 
using renewable electricity and their ability to opt out of the BCCE 
program at no cost if the rates are no longer comparable to or provide 
savings compared to standard service. 
● The project team will also work to determine what utility incentives are 
available, feasibility of mass timber construction and opportunities to 
reduce embodied carbon through material studies. 
The proposed scope of any in-kind work agreed to by the Proponent shall be 
developed in consultation with the BPDA and appropriate city agencies, 
departments, and commissions and the allocation of any financial contributions 
shall first be provided to the BPDA for disbursement to the specified entity or

Proponent and the BPDA. To the greatest extent possible, the Proponent will

and community benefits have been satisfied.
