feet (inclusive of mechanical 
penthouse). 
 
For purposes of the Development Plan, the term “Lot Area” or “total area of the Lot”, as 
defined in Article 2, shall mean 175,966 square feet, which measurement is inclusive of areas 
that will be devoted to new streets (and other site improvements) on the Project Site but 

5 
exclusive of the 3,000 square feet of area intended, if possible, to be licensed from the MBTA 
adjacent to the site and the 15,000 square feet of proposed offsite improvements in the rail bed 
on D Street, which are subject to MBTA and Massport review and approval. 
 
The Project’s bulk and dimensional aspects shall be subject to design, environmental and 
other development review by the BPDA, and any bulk and dimensions approved as part of such 
review shall be deemed to be consistent with this Development Plan upon the issuance of one or 
more partial or final Certifications of Consistency in accordance with Section 80C-8 of the 
Code. 
10. 
Proposed Open Space and Landscaping: The Project will provide privately 
owned, publicly accessible open spaces for use by the general public and tenants and their 
employees, guests and other visitors to the Project comprising approximately 23% of the Project 
Site, approximately as categorized in Exhibit D (subject to modification of site improvements 
shown thereon such as the location of walkways and paths in connection with further design 
review pursuant to Article 80B-5 of the Code). The Project includes a planned active, vibrant, 
Shared-Use Connection, including a path of no less than 10 feet in width, through the site to 
improve neighborhood access to/from the Sullivan Square MBTA Station and create a 
meaningful linkage to Hood Green and the Stack Street corridor through a network of activated 
open spaces, which further the goals of the PLAN and the contemplated Charlestown Green 
Loop. In all, approximately 41,000 square feet of the Project Site will be designed for use as 
open space. In addition, the Project includes up to approximately 10,000 square feet of ground 
floor area designed for Retail Uses and Restaurant Uses and other commercial uses. The 
Project’s open space shall be subject to design, environmental and other development review by 
the BPDA, and any open space or landscaping approved as part of such review shall be deemed 
consistent with this Development Plan upon the issuance of one or more partial or final 
Certifications of Consistency in accordance with Section 80C-8 of the Code. The Project, if built 
in accordance with the Development Plan, will be deemed to meet the requirements of the Code 
applicable to open space and landscaping. 
11. 
Proposed Traffic Circulation; Parking and Loading Facilities. The Project 
will provide access and traffic circulation as generally shown on Exhibit E. As described above, 
the Project features a subsurface parking structure, which will provide direct, secure access to 
each of the buildings on the Project Site and will streamline vehicular circulation, with all 
passenger vehicles entering and exiting the parking structure through an entry/exit via a private 
service road located on the Project Site beyond the western terminus of D Street, near the 
southwest corner of the Project Site. The Project will provide a maximum of 487 off-street 
parking spaces. 
 
The Proposed Project will be in compliance with the City’s Bike Parking Guidelines, will 
include at least 325 secure bike storage spaces, at least 43 outdoor publicly accessible bike 

6 
spaces, showers available for use by building occupants, and lockers available for use by 
building occupants. The Project will also provide space for a 19-dock bikeshare station on or 
near the Site. 
 
Also included in the Project are dedicated loading areas within each Building with a 
shared loading zone on the west end of the Project Site, as generally shown on Exhibit E. All 
deliveries, as well as trash and recycling pick-up activity for each Building, will occur in the 
respective loading areas. The Project’s parking and loading facilities and traffic circulation shall 
be subject to design, environmental and other development review by the BPDA, and the parking 
and loading facilities and traffic circulation approved as part of such review, together with the 
bikeshare station, shall be deemed to be in compliance with this Development Plan upon 
issuance of one or more partial or final Certifications of Compliance and Certifications of 
Consistency pursuant to Sections 80B-6 and 80C-8 of the Code, respectively. The Proponent 
will also execute a Transportation Access Plan Agreement (TAPA) with Boston Transportation 
Department, which will dictate traffic, parking, circulation, bike parking, transportation demand 
management program, and in-kind transportation investments to be completed by the Project as 
further set forth therein and subject to the terms thereof. 
12. 
Access to Public Transportation. The Project Site is well served by public 
transportation, with access to two Orange Line MBTA stations (Sullivan Square and Community 
College) and 12 nearby bus routes. The Sullivan Square MBTA station is located approximately 
300 feet north of the Project Site and provides access to the Orange Line and the MBTA bus 
routes. Community College station is approximately 0.6 miles from the Project Site and is 
accessible via Rutherford Avenue. Together, these public transportation nodes provide 
convenient access to the residents of the City of Boston. 
13. 
Signage. Signs shall be permitted on the Project Site as approved from time to 
time through Article 80 design review by the BPDA. Any sign approved as part of such review 
will be deemed to be in compliance with this Development Plan and the Code. 
14. 
PDA Plan Approval Standards. Section 62-23 of the Code provides that the 
BPDA may approve a planned development area development plan in the CND District as 
meeting the requirement of Section 80C-4 if the BPDA finds that such development plan 
proposes a plan for public benefits, including two or more of the following: (a) significant 
mobility improvements through the addition of, but not limited to, streets, sidewalks, and bike 
lanes; (b) improvements to existing open space or the creation of new open space, particularly 
parks; (c) preservation of historically significant buildings through adaptive reuse; (d) provision 
of affordable housing exceeding that which is required by city policy; or (e) diversification and 
expansion of Charlestown's economy and job opportunities through economic activity, such as 
private investment in commercial and cultural uses, or research and development. As addressed 
in Section 15 and other Sections of this Development Plan, this Development Plan proposes a 

7 
comprehensive plan of public benefits to be derived from the Project, consistent with Section 62-
23 of the Code. 
15. 
Public Benefits. The Project’s public benefits include the following: 
a. 
Economic Health and Diversity. The Project will contribute extensively to 
the economic health and well-being of the Charlestown neighborhood, and the City of 
Boston more generally, by generating substantially increased property taxes, new tax 
revenues, and diverse job opportunities. 
b. 
Open Space Improvements and Creation. The Project will include 
enhancements to existing open space and create new open spaces, including: 
1) A new, accessible Shared-Use Connection, including a path of no less 
than 10 feet wide, through the Project Site between D Street and 
Cambridge Street that creates a welcoming pedestrian and bicycle 
experience between Sullivan Square Station, the Lost Village, Hood 
Park, and Stack Street; 
2) The creation of approximately 41,000 square feet of open space on the 
Project Site, approximately as shown in Exhibit D; and 
3) The improvement of approximately 18,000 square feet of open space 
provided on adjacent parcels, subject to MBTA and Massport review 
and approval; 
c. 
Mobility Improvements and Transportation Demand Management 
measures: The Proponent has committed to undertake improvements that enhance the 
public realm in the area of the Site. These enhancements include: 
1) Subject to the cooperation of Massport, improving the existing roadway 
known as D Street between Spice Street and the westernmost edge of 
the Project Site with a new roadway surface, sidewalk, accessible ramps 
and crosswalks, enhanced storm drainage, granite curbing, street trees, 
and street lighting. 
2) An annual financial contribution to the Charlestown Link shuttle service 
(or equivalent) commencing upon first Certificate of Occupancy and 
continuing for the duration of the service; 
3) At the Cambridge Street/I-93 off ramp intersection, the Proponent will 
design, permit, and construct safety improvements, signal upgrades, 
ADA-compliant ramps, and expanded sidewalk/curb extensions. If 

8 
feasible, in consultation with BTD and MassDOT, a new crosswalk at 
the eastern leg of the intersection will be added across Cambridge 
Street. Each of the activities associated with this mitigation measure is 
subject to BPDA, BTD, PWD, and other city or state agency timely 
review and approval as needed. PIC approvals for proposed 
improvements shall be completed before building permit issuance for 
the Proposed Project. The physical mitigation improvements must be 
completed upon Certificate of Occupancy. Alternatively, if the 
Proponent is unable to obtain or is delayed in obtaining the necessary 
approvals to construct the improvements, the Proponent shall contribute 
funds equivalent to the cost of the improvements to be used towards the 
improvements if implemented by the applicable agencies at a later date; 
4) The construction of a new 19-dock Bluebikes station at the Project Site 
and a one-time contribution of $228,260 to Boston Transportation 
Department (“BTD”) to support operations of the bikeshare system; 
5) Consistent with BTD guidelines, secure bicycle spaces for the office and 
life science/R&D employees and will also provide showers and lockers 
for employees. In addition, the Project will provide outdoor publicly 
accessible bicycle spaces for visitors; and 
6) The Project will comply with the Boston Transportation Department 
Transportation Demand Management Points System. The selected 
strategies will be specified and codified in the Transportation Access 
Plan Agreement (“TAPA”). For this project, the Proponent has agreed 
voluntarily to achieve 100 TDM points. The TDM program is expected 
to include a transit subsidy of at least 25% for building occupants 
incorporated into lease agreements with tenants, Gold-level bikeshare 
membership, and EV car share provided on site. 
7) As a bridge from the Project’s proposed parking ratio (0.6) to the future-
oriented ratio envisioned by PLAN: Charlestown (0.4), the Proponent 
commits to reevaluate on-site parking supply and demand when key 
PLAN: Charlestown Public Improvements are implemented, including 
(1) 4.5 minute headways on the Orange Line, (2) Rutherford 
Avenue/Sullivan Square Design Project, (3) MBTA Bus Network 
Redesign routes and frequencies, (4) Bus Rapid Transit service on 
Rutherford Avenue, (5) Commuter Rail service at Sullivan Square, and 
(6) three neighborhood shuttle routes to supplement MBTA service 
within the neighborhood, as follows: 

9 
i. 
Prior to issuance of a full or partial Certificate of Completion, 
the Proponent will prepare and submit to BPDA and BTD an 
analysis of the on-site parking supply and demand and explore 
the feasibility of reducing on-site parking demand to achieve a 
ratio lower than 0.6/ksf which analysis may be completed and 
submitted prior to or during construction. 
ii. 
Commencing 1 year after at least three (3) of the PLAN: 
Charlestown Public Improvements listed above are completed, 
the Proponent will prepare and submit to BPDA and BTD an 
analysis of the on-site parking supply and demand and explore 
the feasibility of reducing on-site parking demand to achieve a 
ratio of 0.5 per 1,000 sf of approved Gross Floor Area. 
iii. 
Commencing 1 year after at least five (5) of the PLAN: 
Charlestown Public Improvements listed above are completed, 
the Proponent will prepare and submit to BPDA and BTD an 
analysis of the on-site parking supply and demand and explore 
the feasibility of reducing on-site parking demand to achieve a 
ratio of 0.4 per 1,000 sf of approved Gross Floor Area (with no 
spaces allocated to the Project’s up to 10,000 square feet of 
retail/restaurant/other commercial space on the ground floor). 
iv. 
In connection with such evaluations, the Proponent and the 
BPDA will explore whether any available sharing or reuse of 
parking spaces that will not be needed to meet the 66 Cambridge 
development’s parking demands may support nearby 
projects/uses with the goal of reducing new parking construction 
in the area. 
8) Within 2 years of issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy for Building A 
or Building B, and continuing every 2 years after (until the parking 
studies required above commence), the Proponent will study and share 
results of employee, visitor, and/or patron transportation habits/patterns, 
vehicle and bike parking demand and utilization, and the status of 
required TDM measures. 
d. 
Urban Design Benefits. The Project will create a welcoming and inclusive 
transit-oriented development on an existing, auto-centric industrial site that has been 
closed off for many decades, enabling previously unavailable commuter connections 
through the site to Sullivan Square Station from Hood Green and points south. The 
Project will buffer the noise, air quality, and visual impacts of the elevated I-93 structure 

10 
from Charlestown with attractive, site-appropriate improvements and significantly 
increase the neighborhood’s tree canopy, through enhanced landscaping of exterior 
ground level spaces as well as elevated building areas. 
e. 
Smart Growth/Transit-Oriented Development. The Project exemplifies 
smart-growth and transit-oriented development by concentrating commercial uses in 
close proximity to major MBTA hubs and bus lines that provide easy access to the 
Project Site from all of the City’s neighborhoods. 
f. 
Sustainable Design. The Project will comply with the requirements of 
Article 37 of the Code. The Project team will use the U.S. Green Building Council’s 
Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (“LEED”) green building rating system 
to evaluate sustainable design measures, in accordance with Article 37 of the Code. The 
Project, as designed, will target a LEED Gold level certifiability at a minimum. 
g. 
Resiliency. The proposed Project will increase the first-floor elevation to 
21.5 feet BCB to address the City’s 2070 Sea Level Rise Design Flood Elevation. All 
critical mechanical and electrical equipment will be at or above 22.5 BCB. The 28% 
reduction in on-site impervious area and, if permitted to be implemented by the MBTA, 
new green space in the rail bed along D Street will help reduce the heat island effect on 
site and in the surrounding neighborhood. 
16. 
Development Review Procedures. All aspects of the proposed Project design 
will be subject to ongoing development review and approval by the BPDA under Article 80B of 
the Code. In accordance with these development review procedures, the Proponent filed a Project 
Notification Form for the Project on July 27, 2022, initiating the Large Project Review process 
with the BPDA. On January 11, 2023, the BPDA issued a Scoping Determination on the PNF, 
and the Proponent filed a Draft Project Impact Report (“DPIR”) in response to the Scoping 
Determination on September 28, 2023. 
In addition to BPDA approval of the Project and the DPIR pursuant to Article 80B of 
the Code and the approval of this Development Plan, the Proponent will seek such further 
permits and approvals from other governmental agencies as are necessary to undertake 
construction of the Project. 
17. 
Subdivision; Condominium Regime. The Project Site may be reconfigured into 
multiple parcels, which may be (i) held pursuant to a ground lease or leases, (ii) held under 
common or separate ownership (including as part of one or more condominium structures), (iii) 
developed sequentially or simultaneously, and (iv) constructed and/or financed separately (each 
such component, a “Project Component”). Notwithstanding anything contained in this 
Development Plan or in the Code to the contrary, in the event that the Project Site is divided into 
Project Components, compliance of the individual Project Components with the requirements of 

11 
the Code and this Development Plan will be determined on an individual Project Component 
basis, and the compliance or non-compliance of any one Project Component will not affect the 
compliance of any other Project Component. A Certification of Consistency may be issued for 
any Project Component. In addition, this Development Plan approves any zoning nonconformity 
created or increased solely as a result of (i) the separation of ownership of individual Project 
Components, (ii) the subdivision or combination of the parcels that compose the Project Site, 
and/or (iii) the submission of one or more Project Components to a condominium regime; 
provided that: (a) the use provisions of this Development Plan are not violated by the resulting 
Project Components, (b) the Project’s Site-wide FAR (as defined above) does not exceed the 
maximum density permitted under this Development Plan for the Project Site as a whole, (c) the 
open space, parking and loading space requirements of this Development Plan are met with 
respect to the Project Site as a whole; and (d) the public benefits obligations set forth in this 
Development Plan are not decreased without the prior written consent of the Director of the 
BPDA, and the scope of the public benefit obligations set forth in this Development Plan are not 
diminished. Elements of the Project that may be located on separately owned lots at any time and 
from time to time within the Project Site shall be treated as a single lot for purposes of 
calculating FAR if there is a recorded condominium document, easement agreement or other 
agreement between the owners of such lot that allocates the gross floor area of the Project so that 
the total FAR of such lots together does not exceed the total FAR allowable in this Development 
Plan. 
18. 
Applicability. In accordance with Section 80-C of the Code, consistency of the 
Project with this Development Plan constitutes compliance with the dimensional, use and all 
other requirements of the Code to the extent such requirements have been addressed in this 
Development Plan. This Development Plan shall constitute permanent zoning for the Project 
Site. To the extent that any aspect of proposed uses and proposed structures addressed in this 
Development Plan are in conflict with any requirement of the Code, this Development Plan shall 
govern. 
19. 
Amendments. Any owner of an individual Project Component may seek 
amendment of this Development Plan as to such Project Component in accordance with the Code 
without the consent of any other Project Component owner(s). In the event that any amendment 
affects the overall compliance of the Project with this Development Plan, this Development Plan 
will be deemed amended with respect to the Project as a whole to the extent necessary for the 
overall Project and each Project Component to comply with this Development Plan. 
20. 
Minor Modifications to Plans. This Development Plan sets forth the bulk, 
dimensional, use and other zoning requirements for the Project and the Project Site. Once this 
Development Plan is approved, final plans and specifications for the Project will be submitted to 
the BPDA pursuant to Section 3-1A, Article 80B, and Article 80C of the Code for final design 
review approval and certification as to consistency with this Development Plan, and to other 

12 
governmental agencies and authorities for final approval. In light of the comprehensive public 
reviews needed to secure all required permits and approvals for the Project, the Proponent may 
find that modifications and adjustments to the Project may be necessary. Accordingly, minor 
modifications to the Project (which may include changes in height and massing within the 
parameters set forth in this Development Plan) that are consistent with the Building Height and 
density limitations set forth in this Development Plan, subject to BPDA design review approval 
and in accordance with Section 80A-6 of the Code, may be approved without requiring an 
amendment to this Development Plan or further BPDA action, as evidenced by a Certification of 
Consistency issued pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Code. 
Subject to further urban design review pursuant to Section 80B-5 of the Code, minor 
modifications shall be deemed to include reallocations of the building square footage between 
Buildings A and B and the improvements associated with them (e.g., a podium, if applicable), 
adjustments of height of the Buildings within the constraints established for the maximum height 
of a building within this Development Plan, and other massing modifications within the 
constraints established by Code as affected by this Development Plan. 
21. 
Estimated Development Schedule. The Proponent anticipates that the Project 
will be constructed in multiple phases or sub-phases, which phases or sub-phases may proceed 
sequentially or simultaneously. The Proponent estimates that construction of the Project, if 
completed in one phase, will take approximately 36 months from issuance of a full building 
permit, subject to customary delays, pre-leasing, market forces, force majeure events, and similar 
circumstances. If the Project is completed in one or more phases or Project Components, the 
Proponent estimates that construction of the first Project Component will take approximately 33 
months from issuance of a full building permit, subject to customary delays, pre-leasing, market 
forces, force majeure events, and similar circumstances, and the second will take approximately 
30 months from issuance of a full building permit, subject to customary delays, pre-leasing, 
market forces, force majeure events, and similar circumstances. Staging and logistics plans for a 
second Project Component will impact the delivery timing for open space improvements. 
22. 
No Obligation to Proceed. Notwithstanding anything set forth in the Code or in 
this Development Plan to the contrary, under no circumstances shall the Proponent (or any owner 
of all or any portion of the Project Site) be obligated to proceed with the Project or any portion 
thereof, nor shall the Proponent (or any owner of all or any portion of the Project Site) be 
obligated to complete the Project should it decide to proceed with all or any portion of the 
Project.

RE: 66 CAMBRIDGE STREET, CHARLESTOWN
Dear Board Members,
I am writing to express my support for the 66 Cambridge Street proposal in Charlestown. The
project site is located within walking distance of the MBTA Orange Line Sullivan Square station,
and provides a unique opportunity to increase connectivity of this area to the rest of the
neighborhood due to its current industrial, underutilized state.
The proponents, 60 Cambridge Development LLC c/o The Fallon Company LLC, have made
commitments to public realm improvements, local workforce development, and advances in
mobility upgrades that support a multi-modal environment in this transit-oriented location.
Additionally, the proponent has committed to providing $9.3 million linkage contribution
towards affordable housing and $1.7 million linkage contribution towards jobs training. In their
financial commitment to job training, the proponent has stipulated plans to include a workforce
development program geared towards Charlestown and local residents. I ask that the proponent
consider students in and about to graduate from Charlestown High School as part of this
program, so that they and their families can benefit from the BioLab economic development of
this project.
The proponent has promised to improve pedestrian safety and invest in multiple strategies that
will increase bike, walking, and public transportation use. The proposal offers 325 long-term
secure bike parking spaces and 41 visitor publicly accessible bike parking spaces and an annual
financial contribution to the Charlestown Link shuttle service which will begin after the first
Certificate of Occupancy is administered. However, there is still a concern regarding the
Project’s proposed parking ratio (0.6) which is higher than recommended by PLAN: Charlestown
(0.4). I would like to see the proponent follow through on their written commitment to reevaluate
on-site parking when PLAN: Charlestown public improvements are implemented. Traffic

mitigation and limiting impacts on the existing gridlock in Sullivan Square are crucial to making
sure Charlestown residents are able to enter and exit their own community.
Through this project, this major transit corridor will now have 10,000 square feet of commercial
space for potential retail, restaurant, and other businesses. As a mixed-use project, I implore the
proponent to ensure that ground floor retail space available is affordable and that a preference be
given to Charlestown small businesses.
Finally, my understanding is that this proposal meets the requirements of PLAN: Charlestown,
and was created with the new zoning changes in mind. In addition to providing mixed-use
density in a transit-oriented corridor, and renovating mobility infrastructure in Sullivan Square,
the project will provide 41,000 square feet of open space improvements, which is deeply needed
in this neighborhood. Investments include the creation of an accessible shared-use path through
the proposed site between D Street and Cambridge Street that provides safe pedestrian and
bicycle access between Sullivan Square Station, the Lost Village, Hood Park, and Stack Street.
If you have any questions, please feel free to contact me directly at gabriela.coletta@boston.gov
and (617) 635-3200.
Sincerely,
Gabriela Coletta
Boston City Councilor

Dear Director Jemison: 
On behalf of the Massachusetts Port Authority (Massport), thank you for the opportunity to comment on 
the Application for Approval of the Planned Development Area (PDA Application) Development Plan for 
the proposed development at 60-66 Cambridge Street in Charlestown (the "Project"). 60 Cambridge Street 
Development LLC (the "Proponent") proposes to develop approximately 802,000 square feet (sf) of 
commercial office and life science space in two buildings, including 10,000 sf of ground floor retail and 
restaurant use, 41,000 sf of new publicly accessible open space, and approximately 487 below-grade 
parking spaces. The PDA will function as the Project's permanent zoning and establishes the location, uses, 
density and dimensions of all structures; open space and landscaping; traffic circulation; parking and 
loading facilities; public transportation access; and public benefits provided by the Project. 
Massport has been coordinating with the Proponent through the planning and design of the Project 
regarding land the Authority owns adjacent to the Project site. In the early 2000s, Massport purchased the 
Mystic Wharf Branch Railroad right-of-way (ROW) with the support of the Massachusetts Department of 
Transportation (MassDOT) to preserve the corridor to enable potential future resumption of rail 
operations serving marine industrial uses in Charlestown within the Mystic River Designated Port Area. The 
ROW runs to the south of the Project site and includes a narrow private road (referred to as "D Street"), 
which is proposed by the Proponent to be the Project's primary means of vehicular access. D Street also 
serves as the primary means of access for stakeholders west of the Project site such as MassDOT 
operations and Boston Sand and Gravel. 
The Proponent holds existing easements for vehicle access on a portion of the ROW. Massport is in the 
midst of discussions with the Proponent to amend the easements to allow for an increase in access as well 
as necessary roadway geometry improvements and new utility connections to serve the Project. The PDA

The Project will significantly increase vehicular traffic on D Street as it will provide the main vehicular

The Proponent must take the lead to design and vet a safe and an efficient roadway alignment in close

Massport supports the inclusion in the Traffic Circulation, Parking, and Loading Plan of a pull-up/drop-off

on D Street and the railroad ROW to serve the primary pedestrian desire lines. 
Massport understands the City has plans to develop a signalized intersection at the eastern end of D Street

Dear Sarah: 
 
The MBTA appreciates the opportunity to provide initial comments on the 66 Cambridge Street project, a 
transit-oriented development consisting of several parcels adjacent to Sullivan Square station. As the 
proponent notes, this area is rich in transit: hosting a dozen bus routes, as well as Orange Line at Sullivan, 
and the recently completed Green Line Extension a short distance away at East Somerville station. The 
proposed development also abuts several MBTA parcels, including active and inactive ROW. 
The 66 Cambridge Street project envisions the redevelopment of approximately 4.04 acres near Sullivan 
Square station, resulting in 812,000 square feet of new construction, including 802,000 square feet of 
Research & Development and Office space, and 10,000 square feet of retail. The build-out proposed by 
the project will bring an estimated 3857 new riders to and from the neighborhood, most of whom will 
make use of the available transportation network on a daily basis given the project location near multiple 
bus routes and the Orange Line. 
The MBTA is supportive of Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) within walking distance of stations and 
transit stops but is also mindful of the impacts of proposed development to transportation and facilities in 
the immediate area. The following comments were compiled collaboratively by MBTA Departments, 
including Real Estate, and Transit-Oriented Development, in response to the publicly available project 
documents, such as the recent Draft Project Impact Report (DPIR), and the Planned Development Area 
(PDA). 
MBTA Comments 
Supporting Transit & Charlestown Neighborhood Goals 
It is vital to recognize that the 66 Cambridge Street project falls within the Expand Neighborhood area of 
Imagine Boston 2030, the citywide plan. This mandates the City of Boston and new developments 
"Improve Transportation Connections". The MBTA appreciates the project efforts to provide a direct

A key component of PLAN: Charlestown involves future development projects contributing to

Resiliency and Sustainability 
The MBTA would like to provide comments on resiliency concerns with the site location: 
 
• 
The project must manage all stormwater on site, in accordance with BPDA Article 24A, BPDA’s 
Climate Resiliency Checklist and the Smart Utilities Checklist and reduce the amount of 
stormwater from the site that currently flows onto the MBTA Right of Way. 
• 
The Proponent may consider a flood protection structure (berm or flood wall) along the ROW to 
reduce flood risk to the MBTA tracks and mitigate flood water from the Proponents’ property 
from moving onto MBTA tracks. 
• 
The Proponent must ensure that any trees planted on the development are kept a minimum of 25’ 
away from the ROW for safety and to reduce the likelihood of branches coming down onto MBTA 
tracks during a windstorm. 
 
Enabling Phase and Project Construction 
The MBTA has worked with the proponent to undertake a land transaction to allow for relocation of 
current MBTA facilities from the site and integrate them into the ROW. This work includes relocation of 
siding track and relocating and rebuilding an MBTA power substation. The MBTA looks forward to the start 
of this work in late 2024. 
 
As additional construction for the project moves forward on the site, the MBTA notes that due to the 
proximity of the project to MBTA property, the Authority’s Zone of Influence policy may apply to areas of 
the project which are within thirty feet of the MBTA’s property line, a licensing process will be required 
before work can commence. This will include reviewing design and construction plans as well as potential 
construction phase support, if deemed necessary. License applications may be submitted at 
mbtarealty.com/licenses. 
 
Project Transportation Impacts 
Bus Access, Circulation, and Traffic Improvements 
The MBTA anticipates coordination with the City and Proponent on future transit priority infrastructure in 
order to ensure that such infrastructure meets operational and regulatory requirements. Safety, 
accessibility, and alignment with the Better Bus Project are key requirements for any planned 
infrastructure, and all planned crosswalks, bus stops, and bus lanes must be adequately reviewed by 
MBTA staff prior to implementation. Specifically, the MBTA has concerns regarding traffic on Cambridge St 
outside of Sullivan Station and ensuring that all bus movements avoid potential delay wherever possible. 
The MBTA looks forward to working with the Proponent and City on the contemplated improvements for 
this corridor.

Transit Impacts 
The MBTA has reviewed the project’s ridership impacts to the transit network, including Orange Line 
subway service and Sullivan Square bus service. Sullivan Square is an important transfer point in the 
MBTA’s network, allowing riders to change from bus to rapid transit service into the downtown core, or 
choose from a dozen bus routes to travel to points in Somerville, Cambridge, Everett, Malden, and Revere. 
 
Based on the MBTA’s own transportation impact methodology there will be approximately 3,857 new 
daily transit trips generated by the completed development, as well as an additional short-term increase 
in ridership generated by the construction workforce traveling to and from the project site.

Parking Supply and Management 
The proponent highlights the transit-oriented nature of the project as part of the development’s overall 
parking strategy with an emphasis on promoting walking, biking, and transit in the neighborhood for 
future tenants and employees. The project’s parking strategy states that it will provide a TDM strategy to 
reduce reliance on single-occupancy vehicles while supporting neighborhood demand, including 487 
spaces of onsite parking. 
The MBTA notes that successful Transportation Demand Management measures include: 
• 
Accessibility upgrades, where necessary. 
• 
Installation of amenities, such as alternative mobility options, enhanced bus stops, and active 
transportation improvements. 
• 
Alternative transportation membership programs, such as the MBTA’s Perq program, alternative 
mobility, and subsidized transit passes. 
 
While the DPIR states that the “Proponent will commit to reevaluate on-site parking supply and demand 
when key PLAN: Charlestown Public Improvements are implemented”, the MBTA would encourage the 
proponent to plan for further reductions in parking demand by decreasing planned parking supply. Similar 
to how the proponent is planning to financially assist the Charlestown Link shuttle service the proponent 
could instead assist the MBTA in making improvements to the rapid transit and bus transit systems at 
Sullivan Square which will connect to other areas of Charlestown and Everett. Such assistance could

Dear Secretary Tepper: 
 
The Metropolitan Area Planning Council (MAPC) regularly reviews proposals deemed to have regional 
impacts. The Council reviews proposed projects for consistency with MetroCommon 2050, MAPC’s 
regional land use and policy plan, consistency with Complete Streets policies and design approaches, as 
well as impacts on the environment. 
 
60 Cambridge Development, LLC, the Proponent, has submitted a Draft Environmental Impact Report 
(DEIR) for the redevelopment of an approximately 4-acre site at 60-66 Cambridge Street in the 
Charlestown neighborhood of Boston. Currently, the site contains warehouse, parking, and vehicle 
storage uses, an Eversource/MBTA electrical substation structure, and an MBTA spur track. The 
proposed redevelopment will include approximately 802,000 square feet (sf) of life 
sciences/office/research and development (R&D) space in two buildings and approximately 10,000 sf of 
retail/restaurant/commercial space (the Project). 
 
The Project site is well served by transit services, with access to two Orange Line MBTA stations 
(Sullivan Square and Community College) and numerous nearby bus routes. The Sullivan Square 
MBTA station is located approximately 300 feet north of the Project site and Community College station 
is approximately 0.6 miles from the Project site. This Project proposes a total of 482 parking spaces.

amount given the site’s proximity and access to rapid transit (both existing and planned). According to 
the Proponent, the predicted traffic net CO2 emissions generated by this project will be 442 
tons/year1.

recommends that the Proponent make a few key adjustments to this project prior to their next 
submission. However, we would like to note that, overall, we find this project to be well planned and 
suited for an otherwise challenging and underutilized site in the shadow of an elevated highway, with

Parking 
 
While the proposed ratio of 0.6 per 1,000 sq ft parking ratio is decent, we urge the Proponent to reduce 
this ratio to .4 per 1,000 sq ft to keep pace with surrounding developments2 and to reflect the goals of 
PLAN: Charlestown which outlines .4 parking spaces per 1,000 sq ft for commercial development3. We 
note that the Proponent does state (in Section 5) that the proposed number of parking spaces (not to 
exceed 482 spaces) will be reevaluated for on-site parking supply and demand when key PLAN: 
Charlestown Public Improvements are implemented. However, it is preferable to comply with PLAN’s 
objectives now, rather than making a conditional promise to remove parking spaces at an unspecified 
date in the future. 
 
To minimize demand for employee parking, incentivize use of transit, and reduce vehicle trips to the 
site, we strongly urge that the Proponent require employers to charge for parking on a daily, rather than 
monthly or even weekly, basis. Research4 consistently supports that availability of parking at the 
worksite is the top determinant of employees’ decision to drive to work over other available options, 
and that when parking is free, or even offered through a monthly pass (therefore seen as a “sunk cost”), 
all other efforts to induce mode shift away from driving are significantly diminished. 
 
To further reduce demand for parking, and to reflect the goals of the Transportation Demand 
Management (TDM) Point System Tool of the Boston Transportation Department (BTD), we commend 
the Proponent for “unbundling” the cost of parking from rent and leasing costs. By providing tenants 
with the option to lease or purchase building space without inclusion of a market rate price for on-site 
parking, companies are encouraged to rethink the value of parking at their worksite and to invest 
instead in other multimodal options. This can effectively reduce vehicle trips as well as dangerous 
emissions generated because of the project. 
 
Commuter Incentives 
 
To make transit a competitive choice for employees, it must be incentivized through subsidies on par 
with or superior to driving. MAPC commends the Proponent for committing to a minimum 25% T-pass 
subsidy for the property owner or employer. However, this commitment should also be included as a 
condition of lease agreements. This commitment is particularly critical if parking continues to be offered 
at no cost, which we strongly discourage (see above).

initial community feedback from the planning process. Until topics such as land use, urban

guidance on whether the proposal’s approach to these issues complies with PLAN:
Charlestown. When complete, PLAN: Charlestown will establish a comprehensive and
coordinated plan to ensure the equitable provision of infrastructure to support future land
uses and development; mobility connections into and within Charlestown; parks and open
space; climate resiliency; affordable housing; and strategies to enhance the existing
community and preserve its historic assets. Staff feedback is subject to change based on
the completion of PLAN: Charlestown.

Dear Ms. Black,
The City of Boston’s Age Strong Commission is submitting the following comments on the
PNF for the 66 Cambridge St project currently proposed by The Fallon Company and
Owens Companies. Age Strong is pleased to see an underutilized space converted into a
multi use district that enhances transit connections in a neighborhood underserved by
transit and provides valuable public space This is a difficult area to navigate for pedestrians
so we particularly support the pedestrian connection between the project site and the
Sullivan Square MBTA station and the addition of multiple large public open spaces. We
would like to note several age friendly features; a covered ramp that is adjacent to a
staircase to give equal treatment to the accessible entry, wayfinding signage, and the
Woonerf Zone to designate passenger pickup and dropoff.
A. Older Adults in the Workforce
We appreciate the inclusion of jobs for all ages in your project. Age is an often
overlooked diversity in employment and older adults face high rates of
unemployment and underemployment in Boston. We hope you will incorporate skills
training or reverse mentorship for older workers into your workforce training
program.
B. New Trees
Tree canopy is an essential physical and mental health tool to address heat related
illnesses in older adults and the effects of lack of green space in an urban
environment. This industrial area is underserved by plants and trees. Age Strong
supports the planting of new trees and vegetation. We would like to see details
about the design of tree pits, which should maintain accessibility while preserving
the health of the tree. We would also like to see plans for maintenance to ensure the
health of the plantings as well as keep the area accessible and safe.
C. Age Friendly Seating
We recommend adding benches at regular intervals along pedestrian paths and
corridors and incorporating some age friendly seating into any open or common
spaces that feature seating. Seating that is age-friendly includes armrests for ease of
access and vertical backrests for additional support. When siting outdoor benches,
cite them if possible under an overhang, awning or tree to provide shade.

driveway. However, the infrastructure should prioritize the responsibility of drivers
to spot pedestrians.

On behalf of the Massachusetts Port Authority (“Massport”), we welcome the opportunity to submit comments on 
the Project Notification Form filed recently by the 60 Cambridge Development LLC (the “Proponent”) for the 
redevelopment of that certain property containing approximately 4 acres and located at 66 Cambridge Street in 
Charlestown (the “Property”) near Sullivan Square. The Proponent proposes to redevelop the Property for 
approximately 812,000 square feet of commercial office and life sciences space and approximately 646 below 
grade parking spaces. As the owner of the narrow private right-of-way (commonly referred to by parties other 
than Massport as “D Street”) that abuts the Project, which is proposed to be the primary means of access to the 
Property, Massport’s primary interest is in understanding how the Project will impact Massport’s ownership and 
long-term use of the Mystic Wharf Branch Rail Right-of-Way (the “ROW”) as well as the Project’s required use 
of the ROW for vehicle and other access and egress, and what the potential impacts of that use will have on the 
existing rights of other businesses that utilize the ROW. In the early 2000’s, Massport purchased the ROW with 
the support of the Massachusetts Department of Transportation (“MassDOT”) to preserve the ROW upon a 
portion of which are the rail serving the Mystic River Designated Port Area. 
 
Mystic Wharf Branch Rail Right of Way (so-called ”D Street”). As an abutter and the owner of the ROW, 
which includes the private way commonly referred to as D Street, Massport is interested in understanding how the 
additional new daily vehicle trips generated by the Project (once finally determined) will impact access/egress to, 
and maintenance and operations along Massport’s ROW, which is a private way. 
 
We recognize that the Project is still in the early stages and details still remain on the final development program, 
vehicle trips, utility needs and other elements that may impact Massport’s ROW, which is in active use by 
adjacent industrial businesses and MassDOT’s District 6 Satellite Maintenance Facility and Emergency Response 
Station 10 on its western end of the Project, and to the Graphic Lofts residences (32 Cambridge Street) to the 
eastern end intersecting with Rutherford Avenue. In addition, the 1.7 million square for Hood Park development 
just to the south will also have access to the ROW as well as crossings over the rail tracks (the “ROW Rail”). All 
of whom have varying easement rights for use of the ROW. It will be important to understand as the Project 
continues to evolve what the proposed usage of the ROW will be and what impacts it will have on these pre-
existing rights holders. Given that many of these are heavy industrial users with frequent truck movements, we 
will also need to understand the safety measures planned to minimize potential conflicts with these 
commercial/industrial trucks and pedestrians and bicycles that may also use the ROW as a result of the Project, 
and encourage the Proponent to direct these modes of access to the Property at other points away from the ROW.

SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority

to: (1) issue a Certification of Approval for the proposed development located at 66

PROJECT SITE 
 
The Proposed Project is located at 66 Geneva Avenue in Roxbury (the “Project Site”). 
The Project Site consists of one (1) parcel which contains approximately 19,673 
square feet, which is currently improved with a single floor structure encompassing 
approximately 17,200 square feet. The Proposed Project is ideally situated within 
walking distance from the Four Corners/Geneva MBTA Commuter Rail Station and 
is well served by multiple MBTA Bus Routes.

DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
 
The Proponent proposes the construction of a five-story residential building 
totaling approximately 48,912 gross square feet which will contain approximately 
fifty (50) homeownership units, including eight (8) IDP Units, and seventeen (17) at-
grade garage parking spaces (the “Proposed Project”). The building will contain 
eight (8) studio units, sixteen (16) one-bedroom units, eighteen (18) two-bedroom 
units, and eight (8) three-bedroom units. The Proposed Project will include a 
maximum of seventeen (17) parking spaces and fifty (50) interior secure resident 
bike spaces and ten (10) exterior visitor post-and-ring bike parking spaces. 
 
The Proponent plans to commence construction of the Proposed Project in the 
second quarter of 2023. There are an estimated100 construction jobs which will 
contribute to the Proposed Project. The total development cost is approximately 
Fifteen Million Dollars ($15,000,000). 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On June 29, 2022, the Proponent filed a Small Project Review application with the 
BPDA for the Proposed Project, pursuant to Article 80E of the Code. The BPDA 
sponsored public meetings on July 18, 2022, and October 6, 2022 via Zoom. The 
meeting was advertised in the relevant neighborhood newspaper, the Bay State 
Banner. The public meeting was posted on the BPDA website, a notification was 
posted to the BPDA website, and a notification was emailed to all subscribers of the 
BPDA’s Dorchester neighborhood update list. The BPDA comment period, with 
extensions to allow for comments on project updates, ended on October 14, 2022. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT AND CITY STAFF REVIEW 
The Proposed Project is located within the planning boundaries of the Roxbury 
Strategic Master Plan (“RSMP”), a strategic framework, adopted in 2004, to guide 
change and economic growth in Roxbury over the next ten to twenty years. 

The Proposed Project makes significant contributions towards the realization of the 
RSMP’s goals of providing a wide range of housing opportunities by proposing 
100% homeownership condos totaling to 50 residential units with 16% of the units 
designated under the Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”). The units vary in size 
from studio to 3-bedroom which serves the projected needs based on the 
demographics of households in the area. The Proposed Project further advances 
RSMP’s goals of promoting a diverse and sustainable economy by proactively hiring 
local, minority and women-owned businesses as part of the workforce in the 
development of the Proposed Project. Further, the Proponent has committed to 
pedestrian improvements along Geneva Avenue improving the pedestrian 
experience on Geneva Avenue. Additionally, the parking ratio is below the 
maximum parking ratios per citywide guidelines which advances both mobility and

BACKGROUND AND CONTEXT 
Roxbury Preparatory Charter School (“Roxbury Prep”) was founded in 1999 with a 
single middle school located in Mission Hill. Today Roxbury Prep consists of three 
middle schools and a high school with a total of approximately 1,600 students, over 
90% of whom are Boston residents. Roxbury Prep is part of the Uncommon 
Schools, Inc. network and its mission is to prepare students to enter, succeed in, 
and graduate from college. Roxbury Prep is free and open to all families living in 
the City of Boston and, in accordance with state law, accepts students by random, 
public lottery. The current student body is 97% Black and LatinX and 76% 
economically disadvantaged. 
 
Roxbury Prep High School opened in 2015 and has been housed in temporary and 
split campuses since its opening. Currently the High School is in leased space in 
Cleary Square, Hyde Park and Nubian Square, Roxbury. The temporary nature of 
the facilities, the missing program elements (such as a gymnasium), and the six 

 
 
miles separating the campuses combine to present significant operational, 
educational, and cultural challenges. The Proposed Project will permit the school to 
serve all its students in one facility at a location accessible to its student body by 
public transit and within its core student demographic area. 
 
With the development of this new state-of-the-art high school facility, Roxbury Prep 
High School scholars will be able to excel in the learning environment they deserve 
and the larger organization will have a permanent flagship campus to which all its 
students can aspire. 
 
DESCRIPTION OF PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
The Proposed Project involves the demolition of the existing buildings on the 
Project Site, and the construction of a new four-story academic facility of 
approximately 83,500 square feet of gross floor area. The new school facility will 
include a cafeteria, high school regulation gymnasium, art room, four science labs, 
engineering space, over thirty core classrooms, special education spaces, and 
administrative space. In addition, it will include approximately 46 on-site vehicular 
parking spaces located at grade, with a portion of the parking area located below a 
cantilevered section of the building. Over 200 feet of the sidewalk on both Proctor 
Street and Magazine Street in front of the school building will be widened and 
rebuilt to create a welcoming public space for Roxbury Prep students, staff, visitors, 
and the public. 
 
The Proposed Project will comply with the Boston Transportation Department’s 
Transportation Demand Management Points System. The Proposed Project will also 
comply with the Boston 2020 Bike Parking Guidelines. Exterior bike racks will be 
located near the front entrance on Proctor Street and an interior bike storage room 
will be accessible from Proctor Street without transiting through the main entrance 
lobby. 
 
PUBLIC BENEFITS AND MITIGATION 
 
The Proposed Project will provide high quality, free, public education to 
approximately 800 high school students, almost all of whom are Boston residents, 
at a location which is easily accessible by public transportation. 
 
In addition, the Proposed Project will: 

 
 
● Introduce a well-established, highly successful institutional presence to the 
Newmarket district which will serve as a neighborhood anchor, catalyze high 
quality development, and contribute toward the overall stewardship of the 
public realm. 
 
● Provide a measure of transparency into the cafeteria and lobby areas along 
Proctor Street in order to activate the streetscape. 
 
● Remove blight with over $1,000,000 of investment into site clearance, 
environmental mitigation, ground improvements, and utility infrastructure. 
 
● Reconstruct 375’ of public sidewalks, accessible pedestrian ramps, a 
crosswalk, curb cuts, and new street trees in compliance with Boston 
Complete Streets Guidelines. 
 
● Become a new active member and substantial contributor to the newly 
formed Newmarket Business Improvement District. 
 
● Increase educational opportunities for students in the neighborhood. 
 
● Provide after-hour public access to a meeting space and a gymnasium. 
 
● Create approximately 175 construction jobs subject to the Boston Resident 
Jobs Policy. 
● Comply with the City’s Bike Parking Guidelines as it relates to bike parking 
and required Bluebikes contribution, to be finalized with BPDA and BTD prior 
to Certificate of Occupancy.. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The Proposed Project is located within the area which is currently the focus of 
PLAN: Newmarket, a BPDA planning initiative for the Newmarket District which 
commenced in 2020. The PLAN: Newmarket initiative has involved many robust 
discussions with community members and businesses which have resulted in an 
evolving vision for the district. Major goals of the PLAN include preservation and 
enhancement of employment opportunities provided by commercial businesses in 
the district, activation of ground floor street front spaces, improvement of transit 
routes, climate resiliency measures, and safety enhancements. 
 
While the educational use has not been specifically identified as a target land use in 
the PLAN, the Proposed Project is consistent with the PLAN objectives: 

 
 
 
● Together staff and students represent close to 1,000 new consumers in the 
neighborhood to support local businesses. 
 
● The Proctor Street frontage will offer significant street presence by virtue of 
the widened and improved sidewalk terrace and entrance plaza, and the light 
and transparency to the school cafeteria. 
 
● School traffic on Magazine Street, which was identified as a commercial 
transportation route, is limited to only 46 staff auto trips and occasional 
deliveries and trash removal. There is no pedestrian access to the school 
from Magazine Street. However, the Magazine Street frontage is an 
important pedestrian experience, as it connects many residents from 
neighboring transit facilities in Roxbury to public facilities in Newmarket. 
 
● The Project will be developed to be climate resilient. 
 
● The school’s presence facing directly out onto Clifford Park will provide a 
constant visual connection during school hours, thus enhancing safety and 
stewardship of the public park. 
 
Roxbury Prep has committed to establishing itself as a community anchor and 
economic driver dedicated to deep relationships with its neighboring institutions. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
Following several pre-filing meetings with the BPDA, the Proponent filed a Project 
Notification Form (“PNF”) for the Proposed Project on June 16, 2022. Notice of 
receipt by the BPDA of the PNF was published in the Boston Herald on June 29, 
2021, initiating a thirty (30) day public comment period which was extended until 
August 19, 2022. The notice and the PNF were sent to the City’s public agencies 
pursuant to Section 80A-2 of the Code. 
 
Pursuant to Section 80B-5.3 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”), a Scoping 
Session was held on July 11, 2022, with the City’s public agencies during which the 
Proposed Project was reviewed and discussed. On July 25, 2022, the BPDA held an 
Impact Advisory Group (“IAG”) Meeting and on July 28, 2022 the BPDA held a Public 
Meeting. 
 

 
 
Large Project Review under Article 80 of the Code also covers climate change 
preparedness and resiliency, carbon neutral building assessment, handicap 
accessibility, green building standards, and smart utilities. Determination was 
made that the Proposed Project would not require review by the Boston Civic 
Design Commission. 
 
SUSTAINABILITY 
 
The Proposed Project will be designed to meet or exceed LEEDv4 Gold 
requirements. The building will feature an all-electric heating and cooling system 
and, with the sole exception of fuel for the back-up generator, will utilize no fossil 
fuels. In support of Boston’s carbon neutrality goals, the Roxbury Prep modeling 
currently shows that the Proposed Design achieves a 39% energy savings against a 
baseline building and will be compliant with existing City of Boston Carbon 
Emission Intensity (CEI) limits beyond 2035 with a predictive modeled performance 
of 2035 Carbon Emission Intensity of 1.37 kg CO2e/sf-yr. The building will be 
constructed solar PV ready, and the Project Team is in discussions with PV 
providers to install a system immediately upon construction completion. 
Compliance with Article 37 is a requirement of standard design review which takes 
place following Article 80 and as a precursor to issuance of Certificate(s) of 
Compliance. 
 
ZONING 
 
In order to carry out the Proposed Project, under Article 50 Roxbury Prep is seeking 
zoning relief from the Boston Zoning Code (“Zoning Code”)with respect to certain 
aspects of the Proposed Project. Per the Zoning Code Map 6A/6B/6C, the Project 
Site is located within the Roxbury Neighborhood District and within the Newmarket 
Industrial Development Area (IDA) Subdistrict. The Project Site is not located in any 
overlay districts. The Project Site is located within 100 feet of a City-owned Park, 
which means that the Project will require approval of the Boston Parks and 
Recreation Commission per City of Boston Municipal Code Section 7-4.11. 
 
Per the Zoning Code, the Proposed Project will require Zoning Relief from the Board 
of Appeals for the following: 
 
1. Conditional Use Permit for elementary or secondary school per Article 50, 
Table A, pursuant to Section 50-32 of the Code. 
 

 
 
2. Dimensional variance from the terms of Article 50, Table G of the Code for 
deviation from required Maximum Floor Area Ratio of 2.0. The Proposed 
Project will have a Floor Area Ratio of approximately 2.39.

Neighborhood District within a Multifamily / Local Services (MFR/LS) Subdistrict,

proposed mix of active ground floor use and residential on upper stories aligns well 
with the MFR/LS zoning, and the built environment of mixed-use context of this 
portion of East Broadway.

staff review of the project, the amount of usable open space was increased through 
the addition of rear balconies. Streetscape improvements were designed in 
collaboration with staff to ensure compliance with Complete Street Guidelines 
along with the addition of three street trees. 
 
The proposed height and floor area ratio exceeds the maximum dimensions 
established by Article 68. However, zoning relief is appropriate given the Proposed 
Project’s consistency with an established dimensional context found on this section 
of East Broadway, as well as the general purpose and intent of the Code.

The Commission has the following comments regarding the proposed project. 

General 
1. 
Prior to the initial phase of the site plan development, ST A TS, should meet with the 
Commission's Design and Engineering Customer Services Departments to review water 
main, sewer and storm drainage system availability and potential upgrades that could 
impact the development. 
2. 
Prior to demolition of any buildings, all water, sewer and storm drain connections to the 
buildings must be cut and capped at the main pipe in accordance with the Commission's 
requirements. The proponent must complete a Cut and Cap General Services Application, 
available from the Commission. 
3. 
All new or relocated water mains, sewers and storm drains must be designed and 
constructed at ST A TS, expense. They must be designed and constructed in conformance 
with the Commission's design standards, Water Distribution System and Sewer Use 
regulations, and Requirements for Site Plans. The site plan should include the locations 
of new, relocated and existing water mains, sewers and drains which serve the site, 
proposed service connections, water meter locations, as well as backflow prevention 
devices in the facilities that will require inspection. A General Service Application must 
also be submitted to the Commission with the site plan. 
4. 
The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), in cooperation with the 
Massachusetts Water Resources Authority (MWRA) and its member communities, has 
implemented a coordinated approach to flow control in the MWRA regional wastewater 
system, particularly the removal of extraneous clean water ( e.g., infiltration/inflow (I/I)) 
in the system. The Commission has a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System 
(NPDES) Permit for its combined sewer overflows and is subject to these new 
regulations [314 CMR 12.00, section 12.04(2)(d)]. This section requires all new sewer 
connections with design flows exceeding 15,000 gpd to mitigate the impacts of the 
development by removing four gallons ofl/I for each new gallon of wastewater flow. In 
this regard, any new connection or expansion of an existing connection that exceeds 
15,000 gallons per day of wastewater shall assist in the 1/1 reduction effort to ensure that 
the additional wastewater flows are offset by the removal of 1/1. Currently, a minimum 
ratio of 4:1 for 1/1 removal to new wastewater flow added is used. The Commission will 
require proponent to develop a consistent inflow reduction plan. The 4: 1 requirement 
should be addressed at least 90 days prior to activation of water service and will be based 
on the estimated sewage generation provided on the project site plan. 
5. 
The design of the project should comply with the City of Boston's Complete Streets 
Initiative, which requires incorporation of"green infrastructure" into street 
designs. Green infrastructure includes greenscapes, such as trees, shrubs, grasses and 
other landscape plantings, as well as rain gardens and vegetative swales, infiltration 
basins, and paving materials and permeable surfaces. The proponent must develop a

maintenance plan for the proposed green infrastructure. For more information on the

demand for residential, irrigation and air-conditioning make-up water for the project.

1.

(MTU) and connect the device to the meter. For information regarding the installation of

ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
 
On November 13, 2023, the Proponent filed a Notice of Project Change (“NPC”) with 
the BPDA for the Proposed Project, pursuant to Article 80E of the Code. The NPC 
was sent to the City’s public agencies/departments and elected officials pursuant to 
Section 80A-2 of the Code. 
 
On January 10, 2024, a Virtual Public Meeting was held. The Virtual Public Meeting 
was advertised in the local Bay State Banner, listed on the BPDA website, and 
distributed to those enrolled in the BPDA Roxbury email list. The public comment 
period ended on January 16, 2024. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The Proposed Project is located at the intersection of Dudley Street and Guild Row, 
directly across from the Dudley Square Plaza. The site is located in the center of 
Nubian Square, Roxbury’s commercial and cultural center. The proposed building 
scale is consistent with the context of the immediate built environment, which 
contains a mix of residential, commercial, and civic uses. 
 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
26 
The Roxbury Strategic Master Plan (2004), serves as the area plan for this location, 
and the Roxbury neighborhood as a whole. Key elements of this plan include the 
enhancement of the civic and cultural environment, promotion of a diverse 
economy and range of housing options, and creation of safer transportation 
connections and a lively public realm. The Proposed Project helps fulfill these 
planning goals through the creation of new income-restricted housing on currently 
vacant land. In addition to net new housing production, proposed site 
improvements will enhance the parcel’s edges, improving the public realm 
experience of this block. 
 
The Proposed Project is also located in the PLAN: Nubian Square study area. This 
parcel was cited by the plan as an exemplary location for infill development in the 
context of an established neighborhood fabric. In use and form, the proposal is 
well-aligned with the planning goal of ensuring that new development is both 
responsive to neighborhood context, and consistent with surrounding uses. 
 
 
ZONING 
 
The Project Site is situated within the Roxbury Neighborhood District and is 
governed by Article 50 of the Code. The previously Proposed Project was granted 
zoning relief from the following: Multifamily Residential Zoning, Minimum Lot Size,

Building Height (Stories), Maximum Building Height (Feet), Minimum Usable Open 
Space Per D.U., Minimum Front Yard, Minimum Side Yard (With Front Yard Special 
Provisions for Corner Lots, Section 50-44), Minimum approval of the project 
changes (from higher to lower density) from the ZBA acting Rear Yard, Minimum 
Number of Parking Spaces, Minimum Number of Off-Street Loading Bays, and 
Traffic Visibility Across Corner. 
 
The previous version of this Project had received zoning approval and relief which 
the Proponent has requested to extend. This request will be voted on at the March 
12, 2024, Board of Appeal meeting. Because of the previous zoning relief, the 
Proponent plans to request approval of the project changes (from higher to lower 
density) from the ZBA acting as board final arbiter. No additional relief is needed 
due to these design changes.

Projects financed as one entity and where at least forty (40) percent of the units are

fifteen (15) income restricted units, or 100 percent of the total units, surpassing 40 
percent of the total units. As such, the Proposed Project is exempt from the 
Inclusionary Development Policy.

affordability of the project will be finalized through the public funding process and 
the ongoing affordability of the project will be monitored by the City of Boston

the site at 75 Tremont Street includes a steep grade differential of approximately

DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
 
The Proponent seeks to activate this oversized and underutilized parcel of vacant 
land with a residential condominium development of appropriate scale, with 
innovativeprogramming and family-sized housing. The Proposed Project would 
include approximately 70 condominium homeownership units in a building of 
approximately 74,853 gross square feet, with 70 residential garage and covered 
surface parking spaces, along with widened sidewalks, open space and related 
amenities, and overall site upgrades (collectively, the “Proposed Project”). 
 
The scope and scale of the development program is also intended to advance the 
policy goals of the City of Boston’s 2030 Housing Plan and its Affirmatively 
Furthering Fair Housing initiative, by creating more on-site affordable housing with 
greater family-sized units, in excess of the City’s Inclusionary Development Policy 
(the “IDP”). Furthermore, and in response to public feedback provided by the 
Impact Advisory Group during the Article 80 process, the Proposed Project will 
include provisions to require that at least sixty-five percent (65%) of its total units 
will be owner-occupied, as part of its future condominium program. 
 
Prior to filing with the BPDA, the Proponent engaged in nearly four (4) years of 
extensive preliminary outreach and advisory review with the BPDA staff and 
neighborhood leadership. As a result of this process, the Proposed Project was 
significantly reduced in scale, unit density and lot coverage (from 120 rental to 70

74,853 gross square feet of total floor area), with lush landscaping and vast usable 
open spaces; and changed, as noted from rental to homeownership, with larger 
family-sized units, including voluntary additional three (3) bedroom IDP units, and 
programming for mature buyers seeking to downsize in Brighton. 
 
The Proposed Project will transform the currently vacant and neglected Project Site 
into an active and pedestrian friendly area, and bring diverse housing into the 
neighborhood. Its new building has been carefully designed to address and 
respond to the steep change in grade, which uniquely burdens the Project Site, and 
to comport with the character and context of the surrounding neighborhood. The 
new building’s frontage will be modal and aligned with its adjacent structures along 
Tremont Street, with a variety of ground floor amenities, new widened sidewalks 
and improved open spaces, a robust street tree canopy and native plantings to 
better activate the streetscape. 
 
Covered parking will be shielded behind the amenity uses on the ground floor, with 
solar on parking roof for sustainable on-site energy production. Vast usable open 
space for the building residents will be created at an internal courtyard on the 
second floor (at the west), along with a southern-facing roof terrace on the 5th level 
of the new structure, in addition to private unit patios (which open to the second-
floor courtyard). Outdoor programming and amenity spaces at the improved 
overall Project Site will also include gardening plots, a walking trail and pet relief 
areas. 
 
Due to the steep grade differential from Tremont Street to the rear of the Project 
Site, the building height steps up with four (4) floors along Tremont Street and two 
(2) visible floors of units at the rear elevation at the top of the hill. The vehicular and 
service access to the Project Site is from a single new curb cut on the east property 
edge. The existing bus stopswill be relocated to better accommodate a new mid-
block crossing and will be provided with a new covered bus shelter as a public 
amenity, and as a part of the Proponent’s mitigation, for the neighborhood along 
with some new landscaped seating area adjacent to the bus stop.

The Proposed Project is located within the Allston-Brighton Mobility Study area

project’s proximity to Oak Square and the surrounding residential fabric. Special 
consideration was given to the need to provide a landscape plan that incorporates 
quality flora given that the existing condition of the site is deficient in diverse

The Proposed Project contributes to the overall walkability and transit-oriented 
development described in the Allston-Brighton Mobility Study through the 
commitment to add a raised concrete island and moving the MBTA Bus Stop near

subdistrict that permits uses like the multifamily residential proposed in the 
project. While the Project will need relief from the Zoning Board of Appeals, it

requires a Variance for its proposed Multifamily Residential Use. With

PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The Proposed Project is located within the Allston-Brighton Mobility Study area 
which focuses on increasing mobility for all. During review, BPDA staff considered 
future conditions proposed in the Allston Multimodal Project (also known as the I-
90 Interchange Project) by the Massachusetts Department of Transportation 
(MassDOT), which includes the creation of a commuter rail station known as West 
Station. Due to the site’s proximity to and prime access to the future West Station, it 
is imperative that a primarily residential project be developed to support 
multimodal infrastructure. 
 
The Proposed Project contributes to the overall walkability and creation of transit-
oriented development described in the Allston-Brighton Mobility Study and the 
Allston Multimodal Project by offering the necessary easements to connect the 
future West Station to Brighton Avenue and Commonwealth Avenue through 
Malvern Street. Also, BPDA staff recommended that the interim condition of the 
future easement to West Station to the west of the proposed project not stray far 
from the site's long-term use with the goal of minimizing community disruption in 
the future. 
 
Additionally, during review staff considered the proposed project’s zoning context. 
The proposed project is in the Ashford Street Local Industrial (LI-1) subdistrict of the 
Allston/Brighton Neighborhood zoning district and is neighbor to the Boston 
University Institutional Master Plan (IMP) and a 3F-4000 subdistrict. While the 
Project will need relief from the Zoning Board of Appeals, the proposed project 
provides major multimodal infrastructure improvements that will benefit the 
Allston-Brighton neighborhoods. The proponent team should continue 
coordination with the City of Boston, MassDOT, and the MBTA to ensure alignment 
with ongoing planning efforts in the area.

(7) minute walk of MBTA Green Line and bus service (Babcock Street 
Station) and is located immediately adjacent to the future 
MBTA/MassDOT West Station transportation hub. 
 
● Community Oriented & Affordable Retail Space 
 The Proposed Project includes two (2) ground floor retail spaces that 
collectively comprise approximately 1,875 square feet. One (1) of the 
retail spaces will be made available to a local, community based retail 
tenant at a below market-rate rent. 
 
● MassDOT/MBTA West Station Roadway Connection 
 MassDOT has been leading a multi-agency planning effort for the Allston 
Multimodal Project. The proposed infrastructure project creates an 
opportunity to dramatically improve livability and connectivity for 
residents of the Allston neighborhood while preserving and enhancing 
regional mobility through improvements to I-90 and its abutting 
interchange and the creation of a new stop on the 
Worcester/Framingham Commuter Line to be known as West Station.

11 
 
MassDOT’s I-90 task force identified the Project Site as a vital part of the 
plan for the proposed infrastructure project. This parcel, directly abutting 
the future proposed location of West Station, is a key access point for 
pedestrian, bicycle, and bus traffic from the existing neighborhood. The 
Project Site is the only parcel abutting the planned station that would not 
require the removal of residential property or existing properties that are 
integral parts of the Boston University campus. Soon after acquiring the 
Project Site, the Proponent approached the MassDOT I-90 task force 
members and subsequently spent years working with them to 
incorporate the proposed multimodal connection into the Proposed 
Project plans. After multiple rounds of revisions to the plans, the current 
scheme for the Proposed Project includes an allocation of an 
approximately 16,545 square foot portion of the lot for this connection 
and constrained the Proposed Project to the remaining portion of the lot. 
 As an interim condition, while MassDOT, MBTA, and other applicable 
agencies, complete their infrastructure plans and obtain the necessary 
funding, the Proponent shall design and construct the approximately 
16,545 square foot portion of the Project Site as a staging area for the 
future roadway. Upon MassDOT’s (or another state entity) acquisition of 
the 16,545 square foot Project Site, MassDOT, MBTA, or other applicable 
agency will be responsible for final the design and construction of the 
permanent roadway condition. 
 
● Additional Affordable Housing Creation 
 In addition to the thirty six (36) on-site IDP units, the Proponent shall 
make a voluntary financial contribution of up to $4.5 million with the 
exact amount to be determined by the final Purchase and Sale Agreement 
of an approximately 16,545 square foot portion of the Project Site or 
equivalent thereof with MassDOT and/or other related entities, to the 
City’s Special IDP Fund. The financial contribution will be derived from the 
land transaction with MassDOT which consists of the sale of an 
approximately 16,545 square foot portion of the Project Site. Based on an 
appraisal done for that portion of the Project Site, the sale amount is 
anticipated to yield the creation of up to fifteen (15) additional income-
restricted units (using the off-site housing contribution calculation 
outlined in the 2015 City IDP, as the basis), which would raise the project’s 
IDP unit creation from thirty-six (36) on-site IDP units (14.2%) to up to fifty-
one (51) income-restricted units (36 on-site IDP units and up to 15 off-site

transaction closing between the Proponent and MassDOT or the

● Sustainable Design/Green Building
