existing IMP was approved by the BRA in 2009. In 2013 the IMP was renewed for 
four years, and then again was renewed in 2017 for four years. In 2021 it was 
renewed for two years, and most recently in 2023 it was renewed for another two 
year period through October 14, 2025. 
 
The existing IMP identifies the location of the Proposed Project as a site for future 
library storage. Staff have determined that the proposed use is well aligned with 
the intended use described by the site’s existing IMP zoning. The existing IMP 
describes the storage facility on this site as a 40 foot, 14,000 square foot addition to 
an existing library. The Proposed Project’s dimensions have increased to 55 feet 
and 44,000 square feet. The proposed dimensions would facilitate new storage 
demands of the library and achieve program goals of the school outlined in the 
purpose of the IMP, while having minimal impact on the surrounding context. 
 
Parking requirements will be satisfied by two accessible parking spaces, two service 
parking spaces and a loading area in front of the entrance to the Proposed Project. 
 
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS

Adequacy Determination approving the proposed Fifth Amendment to the Boston 
College 2009-2025 Institutional Master Plan (the “Fifth Amendment to the BC IMP”), 
and issue a Certification of Approval for the proposed development located at 117 
Lake Street and take any other actions and execute any other agreements and 
documents that the Director deems appropriate and necessary in connection with 
the Proposed Project. An appropriate vote follows:

FROM:

SUBJECT:

_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency ("BPDA") authorize the 
Director to: (1) issue a Scoping Determination Waiving Further Review for 
the proposed Building 108 project located at 108 Third Avenue in 
Charlestown (as defined below, the “Proposed Project”), in accordance 
with Article 80B, Large Project Review of the Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Code”); (2) issue a Certification of Compliance under Section 80B-6 of 
the Code upon successful completion of the Article 80 review process for 
the Proposed Project; and (3) enter into a Cooperation Agreement, and 
any and all other agreements and documents, and to take any and all 
other actions that the Director deems appropriate and necessary in 
connection with the Proposed Project. 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
PROJECT SITE 
 
The Proposed Project is located at 108 Third Avenue on a portion of Parcel NY-1 in the 
Historic Monument Area of the Charlestown Navy Yard within the Charlestown Urban 
Renewal Area, Project No. Mass. R-55. The Proposed Project is also located within the 
Harborpark: Charlestown Waterfront zoning district, and the Charlestown Navy Yard 
subdistrict, consisting of approximately 40,688 total square feet of land (the “Project 
Site”) and is within the Historic Monument Area of the Navy Yard. The Project Site was 
previously occupied by Building 108, the former power house for the Charlestown 
Navy Yard, which provided electricity, heat, and steam for the buildings throughout 
the Navy Yard. Building 108 was in a state of substantial disrepair and had a 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
25 
 
 
significant amount of hazardous materials throughout, including asbestos containing 
materials, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), lead, in addition to petroleum 
contamination in the soil. Demolition and remediation of that building has been 
completed. 
 
DEVELOPMENT TEAM 
The development team includes: 
 
Proponent:

PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
Power House CNY, LLC (the “Proponent”) proposes the redevelopment of the Project 
Site with the construction of an approximately 99,600 GSF building with 78,370 SF of 
research and development (R&D) space, 1,800 SF of restaurant/café space, and 39 
below-grade parking spaces. The ground floor will consist of an 8,150 SF lobby space, 
14,040 SF of R&D space, the 1,800 SF café, bicycle storage, restrooms, and utility 
space including a trash room for the nearby Ropewalk. 
 
The table below summarizes the Proposed Project’s key development metrics.

PLANNING AND ZONING CONTEXT 
 
The Proposed Project is located at 108 Third Avenue on a portion of Parcel NY-1 in the 
Historic Monument Area (HMA) of the Charlestown Navy Yard within the Charlestown 
Urban Renewal Area, Project No. Mass. R-55. The Project is also located within the 
Harborpark: Charlestown Waterfront zoning district, and the Charlestown Navy Yard 
subdistrict. 
 
The Charlestown Navy Yard (“CNY”), the Property’s neighborhood, is nationally 
significant as one of the earliest naval shipyards in the United States. 
Decommissioned in 1974, the CNY has retained many of its historic components, and 
is a significant site which illustrates aspects of the naval, industrial, and technological 
history of the United States. It is listed on the National Register of Historical Places 
and is a designated National Historic Landmark. 
 
Today, the CNY is an active hub of both historic and modern uses for residents, 
employees and visitors. In addition to residential properties and a marina with more 
than four hundred slips, it is also home to multiple restaurants, a hotel, and a 
terminal for the MBTA Charlestown-Downtown Boston ferry. The area boasts historic 
resources including a section of the Freedom Trail and the USS Constitution Museum, 
as well as first quality open space, such as Shipyard Park and Menino Park. The area 
is a hub for health care research and practice, including development and 
administrative affiliates of Partners Health Care and the Spaulding Rehabilitation 
Hospital. 
 
Historic preservation where possible has maintained the original form and character 
of the CNY, while public and private investment have revitalized the area and the 
larger Charlestown neighborhood. 
 
The Proposed Project must be consistent with the 1991 Municipal Harbor Plan and 
the 1990 Charlestown Navy Yard Master Plan. Because the Premises is within the 
Historical Monument Area of the CNY, redevelopment of the Project Site must also be 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
25 
 
 
consistent with the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for the Treatment of Historic 
Properties, the Charlestown Navy Yard Design Guidelines for Reuse for the Historic 
Monument Area, and the Charlestown Navy Yard Program for Preservation and Use. 
Final design approval of the Proposed Project will be required from National Park 
Service (“NPS”) and Massachusetts Historical Commission (“MHC”). The Proponent will 
engage in design review with BPDA, NPS and MHC. The Proponent will also engage 
with MHC and the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation to complete the Section 
106 review process under the National Historic Preservation Act. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On March 7, 2023, the Proponent filed a Project Notification Form (“PNF”) with the 
BPDA for the Proposed Project, pursuant to Article 80B of the Code. The BPDA 
sponsored and held a virtual Impact Advisory Group Meeting on May 15, 2023, and a 
virtual Public Meeting on May 17, 2023, both via Zoom. The public comment period 
ended on May 31, 2023. An additional Public Meeting and IAG meeting were held on 
June 23, 2025 via Zoom. The IAG and Public Meetings were advertised in the local 
newspapers, posted on the Planning Department website, and a notification was 
emailed to all subscribers of the Planning Department’s Charlestown neighborhood 
update list. 
 
MITIGATION AND COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
The Proposed Project will include mitigation measures and community benefits to the 
neighborhood and the City of Boston (the “City”), including: 
● Removal of the hazardous environmental conditions that have been present 
for over 50 years. The building will be replaced with a state-of-the-art facility 
designed to complement the historic buildings in the Historic Monument Area; 
● Landscaping along the street edges and between the Ropewalk and Building 
108, opening up the entire open space between the Ropewalk, Building 108, 
and Building 107, providing a cloistered and inviting space away from active 
streets; 
● $1 million in real estate taxes each year and pay into the Navy Yard’s Common 
Area Maintenance (CAM) fund; 
● Creation of approximately 150 construction jobs over the two-year 
construction period, exclusive of the jobs created by the remediation and 
demolition of the Site and once completed, the Proposed Project can be 
expected to provide for at least 100 to 125 jobs associated with the Research & 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
25 
 
 
Development/Lab space, plus 10 jobs associated with the operation of the new 
building; 
● Creation of safe, continuous, and ADA/AAB-compliant pedestrian and bicycle 
access to the site to complete the established street network and public realm 
within the Charlestown Navy Yard. 
 
SUSTAINABLE DESIGN/ GREEN BUILDING 
Article 37 encourages sustainable design, energy efficiency, resiliency, and resource 
efficiency by requiring projects subject to Article 80B, Large Project Review to also 
comply with Article 37 of the Code and demonstrate that a proposed project will 
meet the minimum requirements to become LEED Certifiable under the US Green 
Building Congress (USGBC). 
The Proponent and the design and engineering team are committed to these values 
and will prioritize increasing energy performance and seek strategies that support 
low-carbon building operations, integration of renewable energy resources, 
embodied carbon reduction via adaptive reuse, and will target LEED Gold 
certifiability. The facility will be designed and constructed to provide infrastructure 
and space for future 100% electrification. 
As a proviso of this memo, the Proponent will provide an updated energy model 
and Climate Resiliency check list based upon current design within 6 months of 
Board approval 
SMART UTILITIES 
The Proponent and design and engineering team will comply with the Smart Utilities 
requirements found in Article 80B of the Code. The Proposed Project shall meet or 
exceed the 1.25” of stormwater infiltration per square inch of impervious 
development as indicated in the PNF and will incorporate best practice green 
infrastructure standards within the public realm, when applicable. These elements 
include but are not limited to porous curb extensions, bio-retention strategies 
and/or rain gardens. The Proposed Project will also include smart streetlights 
standards for new sidewalks, including city shadow conduit and dual handholes in 
accordance with Public Improvement Commission requirements. Utilities in any City 
right of way will be designed to conform with Public Works Department standards 
and will undergo further review to ensure they are not in conflict with any 
landscape design feature such as tree pits and/or other green infrastructure 
elements. Utilities on site will be designed to ensure that there is no conflict with 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
25 
 
 
any proposed landscape features and shall be coordinated with neighboring utility 
infrastructure including the existing Ropewalk geothermal borefield as design 
progresses. The Proposed Project will also provide access for local telecom and fiber 
providers to ensure broadband equity and possible future deployment of smart 
technologies 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
The Proposed Project complies with the requirements set forth in Section 80B of the 
Code for Large Project Review. Therefore, staff recommends that the Director be 
authorized to: (1) issue a Scoping Determination Waiving Further Review for the 
proposed Building 108 project located at 108 Third Avenue in Charlestown, in 
accordance with Article 80B, Large Project Review of the Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Code”); (2) issue a Certification of Compliance under Section 80B-6 of the Code upon 
successful completion of the Article 80 review process for the Proposed Project; and 
(3) enter into a Cooperation Agreement, and any and all other agreements and 
documents, and to take any and all other actions that the Director deems appropriate 
and necessary in connection with the Proposed Project. 
 
VOTED: 
That the Director of the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) be, and 
hereby is, authorized to issue a Scoping Determination Waiving Further 
Review under Section 80B-5.3(d) of the Boston Zoning Code for the 
project located at 108 Third Avenue in the Charlestown neighborhood of 
Boston (the “Proposed Project”) which: (i) finds that the Project 
Notification Form submitted on March 7, 2023, adequately describes the 
potential impacts arising from the Proposed Project in the Charlestown 
area, and provides sufficient mitigation measures to minimize these 
impacts; and (ii) waives further review of the Proposed Project under 
Section 80B-5 of the Code, subject to continuing design review by the 
BRA and other parties noted above; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue a Certification of 
Compliance or one or more Partial Certification of Compliance under 
Section 80B-6 of the Code for the Proposed Project upon the successful 
completion of all Article 80 processes for the Proposed Project or any 
phase thereof; and 
 
FURTHER

That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to execute a Cooperation 
 
 
Agreement, and any and all other agreements and documents that the 
 
 
Director deems appropriate and necessary in connection with the 
 
 
Proposed Project, all upon terms and conditions determined to be in the 
 
 
best interest of the BRA.

To Whom It May Concern, 
I am writing to express my support for the proposed redevelopment of Building 108 in 
the Charlestown Navy Yard by Power House CNY, LLC. This project represents a 
thoughtful and forward-looking reuse of a historically significant, yet environmentally 
compromised site. It aligns well with the broader goals outlined in the Charlestown Navy 
Yard Master Plan. 
 
The proposed scale and use of the site are appropriate and do not present any adverse 
effects for the National Park Service, though further collaboration is required to resolve 
structural and boundary issues at the Connector Building. The redevelopment of the 
Building 108 site offers a transformative opportunity to revitalize a key location within 
the Navy Yard, support Boston’s innovation economy, and promote sustainable urban 
development. 
 
I encourage the BPDA to continue supporting this important project. 
Sincerely,

SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(“BRA”) d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) 
authorize the Director to: (1) issue a determination pursuant to Article 
80, Section 80A-6 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”) in connection 
with a Notice of Project Change (the “NPC”) filed by Jamaica Plain 
Neighborhood Development Corporation (“Proponent”) on March 8, 
2023, for the Cheney Street Homes project in the Dorchester 
neighborhood of Boston (as further described below, and as modified 
by the NPC, the “Proposed Project”); (2) issue a Certification of 
Compliance under Section 80B-6 of the Code upon successful 
completion of the Article 80 review process for the Proposed Project as 
modified by the NPC; and (3) execute and deliver a Cooperation 
Agreement which will include a provision regarding a Boston Residents 
Construction Employment Plan, and any and all other agreements and 
documents that the Director deems appropriate and necessary in 
connection with the Proposed Project as modified by the NPC. 
 
 
 
 
1Effective October 20, 2016, the BRA commenced doing business as BPDA. 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
17 
 
 
PROJECT SITE 
The Proposed Project is located at 4-18 Cheney Street in Dorchester (the “Project 
Site”). The site is located near Franklin Park and close to a vibrant commercial 
district on Blue Hill Avenue. Nearby services include the Grove Hall Branch Public 
Library, a Stop & Shop grocery store, a US Post Office, and the Jeremiah E. Burke 
High School. The three (3) sites are arrayed on a slope, with edges along Cheney, 
Hartwell, and Schuyler Streets. An existing one-story industrial building 
encompasses the 4-18 Cheney Street parcel. 
 
Although the original BPDA approval covered two (2) adjacent properties (3 
Schuyler and 20-28 Cheney), the NPC seeks BPDA approval only for changes related 
to the apartment building located at 4-18 Cheney St (“Cheney Homes”). Any 
changes to the program at the other two properties, 3 Schuyler and 20-28 Cheney, 
may be the subject of a future Notice of Project Change. 
 
DEVELOPMENT TEAM 
 
The Development Team for the Proposed Project has not changed since the filing 
by the Proponent of the Project Notification Form ("PNF") for the Proposed Project 
on or about October 1, 2020, and consists of: 
 
Proponent:

DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
The Proposed Project as modified by the NPC reflects the Proponent’s desire to 
maximize production of affordable units in a way that incorporates a deep level of 
community input. The original proposal included new construction at three 
locations that triggered BPDA review. This current iteration includes new 
construction at the same three locations, but with less density/impact, as requested 
by local community groups during an extensive public review process. 
 
The overall Cheney Street project, as modified by the NPC (the “Proposed Project”), 
will consist of new construction of three separate residential buildings with an 
aggregate of sixty (60) new affordable housing units, forty-eight (48) senior rental 
units and twelve (12) homeownership units for families. As originally proposed, the 
overall Cheney Street project was to consist of three separate residential buildings 
with an aggregate of seventy-four (74) new affordable housing units, fifty-nine (59) 
senior rental units and fifteen (15) homeownership units for families. Since the 
original BPDA approval, the developer has revised the unit count. The overall 
project concept, which is unchanged by the NPC, combines rental housing and 
affordable homeownership and will facilitate comprehensive resident services for 
tenants, including PACE services for any neighborhood resident enrolled in the 
program and other services for special needs populations as appropriate. 
 
Due to funding constraints, the development of the senior rental housing is now on 
a different timeline from the development of the homeownership units. The 
funding deadlines for the rental component necessitate securing BPDA approval of 
a Notice of Project Change at this time. The homeownership project may come 
before the BPDA board at a future date as the project evolves. 
 
For purposes of this board vote, the Proposed Project includes the demolition of an 
existing vacant industrial building, and the construction of a new residential 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
17 
 
 
building. The Proposed Project will provide approximately 5,500 sf of community 
space, a total parking count, as modified by the NPC, of 37 spaces (increased from 
34 spaces as originally proposed) (with 25 parking spaces now to be located under 
the mid-rise rental building). The Project will have a mix of affordable rental 
units at 30% AMI, 50% AMI, and 60% AMI; as well as affordable homeownership 
units at 80% AMI and 100% AMI. 
 
Building A: 4-18 Cheney Street comprises a four-story building located on the north 
side of the Project site. The building, as modified by the NPC, is now proposed to 
include approximately forty-eight (48) senior residential rental units (decreased 
from fifty-nine (59)), with a mix of one and two-bedroom apartments all ranging 
from 30%, 50% and 60% of AMI with approximately 5,500 sf of community space. 
The building will include approximately 25 at-grade level parking spaces (reduced 
from 28) tucked under the building and accessed from Cheney Street. The ell-
shaped building will frame a landscaped courtyard. As requested by community 
input, building height and floor area ratio have been reduced, and the building has 
been pushed back further off the street. 
 
The Proponent anticipates the construction of Building A in late 2023, with all 
construction completed within approximately sixteen to eighteen months. The 
total development cost of Building A is approximately Thirty-Five Million Dollars 
($35,000,000).

ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On September 20, 2020, in accordance with the BPDA’s policy on mitigation as 
outlined in the Mayors Executive Order Relative to the Provision of Mitigation by 
Development Projects in Boston, the Proponent submitted a Letter of Intent to 
develop the Cheney Apartments at 4-18 Cheney Street, 20-28 Cheney Street and 3 
Schuyler Street in Dorchester. 
Letters soliciting nominations to the IAG for the Proposed Project were delivered via 
email to then City Councilor Andrea Campbell, State Senator Nick Collins, State 
Representative Chynah Tyler. Additional letters seeking recommendations were 
delivered via email to the Office of Neighborhood Services and the City Councilors 
at large. There were no responses from any of the elected officials and as a result 
there was no IAG formed. 
On or about October 1, 2020, the Proponent filed the PNF with the BPDA pursuant 
to Article 80B of the Code. A Scoping Session for City and State officials was held on 
October 19, 2020. 
On July 29, 2021, a public meeting was held virtually via Zoom. The Public Meeting 
was advertised in the Dorchester Reporter and the Bay State Banner and posted on 
the BPDA website, and was distributed to the BPDA Dorchester email list. In 
addition, JPNDC hosted 5 Community Meetings between May 2019 and April 2021. 
JPNDC also presented at 6 community meetings including Project R.I.G.H.T., the 
Garrison Trotter Neighborhood Association, Massachusetts Senior Action Council 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
17 
 
 
and Grove Hall Main Streets. Lastly, the team held 4 meetings with elected officials, 
bringing the total meeting/community presentation count for the Cheney Street 
Project to 15. The initial comment period ended on October 30, 2020. The 
comment period was extended to August 13, 2021. 
The Proposed Project has received all necessary zoning relief from the Boston 
Zoning Board of Appeal, beyond the applicable appeal periods. 
The BPDA approved the Proposed Project, as initially proposed, on September 13, 
2021. The first ZBA hearing took place on December 14th, 2021. During this hearing, 
community groups raised concerns about height, density, and parking. The ZBA 
deferred the vote until March 22, 2022, in order to allow time for JPNDC to meet 
and incorporate feedback from community groups. Between January and March 
2022, JPNDC held 6 meetings with these groups and 5 meetings with elected 
officials. The project was approved by the ZBA on March 22, 2022, with support 
from community groups. After ZBA approval, the development team continued to 
work in close collaboration with the City of Boston’s Mayor’s Office of Housing, 
community group representatives, and neighborhood residents to adjust the site 
plan and program. The changes to the program triggered ZBA Board Final Arbiter 
review and approval, as well as a Notice of Project Change. ZBA Board Final Arbiter 
approval was granted on September 12, 2022. 
 
PUBLIC BENEFITS 
The Proposed Project, as modified by the NPC, will result in a number of public 
benefits to the Dorchester neighborhood and the City of Boston as a whole, and 
these benefits, which are undiminished by the NPC, include: 
 
● Permanently Affordable Housing: The new apartments will be permanently 
deed-restricted to households earning up to 30%, 50% and 60% of the Area 
Median Income (“AMI”). 
 
● Ground-Floor Community Room and Resident Space: The Proposed Project 
will include several accessible and flexible ground floor common spaces such 
as a multipurpose room, and resident space to enliven the street and 
promote intergenerational activity. The Proponent also welcomes the 
broader community to use its proposed community room to host 
neighborhood events and to take part in many activities in its buildings such 
as lecture series, health and wellness events, and programming. 
 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
17 
 
 
● Sustainable Design/Green Building: In support of Boston’s carbon neutral 
goals, the buildings will be design to achieve Zero Net Carbon performance 
and Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (“LEED”) certifiable to at 
least the Gold level in accordance with Article 37 of the Boston Zoning Code 
and Mayor’s Office of Housing requirements. 
 
● Access to Innovative Healthcare: The Proposed Project will include an 
approximately 3,000 square foot PACE programming space, a comprehensive 
health and wellness program that helps frail seniors meet their health care 
needs in the community instead of going to a nursing home, and is 
particularly beneficial for extremely low-income nursing home eligible older 
adults who are both Medicare and Medicaid eligible. 
 
The community benefits described above will be set forth in the Cooperation 
Agreement for the Proposed Project. 
 
SMART UTILITIES 
The Proponent agrees to complete the Smart Utilities review prior to obtaining a

DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
The Project contemplates moderate renovations to an approximately 78,000 sf 
portion of Building 150 that comprises the former Constitution Inn. The 147 existing 
hotel-style, one-bedroom units will be converted into 100 rental units consisting of 
approximately 64 studios, approximately 14 one-bedrooms, and approximately 22 
two-bedroom units. Consistent with the existing condition, no vehicle parking will 

 
BOARD APPROVED

be provided on site. One hundred and six (106) secure bike parking spaces will be 
provided within the building for resident and YMCA employee use in addition to 24 
exterior, visitor parking spaces. The remaining approximately 18,000 sf of the 
building’s interior space will be leased back to the YMCA which will renovate it for 
the continued operation of a fitness and wellness facility including the existing 
swimming pool. 
 
The Proponents propose to renovate the existing building for use as a 100% 
permanent affordable housing community, with 100 affordable rental units. Fifty-
two (52) of the total 100 units will be leased to households earning not more than 
80% of Area Median Income (AMI), and 48 of the 100 units will be dedicated to the 
Permanent Supportive Housing (PSH) model and are designated as PSH units in the 
proposed building plans. The PSH units will be leased under written leases to 
households earning no more than 30% AMI and will include on-site services for 
vulnerable populations that support stable tenancies. The PSH model combines 
providing deeply affordable, permanent, leased housing for individuals 
experiencing homelessness with tailored individualized services to assist people 
with disabilities to live successfully in the community long term.

By redeveloping an underutilized building and creating a diverse range of new

alleviate the housing crisis, supporting community members and local affordability, 
equity, and carbon reduction policy objectives, as well as contributing to the local 
economy. 
Community Diversity and Access to Opportunities 
Affordable housing is more powerful as a foundation for positive individual and 
collective outcomes when it is located in areas of opportunity, allowing residents to 
manifest their potential by accessing local resources and building a reciprocal 
relationship with their community that strengthens those resources. The Project

Furthermore, the Project is close to existing rapid transit, transportation, and bus 
routes for residents, allowing for easy access to various amenities in the 
Charlestown Navy Yard, the greater Charlestown neighborhood, and other parts of 
Boston. This transit access increases job opportunities and access to services for 
prospective residents. Given that the census tract has a median income at 112% of

The Commonwealth of Massachusetts and the City of Boston have identified hotel 
conversions as desirable projects because they can lend themselves to creating 
more permanent housing more easily than other adaptive projects architecturally, 
financially, and in terms of zoning. The Project reflects these advantages, and the 
reuse and renovation of an existing vacant building also avoids displacement and

Project Specific Scope Considerations:
The developer should coordinate with BTD and PWD to develop safety and accessibility improvements for
pedestrians. The developer should verify the compliance of the existing pedestrian ramps as needed, specifically
those at Third Ave and 9th Street, at Third Ave and 7th Street, at First Ave and 9th Street, at First Street and 7th
Street intersections. The developer should provide perpendicular pedestrian ramps at these intersections. The
developer should also coordinate with the Parks Department regarding the street tree plantings.
Site Plan:
The developer must provide an engineer’s site plan at an appropriate engineering scale that shows curb
functionality on both sides of all streets that abut the property.
Construction Within The Public Right-of- Way (ROW):
All proposed design and construction within the Public ROW shall conform to PWD Design Standards
(https://www.boston.gov/departments/public-works/public-works-design-standards). Any non-standard materials
(i.e. pavers, landscaping, bike racks, etc.) proposed within the Public ROW will require approval through the Public
Improvement Commission (PIC) process and a fully executed License, Maintenance and Indemnification (LM&I)
Agreement with the PIC. Please note that the comments below are specific to proposed work within the Public
ROW.
Sidewalks:
The developer is responsible for the reconstruction of the sidewalks abutting the project and, wherever possible, to
extend the limits to the nearest intersection to encourage and compliment pedestrian improvements and travel
along all sidewalks within the ROW within and beyond the project limits. The reconstruction effort also must meet
current Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)/Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (AAB) guidelines,
including the installation of new or reconstruction of existing pedestrian ramps at all corners of all intersections
abutting the project site if not already constructed to ADA/AAB compliance per Code of Massachusetts Regulations
Title 521, Section 21 (https://www.mass.gov/regulations/521-CMR-21-curb-cuts). This includes converting apex
ramps to perpendicular ramps at intersection corners and constructing or reconstructing reciprocal pedestrian
ramps where applicable. Plans showing the extents of the proposed sidewalk improvements associated with this
project must be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval. Changes to any curb geometry
will need to be reviewed and approved through the PIC.
Please note that at signalized intersections, any alteration to pedestrian ramps may also require upgrading the
traffic signal equipment to ensure that the signal post and pedestrian push button locations meet current ADA and
Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) requirements. Any changes to the traffic signal system must
be coordinated and approved by BTD.
All proposed sidewalk widths and cross-slopes must comply to both City of Boston and ADA/AAB standards.

Dear Ms. Black: 
The Boston Water and Sewer Commission (Commission) has reviewed the Project 
Notification Form (PNF) for the proposed Constitution Inn project located at 150 Third 
Avenue in the Charlestown neighborhood of Boston. 
The proposed project is located on an approximately 14,762 square foot (sf) BPDA owned 
site currently occupied by a six-story building known as Building 150. Building 150 is 
currently ground leased to the YMCA. The proponent, Planning Office for Urban Affairs and 
St. Francis House (POUA/SFH), intends to acquire the YMCA's ground leasehold and 
renovate an approximately 78,000 sf portion of Building 150 that compromises the former 
Constitution Inn. The 14 7 existing hotel style, one-bedroom units will be converted into 
approximately 64 studios, approximately 14 one-bedrooms and approximately 22 two-
bedroom units. The remaining approximately 18,000 sf of the interior space will be leased 
back to the YMCA which will renovate it for continued operation of a fitness and wellness 
facility. The project site is bounded by Third Avenue to the north, Ninth Street to the east, a 
pedestrian walkway to the south and a commercial building to the west. There is no vehicle 
parking associated with the project. 
According to the PNF, the project's proposed water demand is approximately 11,000 gallons 
per day (gpd). The Commission owns and maintains an 8-inch Northern Low DICL water 
main installed in 1985 in Third Avenue, a 12-inch Northern Low DICL water main installed 
in 1985 in Ninth Street and an 8-inch Northern Low DICL water main installed in 1985 in 
Second A venue. 
According to the PNF, the proposed sewage generation is 11,010 gpd, a decrease of 5,170 gpd 
under existing conditions. For sewage and storm drainage service, the site is served by a 12-
inch sanitary sewer and a 12-inch storm drain in Third A venue, a 10-inch sanitary sewer and a 
24-inch storm drain in Ninth Street and a 30-inch storm drain in Second Avenue. 

The Commission has the following comments regarding the PNF: 
General 
1. 
Prior to the initial phase of the site plan development, POUA/SFH should meet with 
the Commission's Design and Engineering Customer Services to review water main, 
sewer and storm drainage system availability and potential upgrades that could impact 
the development. 
2. 
All new or relocated water mains, sewers and storm drains must be designed and 
constructed at POUA/SFH's expense. They must be designed and constructed in 
conformance with the Commission's design standards, Water Distribution System and 
Sewer Use regulations, and Requirements for Site Plans. The site plan should include 
the locations of new, relocated and existing water mains, sewers and drains which 
serve the site, proposed service connections, water meter locations, as well as back 
flow prevention devices in the facilities that will require inspection. A General 
Service Application must also be submitted to the Commission with the site plan. 
3. 
The design of the project should comply with the City of Boston's Complete Streets 
Initiative, which requires incorporation of "green infrastructure" into street designs. 
Green infrastructure includes greenscapes, such as trees, shrubs, grasses and other 
landscape plantings, as well as rain gardens and vegetative swales, infiltration basins, 
and paving materials and permeable surfaces. The proponent must develop a 
maintenance plan for the proposed green infrastructure. For more information on the 
Complete Streets Initiative see the City's website at http://bostoncompletestreets.org/ 
4. 
The water use and sewage generation estimates do not appear to be correct. The 
• Commission requires that these values be recalculated and submitted with the Site 
Plan. POUA/SFH should provide separate estimates of peak and continuous maximum 
water demand for residential, irrigation and air-conditioning make-up water for the 
project. Estimates should be based on full-site build-out of the proposed project. 
POUA/SFH should also provide the methodology used to estimate water demand for 
the proposed project. 
5. 
For any proposed masonry repair and cleaning POUA/SFH will be required to obtain 
from the Boston Air Pollution Control Commission a permit for Abrasive Blasting or 
Chemical Cleaning. In accordance with this permit POUA/SFH will be required to 
provide a detailed description as to how chemical mist and run-off will be contained 
and either treated before discharge to the sewer or drainage system or collected and 
disposed of lawfully off site. A copy of the description and any related site plans must 
be provided to the Commission's Engineering Customer Service Department for 
2 

review before masonry repair and cleaning commences. POUA/SFH is advised that 
the Commission may impose additional conditions and requirements before permitting 
the discharge of the treated wash water to enter the sewer or drainage system. 
6. 
It is POUA/SFH's responsibility to evaluate the capacity of the water, sewer and 
storm drain systems serving the project site to determine if the systems are adequate to 
meet future project demands. With the site plan, POUA/SFH must include a detailed 
capacity analysis for the water, sewer and storm drain systems serving the project site, 
as well as an analysis of the impacts the proposed project will have on the 
Commission's water, sewer and storm drainage systems. 
1. 
POUA/SFH must provide separate estimates of peak and continuous maximum water 
demand for residential, commercial, industrial, irrigation of landscaped areas, and air-
conditioning make-up water for the project with the site plan. Estimates should be 
based on full-site build-out of the proposed project. POUA/SFH should also provide 
the methodology used to estimate water demand for the proposed project. 
2. 
POUA/SFH should explore opportunities for implementing water conservation 
measures in addition to those required by the State Plumbing Code. In particular, 
POUA/SFH should consider outdoor landscaping which requires minimal use of water 
to maintain. If POU A/SFH plans to install in-ground sprinkler systems, the 
Commission recommends that timers, soil moisture indicators and rainfall sensors be

and to obtain a Hydrant Permit.

Engineering Code Enforcement, with regards to backflow prevention. 
5. 
The Commission is utilizing a Fixed Radio Meter Reading System to obtain water

Transmitter Unit (MTU) and connect the device to the meter. For information

Sewage I Drainage 
1. 
In conjunction with the Site Plan and the General Service Application POUA/SFH 
will be required to submit a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan. The plan must: 
• 
Identify specific best management measures for controlling erosion and preventing 
the discharge of sediment, contaminated stormwater or construction debris to the 
Commission's drainage system when construction is underway. 
• 
Include a site map which shows, at a minimum, existing drainage patterns and

stormwater, and the location of major control structures or treatment structures to

• 
Specifically identify how the project will comply with the Department of

2. 
The Commission encourages POUA/SFH to explore additional opportunities for

POUA/SFH must fully investigate methods for retaining stormwater on-site before the

Sanitary sewage must be kept separate from stormwater and separate sanitary sewer

construction of Building 1 as Phase 1, and Buildings 2 and 3 being built together as

plan is anticipated to be required.

transportation upgrades to Tremont Street, and approximately 23,000 SF of the 
Proposed Project’s open space, and up to 35 interim surface parking spaces for the

preservation of existing trees on site as an interim condition. Additionally, Phase 1 
will construct the pick up/drop off for Building 1 in coordination with Whittier 
Choice. The Phase 1 Site Plan is attached hereto as Exhibit B.

underneath Buildings 2 and 3, the improvements to the Ruggles Street, the Melnea 

 
 
Cass Boulevard and Raynor Circle edges of the Project Site, the renovation of St. 
Katharine Drexel Church, the new ABCD daycare space and playground, and the 
remaining open space for the Project Site. Phase 2 will replace the 35 surface 
parking spaces provided as part of Phase 1. 
 
PLANNING AND ZONING CONTEXT 
 
The Proposed Project is within the planning boundaries of the Roxbury Strategic 
Master Plan (“RSMP”) adopted in 2004 and PLAN: Nubian Square (“Plan Nubian”) 
adopted in 2018, and responds to the BPDA’s RFP for the Crescent Parcel, as 
explained in the RFP Issuance and Selection section below. 
 
The Roxbury Strategic Master Plan (RSMP) identifies the portion of Melnea Cass 
Boulevard between Tremont Street and Massachusetts Avenue as a “Crosstown 
Corridor” (the “Corridor”) that provides great potential for economic development 
with numerous parcels that could be redeveloped. The RSMP establishes principles 
for the Corridor, including (i) developing the western portion of Melnea Cass 
Boulevard in a way that re-knits the neighborhoods on either side of it, (ii) 
developing the public parcels with uses that generate good jobs and potentially 
housing, and (iii) making Melnea Cass Boulevard “more inviting for pedestrians in 
order to help reduce the perception of a divide between Upper and Lower 
Roxbury.” 
 
Plan Nubian was intended to (i) revisit the RSMP, (ii) identify current community 
needs, including the economic context, and (iii) provide guidance for the disposition 
of publicly owned vacant land in Nubian Square to best provide public benefit, 
including the Crescent Parcel which is the site of the Proposed Project. Specifically, 
Plan Nubian recommends providing new housing at a range of income levels 
including deeply affordable units and homeownership opportunities. Specifically, 
the PLAN documents that community members strongly expressed support for 
projects that provide the following: 
• A range of affordability levels, such as ⅓ for low-income, ⅓ for low to 
moderate income, and ⅓ market-rate, 
• Deep affordability that requires public subsidy, and 
• Homeownership and cooperative ownership opportunities. 
 
 

 
 
The PLAN also establishes an urban design framework to ensure coherent 
development while reinforcing the cultural and architectural identity of Nubian 
Square. The Plan Nubian notes that the site of the Proposed Project “has the 
potential to become a major mixed-use transit-oriented hub” that is a dynamic 
gateway with “strong pedestrian connections from Ruggles Station to Nubian 
Square.” Across the study area, the planning process examined three development 
scenarios ranging from six to twelve stories, with the expectation of establishing 
specific massing and height guidance during parcel-specific community meetings. 
 
The Proposed Project has been informed by Plan Nubian and the RSMP, the RFP, as 
described below, and feedback from City staff and members of the public during 
the RFP and review processes. It is noted by City staff that the Proposed Project is 
designed in order to (i) maintain the existing mature trees on the corner of Tremont 
Street and Melnea Cass Boulevard, (ii) integrate the existing St. Katharine Drexel 
church building, and (iii) provide a robust pedestrian connection from Raynor Circle 
to the corner of Ruggles Street and Tremont Street. The protection of the trees and 
St. Katharine Drexel Church reduces the size of the potential footprint of the 
proposed buildings and therefore resulted in an increase in the proposed building 
heights. 
 
The proposed project is within the Roxbury Neighborhood Multifamily Residential 
(MFR) subdistrict and an Urban Renewal Area Overlay District (the “U District”). A 
portion of the Project Site abutting Tremont Street and Melnea Cass Boulevard is 
within the Boulevard Planning District. The U District supersedes the base zoning: 
the accompanying Development Regulatory Agreements will effectuate use and 
dimensional controls for the Project Site.

RFP ISSUANCE AND SELECTION 
 
In January 2021, after an extensive community process through the Plan Nubian 
planning effort and five 5 community meetings held just for the RFP Parcels over 13 
months between 2019 and 2020, the BPDA released an RFP for the redevelopment 
of the RFP Parcels. The development objectives of the RFP reflected Plan Nubian 
Square planning principles, which include but are not limited to economic 
development, sustainable and resilient development, development without 
displacement, and diversity and inclusion in the development team. In response to 
community requests, the RFP’s Urban Design Guidelines emphasize preserving 
trees, providing open space that serves as a gateway to Nubian Square, enhancing 
the public realm, and ensuring convenient connections through the Project Site to 
community amenities, such as transit. 
 
In April 2021, the BPDA received three proposals in response to the RFP. Following 
a robust public evaluation process, including the convening of a Project Review 
Committee (“PRC”) made up of community residents and stakeholders. On October 
4, 2021, the PRC presented its recommendation of the Proponent to the Roxbury 
Strategic Master Plan Oversight Committee (the “RSMPOC”) as the developer of the 
Project Site. 
 
Based on its evaluation, and taking into account the recommendation of the 
RSMPOC, the selection committee determined that the proposal submitted by the 
Proponent was the most highly advantageous, and ultimately voted to recommend 
that the BPDA award tentative designation to the Proponent. The Proponent was 
awarded Tentative Designation status for the Project Site on November 18, 2021 
pursuant to a BPDA Board Vote. The Proponent is an affiliate of the Planning Office 
for Urban Affairs, Inc. and JGE Development LLC. 
 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On December 12, 2022, the Proponent filed a Letter of Intent (“LOI”) with the BPDA 
in accordance with the BPDA’s policy regarding Provision of Mitigation by 
Development Projects in Boston. 

 
 
 
On October 6, 2023, the Proponent filed a Project Notification Form ("PNF") with the 
BPDA pursuant to Article 80B of the Code, which commenced a comment period 
that ran through December 11, 2023. A Scoping Session for City of Boston and 
Commonwealth of Massachusetts officials was held on November 16, 2023. 
 
The BPDA hosted a virtual Impact Advisory Group (“IAG”) meeting on November 20, 
2023. The BPDA hosted a virtual public meeting on November 28, 2023. The public 
comment period in connection with the PNF concluded on December 11, 2023. 
 
The public meetings were advertised in the Bay State Banner, El Mundo, and El 
Planeta newspapers, while the public meeting and PRC/IAG meeting were posted 
on the BPDA calendar and website, and email notifications were sent to all 
subscribers of the BPDA's Roxbury neighborhood email update list. Local elected 
officials and their staff were also notified of all meetings. 
 
The Proposed Project was presented to the Boston Civic Design Commission 
(“BCDC”) on July 9, 2024. Subsequent to the initial presentation, the Proponent 
presented to BCDC Subcommittee on August 20, 2024, and October 22, 2024. The 
Proposed Project received BCDC approval on December 3, 2024.

HOUSING PROGRAM AND INCLUSIONARY DEVELOPMENT 
 
Projects financed as one entity and where at least forty (40) percent of the units are 
income-restricted are exempt from the Inclusionary Development Policy, dated 
December 10, 2015, The Proposed Project is financed as one entity and contains 
approximately one hundred ninety (190) income-restricted units, for approximately 
85 percent of the total units, surpassing 40 percent of the total units. As such, the 
Proposed Project is exempt from the Inclusionary Development Policy. 
 
As currently proposed, approximately fifty (50) rental units will be made available to 
households earning not more than 30% of the Area Median Income (“AMI”), as 
published by the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development 
(“HUD”), approximately ten (10) rental units will be made available to households 
earning not more than 50% of AMI, approximately sixteen (16) rental units will be 
made available to households earning not more than 60% of AMI, sixty (60) rental 
units will be made available to households earning not more than 80% of AMI, and 
twenty-two (22) rental units will be made available to households earning not more 
than 100% of AMI. Further, as currently proposed, approximately twenty-two (22) 
homeownership units will be made available to households earning not more than 
80% of AMI, and approximately ten (10) homeownership units will be made 
available to households earning not more than 100% AMI. The affordability of the 
Proposed Project will be finalized through the public funding process and the 
ongoing affordability of the project will be monitored under a MassDocs 
agreement. The BRA’s Ground Lease for the Project Site will provide for the 
marketing of the residential units to include a tenant and homebuyer preference to 
be given to Urban Renewal Displacees.

The Proposed Project at 175 Ruggles Street (‘the Proposed Project’) is located on an approximately
110,400-square foot (sf) site at the southeast corner of the intersection of Melnea Cass Boulevard
and Tremont Street. The Proposed Project seeks to develop three buildings composed of
approximately 346,022 sf. The project includes 217 residential rental and homeownership units,
1,594 sf of retail space, 10,333 sf of amenity space, 2,000 sf of community space and 11,900 sf of day

Context
Go Boston 2030, the City of Boston’s long-term transportation action plan, envisions a city where all
residents have better and more equitable travel choices, where efficient transportation networks
foster economic opportunity, and where the City has taken steps to prepare for climate change.
Whether traveling by transit, on foot, on a bike, or by car, Bostonians will be able to access all parts
of the city safely and reliably. This vision was created with the help of thousands of Bostonians
through a significant public engagement process.
This vision establishes foundational priorities for all transportation projects in the City, including
development proposals as they impact transportation networks and the public realm. Go Boston
2030’s primary goals—expanding access, improving safety, and ensuring reliability—help us hold all
projects accountable to this vision. Its aspirational targets clearly establish a yardstick for measuring
success.
In short, when reviewing proposals we must ask ourselves: does the project bring the City closer to
achieving its transportation vision, goals, and targets?
Expanding Access:
●
Goal: Make Boston’s neighborhoods interconnected for all modes of travel.
●
Aspirational Target: Every home in Boston will be within a 10-minute walk of a rail station or
key bus route stop, and Bluebikes station, and car share.
Improving Safety:
●
Goal: Substantially reduce collisions on every street through education, enforcement, and
designs that reallocate street space to prioritize moving people safely rather than faster.
●
Aspirational Target: Eliminate traffic fatalities and severe injuries in Boston.
Ensuring Reliability:
●
Goal: Prioritize making travel predictable on Boston’s transit and roadway networks.
●
Aspirational Target: Bostonians’ average commute to work time will decrease by 10%

Developments and provide electric vehicle charging infrastructure in their garage, as well as
provide e-bike charging. A detailed strategy plan must be submitted to explain how the

The Boston Transportation Department released Maximum Parking Ratios for Large
Developments that are required to submit a Transportation Access Plan Agreement. We
developed an analysis that right-sizes the amount of parking allowed for new large

developments. The new parking guidelines are complemented by our transportation
demand management (TDM) strategies. TDM strategies allow developers to manage their
tenants' parking demand by investing in sustainable transportation options. The parking
ratios are based on the mobility scores of 0-100, with 0 being the least access to everyday
resources that support a car lite lifestyle and 100 being the most access. The project site is
located within the mobility score category of 70-90. The project site’s mobility score is a 78
out of 100. The site is afforded a wealth of transportation access, as well as food access. The
project site is providing 60 below-grade parking spaces which is less than 50% of the
maximum ratio allowable. Given the access, the supply of parking is appropriately right-sized

along all sidewalks within the ROW within and beyond the project limits. The reconstruction effort also must meet

including the installation of new or reconstruction of existing pedestrian ramps at all corners of all intersections

project must be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval. Changes to any curb geometry
will need to be reviewed and approved through the PIC.

traffic signal equipment to ensure that the signal post and pedestrian push button locations meet current ADA and

be coordinated and approved by BTD.
All proposed sidewalk widths and cross-slopes must comply to both City of Boston and ADA/AAB standards.
The developer is encouraged to contact the City’s Disabilities Commission to confirm compliant accessibility within
the Public ROW.

Project Notification Form 
Dear Mr. Carter: 
The Boston Water and Sewer Commission (Commission) has reviewed the Project 
Notification Form (PNF) for the proposed Drexel Village project located at 175 Ruggles 
Street in the Roxbury neighborhood of Boston. 
The proposed project is located on an approximately 2.46 acre site currently occupied by 
surface parking, vacant open space, a daycare and a church/parish center. The proponent, 
Drexel Village LLC, plans to construct a three building complex containing approximately 
346,022 gross square feet (gsf) including: 
• 
Building One, a 14-story structure with approximately 142 mixed income rental units, 
residential amenity space and a community room, 
• 
Building Two, a 6-story structure with approximately 61 mixed income rental and 
home ownership units, amenity space, a management office and bike storage, 
• 
Building Three, a 4-story structure with approximately 14 rental units, a resident 
lounge, parish program space, daycare space and bike storage. 
The project site is bounded by Melnea Cass Boulevard to the north, Tremont Street to the 
west, Ruggles Street to the south and Raynor Circle to the east. There will be approximately 
60 vehicle parking spaces in an underground garage. 
According to the PNF, the project's proposed water demand is approximately 51,392 gallons 
per day (gpd). The Commission owns and maintains a 12-inch Southern Low DICL water 
main installed in 1982 in Melnea Cass Boulevard, a 12-inch Southern Low DICL water main 
installed in 1982 and a 48-inch Southern Low Steel water main installed in 1946 and 
rehabilitated in 1992 in Tremont Street, a 12-inch Southern Low DICL water main installed in 
1978 in Ruggles Street and an 8-inch Southern Low DICL water main installed in 1975 and 
2017 in Raynor Circle. 

According to the PNF, the proposed sewage generation is 46,524 gpd, an increase of 45,774 
over existing conditions. For sewage and storm drainage service, the site is served by a 30-
inch storm drain in Melnea Cass Boulevard, a 12-inch and a 15-inch sanitary sewer and a 62-
inch by 57-inch storm drain in Tremont Street, a 24-inch by 36-inch combined sewer and a 
15-inch storm drain in Ruggles Street, and a 10-inch sanitary sewer and a 12-inch storm drain 
in Raynor Circle. The Massachusetts Water Resources Authority's Boston Main Drainage 
Tunnel, a 120-inch combined sewer, transverses the project site. 
The Commission has the following comments regarding the PNF: 
General 
1. 
Prior to the initial phase of the site plan development, Drexel Village LLC should 
meet with the Commission's Design and Engineering Customer Services to review 
water main, sewer and storm drainage system availability and potential upgrades that 
could impact the development. 
2. 
All new or relocated water mains, sewers and storm drains must be designed and 
constructed at Drexel Village LLC's expense. They must be designed and constructed 
in conformance with the Commission's design standards, Water Distribution System 
and Sewer Use regulations, and Requirements for Site Plans. The site plan should 
include the locations of new, relocated and existing water mains, sewers and drains 
which serve the site, proposed service connections, water meter locations, as well as 
back flow prevention devices in the facilities that will require inspection. A General 
Service Application must also be submitted to the Commission with the site plan. 
3. 
The Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), in cooperation with the 
Massachusetts Water Resources Authority and its member communities, is 
implementing a coordinated approach to flow control in the MWRA regional 
wastewater system, particularly the removal of extraneous clean water ( e.g., 
infiltration/inflow (I/I)) in the system. In April of 2014, the Massachusetts DEP 
promulgated new regulations regarding wastewater. The Commission has a National 
Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Permit for its combined sewer 
overflows and is subject to these new regulations [314 CMR 12.00, section 
12.04(2)(d)]. This section requires all new sewer connections with design flows 
exceeding 15,000 gpd to mitigate the impacts of the development by removing four 
gallons of infiltration and inflow (I/I) for each new gallon of wastewater flow. In this 
regard, any new connection or expansion of an existing connection that exceeds 
15,000 gallons per day of wastewater shall assist in the 1/1 reduction effort to ensure 
that the additional wastewater flows are offset by the removal of 1/1. Currently, a 
minimum ratio of 4: 1 for 1/1 removal to new wastewater flow added is used. The 
Commission supports the policy and will require proponent to develop a consistent 
2 

inflow reduction plan. The 4: 1 requirement should be addressed at least 90 days prior 
to activation of water service and will be based on the estimated sewage generation 
provided on the project site plan. 
4. 
The design of the project should comply with the City of Boston's Complete Streets 
Initiative, which requires incorporation of "green infrastructure" into street designs. 
Green infrastructure includes greenscapes, such as trees, shrubs, grasses and other 
landscape plantings, as well as rain gardens and vegetative swales, infiltration basins, 
and paving materials and permeable surfaces. The proponent must develop a 
maintenance plan for the proposed green infrastructure. For more information on the 
Complete Streets Initiative see the City's website at http://bostoncompletestreets.org/ 
5. 
Drexel Village LLC should be aware that the US Environmental Protection Agency 
issued the Remediation General Permit (RGP) for Groundwater Remediation, 
Contaminated Construction Dewatering, and Miscellaneous Surface Water 
Discharges. If groundwater contaminated with petroleum products, for example, is 
encountered, Drexel Village LLC will be required to apply for a RGP to cover these 
discharges. 
6. 
It is Drexel Village LLC's responsibility to evaluate the capacity of the water, sewer 
and storm drain systems serving the project site to determine if the systems are 
adequate to meet future project demands. With the site plan, Drexel Village LLC 
must include a detailed capacity analysis for the water, sewer and storm drain systems 
serving the project site, as well as an analysis of the impacts the proposed project will 
have on the Commission's water, sewer and storm drainage systems. 
1. 
Drexel Village LLC must provide separate estimates of peak and continuous 
maximum water demand for residential, commercial, industrial, irrigation of 
landscaped areas, and air-conditioning make-up water for the project with the site 
plan. Estimates should be based on full-site build-out of the proposed project. Drexel 
Village LLC should also provide the methodology used to estimate water demand for 
the proposed project. 
2. 
Drexel Village LLC should explore opportunities for implementing water 
conservation measures in addition to those required by the State Plumbing Code. In 
particular, Drexel Village LLC should consider outdoor landscaping which requires 
minimal use of water to maintain. If Drexel Village LLC plans to install in-ground 
sprinkler systems, the Commission recommends that timers, soil moisture indicators 
and rainfall sensors be installed. The use of sensor-operated faucets and toilets in 
common areas of buildings should be considered. 
3 

3. 
Drexel Village LLC is required to obtain a Hydrant Permit for use of any hydrant 
during the construction phase of this project. The water used from the hydrant must 
be metered. Drexel Village LLC should contact the Commission's Meter Department 
for information on and to obtain a Hydrant Permit. 
4. 
The Commission is utilizing a Fixed Radio Meter Reading System to obtain water 
meter readings. For new water meters, the Commission will provide a Meter 
Transmitter Unit (MTU) and connect the device to the meter. For information 
regarding the installation ofMTUs, Drexel Village LLC should contact the 
Commission's Meter Department. 
Sewage / Drainage 
1. 
A Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) for Nutrients has been established for the 
Lower Charles River Watershed by the Massachusetts Department of Environmental 
Protection (MassDEP). In order to achieve the reductions in Phosphorus loading 
required by the TMDL, phosphorus concentrations in the lower Charles River from 
Boston must be reduced by 64%. To accomplish the necessary reductions in 
phosphorus, the Commission is requiring developers in the lower Charles River 
watershed to infiltrate stormwater discharging from impervious areas in compliance 
with MassDEP. Drexel Village LLC will be required to submit with the site plan a 
phosphorus reduction plan for the proposed development. Drexel Village LLC must 
fully investigate methods for retaining stormwater on-site before the Commission will 
consider a request to discharge stormwater to the Commission's system. The site plan 
should indicate how storm drainage from roof drains will be handled and the 
feasibility of retaining their stormwater discharge on-site. Under no circumstances 
will stormwater be allowed to discharge to a sanitary sewer. 
In conjunction with the Site Plan and the General Service Application the Drexel 
Village LLC will be required to submit a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan. The 
plan must: 
• 
Identify best management practices for controlling erosion and for preventing the 
discharge of sediment and contaminated groundwater or stormwater runoff to the 
Commission's drainage system when the construction is underway. 
• 
Include a site map which shows, at a minimum, existing drainage patterns and 
areas used for storage or treatment of contaminated soils, groundwater or 
storm water, and the location of major control or treatment structures to be utilized 
during construction. 
4 

• 
Provide a stormwater management plan in compliance with the DEP standards 
mentioned above. The plan should include a description of the measures to 
control pollutants after construction is completed. 
2. 
Developers of projects involving disturbances of land of one acre or more will be 
required to obtain an NPDES General Permit for Construction from the 
Environmental Protection Agency and the Massachusetts Department of 
Environmental Protection. Drexel Village LLC is responsible for determining if such 
a permit is required and for obtaining the permit. If such a permit is required, it is 
required that a copy of the permit and any pollution prevention plan prepared pursuant 
to the permit be provided to the Commission's Engineering Services Department, 
prior to the commencement of construction. The pollution prevention plan submitted 
pursuant to a NPDES Permit may be submitted in place of the pollution prevention 
plan required by the Commission provided the Plan addresses the same components 
identified in item 1 above. 
3. 
The Commission encourages Drexel Village LLC to explore additional opportunities 
for protecting stormwater quality on site by minimizing sanding and the use of deicing 
chemicals, pesticides, and fertilizers. 
4. 
The discharge of dewatering drainage to a sanitary sewer is prohibited by the 
Commission. Drexel Village LLC is advised that the discharge of any dewatering . 
drainage to the storm drainage system requires a Drainage Discharge Permit from the 
Commission. If the dewatering drainage is contaminated with petroleum products, 
Drexel Village LLC will be required to obtain a Remediation General Permit from the 
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for the discharge. 
5. 
Drexel Village LLC must fully investigate methods for retaining stormwater on-site 
before the Commission will consider a request to discharge stormwater to the 
Commission's system. The site plan should indicate how storm drainage from roof 
drains will be handled and the feasibility of retaining their storm water discharge on-
site. All projects at or above 100,000 square feet of floor area are to retain, on site, a 
volume of runoff equal to 1.25 inches of rainfall times the impervious area. Under no 
circumstances will stormwater be allowed to discharge to a sanitary sewer. 
6. 
The Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP) established 
Stormwater Management Standards. The standards address water quality, water 
quantity and recharge. In addition to Commission standards, Drexel Village LLC will 
be required to meet MassDEP Stormwater Management Standards. 
7. 
Sanitary sewage must be kept separate from storm water and separate sanitary sewer 
and storm drain service connections must be provided. The Commission requires that 
5 

existing stormwater and sanitary sewer service connections, which are to be re-used 
by the proposed project, be dye tested to confirm they are connected to the appropriate 
system. 
8. 
The Commission requests that Drexel Village LLC install a permanent casting stating 
"Don't Dump: Drains to Charles River" next to any catch basin created or modified as 
part of this project. Drexel Village LLC should contact the Commission's Operations 
Division for information regarding the purchase of the castings. 
9. 
If a cafeteria or food service facility is built as part of this project, grease traps will be 
required in accordance with the Commission's Sewer Use Regulations. Drexel 
Village LLC is advised to consult with the Commission's Operations Department with 
regards to grease traps. 
I 0. 
The enclosed floors of a parking garage must drain through oil separators into the 
sewer system in accordance with the Commission's Sewer Use Regulations. The 
Commission's Requirements for Site Plans, available by contacting the Engineering 
Services Department, include requirements for separators. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this project.

SUBJECT: 
REQUEST AUTHORIZATION AND APPROVALS REGARDING THE 
INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN NOTIFICATION FORM FOR THE 
RENEWAL OF THE EMERSON COLLEGE INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Planning & Development 
Agency (“BPDA”): waive further review of the Institutional Master Plan 
Notification Form for the Renewal of the Emerson College Institutional 
Master Plan (“IMPNF for Renewal”), dated October 16, 2023, and 
approve the renewal of the Emerson College Institutional Master Plan 
(the “Emerson College IMP”) pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 
80D-6, and Section 80D-8 of the Code; and (2) authorize the Director to 
take all actions and execute any and all documents deemed necessary 
and appropriate relative to the IMPNF for Renewal. 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The Emerson College (“Emerson”) Institutional Master Plan (“IMP”) was 
approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) Board on December 5, 
2002 and approved by the Boston Zoning Commission on December 11, 2002. The 
Original IMP was subsequently amended on July 19, 2006; September 26, 2007; 
January 8, 2014; May 20, 2015; March 8, 2017; September 12, 2018; and renewed on 
November 18, 2021. 
 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
16 
DOC No. 8085 
 
 
 
On October 16, 2023, Emerson submitted an IMPNF for Renewal to the Boston 
Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”), signaling its intention to renew the 
Emerson IMP for a period of two years. Emerson is not proposing a “Proposed 
Institutional Project”, as that term is understood in the Code; is not adding new land 
area to the Emerson IMP; is not proposing any changes to the Emerson IMP which 
would constitute a change in use, dimensional, parking or loading elements thereof 
(other than de minimus dimensional changes), and BPDA staff do not anticipate any 
greater impacts from the continuation of the implementation of the Emerson IMP 
than that which were originally evaluated. 
 
 
INSTITUTIONAL TEAM 
 
Proponent: 
Emerson College 
Margaret A. Ings 
Mary Higgins 
 
 
 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW 
 
The IMPNF for Renewal is subject to Institutional Master Plan Review and qualifies 
for a waiver of further review in accordance with Sections 80D-5.2(e) and 80D-6 of 
the Code in that: (i) no new Proposed Institutional Projects are planned; (ii) no 
changes in the Institutional Master Plan are proposed that would constitute a 
change in the use, dimensional, parking or loading elements of the Institutional 
Master Plan (other than de minimus dimensional changes); and (iii) no significantly 
greater impacts would result from continued implementation of the approved 
Institutional Master Plan than were originally projected. The IMPNF for Renewal 
seeks approval of the IMPNF and the Emerson IMP together, as the renewed IMP, 
for a period of two years, until November 16, 2025. 
 
The submission of the IMPNF for Renewal on October 16, 2023, initiated a 30-day 
comment period that ended on November 15, 2023. Notice of submission was 
published in the Boston Herald on October 16, 2023. 
 
CONTINUED COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
16 
DOC No. 8085 
 
 
 
All community benefits currently offered pursuant to the existing Emerson IMP will

BACKGROUND & PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
Windale Developers Inc. (the “Proponent”) proposes to construct twenty-three 
home ownership units in single-family, stacked two-family and semi-detached two 
family unit types totaling 32,200 square feet (“Proposed Project”). 16 of the units will 
be made affordable to those earning between 80% and 100% AMI and the 
remaining 7 units will be market rate. The unit mix of the units include six two-
bedroom units and seventeen three-bedroom units. The Proposed Project will 
include 26 driveway parking spots. 
 
The Proposed Project includes the reopening of Harold Street to further connect 
the new development to the existing neighborhood. 

The Garrison Trotter Project is Phase 4 of this multi-phase engagement with the 
Garrison Trotter Neighborhood. Windale was selected by the BPDA as the 
developer for the project on 05/12/2022. The previous phases of the Garrison 
Trotter Project included Requests for Proposals from the Mayor’s Office of Housing 
to create homeownership opportunities through the Neighborhood Homes 
Initiative. The Neighborhood Homes Initiative was a commitment to promote 
mixed-income communities and expand affordable homeownership opportunities 
for first time home buyers. Working extensively with the Garrison Trotter 
Neighborhood Association (“GTNA”) MOH and BPDA have completed three phases 
of Neighborhood Homes Initiative developments, resulting in the development of 
eighteen (18) homes comprising twenty-nine (29) units of housing that were 
developed by private developers responding to Request for Proposals (“RFP”) 
requiring two thirds of the units as income restricted, affordable housing. The 
developments represent 107,516 square feet of land, including land formerly 
owned by BPDA and the City of Boston.

PLANNING CONTEXT AND CITY STAFF REVIEW 
The Proposed Project is located within the planning boundaries of the Roxbury 
Strategic Master Plan (“RSMP”), a strategic framework, adopted in 2004, to guide 
change and economic growth in Roxbury over the next ten to twenty years. 
The Proposed Project makes significant contributions towards the realization of the 
RSMP’s goals of providing affordable housing opportunities by proposing 100% 
homeownership single- and two-family houses, totaling to 23 residential units with 
16 of the units designated under the Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”). The 
units vary in size from 2- to 3-bedroom which serves the projected needs based on 
the demographics of households in the area. The Proposed Project further 
advances RSMP’s goals of promoting pedestrian improvements along Hollander, 
Harold and Holworthy Streets through landscaping, street lighting, and the 
mitigation of curb cut impacts on the streetscape. Additionally, the parking ratio is 
below the maximum parking ratios per citywide guidelines which advances both 
mobility and climate resiliency citywide planning goals.

DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
 
The Amended and Restated Master Plan governs the Enterprise Research Campus 
project in the Allston neighborhood of Boston, which will be constructed within the 
PDA Area. The Enterprise Research Campus project proposes the construction of 
enabling infrastructure and multiple buildings of approximately 900,000 square 
feet with uses that will include office/lab, residential, hotel and conference center 
uses, retail/restaurant uses, and parking, as described below. Under the 2018 PDA

Master Plan and the proposed Amended and Restated Master Plan, a maximum 
Floor Area Ratio or FAR of 4.0 is allowed for the PDA Area as a whole. 
 
This memorandum, together with the Phase A Development Plan, proposes the so-
called Phase A of the Enterprise Research Campus project (the “Proposed Phase A 
Project”), totaling 900,000 square feet, which is the initial phase of the Enterprise 
Research Campus project and is described in greater detail below. The Proposed 
Phase A Project frontloads delivery of the Enterprise Research Campus project’s 
community benefits and open space. 
 
The Proposed Phase A Project is the initial phase of development in the Allston 
Landing North Economic Development Area, which was created under Article 51 of 
the Code. The 2018 PDA Master Plan reserved locations within the PDA Area for 
subsequent development after the Proposed Phase A Project has commenced. The 
remaining portion of the PDA Area has been proposed to be developed as a second 
phase of the Enterprise Research Campus (sometimes referred to as “Phase B”). 
The Proposed Phase A Project for which BPDA approval is currently being 
requested does not include Phase B, which will require a comprehensive and 
separate BPDA approval process, including the filing and approval of a Phase B 
Planned Development Area Development Plan. 
 
The Proposed Phase A Project will consist of approximately 900,000 square feet of 
mixed-use development including the following elements. 
 
o 
A residential structure that includes two distinct massings, with 
approximately 263,500 square feet of residential and retail and restaurant space 
and approximately 345 units of rental housing, of which 25% will be income 
restricted, with a maximum Building Height of 190 feet; 
 
o 
An office/lab building that includes two distinct massings, with approximately 
440,000 square feet of office/lab and retail and restaurant space, with a maximum 
Building Height of 140 feet; 
 
o 
A hotel of approximately 135,000 square feet, including retail and restaurant 
space and approximately 250 keys, with a maximum Building Height of 190 feet; 
 
o 
A conference center of approximately 61,500 square feet, including retail and 
restaurant space therein, with a maximum Building Height of 100 feet;

PROJECT-BASED COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
With the Proposed Phase A Project, the Proponent is seeking to establish a new 
model for inclusive, equitable, and community focused development. A key focus 
has been to integrate Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) into each phase of the 
development to begin to address the growing racial wealth gap in Boston and 
across the country. The Proposed Phase A Project will also provide a range of public 
and community benefits to promote housing creation, neighborhood enrichment, 
usable new open space, future planned connections to the Charles River and Ray 
Mellone Park, environmental remediation, economic activity, and transportation 
improvements. Those public and community benefits are described below: 
 
Public Realm Benefits and New Tax Revenues 
● 
The accessibility to the PDA Area will be improved through the creation of 
new streets that continue the connections to existing roads and pedestrian/bicycle 
lanes that exist at the edges of the PDA Area.

The Proposed Project will include approximately 2.9 acres of publicly 
accessible open space, including an approximately 1.4 acre east-west greenway. 
● 
The location and massing of buildings within the Proposed Phase A Project 
has been planned to maximize sunlight reaching the Phase A Greenway and to 
shelter the Phase A Greenway from wind impacts, enhancing its attractiveness for 
the Allston-Brighton community and general public and extending seasonal use of 
the Phase A Greenway in the Spring and Fall. 
● 
The Proponent will actively program the Phase A Greenway with a wide 
variety of events and activities that may range from farmer's markets and small

The Proposed Phase A Project will generate substantial new real estate tax 
revenues for the City of Boston estimated to be in excess of $10 million.

also considered the neighborhood context; common themes emerging from other

Avenue Corridor Rezoning Study and other development projects with community
