The Project will transform a historically underutilized site into a vibrant, inclusive mixed-use community. The 
Project is envisioned as a pedestrian-focused urban district that is designed to nurture and inspire creativity and 
exploration, and to be a destination for those from the Allston community and beyond. The central focal point of 
the Project will be a greenway that is part of a public open space network intended, over time, to connect the 
Honan-Allston Library and the Allston neighborhood toward the Charles River. Phase A will contain approximately 
900,000 square feet of mixed-use development consisting of affordable and market-rate residential, office/lab, 
hotel, conference center, restaurant, and retail use, along with approximately three acres of publicly accessible 
open space. The next phase of development ("Phase B") will be subject to review under Article 80 and approval of 
a PDA Development Plan for Phase B.
The Project will include numerous public benefits intended to create a vibrant and inclusive community welcoming
to all. Phase A will include approximately three acres of new, publicly accessible open space, including a central
greenway that will be programmed to create an active and vibrant environment. Twenty five percent of the
residential units in Phase A will be affordable units. The Proponent is committed to diversity, equity, and inclusion
and for Phase A has (i) created an inclusionary ownership program for Black and Latinx investors, (ii) awarded
more than 30% of Phase pre-construciton costs to certified MBE and WBE firms, (iii) committed to using good faith
efforts to award or cause to be awarded 15% of the total value of construction contracts to MBE/WBE firms, and (iv)
committed to allocating ~25% of the retail for local, small, Minority-owned, or Women-owned retailers. 
The Project will include complete streets enhancements on Western Avenue, new complete streets construction of
Cattle Drive and East Drive, and transit priority and bus stop improvements on Western Avenue and other corridors,
all of which will be provided as part of Phase A. The Proponent supports elevating the Route 70 and 86 to Key Bus
Routes at recommended service levels and commits to study and support the implementation of bus transit priority
on Western Avenue and other critical locations. The exact details and structure of the mitigation commitment will be

1.0 
Introduction 
In December 2017, the President and Fellows of Harvard College, acting as Harvard University (together 
with its affiliates, “Harvard”), filed a Master Plan for Planned Development Area No. 115 (the “Original 
Master Plan”) with the Boston Redevelopment Authority d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency

has selected Tishman Speyer ERC Developer, L.L.C. (the “Proponent”) to develop the Proposed Project

In accordance with Sections 3-1A and 80C-3 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”), this plan 
constitutes an Amended and Restated Master Plan for Planned Development Area No. 115 (this “PDA 
Master Plan”) for the development of a portion of the Enterprise Research Campus on Western Avenue in 
the Allston neighborhood of Boston, and amends, restates and supersedes the Original Master Plan in its 
entirety. This PDA Master Plan covers an approximately 14.2-acre (approximately 619,402-square-foot)

buildings and other improvements (the “Proposed Project”), which may be built simultaneously or in 
phases. The Proposed Project consists of (i) the development of an approximately 9.4-acre portion of the 
PDA Area (consisting of approximately 6 acres to be developed as buildings, open space, and related 
improvements, and approximately 3.4 acres of streets and other enabling infrastructure) as shown on 
Exhibit D as the “Phase A PDA Area” pursuant to and in accordance with that certain “Phase A 
Development Plan for Planned Development Area No. 115” (the “Phase A Development Plan”) that is

redevelopment, the “Phase A Project”), and (ii) a second development phase within the PDA Area,

D as the “Phase B PDA Area.” The second development phase (the “Phase B Project”) is subject to future 
Large Project Review under Article 80B of the Zoning Code and will require the submission and approval 
of a separate Planned Development Area Development Plan (the “Phase B Development Plan”).

5.0 
Planning Objectives and Character of Development 
The following planning principles present a summary of the principles guiding the development of this 
PDA Master Plan. 
 5.1 Land Use 
The PDA Area and adjacent portions of the Harvard Enterprise Research Campus site are currently vacant, 
with some areas used from time to time as construction laydown and staging areas. Proposed future uses 
defined by the development of the PDA Area will result in the construction of a diverse mix of uses, 
including office, lab, research space, residential, retail, restaurant and other uses, as well as a range of 
publicly accessible open spaces. A complete list of allowed uses is included on Exhibit E and is described 
further in Section 4.2 above. 
The planning for the PDA Area focuses on goals that include establishing relationships between the future 
commercial and research tenants of the PDA Area and the teaching and research mission of Harvard. 
Simultaneously, the success of the PDA Area as an urban district will also be contingent on the 
establishment of a robust mixed-use development program including office, lab, research space, residential, 
retail, restaurant and other uses, as well as a range of publicly accessible open spaces. This type of mix is 
intended to ensure that the area is vibrant, with activity extending through the day and evening. 

 
 
9 
Along primary streets within the PDA Area, a high degree of porosity and public interface is desired. 
 5.2 Urban Design 
Architectural expression of buildings within the PDA Master Plan will be driven in large part by their 
individual and unique context within the overall PDA Master Plan, and the design of the future buildings 
should emphasize a variety of scale, style, and material to reflect such diversity of experience throughout 
the PDA Area. To this end, individual buildings are encouraged to find creative expression while complying 
with the dimensional requirements and urban design parameters set forth below and on Exhibit G. 
Buildings should create well-defined public spaces and maintain a human scale at the ground level. 
Distinctive, place specific design, durability, and long-term sustainability should drive the architectural 
character of all new construction. Architecture that is expressive of the new trends in housing and 
commercial uses, and derived from the unique mixed-use nature of this district, is encouraged. Façade 
materials and expressions must have appropriate detail and scale-giving elements to contribute to a 
distinctive urban context. A set of design guidelines, attached hereto as Exhibit H, manage how the 
buildings relate to each other and to the adjacent public realm. 
The blocks within the PDA Area are organized by streets, paths, and open spaces that are currently designed 
to break down existing impenetrable areas into a system of development blocks that guide future 
incremental growth. The blocks identify sites within which one or more buildings can be developed in the 
future. Each site can accommodate a variety of building footprints, perimeter open space and courtyards. 
The block plan allows for a mix of building types and scales to coexist in the PDA Area. As planning and 
tenancy evolve, the block plan may need to be adjusted, in accordance with Section 4.1 above. 
The Proposed Project will provide a range of public and community benefits, including new usable, publicly 
accessible open space, economic activity, improved circulation, and a mix of uses and housing options. The 
Proposed Project seeks to provide welcoming, programmable and inclusive open spaces that will 
themselves serve as social hubs and incubators. Additional public and community benefits as they relate to 
urban design are addressed in the Design Guidelines included on Exhibit H. 
Development within the PDA Area should clearly establish gateway treatments at key intersections, 
particularly those that intersect with Western Avenue such as at Cattle Drive. This may involve setback 
conditions or other physical or programmatic treatments that signal entrance to an important urban district 
apart from (although related to) the Harvard academic campus directly to the north. 
Access to internalized building services will be integrated into the landscape design, paving design, and 
architecture, thereby minimizing adverse impact on the pedestrian realm. The intersection between Cattle 
Drive, Science Drive, and the Project Greenway is envisioned as a key urban moment that will have a 
pedestrian focus and create the sense of a plaza or town square rather than a conventional street crossing. 
The arrangement of the buildings, streets, and Project Greenway will allow for the establishment of a critical 
mass and activate the space to create a lively environment in the early phases of development. 
Along the ground floor, the building edges facing Cattle Drive, Western Avenue, and East Drive are 
programmed to be active, both along the streets and along the Greenway. Interruptions to these open spaces 
and sidewalks are minimized through the consolidation of services and loading between buildings. To 
further enhance the character and usability of the publicly accessible open spaces, buildings are sited to 
account for wind conditions, daylight access, and sources of sound pollution. 

 
 
10

● Western Ave - Western Avenue is expected to be the primary arrival point for the PDA Area. Western 
Avenue is intended to prioritize transit service and low-stress bikeways, and to provide a thoughtfully 
designed pedestrian realm. The southern edge of Western Avenue will be activated by the hotel lobby, retail

● Cattle Drive - Cattle Drive, running north-south, will serve as a “Main Street” for the PDA Area,

realm.

 5.3 Public Realm 
The PDA Master Plan will create an open and inviting public realm that aims to connect Allston residents 
with new employees, residents, and visitors of the Proposed Project, along with the Harvard community 
and others. A primary objective of the open space plan is to create an environment that is open and inviting 
to the public. Through a range of engaging publicly-accessible spaces, the Proposed Project seeks to 
establish strong connections with existing amenities, build upon completed portions of the open space 
network, and advance towards a future continuous open space connecting the Honan-Allston Public Library 
to Soldiers Field Road and toward the Charles River. 
The Phase A Project includes approximately 2.9 acres of Publicly Accessible Open Space and Public Realm 
areas within the developable portion of the PDA Area as illustrated on Exhibit D. 
 5.3.1 Streetscape Improvements 
The PDA Master Plan will create a cohesive network of streets, walking paths, bicycle paths and bike 
stations, and green connections. Western Avenue will be upgraded to prioritize transit and will be made to 
be pedestrian- and bike-friendly. Western Avenue is also anticipated to serve as a primary access point for 
motorized vehicles entering and exiting the PDA Area. 
Street planning guidelines for the PDA Area provide for elements which are necessary to create a cohesive 
and sustainable public realm. Principles follow those of Boston’s Complete Streets Guidelines, which state 
that streets should be sensitive to their context, recognized as an essential component of publicly-accessible 
open spaces, supportive of multiple functions, and encouraging of non-motorized uses. Publicly accessible 

 
 
12 
streets will shape the PDA Area physical setting and public realm. Plans should enhance the quality of the 
public realm to create great streets and memorable places. 
Following guidance from Boston’s Complete Streets Guidelines, the street and sidewalk configuration will 
ensure high performance and longevity for the investment in new street trees. Pervious paving and 
structural soil volumes in the planted areas provide horticultural support for the trees, but they also 
significantly increase infiltration and reduce the outflow of stormwater in rain events through below-grade 
detention. Over time, this system should ensure a notable increase in canopy coverage throughout the area 
and will contribute to the evolution of a unified network of streets throughout. 
A coherent pedestrian realm that comprises a diverse urban landscape will be achieved over time. Critical 
ingredients include the organization of buildings, land uses, and memorable spaces that contribute to a 
unique urban quality; activation of the street with extensive programs of public accommodation; and the 
efficient and systematic design of vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian ways. Boston’s Complete Streets 
Guidelines offer guidance on programmatic issues, dimensions, materials and techniques, performance and 
function, and the achievement of comprehensive environmental benefits. In order to provide the best 
pedestrian realm, curb cuts on main streets will be minimized. 
● 
Pedestrian Zone: Sidewalks are planned to have continuous and unobstructed pathways and sight 
lines. Uniform, consistent surfaces are recommended and will be made with poured concrete surface or 
smooth pavers that utilize large dimensions. Any material other than poured concrete should be reviewed 
and approved by the Mayor’s Commission for Persons with Disabilities. The pedestrian zone will line up 
legibly and logically with intersection crosswalks. This system achieves optimal navigation and ease of 
travel for persons with varying disabilities. 
● 
Furnishing Zone: Between the pedestrian zone and the curb of the roadbed, a furnishing zone is 
contemplated to accommodate tree planting and soil infiltration zones, pedestrian and street lighting, street 
furniture, and any fixtures and appurtenances required for transit. Locations and dimensions will vary 
according to specific conditions and roadway configuration, but throughout the PDA Area, this zone is 
envisioned to be 4 to 6 feet in width, plus curb extensions where they exist. By using unit pavers, the 
furnishing zones will have permeability for stormwater infiltration. 
● 
Frontage Zone: The frontage zone will frame the inside edge of the pedestrian zone, extend the 
sidewalk as dimensions allow, and may accommodate sidewalk cafes, store entries, retail displays, and 
landscape elements. The frontage zone can be widened to create plazas and gathering spaces at periodic 
breaks in the street wall. Dimensions and materials in the frontage will vary according to building use and 
building type. 
Given the phased nature of the build-out of the PDA Area, interim roadway and sidewalk improvements 
may be located from time to time on portions of the PDA Area that have not been redeveloped as 
contemplated by the PDA Master Plan. Such interim roadway and sidewalk improvements shall be subject 
to review and approval by BTD as part of the applicable construction management plan, and any temporary 
roads/access shall be designed to facilitate multimodal safety and connectivity in a manner that is informed 
by and does not preclude implementation of subsequent phased development of the PDA Master Plan. 
 5.3.2 Open Space 
The Phase A Project includes approximately 2.9 acres of Publicly Accessible Open Space and Public Realm 
areas within the developable portion of the PDA Area as illustrated on Exhibit D, which will be developed 

 
 
13 
and maintained by the Proponent or Harvard and will be available for use by residents, tenants, workers,

Landscape is an important element which helps to define the character of the PDA Area. The building 
placement and the landscape design will work together to provide form and definition to the Phase A 
Project’s Publicly Accessible Open Space. This PDA Master Plan establishes a network of open spaces and 
increased landscape areas along Cattle Drive which will help to make Cattle Drive an important pedestrian 
destination. It will also enhance landscape function to minimize the impact on ecosystems and water 
resources, reduce drainage impacts of projects, and improve the quality of stormwater management. 
The Proposed Project’s Publicly Accessible Open Space areas include the Project Greenway, a laneway 
connecting Western Avenue to the Project Greenway, as well as smaller planned “sidewalk room” open 
space areas. The sidewalk rooms are areas intended to provide open space where there would otherwise be 
private enclosed space, creating Publicly Accessible Open Space areas that provide greenery, art or other 
visual and physical amenities and pockets of resting space on alternating sides of Cattle Drive. 
The City of Boston’s Imagine Boston 2030 plan commits to investing in new open spaces in areas of new 
housing and job growth, as well as developing family- and kid-friendly environments that promote 
opportunities to play everywhere. The Proposed Project will help increase the area’s open space ratio and 
follow the plan’s goals of envisioning and creating an accessible open space system, enhancing the urban 
natural environment, and improving quality of life and well-being in the city. 
As used in this PDA Master Plan, (1) “Publicly Accessible Open Space” shall mean and include, as

Reduce vulnerability to climate change impacts including natural hazards by integrating climate 
change adaptation into planning and project design;

Promote health, productivity, and safety of the community through design and maintenance of the 
built environment;

Enhance the health of ecosystems and increase the diversity of native species;

● 
Minimize the impact on ecosystems and water resources, and reduce drainage impacts of the

● 
Promote smart use of water, inside and out, to reduce potable water consumption; 
●

 6.4 
Sustainable and Resilient Development 
 
● 
The Proposed Project will advance Boston’s carbon neutral and climate ready goals by 
incorporating a variety of sustainable design and resilient building strategies that will reduce carbon 
emissions, improve water quality, reduce the urban heat island effect, maximize the conservation of energy 
and water, and reduce the risk of flooding due to sea level rise. 
● 
The lab/office, residential and hotel buildings of the Phase A Project will be eligible to receive 
LEED Gold certification at a minimum using the LEEDv4 rating system, exceeding the City’s requirements 
under Article 37 - Green Buildings. The Phase A Project lab/office, residential and hotel buildings will be 
eligible to achieve Fitwel certification (a certification system focused on building health for all, originally 
created by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and U.S. General Services Administration) 
in addition to LEED Gold certification. 
● 
The Phase A Project will reduce energy and stationary source GHG emissions by targeting zero net 
carbon building performance including a 40% reduction in carbon emissions as compared to the Base Case 
(Stretch Code) with 2035 electric grid emissions.

The Phase A Project will prioritize systems and solutions that utilize renewable energy, and will 
explore the feasibility of providing 90% of the Proposed Phase A Lab/Office and Hotel and 100% of the 
Residential and Conference Center building energy needs by electricity when the Proposed Phase A Project 
opens. Additionally, the Proposed Phase A Project will achieve a BERDO emissions standard of 1 kg 
co2e/sf/yr, and will explore a reduction below this level. 
● 
The Phase A Project will utilize a combination of on-site renewable energy and utilities provided 
through the District Energy Facility in connection with the Conference Center, if feasible. 
● 
The Proposed Project will consider incorporating design strategies and construction materials to 
reduce Heat Island conditions, where feasible, including the use of low SRI building wall and roof products 
and site hardscape materials, building and site canopies, and landscape design and plantings. 

 
 
18 
● 
The Proposed Project will incorporate design elements to improve on-site stormwater management 
and reduce risk of precipitation-based flooding. The Proposed Project will provide a significant amount of 
public realm and open space improvements, and the Proposed Project will be designed and engineered to 
manage the 32-year storm (6.7 inches of rainfall), exceeding Boston Water and Sewer Commission 
(BWSC) requirements and will prioritize the use of green infrastructure solutions.

The PDA Area is not within a current FEMA floodplain, and is located outside the boundary for 
the 2070 1% annual chance event used in Climate Ready Boston. While the Proposed Project has limited

performance models for review and approval by the IGBC.

Brighton stakeholders, the City, BPDA, and MBTA, as well as other developers in the area. 
● The Proponent is engaged in specific coordination with Harvard to develop a transit service plan that 
seeks to address the Phase A Project’s trip demand to/from Harvard Square, as well as Harvard University’s 
own needs. 
● The Proponent will include a total of 600 bike parking spaces within the Phase A Project, distributed 
across indoor and outdoor locations and in compliance with the City’s Bike Parking Guidelines. 
● Two Bluebike stations will be installed by the City in connection with the completion of the Phase A 
Project (at locations to be jointly approved by the Proponent and the City). Each such station will 
accommodate approximately 23 docks. Consistent with the City’s Bike Share program, a financial 
contribution of $250,000.00 will be made to the Boston Transportation Department not later than the date 
the Phase A Project obtains its first Certificate of Occupancy. Installation of both stations is anticipated to 
be completed concurrently with substantial completion of the Phase A Project. No other payment will be 
required in connection with the City’s Bike Parking program or implementation. 
● To support needed transit improvements, the Proponent will work with the BPDA, BTD, and the MBTA 
to design and install an eastbound transit lane on Western Avenue directly fronting the Phase A PDA Area. 
Final design requires BPDA, BTD, and MBTA approval. Installation is anticipated to be completed 
concurrently with substantial completion of the Phase A Project. 
● To further support transit improvements for the Phase A Project, and in support of larger transit 
improvements for the Allston community, the Proponent and Harvard University will participate in, and 
the Proponent will provide financial support to the BPDA in the amount of $500,000 for, a holistic study 
and design effort of a “Western Avenue Transitway” which will prioritize transit use, low stress bikeways, 
and generous pedestrian accommodations. This effort will allow the BPDA and BTD to advance work to 
support transit operations that will experience increased demand, and is in line with efforts underway by 
the BPDA through the Western Avenue Corridor Rezoning Study. The Proponent’s financial contribution 
will be made in two installments: the first installment, in the amount of $250,000, will be due concurrently 
with the issuance of a building permit for the Phase A Project; and the second installment, also in the amount 
of $250,000, will be due concurrently with substantial completion of the Phase A Project.

Effect of PDA Master Plan 
 
 10.1 Zoning 
The PDA Area is located within the Allston Landing North Economic Development Area, which is 
governed by Article 51 of the Zoning Code. As shown on the Survey, Exhibit B, the PDA Area contains 
more than five acres of land, and since it is not located in a residential zoning district, treating this 
submission as a Master Plan is authorized by Article 3-1A.a of the Zoning Code. 
This PDA Master Plan sets forth the zoning for all elements of the Proposed Project for the PDA Area. 
Upon approval by the BPDA and the Boston Zoning Commission, any PDA Development Plan for a 
Proposed Project within the PDA Area that is consistent with this PDA Master Plan will be presumed to be 
consistent with underlying zoning and all other provisions of the Zoning Code to the extent that such 
requirements are made applicable and have been addressed in this PDA Master Plan or a subsequent PDA 
Development Plan. A Certification of Consistency for individual buildings described in this PDA Master 
Plan shall be issued pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Zoning Code, in the case of Proponent’s buildings, or 
in the case of the Conference Center, under the provisions of Section 80D-10 of the Zoning Code. 
 9.2 
Parcels 
The PDA Area is an assembly of various legal lots which were acquired by Harvard over a period of time. 
In order to implement the Proposed Project, it is contemplated that new legal lots will be created and that 
one or more of those lots may be leased or conveyed to third parties. A plan of the proposed parcels is 
shown on Exhibit J attached hereto. This plan shows the proposed locations of each building and open 
space with respect to streets, and intended dimensions land area for each parcel, which are subject to 
modification as set forth in this PDA Master Plan. 
Notwithstanding that lots may be in separate legal ownership and separated by streets, the dimensional 
requirements and Floor Area Ratio set forth in this PDA Master Plan shall apply to the PDA Area as a 
whole and not to each individual lot, and a Certification of Consistency may be issued for each separate 
building and/or separately for each of the Phase A Project and the Phase B Project; provided that non-
compliance by a particular building or phase shall not affect compliance by any other currently existing 
building or a building for which a Certification of Consistency has been issued. 
 9.3 
Development Review 
Each building component of the Proposed Project within the PDA Area will undergo review as required by 
Article 80 of the Zoning Code, as well as design review subsequent to the submission of one or more PDA

Development Plans for the Proposed Project. Review of environmental impacts will be studied during the 
Article 80-B Large Project Review process, taking into account the technical studies already performed.

Code, respectively, and to further review by the BPDA of the schematic design, design development and

approvals of other governmental agencies, such as the City of Boston's Public Improvement Commission 
and the Boston Conservation Commission. No permits for any elements of the Proposed Project included 
in this PDA Master Plan, as the same may be amended, shall be required from the Zoning Board of Appeals.

subject to one or more PDA Development Plans submitted and approved in accordance with Article 80C

proposed buildings and/or PDA Development Plans will be required to comply with the governing

Dimensional Requirements and Urban Design Parameters 
 
In addition to other requirements, the PDA Master Plan’s development will be subject to the following 
additional dimensional requirements and urban design parameters: 
 
(i) 
Maximum Building Coverage. The portion of the land area within the PDA Area that is 
occupied by the footprint of buildings shall not exceed 50% in the aggregate, for purposes of 
which all buildings within the PDA Area shall be taken into account, and compared against the 
entire land area of the PDA Area, including without limitation open space and roadways. In 
calculating the portion of land area that is occupied by the footprint of buildings, a building 
footprint shall not include areas located wholly below grade or below open space, roadways, 
courtyards, service areas, and/or other similar areas open to the sky. 
 
(ii) 
Active Uses. Designs for each building shall, to the extent possible, seek to maximize the 
storefront area used for Active Uses (as defined below) on building facades facing on Western 
Avenue and East, Cattle and Science Drives as determined through the BPDA design review 
process. As used in this PDA Master Plan, “Active Uses” shall mean building lobbies, 
conference center uses and any of the following other uses if located on the ground floor: 
Restaurant Uses; Retail Uses; Hotel Uses; Facility of Public Assembly Uses; Neighborhood 
Medical Uses; Educational Uses, Art Uses; Entertainment Uses; Institutional Uses (as outlined 
and limited above); Community and Cultural Uses; and uses accessory thereto, in each case as 
outlined on Exhibit E. 
 
(iii) 
Parking, Service and Loading Dock Entrances; Private Service Driveways. For each 
building, dimensions and locations of curb cuts for parking entrances shall be determined 
through the BPDA design review process. 
 
(iv) 
Façade and Horizontal Building Wall Designs. Designs for each building, including horizontal 
facade massing, shall be determined through the BPDA design review process, as part of which 
buildings facades should be designed to maximize visual interest and avoid being perceived as a 
solid uninterrupted horizontal wall using publicly accessible ground-floor through-openings, or 
other such design features, or by being visually articulated as several smaller masses using 
different materials or colors, vertical breaks, bays, or other architectural elements. In addition, 
buildings should reflect a rhythm and variation appropriate to the urban context. 
 
Any variations from the use and dimensional requirements and urban design parameters set forth above and 
in Section 4.3 shall require approval pursuant to the PDA Development Plan, and for material variations may 
also require an amendment to this PDA Master Plan and the applicable PDA Development Plan, as 
determined by the BPDA.

I. 
Proponent 
Tishman Speyer ERC Developer, L.L.C. 
II. 
Project 
Location 
The PDA Area is an approximately 14.2 acre parcel of land, bounded generally by 
Western Avenue on the north, the Harvard property which is ground-leased to 
National Resilience Inc. on the east, the Harvard University District Energy Facility 
(“DEF”) on the southeast, and Harvard property west of Hague Street on the west. 
III. 
Development 
 Concept 
The PDA Master Plan proposes the construction of multiple buildings that comprise 
Phase A of the Proposed Project, containing a total of approximately 900,000 square 
feet and described conceptually below: 
 
● an office/lab building with approximately 440,000 square feet of office/lab and 
retail and restaurant space, 
● a residential structure having two distinct massings with approximately 
263,500 square feet of residential and retail and restaurant space and 
approximately 345 units, 
● a hotel with approximately 135,000 square feet of hotel and retail space and 
approximately 250 hotel rooms, 
● an approximately 61,500 square foot conference center and retail and 
restaurant space, and 
● up to 580 off-street parking spaces. 
 
The PDA Master Plan also includes various open spaces, including a greenway that 
will bisect the site (the “Project Greenway”). 
 
Those spaces will connect to the west to the network of open spaces beginning 
behind the Honan-Allston Branch Library at Ray Mellone Park and extending 
eastward through Rena Park and continuing east to Soldiers Field Road. 
 
In addition, the PDA Master Plan provides for new roadways and access driveways. 
The most significant of these is Cattle Drive, a new north-south roadway which will 
provide access into and through the PDA Area. In the long-term, Cattle Drive will 
provide a through connection from Western Avenue to Cambridge Street and on to 
the future multimodal West Station commuter rail stop. 
 

 
 
 
EAST\183845827.44 
IV. 
 Project Uses 
Allowed uses for the PDA Area include, among others, office, laboratory, 
residential, cultural, research and development, service, open space (including 
programmed open space), hotel, conference center, and retail and/or restaurant, 
together with accessory and ancillary uses thereto. A limited amount of 
Institutional Uses will be allowed in the Proposed Project, consistent with 
applicable Institutional Master Plan requirements. Uses will also include below-
grade, at-grade, and structured accessory parking for all types of uses as set forth 
in the "Parking" section of the PDA Master Plan. Roadways constructed within 
the PDA Area are expected to serve the PDA uses and adjacent uses, including 
institutional uses. There will also be below-grade utility lines running from the 
DEF to institutional and non-institutional buildings in the vicinity. 
 
 
V. 
Public Benefits 
The development of the Proposed Project contemplated by the PDA Master Plan will 
provide a range of public benefits, including: 
● Increased and improved publicly-accessible open space which connects to a 
broader network of open spaces; 
● New affordable housing units in connection with any residential development 
that comply with City requirements; 
● Housing and job linkage payments from qualifying uses in connection with 
construction of buildings containing such uses; 
● New construction and permanent jobs; 
● Increased tax revenues for the City; 
● Measures to advance Boston’s carbon neutral and climate ready goals by 
incorporating a variety of sustainable design and resilient building strategies 
that will reduce carbon emissions, improve water quality, reduce the urban 
heat island effect, maximize the conservation of energy and water, and reduce 
the risk of flooding due to sea level rise; 
● Measures to promote diversity, equity and inclusion, including the creation of 
investment opportunities for diverse investors, commitments to contract with 
MBE and WBE firms for 15% of the total value of preconstruction and 
construction contracts, and initiatives to allocate 25% of the retail to small, 
local, MBE, and/or WBE retailers, and 
● Transportation improvements, including new complete streets and transit 
service serving both persons living and working at the Proposed Project and 
the general public in the Allston community. 
 
Public benefits associated with each phase of the Proposed Project will be 
included in the PDA Development Plan for such phase.

more than 580 permanent parking spaces, which are to include up to 300 below-grade off-street

this Development Plan) outside the Master Plan PDA Area or surface parking lots within the

 13.3 Workforce, Economic Development, and Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Benefits 
 
● 
The Project is expected to create approximately 2,300 permanent jobs relating to the 
commercial, hotel, retail, restaurant, parking and residential administration components, and to 
create approximately 2,000 construction jobs in a variety of trades. 
● 
Historically there have been disparities in economic opportunities available to under-
represented populations in the commercial real estate industry, particularly for wealth creation 
opportunities and true ownership of institutional-scale development projects. With regard to the 
capitalization of the Project, the Proponent set out to raise investment from Black and Latinx 
investors for a targeted 5% of equity for the Project. Through concerted and wide-ranging efforts 
to identify, source, and structure such investments, the Proponent was able to bring over 150 Black 
and Latinx individuals into the Project’s ownership, including local Boston-area residents, in 
amounts that totaled approximately $30 million. This represents what is believed to be the largest 
such inclusionary investor initiative (in terms of total dollars) for a private development in the 
history of the City of Boston.

To foster small, local, MBE, or WBE retailers, the Proponent is committed to allocating 
25% of the retail at the Project to such retailers, and, as necessary, work with such retailers to 
provide advantageous lease terms. 
● 
As part of the Proponent’s commitment to allocate approximately 25% of the retail at the 
Project to small, local, MBE, and/or WBE retailers, the Proponent will designate a ~1,500 SF 
ground floor retail space in the Project as a flexible arts space that will include a rotating program 
of art and cultural uses, which could include pop up gallery opportunities for local artists to show 
their work. 
● 
The Proponent has committed to awarding at least 15% of the total value of its 
preconstruction contracts for the Project to certified MBE and WBE firms and to awarding at least 
15% of the total value of its construction contracts for the Project to certified MBE and WBE 
firms. 
 13.4 Sustainable and Resilient Development 
 
● 
The Project will advance Boston’s carbon neutral and climate ready goals by incorporating 
a variety of sustainable design and resilient building strategies that will reduce carbon emissions, 
improve water quality, reduce the urban heat island effect, maximize the conservation of energy 
and water, and reduce the risk of flooding due to sea level rise. 

 
 
12 
 
 
● 
The lab/office, residential and hotel buildings of the Project will be eligible to receive 
LEED Gold certification at a minimum using the LEEDv4 rating system, exceeding the City’s 
requirements under Article 37 - Green Buildings. The Project lab/office, residential and hotel 
buildings will be eligible to achieve Fitwel certification (a certification system focused on building 
health for all, originally created by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and U.S. 
General Services Administration) in addition to LEED Gold certification. 
● 
The Project will reduce energy and stationary source GHG emissions by targeting zero net 
carbon building performance including a 40% reduction in carbon emissions as compared to the 
Base Case (Stretch Code) with 2035 electric grid emissions. 
● 
The Project will prioritize systems and solutions that utilize renewable energy, and will 
explore the feasibility of providing 90% of the Project’s Lab/Office and Hotel and 100% of the 
Residential and Conference Center building energy needs by electricity when the Project opens. 
Additionally, the Project will achieve a BERDO emissions standard of 1 kg co2e/sf/yr, and will 
explore a reduction below this level. 
● 
The Project will utilize a combination of on-site renewable energy and utilities provided 
through the District Energy Facility in connection with the Conference Center, if feasible. 
● 
The Project will consider incorporating design strategies and construction materials to 
reduce Heat Island conditions, where feasible, including the use of low SRI building wall and roof 
products and site hardscape materials, building and site canopies, and landscape design and 
plantings. 
● 
The Proposed Project will incorporate design elements to improve on-site stormwater 
management and reduce risk of precipitation-based flooding. The Proposed Project will provide a 
significant amount of public realm and open space improvements, and the Proposed Project will 
be designed and engineered to manage the 32-year storm (6.7 inches of rainfall), exceeding Boston 
Water and Sewer Commission (BWSC) requirements and will prioritize the use of green 
infrastructure solutions. 
● 
The Project Site is not within a current FEMA floodplain, and is located outside the 
boundary for the 2070 1% annual chance event used in Climate Ready Boston. While the Project 
has limited coastal flood risk, first floor elevations are proposed to be raised to 18.5-19.5 feet 
Boston City Base (BCB). 
● 
The Proponent will provide updated individual building Article 37 Initial Filings including 
updated performance models for review and approval by the IGBC. 
 13.5 Smart Utilities 
 
● 
The Project has completed a district energy microgrid feasibility assessment and master 
plan, and reviewed the results with the BPDA. The study included analysis of an ambient water 
loop served by a combination of air to water heat pumps, ground source and electric boilers in

incremental steps to reduce natural gas consumption in buildings for heating and domestic hot 
water demands.

The Phase A Project has assessed the necessary infrastructure improvements for telecom 
conduit and a utilidor, including confirmation of adequate system capacity for the Proposed

● 
The Project will provide for stormwater resiliency storage to accommodate an additional 
1.5 inches of runoff, above the typically-required 1.25-inch water quality volume, for the 
impervious site areas of the Project. Those volumes result in a total of 2.75-inches of stormwater 
storage for the Project. 
 
● 
The Phase A Project has assessed the needs for additional conduit for future electric and 
fiber infrastructure in relevant sidewalks, to support the City’s needs for deployment of future 
smart technology (with such review to be coordinated with the Public Improvement Commission).

The Project will comply with the City of Boston EV Readiness Policy for New 
Developments, including EV chargers and needed infrastructure. Twenty-five percent (25%) of

 13.6 Traffic and Transit Benefits 
 
● The Project will introduce transportation improvements for a wide range of users, including 
new multimodal connections that currently do not exist. Those connections, such as an east-west 
shared-use path (and Project Greenway) and complete streets, will connect pedestrians and 
bicyclists traveling through and to the Project Site from surrounding neighborhoods. The Project 
will prioritize transit improvements and safe pedestrian and bicycling movements on Western 
Avenue. Final design of new and reconstructed roadways, including any and all pick up/drop off 
locations, is subject to further review and approval by the BPDA, BTD, and PIC. 

 
 
14 
 
 
● Proposed transit mitigation measures include working with the MBTA to improve service on 
bus Routes 86 and 70, implementation of supplemental transit services, in cooperation with other 
Allston-area stakeholders, to provide connections to key transit hubs, and transit priority and bus 
stop improvements on Western Avenue. The service plan details for the neighborhood transit 
connections are expected to be determined in collaboration with the City of Boston and Allston-
Brighton Transportation Management Association (ABTMA) via the Allston-Brighton 
Neighborhood Connector Study and with the MBTA via the Bus Network Redesign project. Those 
efforts will include broad input from residents and Allston-Brighton stakeholders, the City, BPDA, 
and MBTA, as well as other developers in the area. 
● The Proponent is engaged in specific coordination with Harvard to develop a transit service 
plan that seeks to address the Project’s trip demand to/from Harvard Square, as well as Harvard 
University’s own needs. 
● The Proponent will include a total of 600 bike parking spaces within the Project, distributed 
across indoor and outdoor locations and in compliance with the City’s Bike Parking Guidelines. 
● Two Bluebike stations will be installed by the City in connection with the completion of the 
Project (location to be jointly approved by the Proponent and the City). Each such station will 
accommodate approximately 23 docks. Consistent with the City’s Bike Share program, a financial 
contribution of $250,000.00 will be made to the Boston Transportation Department not later than 
the date the Project obtains its first Certificate of Occupancy. Installation of both stations is 
anticipated to be completed concurrently with substantial completion of the Project. No other 
payment will be required in connection with the City’s Bike Parking program or implementation. 
● To support needed transit improvements, the Proponent will work with the BPDA, BTD, and 
the MBTA to design and install an eastbound transit lane on Western Avenue directly fronting the 
Project Site. Final design requires BPDA, BTD, and MBTA approval. Installation is anticipated 
to be completed concurrently with substantial completion of the Project. 
● To further support transit improvements for the Phase A Project, and in support of larger transit 
improvements for the Allston community, the Proponent and Harvard University will participate 
in, and the Proponent will provide financial support to the BPDA in the amount of $500,000 for a 
holistic study and design effort of a “Western Avenue Transitway” which will prioritize transit 
use, low stress bikeways, and generous pedestrian accommodations. This effort will allow the 
BPDA and BTD to advance work to support transit operations that will experience increased 
demand, and is in line with efforts underway by the BPDA through the Western Avenue Corridor 
Rezoning Study. The Proponent’s financial contribution will be made in two installments: the first 
installment, in the amount of $250,000, will be due concurrently with the issuance of a building 
permit for the Project; and the second installment, also in the amount of $250,000, will be due 
concurrently with substantial completion of the Project.

Dimensional Requirements and Urban Design Parameters 
 
In addition to other requirements, the Development Plan’s development will be subject to the 
following additional dimensional requirements and urban design parameters: 
 
(i) 
Maximum Building Coverage. The portion of the land area within the Master Plan 
PDA Area that is occupied by the footprint of buildings shall not exceed 50% in the 
aggregate, for purposes of which all buildings within the Master Plan PDA Area shall 
be taken into account, and compared against the entire land area of the Master Plan 
PDA Area including without limitation open space and roadways. In calculating the 
portion of land area that is occupied by the footprint of buildings, a building footprint 
shall not include areas located wholly below grade or below open space, roadways, 
courtyards, service areas, and/or other similar areas open to the sky. 
 
(ii) 
Active Uses. Designs for each building shall, to the extent possible, seek to maximize 
the storefront area used for Active Uses (as defined below) on building facades facing 
on Western Avenue and East, Cattle and Science Drives as determined through the 
BPDA design review process. As used in this Development Plan, “Active Uses” shall 
mean building lobbies, conference center uses and any of the following other uses if 
located on the ground floor: Restaurant Uses; Retail Uses; Hotel Uses; Facility of 
Public Assembly Uses; Neighborhood Medical Uses; Educational Uses, Art Uses; 
Entertainment Uses; Institutional Uses (as outlined and limited above); Community and 
Cultural Uses; and uses accessory thereto, in each case as outlined on Exhibit D. 
 
(iii) 
Parking, Service and Loading Dock Entrances; Private Service Driveways. For 
each building, dimensions and locations of curb cuts for parking entrances shall be 
determined through the BPDA design review process. 
 
(iv) 
Façade and Horizontal Building Wall Designs. Designs for each building, including 
horizontal facade massing, shall be determined through the BPDA design review 
process, as part of which buildings facades should be designed to maximize visual 
interest and avoid being perceived as a solid uninterrupted horizontal wall using 
publicly accessible ground-floor through-openings, or other such design features, or by 
being visually articulated as several smaller masses using different materials or colors, 
vertical breaks, bays, or other architectural elements. In addition, buildings should 
reflect a rhythm and variation appropriate to the urban context. 
 
 
Any variations from the use and dimensional requirements and urban design parameters set forth 
above and in Section 4 shall require approval pursuant to this Development Plan, and for material 
variations may also require an amendment to the Master Plan and this Development Plan, as 
determined by the BPDA.

SUBJECT: 
REQUEST AUTHORIZATION AND APPROVALS REGARDING THE TWO-
YEAR RENEWAL OF THE 2013 INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN FOR 
HARVARD UNIVERSITY’S CAMPUS IN ALLSTON 
______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(“BRA”) d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) Board 
(1) approve a two-year renewal of the 2013 Institutional Master Plan 
for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston (the “Harvard IMP”) 
pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6, Section 80D-8, and 
Section 51-29(6) of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”) and (2) 
authorize the Director to take all actions and execute all documents 
deemed necessary and appropriate by the Director in connection with 
such renewal of the Harvard IMP. 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The 2013 Institutional Master Plan for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston (the 
“Harvard IMP”) was approved by the BRA Board in October 2013 and by the Boston 
Zoning Commission in November 2013. The BRA Board approved five amendments 
to the Harvard IMP; the First Amendment in 2016; the Second, Third, and Fourth 
Amendments in 2017; and the Fifth Amendment on December 15, 2022. The BRA 
Board approved a four-year renewal of the original 2013 Institutional Master Plan in 
December 2017. 
 The term of the 2017 renewal of the Harvard IMP runs until 
 
* Effective October 20, 2016, the BRA commenced doing business as the BPDA. 

2 
 
 
4890-9893-9461, v. 1 
March 20, 2023 pursuant to Chapter 53 of the Acts of 2020, which tolled the 
expiration date of local permits and approvals during the Covid State of Emergency. 
 
On September 8, 2022, Harvard submitted an IMPNF for the Fifth IMP Amendment 
(the “IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment”), for the 92 Seattle Street Project. The IMPNF 
for Fifth IMP Amendment also included a request for the renewal of the Harvard 
IMP (the “Renewal Request”) pursuant to Section 51-29(6) of the Code, which 
provides that colleges and universities in Allston/Brighton are required to renew 
their Institutional Master Plans every four years. The Renewal Request proposes no 
new Proposed Institutional Projects; no changes to the Harvard IMP that would 
constitute a change in the use, dimensional, parking, or loading elements of the 
Harvard IMP; and no significantly greater impacts would result from continued 
implementation of the approved Harvard IMP than were originally projected. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW 
 
The Renewal Request is subject to Institutional Master Plan Review, and qualified 
for a waiver of further review in accordance with Section 80D5.2(e) and 80D-6 in 
that (i) the Renewal Request proposes no new Proposed Institutional Projects; (ii) 
no changes to the Harvard IMP are proposed that would constitute a change in the 
use, dimensional, parking, or loading elements of the Harvard IMP; and (iii) no 
significantly greater impacts would result from continued implementation of the 
approved Harvard IMP than were originally projected. The Renewal Request seeks 
approval of the renewed Harvard IMP for a period of two years. Harvard intends to 
start the process of preparing a new Institutional Master Plan pursuant to Section 
80D-8 of the Code in 2023. 
 
The IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment, which included the Renewal Request, was 
filed on September 8, 2022, initiating a 30-day comment period. Harvard presented 
the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment to the Harvard-Allston Task Force on 
September 22, 2022. The BPDA approved the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment on 
December 15, 2022, with the Renewal Request to be considered separately prior to 
the expiration of the previous renewal. 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, BPDA staff recommends that the BPDA Board authorize 
the Director to (1) approve a two-year renewal of the 2013 Institutional Master Plan 
for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston (the “Harvard IMP”) pursuant to Section 

3 
 
 
4890-9893-9461, v. 1 
80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6, Section 80D-8, and Section 51-29(6) of the City of Boston 
Zoning Code (the “Code”) and (2) authorize the Director to take all actions and 
execute all documents deemed necessary and appropriate by the Director in 
connection with such renewal of the Harvard IMP. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That in connection with the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
for the Fifth Amendment to the 2013 Institutional Master Plan for 
Harvard University’s Campus in Allston, filed by Harvard University on 
September 8, 2022, and after consideration of the request included 
therein (the “Renewal Request”) for the two-year renewal of the 2013 
Institutional Master Plan for Harvard University’s Campus in Allston (as 
so renewed, the “Harvard IMP”) the BRA hereby find that (1) the 
Harvard IMP conforms to the provisions of Article 80D of the Code; (2) 
the Harvard IMP conforms to the general plan for the City of Boston as 
a whole; and (c) on balance, nothing in the Harvard IMP will be 
injurious to the neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public 
welfare, weighing all the benefits and burdens; and 
 
VOTED: 
That the BRA waives further review of the Renewal Request pursuant 
to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6, and Section 80D-8 of the Code 
and approves the Harvard IMP for a period of two (2) years from the 
date of approval of this renewal vote by the BRA, that is January 19, 
2025; and 
 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to execute any and all 
documents deemed necessary and appropriate by the Director in 
connection with the renewal of the Harvard IMP.

CHAIRMAN’S STATEMENT
June 14,2018
This is a public hearing before the Boston Redevelopment Authority doing
business as the Boston Planning & Development Agency, being held in
conformance with Article 80 of the Boston Zoning Code, to consider the Third
Amendment to the Joslin Diabetes Center Institutional Master Plan Amendment.
The hearing was duly advertised on May 30, 2018 in the Boston Herald.
In a BPDA hearing on a proposed petition by the Agency, staff members will
first present their case and are subject to questioning by members of the Agency.
Thereafter, others who wish to speak in favor of the proposed petition are afforded
an opportunity to do so under the same rules of questioning. Following that, those
who wish to speak in opposition may do so, again under the same rules of
questioning. Finally, the proponents are allowed a period of five to ten minutes for
rebuttal if they so desire. In an effort to accommodate all who would like to speak
about this proposal, each person will be given up to two minutes to comment.
BPDA staff will indicate when thirty seconds remain. At that time, please conclude
your remarks so that the hearing may continue and others may be heard.
Ms. Sullivan will now begin the presentation.

INTRODUCTION
An Institutional Master Plan for joslin Diabetes Center (“Joslin” or the “Proponent”)
was first approved by the BRA on May 1, 2003, and approved by the Boston Zoning
Commission on May 28, 2003, and was amended and extended for ten years by the
Joslin Diabetes Center Institutional Master Plan Amendment dated April 29, 2008
(the “First IMP Amendment”), which was approved by the BRA on April 29, 2008, and
approved by the Boston Zoning Commission on May 28, 2008.
On April 6, 201 8, joslin submitted an Institutional Master Plan Notification Form
(“IMPNF”) For Renewal and Amendment oftheJoslin Diabetes Center Institutional
Master Plan (“IMP”) to the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) d/b/a Boston
Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”).
The proposed IMPNF For Renewal and Amendment extends the joslin Diabetes
Center’s IMPfora period of five (5) years from April 29, 2018to April 29, 2023. The
IMPNF For Renewal and Amendment also adds retail uses (excluding adult
bookstores and liquor stores), restaurant uses (including take-out restaurant uses),
and service uses to the allowed uses on the first floor of the building located at 415-
435 Brookline Avenue within the Institutional Master Plan Overlay Area.
PROJECT/IMP REVIEW
The IMPNF For Renewal and Amendment was presented to the community at a
meeting of the Longwood Medical and Academic Area Forum (“LMA Forum”) on
April 23, 2018 and was reviewed at a Scoping Session with public agencies on April
25, 2018. The IMPNF For Renewal and Amendment is subject to Institutional
Master Plan review pursuant to Section 80D of the Boston Zoning Code (the
“Code”).
The IMPNF For Renewal and Amendment meets the requirements for expedited
review pursuant to Section 80D-9.2 of the Code, Expedited Review for Certain Small
Projects. The BPDA may waive the requirement of a Scoping Determination for an
amendment pursuant to Section 80D-5.3(e), given the finding that the IMPNF For

Renewal and Amendment meets the requirements for expedited review pursuant
to Section 80D-9.2 of the Code, Expedited Review for Certain Small Projects.
RECOMMENDATION
Based on the foregoing, BPDA staff recommends that the BPDA: (1) waive the
requirement for the issuance of a Scoping Determination pursuant to Section 80D-
5.3(e) of the Boston Zoning Code (“Code”) in connection with the IMPNF For
Renewal and Amendment and approve the Joslin IMP, together as the renewed and
amended Joslin Diabetes Center Institutional Master Plan pursuant to Section 80D-
9.2 of the Code; (2) authorize the Director to issue an Adequacy Determination
approving the IMPNF For Renewal and Amendment; (3) authorize the Director to
issue one or more Certifications of Consistency or partial Certifications of
Consistency pursuant Section 80D-1 0 of the Code; (4) authorize the Director to
issue one or more Certifications of Approval for the Proposed Project pursuant to
Section 80E-6 of the Code; and (5) authorize the Director to take any and all actions
and execute any and all documents deemed necessary and appropriate by the

2.
Mission and Objectives
2.1
Joslin Mission Statement
The healthcare epidemic of our time, diabetes, affects more than 20 million Americans. In the
face of this public health crisis, Joslin Diabetes Center, a Harvard Medical School-affiliated
institution, is executing the largest categorical attack on the disease in the world.
Joslin is the world’s largest diabetes research center, diabetes clinic and provider of diabetes
education. Its concentrated focus on a single disease allows it to rapidly discover, create and
distribute new knowledge about diabetes prevention, treatment options and research toward a
cure.
Joslin is committed to addressing the challenges of diabetes from all angles, to deliver
exceptional, compassionate care and education to not only treat, but also empower patients and
their families to help manage diabetes and improve their overall health and quality of life.
The ultimate goal of this approach is to help people with diabetes live long, healthy lives and
offer real hope and progress toward prevention and a cure. Our mission is to improve the lives of
people with diabetes and its complications through innovative care, education and research that
will lead to the prevention and cure of the disease.
2.2
Major Operating Divisions
Among the Harvard Medical School-affiliated institutions, Joslin is one of the most research-
intensive academic medical centers and is unique in its sole focus on diabetes.
Founded in 1898 by a single physician, Elliott P. Joslin, M.D., Joslin today employs
approximately 480 individuals in the following major areas:
• Joslin Research: a highly collaborative team of people undertaking the largest research
program aimed at preventing and curing type 1 and type 2 diabetes and their long-
term complications.
• Joslin Clinic, Inc.: the world’s first and most respected diabetes care facility, which
cares for approximately 23,000 adult and pediatric patients a year.
Joslin Education and Care: Provides innovative learning programs that expand the
availability of Joslin knowledge and expertise to people with diabetes and the
clinicians who care for them domestically and across the globe.
Joslin Administration: Provides administrative and operational support in Finance,
Human Resources, IT and other administrative areas.
5
4824-2646-6656.4

2.2.1
Joslin Research
Joslin research comprises the most comprehensive and productive effort in diabetes research
anywhere in the world. Joslin researchers focus on unraveling the biologic, biochemical and
genetic processes that underlie the development of type 1 and type 2 diabetes and related
complications.
Joslin research is highly innovative and imaginative, employing the newest tools in genetics,
genomics and proteomics to identify abnormalities that may play a role in the development of
diabetes and its complications. Joslin Clinic patients, and others with diabetes, have the option of
participating in clinical trials at Joslin to help translate basic research into treatment innovations.
Joslin has one of the largest diabetes training programs in the world, educating approximately
130 physicians and Ph.D. researchers each year, many of whom go on to lead diabetes initiatives
at leading institutions all over the globe. Three Joslin researchers are members of the prestigious
National Academy of Science, a rare accomplishment even in large academic medical and
research institutions.
Joslin’s research budget has grown 15-fold since 1983, with strong support from the National
Institutes of Health. Other support for Joslin research comes from the Juvenile Diabetes Research
Foundation, the American Diabetes Association, as well as from individuals, foundations and
industry.
2.2.2
Joslin Clinic, Inc.
Joslin Clinic, since its inception, has focused on comprehensive care of the patient. Joslin’ s team
consists of board-certified physicians expert in treating diabetes, Certified Diabetes Educators,
Behavioral Health experts providing the patient with all care needed to live a full and productive
life with Diabetes. Joslin has a large patient database and the largest patient population using
insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors. Joslin’s 23,000 patients benefit from highly
specialized care.
Dr. Elliott P. Joslin is credited with creating modern day diabetes care, which utilizes a combined
medical and educational team approach to empower patients to manage their disease in order to
prevent complications. Dr. Joslin was an early champion of tight glucose control and was proven
right 75 years later by the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT).
Today, Joslin’s care teams are made up of highly specialized and multi-skilled experts in all
facets of diabetes, including adult and pediatric diabetes, kidney disease, eye care, mental health
and pregnancy, as well as Certified Diabetes Educators — nurses, dietitians, exercise
physiologists, nurse practitioners and mental health professionals. Joslin clinicians are relentless
in their pursuit of diabetes complications, which are a devastating burden to the patient, their
family and the national healthcare system.
6
4824-2646-6656.4

The impact Joslin has in preventing complications is second to none. Our care model is proof
that with the recommended standard of care and management, complications of diabetes can be
prevented or reversed. Joslin Clinic consistently ranks among the best in the care of patients with
diabetes as measured by national quality indicator data collected by American Diabetes
Association, National Committee on Quality Assurance and numerous private and for-profit
health data consortiiims, including Bridges to Excellence.
Beetham Eye Institute: Integral to patient care is the delivery of the world’s finest diabetes eye
treatment through Joslin’s Beetham Eye Institute. Techniques pioneered at the Beetham have
preserved the vision of more than nine million people around the globe.
Pediatric Health Services: Joslin Clinic provides pioneering care and support of pediatric
patients and their families. Joslin cares for a large portion of children with diabetes in
Massachusetts and more than a quarter of all children with diabetes in New England. Joslin
provides the widest range of patient and family support programs anywhere.
Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center: Joslin Clinic is affiliated with the Beth Israel
Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), a teaching hospital affiliate of Harvard Medical School.
Together, Joslin assists BIDMC primarily in the inpatient setting at the hospital.
2.2.3
Joslin Care and Education Initiatives
Joslin’ s care and education initiatives focus on improving the quality of diabetes care around the
globe. These programs include professional medical education, telemedicine services,
Publications, Affiliated Centers and education provided directly to hospital physicians and nurses
at various locations around the world. Joslin has the largest and most expansive diabetes
continuing medical education program in the world. Since 2002, Joslin professional education
has reached more than 500,000 healthcare providers.
Joslin also provides a wealth of patient education through books, videos and online services,
allowing people around the globe to learn how Joslin experts recommend they manage their
disease.
2.3
Collaboration with Other Institutions
Our affiliation with Harvard Medical School gives Josh11 researchers opportunities to collaborate
with other investigators with complementary interests and expertise. Most Joslin researchers and
clinicians have academic appointments at Harvard Medical School and several are involved in
Ph.D. training at the Medical School.
Our investigators are advancing science at an unusually fast pace due to Joslin’s unique
environment. For example, Joslin’s Diabetes Endocrinology Research Center (DERC) provides
the infrastructure necessary to support research efforts across all the disciplines and encourage
the development of young scientists. The DERC offers researchers specialized technical
assistance as well as a network of colleagues from across the medical and scientific community.
The DERC framework facilitates translational research—that is, the collaboration between basic
7
4824-2646-6656.4

scientists and clinical investigators—resulting in breakthroughs that make a difference to the
millions of people living with diabetes.
These types of collaborations offer an incredibly rich setting in which to work, and provide a
significant asset to our researchers. Two other important examples are our affiliations with Beth
Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School, which enables Joslin researchers
to work with investigators with complementary interests and expertise through such programs as
the Harvard Stem Cell Institute; the Clinical Islet Transplantation Program at Harvard Medical
School; and the Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation Center on Immunological Tolerance in
Type 1 Diabetes. In addition, Joslin is part of the Boston Autologous Islet Replacement Therapy
Program (BAIRT), an academic and industry sponsored research program that looks to link a
patient’s own insulin producing cells to cure Diabetes.
Joslin maintains close links to other LMA institutions, including Children’s Hospital for
pediatrics inpatient care and training of fellows in pediatric endocrinology.

3.
Existing Property and Uses
3.1
Description of Existing Campus
The Joslin campus as it appears today is essentially one building comprised of two separate
wings. The original Joslin research and clinic facility was constructed at the corner of Pilgrim
Road and Joslin Place in 1956 and remains in active use today supporting clinical and research
programs (the “1950s Building”).
A second wing, the Howard F. Root Wing on Brookline Avenue was completed in 1976, to
provide Joslin with additional space for research and clinical activities. This structure was
originally four stories in height (50 feet) and included retail space on the first floor level along
Brookline Avenue. At the time it was constructed, the design allowed for three additional floors.
Joslin subsequently completed the expansion of this building in 1991, by adding three stories
along Brookline Avenue and raising the courtyard to the Pilgrim Road level. A portion of the
courtyard was enclosed for visitor and staff lounge fl4nctions.
Joslin presently occupies approximately 242,300 gsf~ consisting of research, clinic, and
administrative space. In addition, Joslin has historically leased retail, office and restaurant space
on the first floor along Brookline Avenue (approximately 12,000 gsf). At the time of its 1991
expansion, Joslin was issued permission for conditional use and variance from the City of
Boston, Board of Appeal (BZC -15190 dated November 19, 1991) allowing for aFAR of 3.9.
This variance allowed Joslin to achieve a maximum height of 100 feet from average site grade
(eight stories) along Brookline Avenue.
After approval of the IMP Area under the 2008 IMP Amendment, the FAR of the existing
improvements on the IMP Area was increased to approximately 5.4.
3.2
Pedestrian Access
Pedestrian access to the main reception area of Joslin is accessible via Joslin Place. Through the
main entrance Joslin’s Beetham Eye unit can be accessed. The Pilgrim Road access provides
access to Pediatrics and Adult Diabetes clinics on the second floor. All entrances are
handicapped accessible.
3.3
Parking and Loading Facilities
Joslin’s parking needs are provided by garages located in the Longwood Medical Area. Joslin
does not have any parking available of its own. Employee parking is offered through Joslin’s
affiliation with MASCO and area parking companies. Loading dock and trash disposal functions
are accommodated within the completed PDA Project, known as Longwood Center, by virtue of
a lease agreement between the owner of the PDA Project and Joslin.
9
4824-2646-6656.4

4.
Needs of the Institution
4.1
Regional and National Trends
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, diabetes affects approximately
30.3 million Americabs and is the seventh leading cause of death in the U.S. Recently released
data from the American Diabetes Association (ADA) shows that in 2015, diabetes claimed more
than 252,806 lives. Increases in types 1 and 2 diabetes, as well as obesity, are also being
observed in children and adolescents presenting future challenges to the healthcare system.
Meanwhile, the financial burden associated with diabetes is staggering. In 2012, between
healthcare costs and lost productivity, diabetes costs the nation $245 billion annually. The ADA
estimates that one out of every five healthcare dollars is spent caring for someone with diabetes.
4.2
Strengths and Weaknesses of the Existing Campus
Joslin’ s present location in the LMA is ideal for multi-institutional research collaborations and
its major partners for clinical care are located in this area. However, while Joslin’s existing
facilities have served it well in its quest to eradicate diabetes, the prevalence of diabetes
continues. Additional research, alternative health care approaches, and an increased amount of
educational programs are necessary. The cu~ent infrastructure limits Joslin’s ability to expand
its research programs and its staff, to promote innovative approaches, and to support stronger
educational outreach programs. Research and clinical space are used to capacity.
Joslin anticipates that the greatest infrastructure needs will be in three areas:
• Well-trained staff: As the complexity of research and demands for clinical services
increase, the need for well-trained staff with a broad range of expertise will grow.
• Patient care and Administration: Joslin may need additional space to care for the ever
growing diabetic population.
• Lab and Research Facilities: Existing facilities are becoming antiquated and are
increasingly inadequate to optimally house even Joslin’s current programming needs.
The facility age and limitations impede Joslin’s ability to achieve its mission, as well as
the needed growth in research and administrative functions.

5.
Proposed Future Projects
5.1
Long-term Planning
Joslin is in the process of developing long-range space plans (e.g. beyond the 5-year term of this
Institutional Master Plan) that may include renovations of the buildings to ensure suitability for
use as a world-class research and clinical care facility.
5.2
Effect of Approval of the IMP Amendment
Pursuant to Article 80D of the Code, upon approval of this Institutional Master Plan Amendment
by the BPDA, uses or structures existing or described in this Institutional Master Plan will be
deemed to be in compliance with the use, dimensional, parking and loading requirements of
underlying zoning (including special purpose overlay districts) and may be reconstructed after
casualty, notwithstanding any provision of underlying zoning to the contrary and without the
requirement of further zoning relief.
So long as the existing uses or structures are consistent with the provisions of this Institutional
Master Plan, the existing uses or structures may be located on multiple contiguous parcels or
lots, whether or not any portion of the existing uses or structures satisfies the provisions of the
underlying zoning. Consistent therewith, any yard and setback requirements shall be measured
at the exterior property lines of the IMP Area, and shall not apply to any interior lots that may
exist or be created within the IMP Area. Building Height shall have the same meaning as
defined in Article 2A and shall be measured to the top of the last occupiable floor.
5.3
Future Building Renovation and Maintenance Projects
Throughout the term of this Institutional Master Plan, Joslin may conduct ongoing building
renovation projects and other campus improvements which may consist of an erection of
extension of an Institutional Use but which may be below the threshold for IMP Review or Large
Project Review. So long as each such project or improvement are below 20,000 SF GFA in the
aggregate, such work may be conducted without amendment of this Institutional Master Plan and
the permitted FAR under this Institutional Master Plan shall be deemed adjusted accordingly to
not greater than approximately 5.9. In accordance with Article 80D-7 of the Code, Joslin will
submit biannual updates from the date of approval of the IMP. These biannual updates will
include updates on any building renovation and maintenance projects.
5.4
Future Leased or Purchased Space
Joslin has no current plans to purchase or lease additional space located outside of the IMP Area.
Any such facility, to the extent it exceeds IMP exemption thresholds, would not require an
amendment to this Institutional Master Plan as long as the use category of the underlying zoning
which most closely described the use of such facility is either allowed as of right by the
underlying zoning or is allowed by zoning relief obtained by the property owner. This will give
Joslin the needed flexibility to meet its space and parking needs. In accordance with Article 80D-
11

7 of the Code, Joslin will submit biannual updates from the date of approval of the IMP. These
biannual updates will include updates on any future leased or purchased space.
5.5
Future Transfers of Space
During the term of this Institutional Master Plan, it is also unlikely that Joslin will transfer
certain property described in this Institutional Master Plan. In such event, Joslin may, by written
notice to the BPDA, elect to remove such property from the Institutional Master Plan and/or IMP
Area, whereupon:
a)
such transferred property, to the extent that it does not conform to the underlying zoning,
shall be deemed to be lawful prior nonconforming structures; and
b) remaining uses and structures described in this Institutional Master Plan shall be deemed
to be lawful prior nonconforming uses and structures to the extent they do not conform to
underlying zoning, notwithstanding the creation of a new lot as a result of such transfer.
In accordance with Article 80D-7 of the Code, Joslin will submit biannual updates from the date
of approval of the IMP. These biannual updates will include updates on any future transfers of
space.
5.6
Future Reallocation of Certain High Impact Subuses
From time to time during the term of this Institutional Master Plan, Joslin may reallocate Gross
Floor Area among the various Hospital Subuses, including certain High Impact Subuses (Facility
of Public Assemblies and Ambulatory Care Facilities) located within the IMP Area. Any such
reallocation will not require an amendment to this Institutional Master Plan as long as the Gross
Floor Area devoted to High Impact Subuses is not increased. This will give Joslin the needed
flexibility to meet its operational needs.

8.
Community Benefits
8.1
Impact on the Surrounding Area
Joslin is one of the most significant assets to the patient and medical community in Boston, a city
regarded as the country’s preeminent medical center. Here, Joslin plays a vital role as the only
Harvard Medical School Affiliated institution with a sole focus on diabetes. Joslin’s invaluable
educational programs and care resources benefit patients in the surrounding neighborhood, the
City of Boston and the New England region. Some of these benefits include:
• Joslin is aunique resource for people with diabetes and its complications. With 40
physicians on staff—the world’s largest team of board-certified physicians treating
diabetes— Joslin has a concentration of knowledge and support to help people manage
this difficult disease. Joslin has the largest patient database in the world—23,000 active
patients who make more than 70,000 visits a year, commuting to Boston from
surrounding towns and from all over New England for the best diabetes care available.
• Diabetes affects more than 6.2% of the population in Massachusetts. Joslin cares for 51-
76% of kids with diabetes in Massachusetts and 23-34% of kids with diabetes in New
England.
8.2
Special Programs
As part of Joslin’s clinical services, Joslin serves groups at high risk of developing diabetes, such
as African Americans, Latinos and Asian Americans. Two of Joslin’s programs offer unique
opportunities for Latinos and Asian Americans to receive diabetes care that is both linguistically
appropriate and culturally relevant.
8.2.1
Latino Diabetes Initiative (LDI)
The LDI at Joslin is designed to improve health outcomes for Latinos, who are one and one-half
times more likely to develop diabetes than non-Latino Caucasian Americans. Through vigorous
community outreach initiatives that aim to address common myths and perceptions about
diabetes, and in tandem with clinic services in Spanish, Joslin delivers innovative and specialized
care to Latinos in Boston, and from around the world. Outreach programs include: Beisbol y
Salud (Mo Peace Foundation), Bailey Salud (Dance for Health) — community dance program,
group visits, outreach to churches and other community gathering places, Rosa’s Story novella.
8.2.2
Asian American Diabetes Initiative (AADI)
The AADI was established in recognition of the growing challenge of diabetes in the Asian
American population. Joslin has implemented educational outreach programs that increase
awareness of diabetes in Asian communities, and draw these populations to the Joslin Clinic.
Through the AADI, patients receive culturally appropriate diabetes care from a team of doctors,
as well as a JoslinCare ambassador that offers translation services, coordinates appointments,
