SUBJECT: 
LENOX APARTMENTS, ROXBURY – CERTIFICATE OF COMPLETION 
_____________________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(the “BRA”) d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) 
authorize the Director to issue a Certificate of Completion for the 
successful completion of renovations of the buildings included in 
Lenox 2 Apartment (“Lenox 2 Project”) of the Lenox Apartments (the 
“Project”), in accordance with Section C.4 of the Cooperation 
Agreement by and between the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
and BC Lenox Limited Partnership and BC Lenox 2 Limited Partnership 
(collectively, the “Proponent”) dated January 14, 2021. 
 
_____________________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
PROJECT SITE 
 
The Lenox 2 Project is located at 625 Shawmut Avenue in Roxbury (formally a 
portion of 136 Lenox Street) and is bounded by Lenox Street to the northeast, 
Shawmut Avenue to the southeast, and Lenox Apartments (the “Lenox Project”) to 
the north and west, and consists of one (1) 1.9-acre site that is approximately 
82,899 square feet of land (the “Project Site”). 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
22 
 
 
 
 
2 
 
 
The Lenox 2 Project consists of 177 units of rental housing in seven apartment 
buildings as well as a community center building and management office 
containing 160,982 gross sf. In addition to the existing buildings, the Project Site 
includes parking lots for tenant use, a significant amount of green space with 
mature trees, and management office and community building. The Project Site is 
also located approximately 0.4 miles south of the MBTA’s Orange Line 
Massachusetts Ave. Station and is well served by several bus lines operating in 
Lower Roxbury. 
 
BACKGROUND: 
On March 12, 2020, the BPDA authorized the Director to: (1) issue a Scoping 
Determination waiving the requirement of further review pursuant to Article 80, 
Section 80B-5.3(d) of the Zoning Code for the Project; (2) issue a Certification of 
Compliance under Section 80B-6 for the Proposed Project upon successful 
completion of the Article 80 review process; and (3) execute and deliver a 
Cooperation Agreement and any and all other agreements and documents that the 
Director deems appropriate and necessary in connection with the Proposed 
Project. 
 
For financial structuring purposes, the renovations at the Project (as defined herein) 
have been separated into two projects: Lenox Project located at 601 Shawmut 
Avenue (“Phase One”) and Lenox 2 Project located at 625 Shawmut Avenue (“Phase 
Two”) (collectively referred to herein as the “Project”), owned by BC Lenox Limited 
Partnership and BC Lenox 2 Limited Partnership, respectively. The Project is a large 
development with 285 units and because of its size, the renovation work required 
two and a half years to complete. That lengthy project duration posed a challenge 
in attracting tax credit investors. By splitting the project in two, a portion of the tax 
credits may be delivered to the investor sooner—thereby optimizing the terms of 
the investment and eliminating the need for City funding. The two transactions 
closed simultaneously on February 9, 2021. This separation was noted in the BPDA 
Cooperation Agreement, dated January 14, 2021 (“the Cooperation Agreement”). On 
August 11, 2022, the BPDA authorized the Director to issue a Partial Certificate of 
Completion for the successful completion of construction of Phase One. 
 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
22 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
CERTIFICATE OF COMPLETION REQUEST 
On August 16, 2023, the Proponent submitted a request for a Certificate of 
Completion to the BPDA for Phase Two of the Project. A Certificate of Completion 
from the BPDA may be issued upon a determination that the construction of the 
Project has been completed in accordance with the terms and conditions of the 
Cooperation Agreement, and the final working drawings and specifications 
approved by the 
BPDA, and upon receipt of a Certificate of Occupancy from the Inspectional Services 
Department (“ISD”) for the Project. The BPDA staff architect performed a virtual site 
visit of the property on September 21, 2023, and found that the Phase Two of the 
Project was constructed in accordance with the approved plans. The Article 37 
Construction Completion Filing has been reviewed BPDA / IGBC staff and 
determined compliance has been demonstrated. ISD has issued Certificates of 
Occupancy for each of the seven buildings in the Project as well for the community 
building and management office, the last being issued on June 13, 2023. 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
BPDA staff recommends that the Board authorize the Director to issue a Certificate 
of Completion evidencing the successful completion of the Project, based upon the 
BPDA staff architect’s determination that the construction of the Project has been 
completed in accordance with the Cooperation Agreement and the final working 
drawings and specifications approved by the BPDA. Said Certification of Completion 
shall be provided in a form suitable for recording in the Suffolk County Registry of 
Deeds. 
 
An appropriate vote follows: 
 
VOTED: That the Director be, and hereby is authorized to issue a Certificate of 
Completion for the successful completion of Phase Two of the Lenox Apartments 
Project, in accordance with Section C.4 of the Cooperation Agreement by and 
between the Boston Redevelopment Authority and BC Lenox Limited Partnership 
and BC Lenox 2 Limited Partnership, dated January 14, 2021, subject to such terms 
as the Director deems to be necessary and appropriate.

PLANNING CONTEXT 
In December 2020, the BPDA approved the Simmons University Institutional 
Master Plan (“IMP”) intended to regulate development associated with the 
Simmons University campus. The plan focused on renovating and consolidating 
existing academic and residential facilities, which today are located in two 
separate campuses into a single campus. The effort would include the 
construction of a “Living and Learning Center” on the University’s Academic 
Campus, which would accommodate athletic space, a dining hall, and 
approximately 1,100 dormitory beds to replace existing student housing and 
uses on the University’s Residential Campus. The Simmons University 
Residential Campus (the “Residential Campus”) will, in turn, be leased to the 
Proponent to redevelop the Project Site. This Development Plan is a critical step 
to fulfilling the One Simmons vision that will support the continued growth and 
viability of Simmons University in this neighborhood. 

 
4 
 
 
For the redevelopment of the Residential Campus (the Project Site), the 
Development Plan proposes a mix of uses connected to and supported by the 
well-established Research and Development economy associated with the 
Longwood Medical & Academic Area. The Project Site is located within 
Longwood Medical & Academic Area Interim Guidelines study area, adopted by 
the Boston Planning & Development Agency in 2003. The interim guidelines, 
adopted nearly twenty years ago, were intended to be superseded by more 
formal analysis. In the intervening years since the interim guidelines were 
adopted, several long-range planning efforts, including Imagine Boston 2030 
and Go Boston 2030, have provided additional guidance relevant to the 
consideration of the Project. 
An Impact Advisory Group ("IAG") made up of residents, business owners, 
community organizations, and professionals has assisted the BPDA in its review of 
the Development Plan. The IAG has worked closely with BPDA staff, and members 
of the public, to minimize and mitigate any negative impacts, and to provide 
significant public and community benefits for the LMA and the Fenway 
neighborhoods. The BPDA and Proponent remain committed to continued 
engagement with the IAG as future Project filings are available and the Project 
advances through Article 80B Large Project Review. 
 
DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
 
The Development Plan will include approximately 2.6 acres of publicly accessible 
open space and up to 1.7 million square feet of gross floor area (GFA), as that term 
is defined in the Boston Zoning Code, of mixed-use development spread over five 
buildings including residential, community space, retail, laboratory uses, office uses, 
commercial uses, and accessory and ancillary parking in the PDA (the “Proposed 
Project” and “Project”). The buildings themselves will be categorized as either a) 
office/laboratory, research and development or b) residential, with retail and/or 
community spaces envisioned at the ground floor of each building. The Proposed 
Project will be served by up to the total number of parking spaces based upon 
ultimate contemplated full Project build out of the proposed GFA permitted under 
the Development Plan, at ratios of 0.3 parking spaces per 1,000 square feet of 
retail, office/lab, R&D uses, 0.3 parking spaces per rental or condominium unit, and 
zero (0) parking spaces for community use, provided that the overall parking for the 
Proposed Project shall not exceed 520 parking spaces, which will all be available 
upon completion of construction of the below-grade garage (as further described in 
the Development Plan). The Proponent is committed to a reduction in overall 

 
5 
 
 
parking if the full build out of the Proposed Project is less than the proposed GFA 
permitted under the Development Plan. 
 
The currently envisioned building program consists of the following uses and 
approximate square footages: 
● Office/Lab, Research & Development – 1,301,000 SF of GFA 
● Residential – 340,000 SF of GFA with approximately 388 units 
● Retail – 44,000 SF of GFA 
● Community Space - 15,000 SF of GFA 
 
The Proponent will satisfy the City’s Inclusionary Development Policy (IDP) policy 
by providing 20 percent affordable units on-site in each proposed residential 
building as part of the Proposed Project. Should the Proponent ultimately 
propose to not include all/or a portion of the affordable units on site for a 
residential building as part of an Article 80B filing, the Proponent shall be 
required to comply with the then current IDP Policy for such and all future 
residential buildings of the Proposed Project. 
 
Each building or phase of the Proposed Project shall comply with Article 28, 
Boston Civic Design Commission review, and Article 37, Green Buildings, of the 
Code, as well as the BPDA’s Smart Utilities Policy, and any other applicable 
review procedures at that time. Further, each building or phase of the Proposed 
Project shall undergo Large Project Review, in accordance with Article 80B of the 
Code and will be subject, as applicable, to Section 80B-7 of the Code. 
TRANSPORTATION & CIRCULATION 
 
The Project will include a new two-way street (“Mid-Block Street”) at the midpoint of 
the site and in alignment with the Colleges of the Fenway pathway, and a new 
separated pedestrian path and bi-directional bicycle path along Short Street. Both 
Mid-Block Street and the Short Street pedestrian and bicycle pathways will connect 
Brookline Avenue and Pilgrim Road Walking, biking, and transit improvements will 
be made along the Brookline Avenue frontage of the Project Site. 
 
Mid-Block Street will provide the only motor vehicle entrances and exits for the site-
wide below-grade garage and loading structure to serve the Project buildings. The 
Development Plan provides a conceptual layout and location of Mid-Block Street, 
and agreement that the Proponent and Simmons—as fee owner of the land—will 

 
6 
 
 
provide the City an easement for public vehicular travel through the Site, and a 
limited subsurface easement for required City utilities. The specific dimensions and 
details of the easements and Street will be determined through the Public 
Improvements Commission process as the Project proceeds through Article 80B 
Review and advances its design of the buildings, garage, landscape & hardscape 
elements of the Site. 
 
The Proposed Project will be served by up to the total number of parking spaces 
based upon ultimate contemplated full Project build out of the proposed GFA 
permitted under the Development Plan, at ratios of 0.3 parking spaces per 1,000 
square feet of retail, office/lab, R&D uses, 0.3 parking spaces per rental or 
condominium unit, and zero (0) parking spaces for community use, provided that 
the overall parking for the Proposed Project shall not exceed 520 parking spaces, 
which will all be available upon completion of construction of the below-grade 
garage (as further described in the Development Plan). The Proponent is 
committed to a change in overall parking if the full build out of the Proposed 
Project is different than the proposed GFA permitted under the Development Plan. 
All on-site motor vehicle parking and loading will be constructed within a below-
grade parking garage accessible from the Mid-Block Street. The motor vehicle 
parking spaces, permitted by this PDA, may be allocated among allowed uses at the 
discretion of the Proponent. 
 
The Proponent may in the future initiate an amendment to the PDA to seek 
additional motor vehicle parking spaces subject to the prevailing guidance from 
BTD and the analysis findings from the Fenway-Kenmore Transportation Access 
Plan at the time of such approval, including the most recently published Maximum 
Parking Ratio Guidelines and related Mobility Scores. Other than the motor vehicle 
parking space count, the remainder of the Project in compliance with the approved 
PDA will not be subject to further review by such an Amendment. 
 
The below-grade parking garage may also accommodate an additional 148 parking 
spaces for the Winsor School that were approved in the Development Plan for 
Planned Development Area No. 83, the Winsor School Campus (“PDA No. 83”), and 
originally planned to be located on the Winsor School campus. Provision of these 
spaces is subject to an amendment to PDA No. 83, to be sought by the Winsor 
School, for the relocation of these parking spaces, and the potential for 
improvements to the bicycle, pedestrian and landscape connection between Pilgrim 
Road and the Riverway for a safe connection to the Muddy River Path network that 
accommodates Winsor’s operational needs. No amendment to the Development 

 
7 
 
 
Plan (for this PDA #134) shall be needed in order to accommodate the future 
potential provision of these parking spaces for the Winsor School within the PDA 
Area. 
 
The Project at full build-out is anticipated to include approximately 924 long-term 
and 153 short-term bicycle parking spaces based on the Development Plan 
program. The specific amount of bicycle parking for each building will be 
determined during future Article 80B phases, and may be revised in response to 
potential programmatic changes or revisions to City bike parking guidelines. In 
addition, the Project is prepared to sponsor and accommodate on-site bikeshare 
stations for year-round public use, with the number, size, and configuration of 
stations to be determined during the Article 80B process for each building or 
Project phase.

established by Article 32 of the Code, the Restricted Parking Overlay District

allowed pursuant to Section 3-1A.a. of the Code, and the Project Site is over one 
acre, therefore treating this submission as a PDA is authorized by Article 3-1A.a 
of the Code. 
The proposed zoning for the Project Site will be as set forth in the Development

MITIGATION & COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
Urban Design and Public Realm Benefits 
● New Publicly Accessible Open Space: The Development Plan will 
provide a minimum of 2.6 acres of privately owned publicly accessible 
open space consisting of but not limited to: 
o A minimum 31,000 sf “Main Heart” for the Longwood Medical Area 
(“LMA”), publicly accessible active open space that breaks up the 
Site’s street frontage along Brookline Avenue; and 
o A minimum 12,500 sf “Passive Open Space” along Pilgrim Road 
that will provide a place of respite for the public, residents, and 
workers. 
● Public Programming: The Development Plan will provide a mix of active 
and passive programming throughout the Project Site in partnership with 
LMA institutions, industry groups and the City of Boston to activate the 
publicly accessible interior and exterior spaces. The Development Plan will 
also allocate spaces within the ground floor of the buildings to support 
public programming on the Project Site, including providing space for 
storage, access to public bathrooms, and the appropriate infrastructure 
for vendors to set up temporary structures for the public. 
● Parks Mitigation: The Proponent will provide payment equal to $7,000,000 
to create an endowment for use by the Boston Parks and Recreation 

 
10 
 
 
Department to support the needs of significant public City assets. This 
payment will 1) cover a maintenance endowment for the impacted area in 
the Emerald Necklace, 2) study the shadow impacted areas of the Emerald 
Necklace, and 3) develop a policy to prioritize the protection of the 
Emerald Necklace from development impacts. This study will be 
completed within approximately one year from the approval of the 
Development Plan. The study and resulting policy is intended to inform a 
similar effort that will examine the impacts of development on open 
spaces citywide. This payment will be made in two installments. The first 
installment of this payment will be $1,000,000 delivered within 30 days of 
unappealable Zoning approval of this PDA; the second installment of 
$6,000,000 will be delivered within 30 days after issuance of a building 
permit for above grade construction of Phase 1 of the Project. 
 
Following the approval of this project, this study will be conducted to 
better understand the impacts of shadows on parkland and develop a 
policy for protecting these important public assets. 
Streetscape and Transportation Improvements 
The Proponent has worked with the community, BPDA, Boston Transportation 
Department (BTD), and the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA), 
and proposes to reconfigure and improve existing infrastructure to provide safe, 
comfortable, accessible and engaging streetscapes along Brookline Avenue, 
Pilgrim Road, Mid-Block Street, and Short Street, subject to required approvals: 
 
● Pedestrians & Bicyclists 
o Providing upgraded streetscape along the Project Site’s Brookline 
Avenue frontage, including new, wider sidewalks, lighting, visitor bicycle 
parking, landscaping, and other amenities. 
o Designing and constructing a grade-separated bicycle lane along the 
Project Site’s Brookline Avenue frontage. 
o At Mid-Block Street, constructing a new protected, signalized pedestrian 
crosswalk across Brookline Avenue that aligns with the Colleges of the 
Fenway pathway 
o Providing a new, hybrid, dedicated lane along the Project Site’s Pilgrim 
Road frontage that can accommodate vehicles that are queuing while 
waiting to drop-off and pick-up Winsor students, and a new, hybrid 

 
11 
 
 
dedicated lane along the northwest wide of Pilgrim Road to 
accommodate approximately two Winsor athletic buses. 
o Re-designing and re-aligning the intersection of Brookline Avenue and 
Pilgrim Road by extending the curbs to reduce crossing distances for 
pedestrians and bicyclists, reduce vehicular turning speeds, and add 
landscaping. 
o The Project will construct Mid-Block Street that will provide primary 
access and egress for passenger cars and service vehicles to and from 
the Project, and a connection between Pilgrim Road and Brookline 
Avenue. 
o Providing new dedicated pedestrian and bi-directional bicycle paths 
connecting Brookline Avenue and Pilgrim Road, and separated by a 
landscape buffer along the PDA’s frontage on Short Street. These 
pedestrian and bicycle pathways will connect into the existing signalized 
intersection at Brookline Avenue and the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical 
Center driveway, and include an expanded accessible crosswalk, two-
way bicycle crossing, and new or relocated traffic, pedestrian, and 
bicycle signal equipment 
o Moving all service and loading of the PDA below-grade, thereby 
removing all loading activities from the public realm. 
o Sponsor and accommodate on-site bikeshare stations for year-round 
public use. 
● Public Transit 
o Working with the MBTA and the BTD to relocate and reconstruct two 
existing MBTA/LMA shuttle bus stops adjacent to the Project Site on the 
west side of Brookline Avenue with floating bus stops and new shelters 
o Becoming an active member of the Longwood Collective 
Transportation Management Association (“TMA”) and partner with the 
TMA to improve last mile connections between the Project Site and 
nearby MBTA Green Line, Orange Line, and commuter rail services. 
o Providing a contribution to help implement area transportation 
recommendations developed through the Fenway-Kenmore 
Transportation Action Plan that is equivalent to the greater of $5 per

Article 37 - Sustainability and Greenhouse Gas Emissions 
● LEED Certification: The Development Plan seeks to achieve LEED Gold 
certification at a minimum for each building using the most up to date 

 
12 
 
 
LEED rating system for all the office, laboratory, and residential 
building typologies. 
● Energy Efficient Commercial Buildings: The Development Plans will 
target a 90% reduction in building fossil fuel use for the lab buildings 
using efficient heat pump technologies (minimum 25% heat pump 
capacity). 
● All Electric Residential Building: The Development Plan will target all 
electric residential buildings / fossil-fuel free for normal operations 
● Climate resiliency: The Development Plan will address climate change 
resiliency related to more extreme weather by creating a minimum of 
2.6 acres of publicly accessible open space and public realm, 
integrating greenery, trees, green infrastructure, shading structures, 
and materials with high solar reflectance, to the extent feasible, to 
reduce urban heat island impacts. 
● Travel Demand Management ("TDM"): TDM measures, in accordance 
to BTD’s TDM Points system, will be identified during Article 80B 
review processes and implemented to reduce vehicular trips. 
● Stormwater Management: The Development Plan will adhere to 
sensible stormwater management practices as required by the 
City. 
● Tree Canopy: The Development Plan is committed to meeting or 
exceeding existing total caliper of existing trees on site, replacing 
unhealthy street trees, and saving at least one existing mature tree to be 
reused in the PDA. 
 
Community and Public Benefits 
In addition to the aforementioned urban design and public realm benefits, 
streetscape and transportation improvements, and sustainability and 
greenhouse gas emissions considerations, the Proponent has also committed 
to providing Community and Public Benefits, which include: 
 
● 
Housing Creation: Providing approximately 388 new rental units, with a 
wide range of unit sizes and layouts to accommodate a diverse array of 
household types, and which exceed the current City’s Inclusionary 
Development Policy (“IDP”) by providing 20% affordable units in each 
proposed residential building. 
● 
Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (“DEI”): Engaging a team of DEI advisors to 
create the design and execution of a Strategic DEI Framework that will 
seek to imbed DEI principals, practices and target goals in the following 

 
13 
 
 
areas of focus: labor and workforce development, youth education, 
supplier diversity procurement measures, community engagement, and

Community Space and Workforce Development: Dedicating 
approximately 15,000 sf of ground floor space as community space, a 
portion of which could be used to create a workforce development and 
life science training hub for the LMA and the Fenway in partnership with

the Proponent is committed to dedicating approximately 10,000 sf to the

● 
Employment and Job Creation: Creating approximately 5,000 on-site jobs 
relating to office/R&D/lab, life sciences, residential, retail, and parking 
uses within the Development Plan and creating approximately 5,000 
construction jobs during the build out of the Development Plan. 
● 
Retail and Small Businesses: The Development Plan will bring much 
needed new retail offerings to the LMA in the form of both temporary 
and permanent spaces. The Proponent will prioritize allocating retail 
space in the PDA to small, local, Minority Owned Business Enterprises or 
Women Owned Business Enterprises retailers. 
● 
Public Arts Program: The Project will sponsor and fund permanent and 
rotating/short-term art installations throughout the Site by a diverse 
range of artists. The Project will consult with local organizations and 
institutions like the Massachusetts College of Art and Design and the

Linkage Payments: Based on current rates, and assuming a maximum

Construction Mitigation: Committing to working with abutting property 
owners prior to commencing construction activities on-site to ensure

disruption to the surrounding neighborhood.

The Proposed Project will include up to 1.70 million square feet of gross floor area (GFA) of mixed-use 
development distributed over five buildings including residential, community space, retail, laboratory/office uses, 
and accessory and ancillary parking. The Proposed Project will be a stark contrast to the private, insular residential 
campus that exists today; because of the need for security and privacy on the existing campus, this land has been 
gated off from the community for decades. The Proposed Project, by contrast, will not only open up the PDA Area 
to the neighborhood, but by featuring approximately 2.6 acres of publicly accessible open space, it will also invite 
the public in to experience the PDA Area likely for the first time for most. The Proposed Project will provide a 
community gathering place and public amenities, which are lacking in the LMA neighborhood. 
This transformational project will bring much needed amenities and community-oriented retail to the 
neighborhood to support front line medical workers, patients and local residents, new affordable and market rate 
housing, new research, office space and cross-disciplinary spaces to support Boston's life-saving innovation, 2.6 
acres of publicly accessible open space, new interior community space, and over $12 million in public realm 
improvements that will transform this area for those traveling by all modes of transportation. Most importantly, 
this project will fulfill the One Simmon’s vision that supports the continued growth and viability of Simmons 
University. 
A transportation study has been developed to understand and mitigate the transportation impacts associated 
with the Project and to devise a comprehensive transportation mitigation and improvement plan in the vicinity of 
the Project that supports future operations of the Project and provides area-wide transportation improvements to 
the LMA. At this PDA stage the Project is providing over $8 Million in public realm and transportation 
improvements, which include but are not limited to new bike lanes and bus shelters, wide sidewalks, a new 
accessible crosswalk across Brookline Avenue, and a re-designed intersection at Brookline Avenue and Pilgrim 
Road to improve pedestrian safety. The Project will also create new dedicated pedestrian and a bi-directional 
bicycle paths separated by a landscaped buffer along the Project’s frontage on Short Street.

1.0 Introduction 
In accordance with Sections 3-1A and 80C-3 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Zoning Code”), 
This plan constitutes the Development Plan for Planned Development Area No. 134, Longwood 
Place (the “Development Plan”) for the development of the parcels located at 259, 275, 291, 305, 
321 Brookline Avenue & 38, 46, 62 Pilgrim Road in the Fenway/Longwood Medical Area 
(“LMA”) neighborhoods of Boston (currently known as the Simmons University Residential 
Campus, referred to herein as “305 Brookline” and/or “Longwood Place”). As more particularly 
described below, the Development Plan contemplates the construction of multiple buildings and 
public realm (the “Proposed Project” and/or the “Project”), which are currently expected to be 
completed in phases within 5-to-10-years from the start of construction (each phase(s) referred to 
herein as a “Phase(s)” or “Project Component(s)”). The Development Plan covers an 
approximately 5.89-acre (approximately 256,455 square-foot) area of land referred to as the 
“PDA Area.” A figure depicting the location of the PDA Area is included as Exhibit A, and a 
site context map is provided as Exhibit B. The legal description and survey plan of the PDA 
Area are included as Exhibit C. 
 
The PDA Area is comprised entirely of land owned by Simmons University subject to a long-
term ground lease with SCD Pilgrim Road Master Planer LLC (the “Proponent”). 
 
The Proposed Project will include up to 1.70 million square feet of gross floor area (GFA)1 of 
mixed-use development distributed over five buildings including residential, community space, 
retail, laboratory/office uses, and accessory and ancillary parking. The Proposed Project will 
open up the PDA Area to the neighborhood, by featuring approximately 2.6-acres of on-site 
publicly accessible open space and exterior public realm, which is equivalent to 43 percent of the 
project site (excluding roadways), as shown and defined on Exhibit O attached hereto and 
incorporated herein (the “Open Space”), and inviting the public into the PDA Area. The 
Proposed Project will provide a community gathering place and public amenities, which are 
severely lacking in the neighborhood. 
 
Overall, the Proposed Project’s development aims to create a vibrant nucleus of sustainable and 
innovative workspaces, active community amenities, much needed housing, and an inclusive 
public realm in the LMA. The Project is committed to executing a holistic diversity, equity & 
inclusion (DEI) strategy that seeks to employ successful DEI principles and practices throughout 
each stage of the Project development (Design/Construction/Operation). It will reinvigorate a 
long dormant stretch of Brookline Avenue with retail, exterior publicly accessible open space, 
indoor public amenities, streetscape improvements, wider sidewalks and bike accessibility, and 
improved circulation for all modes of movement in the neighborhood. 
 
The proposed exterior open space and publicly accessible ground-level indoor amenity spaces 
are envisioned to accommodate a mix of passive and active programming in mind that are 
intended to be welcoming to all from the Fenway/LMA neighborhoods and promote a sense of 
belonging for visitors from all cultures. It will draw people onto, into, and through the PDA

The PDA Area is comprised of seven parcels with the following street addresses: 259, 275, 291, 
305, 321 Brookline Avenue & 38, 46, 62 Pilgrim Road (the “Site”). The PDA Area is bounded 
generally by Brookline Avenue, Pilgrim Road, and Short Street. Collectively, this Site is the

3.0 The Proposed Project 
 
The Proposed Project reimagines the Site as a vibrant mixed-use neighborhood, opening 
significant opportunities to infuse the Fenway/LMA with a variety of offerings for both public 
and private uses. As illustrated in the conceptual site plan in Exhibit C, the diagrammatic 
ground floor plan in Exhibit E, and the conceptual renderings in Exhibit K, this Development 
Plan proposes five new buildings on the Site, including various uses as set forth below, while 
also creating abundant exterior publicly accessible spaces at the ground level that welcome the 
local community and Boston as a whole. As set forth herein, this Development Plan shall set 
forth maximum densities and heights for the Proposed Project, and minimum open space and 
setbacks from roadways; these dimensional regulations shall be made a permanent part of the 
zoning for this Project. 
 
The Proposed Project engages with visitors, residents, and a new, strong workforce, in an 
inclusive and inviting manner, promoting health, wellness, and vibrant life throughout the 
entirety of the Site. It is particularly noteworthy that the Proposed Project plans for 
approximately 2.6 acres of publicly accessible exterior open space, which acreage excludes the 
vehicular portions of the new two-way street at the midpoint of the Site (the “mid-block street”). 
The proposed open space amounts to approximately 43 percent of the total lot area of the Site.

3.1 Building Program 
 
The Proposed Project’s building program is anticipated to include commercial and residential 
uses with a base of retail and community spaces at the ground floor. The Site proposes a 
maximum buildout of 1.70 million square feet of GFA that results in a Floor Area Ratio (FAR) 
of 6.7. The program is currently envisioned, approximately, as follows: 
 
● approximately 1,301,000 gross square feet of commercial, office, laboratory/research and 
development uses. 
● approximately 340,000 gross square feet of residential uses with approximately 388 units. 
● approximately 44,000 gross square feet of retail uses. 
● approximately 15,000 gross square feet of civic/cultural/community uses; and 
● to include approximately up to the total number of parking spaces based upon ultimate 
contemplated full Project build out of the proposed GFA permitted under the 
Development Plan, at ratios of 0.3 parking spaces per 1,000 square feet of retail, 
office/lab, R&D uses, 0.3 parking spaces per rental or condominium unit, and zero (0) 
parking spaces for community use, provided that the overall parking for the Proposed 
Project shall not exceed 520 parking spaces. 
 
The buildings themselves will be categorized by the following uses, however, in addition to the 
uses listed below, all of the uses listed in Exhibit L shall be permitted at the Project Site: 
 
● Building 1 –laboratory/research and development, and/or office; retail; community uses; 
cultural uses. 
● Building 2 –laboratory/research and development, and/or office; retail; community uses; 
cultural uses. 
● Building 3 –laboratory/research and development, and/or office; retail; community uses; 
cultural uses. 
● Building 4 – residential; retail, community uses; cultural uses. 
● Building 5 – residential; retail, community uses; cultural uses. 
 
The Proposed Project will also create new exterior publicly accessible spaces in addition to those 
outlined above. A conceptual site plan showing the components of the Proposed Project is 
included as Exhibit D.

3.3 Parking and Loading 
 
This Development Plan will permit up to the total number of parking spaces based upon ultimate 
contemplated full Project build out of the proposed GFA permitted under the Development Plan, 
at ratios of 0.3 parking spaces per 1,000 square feet of retail, office/lab, R&D uses, 0.3 parking 
spaces per rental or condominium unit, and zero (0) parking spaces for community use, provided 
that the overall parking for the Proposed Project shall not exceed 520 parking spaces, which will 
all be available upon completion of construction of the below-grade garage (the “Allowed 
Parking”). All on-site parking and loading serving the Project Components will be constructed 
within a below-grade parking garage accessible only from the mid-block street. The parking 
spaces, permitted by this Development Plan, may be allocated among allowed uses at the 
discretion of the Proponent. The Allowed Parking as set forth above and herein shall not be 
subject to reduction based on or due to any regulation, legislation, guidance, guidelines, planning 
studies or the like that is not now in full force and effect as of the effective date of the adoption 
of this Development Plan. 
 
The Proponent shall have the right to seek an amendment to this Development Plan for 
additional parking allowed on the project site, subject to prevailing BPDA and BTD Article 80 
policies and guidelines including the most recently published Maximum Parking Ratio 
Guidelines and related Mobility Scores, and the analysis findings and roadway changes arising 
from the Fenway-Kenmore Transportation Action Plan at the time of such approval. Other than 
changes to the quantity of on-site parking spaces in excess of the Allowed Parking, the remainder 
of the Project in compliance with this Development Plan will not be subject to further review by 
such an Amendment. The Proponent shall provide any and all studies and evidence to 
demonstrate additional parking needs at the time of this future request. The studies needed will 
be determined in coordination with the BPDA and BTD and will include employee surveys, 
Transportation Demand Management effectiveness, transit service and roadway network 
capacity, and parking supply and occupancy, etc. 
 
All service and loading will be located below-grade, thereby removing all loading activities from 
the public realm, and minimizing impacts to Pilgrim Road, Brookline Avenue and abutting

3.4 Proposed Traffic Circulation 
 
All vehicular access and egress to the Project will be provided via the new mid-block street, 
which will create a new vehicular and pedestrian street that will bisect the Project Site, connect 
Pilgrim Road and Brookline Avenue, connect to Parking garage driveways, and provide a safe 
and accessible pedestrian crossing between the Central Connector and Winter Garden within 
Building 3 (Refer to Exhibit F for a circulation and access plan). The mid-block street will be 
the main point of access for service vehicles and points of access to the below-grade parking 
garage. Vehicular pick-up/drop-off areas will be provided on either side of the new street to 
support the new commercial buildings. New signal equipment will be installed at the Brookline 
Avenue intersection to control entering and exiting traffic and facilitate safe and convenient 
pedestrian and bicycle movements. This new road will serve as a gateway into the Project Site 
and a front door for the new buildings, creating an open, urban street that welcomes building 
users as well as the general public. The precise design, dimensions and operations of the mid-
block street will be advanced during the Article 80B Review process and anticipated PIC 
processes; the street will be laid out conceptually as set forth herein and as shown in the 
attachments hereto, with the direct intention to create a visual and physical connection across 
Brookline Avenue to the Colleges of the Fenway pathway, and with the Boston University 
driveway off Pilgrim Road. The mid-block street will be designated as a public way but the 
proponent may retain fee interest in the land. A highway easement will be provided to the City 
through the usual PIC process. The grantor of the easement(s) will retain the right to install 
reasonable utility infrastructure and building elements above and/or beneath the mid-block street 
pending typical City processes, including retention of the right to construct, operate, and 
maintain portions to be determined of the below grade garage and loading facility contemplated 
in this PDA at a depth of no less than 6 feet below the mid-block street. Grantor will also retain 
the right to relocate, modify, or remove the mid-block street through applicable City processes. 
 
Curb space along the mid-block street is intended to be used for sidewalks, an accessible 
pedestrian crossing, and vehicular pick-up/drop-off. The Pilgrim Road curb space is intended to 
be used for sidewalks and vehicular pick-up/drop-off. The curb space along Brookline Avenue is 
intended to be used for expanded roadway space for public transit infrastructure and stations, 
separated bike lanes, sidewalks, and vehicular pick-up/drop-off. 
 
The exact size and location of these pick-up/drop-off areas will be coordinated with the BTD and 
the BPDA as the Project planning advances. Specific PIC approvals will be required and will be 
determined with the City during the Article 80B process. 
 
At the southernmost end of the Proposed Project, along the existing Short Street alley the 
Proponent will design and construct a new separated pedestrian path, bi-directional bicycle path, 
and landscaped buffer spaces connecting Brookline Avenue and Pilgrim Road. The Proponent 
will work with the City and the Winsor School during Article 80B Review to refine the design of 
this critical active transportation connection.

3.5 Open Space and Public Realm 
 
The Project will provide a minimum of 2.6-acres of on-site publicly accessible open space and 
exterior public realm, which is equivalent to 43 percent of the project site (excluding roadways), 
as shown and defined on Exhibit O attached hereto and incorporated herein (the “Open Space”). 
The Project will create new, publicly accessible open space throughout the Project Site, adjacent 
to retail, restaurants, cafes, and active ground level uses. At the southern edge of the Site along 
Brookline Avenue the Proponent proposes a minimum 31,000 SF open space envisioned for both 
active and passive uses (the “Main Heart”). At the northern end of the Site to the northwest of 
Building 2, the Project proposes a minimum 12,500 SF publicly accessible open space 
envisioned for quiet, passive activities (the “Passive Open Space”). 
 
Throughout the Site the Project also proposes smaller open space areas, including: 
● Riverway Gateway: At the southern edge of the Site the Project envisions a plaza that 
would draw the character of the Emerald Necklace parks into the Site (the “Riverway 
Plaza Gateway”). Located at a key pedestrian and vehicular node, the design intent of the 
Riverway Plaza is to provide a safe intersection for pedestrians and bicyclists to connect 
to Pilgrim Road and beyond, and to provide space for temporary activation like market 
stalls or food vendors. 
● Fenway Gateway: At the northern edge of the Site the Project envisions a small plaza 
that would serve as an extension of the Brookline streetscape (the “Fenway Gateway”). 
The Fenway Gateway is envisioned to provide a variety of seating opportunities, planting 
areas, and offers a unique public art opportunity that could define this exciting and active 
gateway into the Site and the LMA. 
● Pocket Plazas: The Proponent envisions smaller, intimate moments between Buildings 3 
and 4, and Buildings 2 and 5 that are envisioned as landscaped and hardscaped plazas 
(“Pocket Plazas”). These Pocket Plazas will provide accessible places of respite and quiet 
that do not exist in the LMA today. 
● Central Connector: The Proponent envisions an active movement corridor between 
Buildings 1 and 3 that would connect the northern and southern halves of the Site (the 
“Central Connector”). The Central Connector could include a variety of seating 
opportunities, water features, public art or creative lighting – and is envisioned as an 
exciting contrast to the other publicly accessible open spaces envisioned within the 
Project.

The current Site is surrounded on all sides by existing sidewalks, many of which are minimal in 
width and do not contribute to a positive pedestrian experience. The Proposed Project will

the Site along with generous street frontages beyond the sidewalk minimums, creating plentiful 
open and welcoming edges that promote safe and comfortable circulation throughout. Specific

3.6 Community Space 
 
In addition to exterior spaces, publicly accessible open space extends into the ground floor 
interiors of the buildings within the Proposed Project. Community spaces are envisioned adjacent 
to the exterior public realm to extend the use of the Site and the public programming 
opportunities beyond the warmer months of the year and allow for occupancy and use all year 
round. Operable walls and large doors will be explored to allow for the seamless passage of 
people and activities between the interior and exterior public realm, removing boundaries and 
welcoming the public deeper into the Site and the buildings. The aim is to achieve a variety of 
scales of open space that can accommodate large gatherings as well as smaller intimate groups 
within smaller open spaces. 
 
Subject to city and state permitting, the Proponent plans to dedicate 15,000 SF of interior 
community space within the Project. To the extent feasible, the community space will be located 
on the ground-floor of the proposed buildings. The Proponent will dedicate up to 10,000 SF of 
this space within one building as mutually determined with the City, to create a workforce 
development and life science training hub for the LMA and the Fenway in partnership with the 
City of Boston. The exact location and phasing of the training hub will be confirmed in 
collaboration with the City through the Phase 1 Article 80B Review process. 
 
The Proponent will partner with LMA institutions, industry groups and the City of Boston to 
deliver relevant and robust programming within this space that addresses community priorities, 
including but not limited to STEM training, workforce development, incubator and meeting 
space, and leadership programs that will develop a diverse talent pipeline of local students and 
residents seeking careers in the life science sector. The Proponent will allocate space within the 
buildings to support these kinds of programs including providing space for storage, access to 
public bathrooms, and the appropriate infrastructure for vendors to set up temporary structures 
for the public. The calculation of the 15,000 SF of community space will not include storage or

other facilities that otherwise serve the function of the building, nor will it include storage or 
bathrooms to the extent already required for the ground floor space under the building code 
without regard to the community space. 
 
Additionally, as part of this Development Plan, the Project is committed to designing an interior, 
publicly accessible ground-floor portion of Building 2 that will invite the public to engage with 
and pass through the building’s lobby and could include amenities like a winter garden. Refer to 
Appendix C, design guidelines for additional details on the proposed publicly accessible ground 
floor portion of Building 2. 
 
3.7 Proposed Project Phasing 
 
The Proposed Project is expected to be completed in phases within 5-to-10-years from the start 
of construction. The initial phase of construction for the Proposed Project will begin upon the 
completion and occupancy of the new Simmons Living and Learning Center on the Simmons 
Academic Campus, which allows the existing uses on the Site to be relocated. 
 
The Project will make a substantial commitment to the public realm during Phase 1; however, it 
is anticipated that each building construction phase will include portions of the exterior public 
realm to ensure community space and exterior amenities are accessible to the neighborhood 
throughout the development and duration of construction. As more precise construction 
sequencing and phasing plans are developed, they shall be submitted as part of the Article 80B 
Large Project filings for the individual buildings. The foregoing conceptual phasing of the 
Proposed Project shall not limit or restrict updates to the phasing that may be proposed in 
response to evolving market conditions.

4.0 Project Benefits 
 
The following Project Benefits summary is grounded in a belief that real community benefits 
seek to generate long-term, sustainable outcomes rather than being satisfied by short-term 
outputs. The development of the Proposed Project contemplated by this Development Plan will 
provide a range of public benefits described below. Modifications to the proposed improvements 
described below during the Article 80B process are expected. 
4.1 Open Space and Public Realm 
 
Provide New Publicly Accessible Open Space 
 
The Project will provide a minimum of 2.6-acres of on-site privately owned publicly accessible 
open space and expanded public realm including but not limited to: 
 
● A minimum 31,000 SF “Main Heart” for the LMA, publicly accessible active open space 
that breaks up the Project’s street frontage along Brookline Avenue and reinforces the 
Project’s importance as a new public destination, and 
● A minimum 12,500 SF Passive Open Space along Pilgrim Road that will provide a place 
of respite for the public, residents and workers. 
 
The Project will provide a minimum of 2.6-acres of on-site, privately owned publicly accessible 
open space (POPS) that will generally be accessed by the public without a fee except for certain 
specific programs and events to be determined in the future. The on-site exterior open space will 
be listed in the BPDA’s POPS database. During the Article 80B process for each of the open 
space components the Proponent will provide design details and will endeavor to provide details 
on future operations, including when the park will be open to the public, as well as proposed 
design and programmatic features, all of which will be jointly determined by the Proponent and 
the BPDA. 
 
Proposed open space and expanded public realm will be classified in submittals during the 
Article 80B process for each Project phase according to the Open Space shown and defined in 
Exhibit O.

Public Programming

5.0 Technical Studies Performed in Support of Development of the PDA 
 
5.1 Traffic 
The following is a summary of the transportation impacts of the Proposed Project presented in 
this Development Plan. A more detailed analysis is included in the Transportation Impact Study 
(“TIS”) that is included as Appendix A. 
 

 
21 
 
A transportation study has been developed to understand and mitigate the transportation impacts 
associated with the Project and to devise a comprehensive transportation mitigation and 
improvement plan in the vicinity of the Project that supports future operations of the Project and 
provides area-wide transportation improvements to the LMA area of Boston. A major emphasis 
of this proposed redevelopment effort focuses on area mobility, including improved access and 
circulation to support the Site and abutting properties and institutions, access to key transit 
nodes, and significant network pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure improvements. These 
elements are at the forefront of the analysis and future planning. 
 
The following are key mobility strategies to be incorporated into the Project: 
 
● The Project will implement a new mid-block street that will be signalized at Brookline 
Avenue, providing primary access and egress for vehicles (both passenger cars and 
service vehicles) to and from the Project. 
● The new signalized intersection at Brookline Avenue and the mid-block street has been 
conceptualized to also support protected, signalized pedestrian movements across 
Brookline Avenue, lining up with the Colleges of the Fenway path. 
● A new separated pedestrian path and a bi-directional bicycle path is proposed along the 
Project’s frontage on Short Street along the edge of the Main Heart open space. The 
Proponent will work with the City and the Winsor School during article 80B to advance 
this pedestrian and bicycle amenity. 
● Where the Project abuts Brookline Avenue, the existing curb will be relocated providing 
for opportunity to create new protected cycling infrastructure. 
● Two existing MBTA/LMA shuttle bus stops will be reconstructed and will provide new 
shelters. 
● Left turns onto Pilgrim Road from Brookline Avenue will be restricted. 
● Pilgrim Road will be widened slightly to support improved access by residents and parent 
pick-up/drop-off operations for the Winsor School. 
● Drop-off and pick-ups for Buildings 1, 2 and 3 will be accommodated in dedicated 
locations off of the new mid-block street. Residential pick-up/drop-off for Buildings 4 
and 5 will be accommodated in designated areas along Pilgrim Road. 
● All loading/service will be accommodated in below grade loading docks. Service vehicles 
leaving the below-grade garage will be required to exit the Site via the mid-block street to 
Brookline Avenue, and will not be allowed to utilize Pilgrim Road. 
● Electric vehicle provisions will all be implemented consistent with BTD Guidelines. 
● Bicycle Parking will be implemented consistent with BTD Guidelines. 
● On-site bikeshare stations for year-round public use, with the number, size, and 
configuration of stations to be determined during the Article 80B process for each 
building or Project phase, or provide an alternative, as provided in Section 3.3 above; and 
● The Project will incorporate TDM principles as defined in the new BTD TDM Points 
System. 
 
The Proponent is aware that the City is undertaking a coordinated and comprehensive 
transportation planning and analysis process effort in the Fenway neighborhood known as the 
Fenway-Kenmore Transportation Action Plan. As this Project advances through Article 80B 

 
22 
 
review, the Proponent will work closely with the City to advance design solutions that are 
consistent with the goals and outcomes of this planning process.

5.2 Shadow 
The following is a summary of the shadow impacts of the Proposed Project presented in this 
Development Plan. A more detailed visual analysis is shown in the Shadow Study that is 
included as Appendix B. 
The Proponent has carefully considered the massing and heights of the Proposed Project to 
provide thermal comfort in the publicly accessible spaces on site, as well as limit the effect of 
new shadows on important resources like the Emerald Necklace parkland. The Proposed Project 
casts no new shadows on the Emerald Necklace Park for longer than 1 hour during the hours of 
10:00AM and 5:00 PM on March 21. There are no new shadows during midday hours. The PDA 
massings which represent the worst-case impacts, cast limited, fast-moving new shadows on the 
Emerald Necklace during the early morning and late afternoon. The Development Plan allows 
the Proponent to design each Phase of the Project up to the maximum heights and square 
footages set forth by this Development Plan, each Project Phase or building will be carefully 
designed within the Development Plan prescribed height and massing envelope to promote good 
urban design, and the Proponent will work to reduce net new shadows cast on the adjacent 
buildings and the Emerald Necklace Parks where practicable during the Article 80B Review. 
Any regulation, legislation, guideline, planning study or the like not in effect as of the date of the 
effective date of this Development Plan as adopted shall not have any effect on the right of this 
Project to cast the maximum shadows as analyzed in this Development Plan and its appendices, 
nor shall it have the effect of additional shadow related mitigation that has already been 
accounted for in both the design of this Project and the Parks endowment fund set forth above 
and herein. Notwithstanding the foregoing, the preceding shall not effect, limit or prevent any 
impact analysis or studies arising from proposed building shadows during Article 80B Review.

Introduction 
Skanska Building USA is filing a Revised Planned Development Area (PDA) to respond to comments on the PDA 
Development Plan for Longwood Place Project that was submitted to the Boston Planning and Development Agency 
(BPDA) on January 3, 2022 (the “Initial PDA Project”). In this memorandum, we review the Revised PDA Project’s 
development program and its transportation elements to compare the changes. This memo serves to: 
• 
Describe the transportation-related characteristics of the Project, including the revised parking program; 
• 
Quantify the trips that will be generated by the Revised PDA Project and compare those to the Initial PDA 
development program’s trip generation; and 
• 
Demonstrate that the Revised PDA Project is less impactful than the Initial PDA Project in terms of trip 
generation and parking requirements, and that the submitted Initial PDA analysis is conservatively high as 
compared to the Revised PDA Project. 
A comprehensive vehicle capacity analysis and transportation evaluation, based on the Initial PDA program, can be 
referenced in the previously submitted PDA technical studies material. As seen in the results of the revised PDA 
program’s trip generation, the currently proposed program will result in more than a 10 percent decrease in peak-
hour vehicle trips, as compared to the Initial PDA program. 
Background 
The site continues to include the entire property historically known as the Simmons University Residential Campus (the 
“Site”). Simmons looks to employ a master plan strategy that would include the consolidation of all academic 
functions, including student dormitory and athletic uses, onto its Main Academic Campus. The disposition of its 
Residential Campus via a long-term ground lease is a critically important element to the implementation of this 
strategy. 
The Project will also include the demolition of all existing residential and athletic facilities that are on the Residential 
campus (approximately 334,200 sf in total) and 28 surface parking spaces.

Revised PDA Project Trip Generation 
Trip generation estimates were developed based on the same methodologies in this Revised PDA that were presented 
previously in the Initial PDA. See the following sections for a brief description of how Project Trips were calculated and 
a comparison of Project Trips between the Revised PDA Project and the Initial PDA Project. 
Project Trip Generation 
Trip generation estimates for the Project are based on standard Institute of Transportation Engineers’ (ITE) data1 
paired with empirical trip rates. The following section discusses how the unadjusted trip generation will be converted 
to new trips on the surrounding roadway networks for the purpose of conducting the transportation analysis. 
Memorandum 

 
 
 
 
Unadjusted Vehicle Trip Generation 
The ITE Trip Generation Manual categorizes various land uses and provides weekday daily, weekday morning peak 
hour, and weekday evening peak hour unadjusted vehicle trip generation estimates for each use. Trip generation 
estimates for the proposed residential and retail uses were projected using data published in the ITE data for LUC 221 
(Mid-Rise Residential) and LUC 820 (Shopping Center). These ITE rates were paired with empirical trip rates collected 
from local, available transportation monitoring report projects for the Office and R&D land uses.1 
Person Trips 
The unadjusted vehicle trips estimated using ITE data were subsequently converted into person trips by applying 
average vehicle occupancy rates (VOR)2 for each use. The national average vehicle occupancy rates applied were 1.18 
persons/vehicle for office, research and development, and residential trips, and 1.82 persons/vehicle for retail trips. 
The national rates are typically applied when converting vehicle trips into person trips to be consistent with ITE data, 
which is also based on national data. The unadjusted vehicle trips were converted into person trips to apply the 
internal capture credits and applicable mode share credits discussed below. 
Internal Capture 
As described in the ITE Trip Generation Handbook,3 “because of the complementary nature of these land uses, some trips 
are made among the on-site uses. This capture of trips internal to the Development Site has the net effect of reducing 
vehicle trip generation between the overall Development Site and the external street system (compared to the total number 
of trips generated by comparable land uses developed individually on stand-alone sites) an internal capture rate can 
generally be defined as the percentage of total person trips generated by a site that are made entirely within the 
Development Site. The trip origin, destination, and travel path are all within the site.” 
As the Project proposes a mixture of uses, the trip generation characteristics of the Project will be different from a 
single-use project. Some of the trip activity generated by the Project will be contained on-site as “internal” or “shared 
vehicle” trips. This concept means that some patrons could visit more than one of the uses on the Site. For example, 
workers at the R&D/office space on-site may patronize the retail shops after work, or residents who live in the 
development may also work in an office on-site. While these shared trips represent new trips to the individual land 
uses, they would not necessarily register as new trips on the surrounding roadway or transportation network. 
Based on the methodology outlined in the ITE Trip Generation Handbook, internal capture rates were applied to the 
gross person trips, resulting in adjusted person trips. Trip generation calculations, including the internal capture 
worksheet, are included in the Appendix of the PDA.

transportation conditions within the Project Study Area. The transportation study has 
been developed to understand and mitigate the transportation impacts associated 
with the Project and to devise a comprehensive transportation mitigation and 
improvement plan in the vicinity of the Project that supports future operations of 
the Project and provides area-wide transportation improvements to the Longwood 
Medical and Academic Area (LMA) of Boston. A major emphasis of this proposed 
redevelopment effort focuses on area mobility, including improved access and 
circulation to support the site and abutting properties and institutions, access to key 
transit nodes, and significant network pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure 
improvements. These elements are at the forefront of our analysis and future 
planning. 
The purpose of these analyses is to: 
› 
Define and quantify existing transportation conditions in the Project Study 
Area; 
› 
Estimate the transportation impacts that will be generated under future 
conditions based on the anticipated program for the Project; 
› 
Develop a set of mitigation strategies and improvement measures which will 
help lessen the transportation demand effects of the Project; 
›

mitigation efforts will meet or exceed BPDA and BTD requirements and will 
serve as exceptional public benefits; and 
› 
Illustrate the Project’s prioritization of pedestrian and bicycle modes as part 
of the overall TDM strategy and commitment to modern mobility. 
Recognizing that transportation is a key policy priority at both the city and state 
levels, this study has been conducted in conformance with both MassDOT and BTD 
guidelines and uses standard methodologies, including the Institute of 
Transportation Engineers’ (ITE) Trip Generation Manual, 10th Edition paired with 
local empirical trip rates, and local travel characteristics as defined in Access Boston 
2000-2010 and the Go Boston 2030 Action Plan.

A.3 Study Methodology 
The transportation analysis has been performed in conformance with both BTD and 
MassDOT Transportation Access Plan Guidelines. It also has been prepared to be 
consistent with the goals and overall vision of Go Boston 2030.2 
The transportation assessment was prepared in three stages. The first stage involved 
an assessment of existing transportation conditions within the Project Study Area, 
including: 
› 
Pedestrian activity along Project Study Area roadways, and at Project Study 
Area intersections. 
› 
Bicycle activity and accommodations. 
› 
Public transportation options within the Project Study Area, including the 
Green Line, Commuter Rail, and multiple bus options. 
› 
An inventory of the transportation infrastructure within the Project Study 
Area, including its geometric and operational characteristics. 
› 
Geometric and operational characteristics of Project Study Area roadways 
and intersections. 
› 
Existing traffic control at Project Study Area intersections (i.e., traffic 
signalization, stop signs, one-way streets, etc.). 
› 
Transportation characteristics of current weekday operations at the Project 
Site and abutters (including the Winsor School). 
› 
Area off-street and on-street parking supply. 
In the second stage of the study (Evaluation of Long-Term Transportation Impacts), 
future transportation conditions were projected within the Project Study Area. The 
future No-Build condition includes an assessment of future transportation including 
planned transportation infrastructure improvements and growth related to other 
proposed projects within the Project Study Area (without consideration of the Project). 
The future No-Build Condition takes into consideration many of the projects that are 
planned and/or under construction within the area including those listed in 
Section A.5.1. The future Build Condition assesses the No-Build Condition plus 
estimated traffic generated by the Project. The year 2028 was selected as the design 
year for analysis for the preparation of this study to reflect completion of the Project, 
providing a seven-year time horizon in accordance with the standard MassDOT 
guidelines. 
The third and final stage of the study discusses potential measures to improve 
existing and future transportation operations in the area and to offset the 
transportation-related impacts associated with the development of the Project.

Directive (published on May 11, 2020) included guidance on the use of traffic count 
data, indicating that historical traffic data may be used on any project to supplement 
and/or replace existing traffic counts as long as it conforms to the latest version of 
the MassDOT guidance. The directive applies to all projects that have not obtained 
count data prior to March 13, 2020. We have adopted this guidance and applied it 
to the City of Boston review process of which this report is a part. 
TMCs from the traffic count data sources are adjusted to the current year (2021) 
using MassDOT Yearly Growth Rates. MassDOT considers 2019 to be existing and no 
growth rate is applied to counts from 2019. 
Since there were a few locations which did not have historical counts available, 
counts were conducted at these locations on Wednesday, September 29, 2021 as 
well as a spot check which indicated that the 2021 traffic volumes on these local 
streets are still about 9% lower on average as compared to MassDOT grown 
historical counts. Since no historical counts were available at these locations, the 
data was used as a basis and the counts were increased along the main roadways 
(Brookline Ave and Riverway) to balance with the adjacent historical counts (which 
were greater).

Crash Analysis 
A detailed crash analysis was conducted to identify vehicle accident trends and 
potential roadway deficiencies in the traffic Project Study Area. Both RMV data and 
City of Boston data are compiled, reviewed and presented here. The MassDOT 
roadway crash database is comprised of crash data from the Massachusetts Registry 
of Motor Vehicles (RMV) Division primarily for use in traffic studies and safety 
evaluations. Data files are provided for entire calendar years, though it is certain that 
some crash records are omitted either due to individual crashes not being reported, 
or the city crash records not being provided in a compatible format for RMV use. 
The most current vehicle accident data for the traffic Project Study Area intersections

was obtained from MassDOT for the years 2014 to 2018 (the most recent five-year 
period available at the time of the data compilation). A summary of vehicle accident 
history at the study intersections based on the available RMV data is demonstrated 
in Table A.5. 
Crash rates are calculated based on the number of accidents at an intersection and the 
volume of traffic travelling though that intersection daily. Rates that exceed 
MassDOT’s average for accidents, at intersections in the district in which the town or 
city is located, could indicate safety or geometric issues for an intersection. As Boston 
is in MassDOT’s District 6, the calculated crash rates were compared to those of 
MassDOT District 6, which are 0.71 for signalized intersections and 0.52 for 
unsignalized intersections. These rates imply that, on average, 0.71 accidents occurred 
per million entering signalized intersections throughout District 6, and 0.52 accidents 
occurred per million vehicles entering unsignalized intersections. 
A review of the accident data indicates that all Project Study Area intersections are 
below the MassDOT District 6 crash rate averages. The intersection of Riverway at 
Longwood Ave has the highest number of crashes in the Project Study Area with a 
total of 51 crashes occurring at the intersection over the five-year period. The most 
common type of crash at the intersection was an angled crash. Six of the 51 crashes 
at the intersection involved non-motorists (either pedestrians and/or bicyclists).

A.4.10 
Winsor School Existing Conditions 
During September 2021 VHB and the Project team conducted detailed observations of 
existing Winsor School pick-up and drop-off activity at the site to assist the design 
team in better understanding school operations, identify access challenges and 
opportunities, and to provide guidance and input regarding the framework of future 
transportation conditions and operations at the school as it co-exists with the success 
of the Proposed Project access and circulation. Note that the Project team also held 
several working meetings with the Winsor School staff, detailed in Section A.5.2. 
Observations were made on Wednesday, September 22 during both the morning 
drop-off and afternoon pick-up. 
General Findings 
› 
Winsor School morning drop-off arrival tends to begin after 7:00 AM and 
ends just before school classes commence. Parent drop-off along Short 
Street Extension, queuing on Pilgrim Road, and bus drop-off in the bus lane 
that is accessed via the Riverway all function reasonably well – as drop-off 
activity is spread out over an approximate 45-minute window. Drop-off 
activity is actively managed by a team of Winsor staff to ensure that student 
movements from vehicles to the School are safe. It is envisioned that there 
will be little overlap between morning school operations and Project 
generated traffic based upon the design considerations for entering 
passenger cars and service vehicles destined for the Project site (see Figures 
A.2.b and A.2.d, presented previously. 
› 
Afternoon pick-up dismissal (vehicles begin to queue around 2:35 PM) 
between 2:35 and 2:55 PM is the time that requires the most management 
of students and parents for an effective and safe pick-up each day. Queues 
are longest in the 10-minute window before students are dismissed. The 
Project intended to widen Pilgrim Road within the Project site property 
between the new mid-block driveway and Short Street Extension to create a 
landscaped hybrid lane for parents to queue. This will keep Pilgrim Road 
open and available to moving traffic and emergency vehicles. It will also 
provide the opportunity for some Winsor parents to pick up students and 
exit the Winsor Campus via Short Street onto Brookline Avenue (instead of 
the Riverway). 
› 
It is envisioned that vehicles exiting the Project Site in the afternoon that are 
destined for the Riverway would do so primarily after the traditional school 
pick-up has ended, thus minimizing the overlap of school operations with 
Project traffic. 
Buses 
› 
Buses arrive via the Riverway and Nessel Way and queue on the curb 
between the Winsor School and the Riverway (the Winsor Bus Lane).

› 
During the observation period, both student and coach buses were 
observed queuing and picking up students. 
› 
There were up to seven buses queued at 2:45 PM and one bus parked on 
the Riverway at this time. 
› 
The Project looks to supplement bus queuing for Winsor by providing an 
opportunity for buses to also queue along the north side of Pilgrim Road 
near Short Street Extension as well as a secondary designated location on 
Short Street that could be accessed via Brookline Avenue. 
Parking + Vehicle Activity 
› 
The staff parking lot is heavily used; and provides parking for approximately 
30 vehicles. 
› 
The staff parking lot is also used to support some parent pick-up/drop-off 
activity during peak pick-up/drop-off periods. 
› 
Parents dropping off and picking up students arrive via Pilgrim Road and 
travel down the road until a queue begins to form. Often, two lanes are 
formed on Pilgrim Road: one for queueing and one for a travel lane. 
› 
During the afternoon pick-up observations, this queue was observed to be 
about 400 feet at its longest (2:50 PM) down Pilgrim Road and dissipated 
shortly after this time. 
› 
After picking up students, vehicles exit Pilgrim Road and take Short Street 
Extension (in front of the Winsor School) to its intersection with the Riverway 
to depart. 
› 
The traffic light at the intersection of Riverway at Short Street provides 
sufficient green time that it does not cause adverse impacts to the Winsor 
School dismissal or arrival periods.

Project Trip Generation 
Trip generation estimates for the Project are based on standard Institute of 
Transportation Engineers’ (ITE) data5 paired with empirical trip rates. The following 
section discusses how the unadjusted trip generation will be converted to new trips 
on the surrounding roadway networks for the purpose of conducting the 
transportation analysis. 
Unadjusted Vehicle Trip Generation 
The Project will consist of approximately 1,750,000 square feet (sf), as defined in 
zoning code, of building space. This building space will include 4 buildings devoted 
to a mix of research & development and office space (approximately 1,516,000 sf), 
retail uses (approximately 47,000 sf), and residential space (approximately 175,000 
sf/ 200 units). Currently the site contains Simmons University’s residential campus 
within a series of buildings. Though the existing site is occupied, no trip credit was 
taken for existing University Housing or Athletic uses in order to conduct a 
conservative analysis. 
The ITE Trip Generation Manual categorizes various land uses and provides weekday 
daily, weekday morning peak hour, and weekday evening peak hour unadjusted 
vehicle trip generation estimates for each use. Trip generation estimates for the 
proposed uses were projected using data published in the ITE data for LUC 221 
(Mid-Rise Residential), and LUC 820 (Shopping Center). In addition, these ITE rates

Person Trips 
The unadjusted vehicle trips estimated using the ITE data were subsequently 
converted into person trips by applying average vehicle occupancy rates (VOR) 
based on national data7 for each use. The national average vehicle occupancy rates 
applied were 1.18 persons/vehicle for office, research and development, and

applied when converting to person trips to be consistent with ITE data, which is also 
based on national data. The unadjusted vehicle trips were converted into person 
trips in order to apply the internal capture credits and applicable mode share credits 
discussed below. 
Internal Capture 
As the Project proposes a mixture of uses, the trip generation characteristics of the 
Project will be different from a single-use project. Some of the traffic to be 
generated by the Project will be contained on-site as “internal” or “shared vehicle” 
trips. This concept means that some patrons could visit more than one of the uses 
on the Project Site. For example, workers at the R&D/office space on-site may 
patronize the retail shops after work or residents who live in the development may 
also work in the office on-site. While these shared trips represent new traffic to the 
individual uses, they would not necessarily register as new vehicle trips on the 
surrounding roadway network. 
As described in the ITE Trip Generation Handbook,8 “because of the complementary 
nature of these land uses, some trips are made among the on-site uses. This capture of 
trips internal to the Development Site has the net effect of reducing vehicle trip 
generation between the overall Development Site and the external street system 
(compared to the total number of trips generated by comparable land uses developed 
individually on stand-alone sites) an internal capture rate can generally be defined as 
the percentage of total person trips generated by a site that are made entirely within the 
Development Site. The trip origin, destination, and travel path are all within the site.” 
Based on the methodology outlined in the ITE Trip Generation Handbook, internal 
capture rates were applied to the gross person trips resulting in adjusted person 
trips. Trip generation calculations, including the internal capture worksheet, are 
included in The Appendix.

A.8 Transit Assessment 
A comprehensive transit capacity analysis was completed to identify bus and rail 
transit service segments in the MBTA system that may need additional service (either 
more frequent service, or adjustments to existing patterns of service trips) to address 
any passenger overcrowding that may be caused by the Project’s development. This 
analysis compares the 2021 Existing, 2028 No-Build, and 2028 Build ridership levels 
and the expected level of performance on these service routes associated with 
passenger crowding, based on the standards and thresholds noted in the MBTA’s 
2017 Service Delivery Policy (“SDP”). 
For this study, the MBTA Routes 8, 19, 47, 60, 65, CT2, and CT3 bus service were 
evaluated for Project impacts on passenger capacity, along with the Green Line D 
branch. 
The analysis requires estimating future passenger activity and establishing 
assumptions for future transit service levels. These future conditions are compared 
against existing conditions. The analysis helps inform how well the transit system can 
accommodate future passenger demands.

A.8.1 
Methodology 
The capacity analysis results in a comparison of the expected demand for transit to 
the existing and planned capacity of the service. Thus, for service routes, we first 
identify the service segments that are expected to be used by riders generated by 
the proposed Project. For each service, we identify the peak passenger load point – 
the service segment that is most crowded, based on existing ridership, for each bus 
trip, commuter rail trip, or half-hour service period on rapid transit. These passenger 
loads are compared against the service’s capacity.
