The capacity threshold of the transit services is based on the MBTA’s Service Delivery 
Policy.12 For the passenger comfort standard, which is based on vehicle capacity and 
riders, the standard sets the level of passenger crowding that is acceptable by transit 
mode and time period (or trip). Generally, the vehicle load assumes all seats on the 
vehicle will be occupied and some passengers may stand as well, before the 
condition is determined to be “overcrowded.” The standard varies by service period: 
generally, high-volume (peak periods) have a higher threshold than low volume (off-
peak) periods. (In other words, the standard “accepts” more crowding during rush 
hour service than at other service periods of the day.) 
The intent of applying this method is to identify segments in the MBTA system that 
may need additional service (more trips) to address overcrowding. These transit 
capacity analyses are performed consistent with MassDOT Office of Performance 
Management and Innovation (OPMI) and MBTA analysis methods used since the 
issuance of the 2017 SDP. 
To estimate the expected growth in transit ridership between the Existing Condition 
and the future No-Build Condition, an average annual passenger growth rate is 
applied based on the Boston MPO’s CTPS Regional Travel Demand Model projections 
for daily ridership by transit service. (These are reported in the Boston MPO’s long-
range regional transportation plan.) The calculated average annual growth rates are 
applied to existing ridership (data provided by the MBTA). The details of the existing 
and future transit capacity analyses are provided in the following sections.

VHB reviewed the MBTA’s data reflecting Fall 2019 Green Line Passenger Load Profiles17 to 
perform a transit capacity (line haul) analysis. The capacity analysis is based on the 
maximum load point on the entire line; the maximum load point is defined as the point 
along the line that carries the greatest number of passengers. The peak load point of the 
Green Line often occurs in the trunk section served by all four branches. 
The passenger loads represent the average condition for the Fall weekday activity, 
which are presented in Figure Series A.22. 
Based on existing conditions, the MBTA meets its current policy passenger load 
threshold along the trunk section of the Green Line for Inbound and Outbound 
Service. The points at which passenger loads most closely approach the threshold 
are called the “shoulder peak” periods, which occur from 9:00 AM to 9:30 AM and 
6:30 PM to 7:30 PM. During these periods, the service frequency changes from six-
minute headways to eight-minute headways, and the policy threshold decreases 
from a peak period policy maximum of 100 passengers per train car to an off-peak 
policy max of 66 passengers per train car. However, the Fall 2019 passenger loads 
during the shoulder periods for both Inbound and Outbound service are consistently 
100 or more passengers below the policy threshold.

Bus Transit Delay Assessment 
This section provides a high-level quantitative assessment of roadway traffic delay 
impacts on the MBTA bus routes operating within the study network. This 
assessment does not constitute a complete transit delay study - the assessment 
instead relies on the results of the standard traffic operations analysis and the 
assumption that intersection approaches which experience high levels of vehicular 
delay create equivalent levels of delay for buses operating in mixed traffic. 
Intersection movements with high levels of bus passenger delay will be identified 
and recommended for further study to determine feasibility of bus transit priority 
measures. This approach aims to replicate the success of the bus transit priority 
component of the MBTA Better Bus Project, which targets opportunities for transit 
priority measures including transit signal priority (TSP), dedicated bus lanes, and 
queue jumps.

Opportunities for Transit Priority 
Intersections and intersection movements with high levels of bus passenger delay 
should be assessed for potential applications of specific transit priority measures. 
Potential measures include: 
› 
Transit signal priority 
› 
Dedicated bus lanes 
› 
Queue-jump lanes 
Transit signal priority could be considered at all intersections, though especially 
when roadway cross section constraints limit bus operations to mixed use traffic 
such as the Brookline Ave/Park Dr SWT movement. Dedicated bus lanes could be 
considered in segments where there are both frequent buses and opportunity to 
redistribute roadway cross section from other uses, including along Brookline 
Avenue and within the Justine Mee Liff Park. Queue jump lanes could be considered 
at intersection approaches where dedicated bus lanes are not feasible, but vehicle 
queuing creates significant bus delay. 
Any potential bus transit priority measures identified should be evaluated in more 
detail for feasibility and potential benefits. 
A.9 Transit Accessibility Assessment 
This section evaluates the accessibility of existing routes between the Project site 
and transit services. The Project site is well-served by nearby MBTA public transit, 
though ensuring convenient and safe access to those existing transit services for 
people walking and using mobility aids is essential to providing useful and equitable 
service. MBTA services that Project site users are expected to utilize include the D 
branch of the Green Line, the Worcester line of the commuter rail, and seven bus 
routes. 
A.9.1 
Existing Transit Access and Access Challenges 
Figure A.25a highlights existing access challenges between the Project site and 
transit services as well as at the stations and stops themselves. These routes and 
access challenges are described in detail below. 
Fenway Station – Green Line 
Site users accessing the Fenway Green Line Station do so via existing sidewalks 
along Brookline Avenue, Riverway, and Park Drive. All pedestrian crossings within the 
Justine Mee Liff Park provide pedestrian signals with push buttons. While not along 
the direct route between the site and Fenway Station, a sidewalk is not provided on 
the west side of Park Drive for one segment within the Justine Mee Liff Park. The 
grass along that segment is visibly worn from frequent foot traffic of this desire line. 
The proposed Fenway Multiuse Path may create additional demand along this

Longwood Station – Green Line 
Access is provided via two routes. One route is via sidewalks along the Short Street 
Extension, then the Short Street Stairs and the Emerald Necklace path within the 
DCR Riverway Park. This route is not considered accessible, as ADA compliant curb 
ramps are not provided at the intersection of Riverway and Short Street Extension, 
and the Short Street Stairs are the only maintained route between Riverway and the 
Emerald Necklace Path. The second route is an approximately two-minute longer 
walk and is via the Brookline Avenue and Longwood Avenue sidewalks to Chapel 
Street which fronts Longwood Station. Both routes provide pedestrian signals at 
signalized intersections. 
Lansdowne Station – Worcester Commuter Rail Line 
Access is via sidewalks along Brookline Avenue and David Ortiz Drive. No access 
challenges are noted. 
Brookline Ave @ Pilgrim Rd/Brookline Ave @ Fenway – Bus Stops 
Access is via sidewalks along Brookline Avenue. The pedestrian ramp angle and 
crosswalk skew at the intersection of Brookline Avenue and Pilgrim road creates a 
challenging crossing for pedestrians with visual disabilities. No bus shelter is 
provided at the Brookline Ave/Pilgrim Rd stop (Stop ID 1777). Both bus stops create 
a potential conflict between buses and people on bikes by placing the stop within 
the bike lane. 
Brookline Ave @ Short St/Brookline Ave opp Short St – Bus Stops 
Access is via sidewalks along Brookline Avenue. At the intersection of Brookline 
Avenue and the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center driveway there is no 
pedestrian ramp serving the crosswalk across Brookline Avenue. Both bus stops 
create a potential conflict between buses and people on bikes by placing the stop 
within the bike lane.

A.11.1 
Bicycle Level of Comfort Analysis 
This section provides a discussion and summary of cyclist comfortability, which was 
conducted to assess area bicycle infrastructure conditions. Figure A.26 provides a 
summary of the bicycle level of traffic stress on the existing area roadways. 
Bicyclists have varying levels of traffic stress depending on the volume, speed, and 
facility in adjacent traffic. The bicycle level of traffic stress (BLTS) used vary from 
either LTS 1 to LTS 4. LTS 1 represents high comfort for users of all ages and abilities. 
LTS 4 represents low comfort, which is intolerable even for most experienced adults, 
often perceived as un-rideable. The City of Boston uses a scale of LTS 1 (high 
comfort) to 4 (low comfort) which is summarized in Table A.20 and visualized in 
Table A.21 below.

A.12 Traffic Operations Analysis 
Consistent with BTD guidelines, Synchro 10 software was used to model Level of 
Service (LOS) operations at the Project Study Area intersections. LOS is a qualitative 
measure of control delay at an intersection providing an index to the operational

considered acceptable. LOS E indicates vehicles experience significant delay while

signalized and unsignalized intersections. Longer delays at signalized intersections

Under Existing Conditions, the intersection of Riverway/Riverway Extension with Park 
Drive/Fenway experiences high levels of delay in both the morning and the evening 
peak hours, operating at LOS E. Under the 2028 No-Build Conditions, operations 
reduce to an LOS F. Although the intersection also operates at LOS F during the 
2028 Build Conditions, delay does not increase significantly with the addition of 
Project-Generated trips (i.e., 8 seconds of additional delay during the morning peak 
hour and 4 during the evening). 
As mentioned previously, the intersection of Park Drive at Brookline Ave/Boylston 
Street will be reconfigured as part of the Boylston Street Corridor Improvements 
Project. The reconfiguration of this intersection is reflected in all 2028 future 
conditions analyses. As demonstrated in this Section, during the morning peak hour, 
the intersection operates at LOS C during both the morning and evening peak hours 
in the 2021 Existing Condition. It operates at LOS D in the 2028 No-Build Condition, 
and, with the addition of Project trips, will operate at LOS E in the 2028 Build 
Condition. No degradation in level of service is expected in the weekday evening 
peak period between the 2028 No-Build and Build conditions. 
The intersection of Brookline Avenue at the Beth Israel Deaconess (BIDMC) Main 
Campus Entrance/Short Street currently operates as a signalized, three-legged 
intersection. In the morning peak hour, operations reduce from LOS D to LOS E 
between Existing Conditions and 2028 No-Build Conditions. As part of the Project, 
the northwest leg of the intersection will be opened to entering and exiting vehicles 
(i.e., Short Street). Vehicles will be permitted to exit the Site via Short Street to 
Brookline Avenue south and north, and to enter the Site by making a right turn onto 
Short Street from the northeast. Left turns onto Short Street from Brookline Avenue 
will be restricted. With the addition of Project traffic and new movements, 
operations do not change in the 2028 Build Condition. This is primarily due to a 
modified phasing plan that removes the all-pedestrian phase in favor of concurrent 
pedestrian phases for Brookline Avenue and the two side street approaches. The 
future configuration will include one crosswalk across Brookline Avenue in between 
the two side street approaches. Because the volume of traffic exiting the Site onto 
Brookline Avenue south is anticipated to be relatively low (3 in the AM, 38 in the 
PM), this crosswalk will run concurrently with southeast-bound traffic from Short 
Street. 
Under Existing Conditions, the intersection of Brookline Avenue at Longwood 
Avenue operates at LOS E during the morning peak hour and LOS D during the 
evening peak hour. In the 2028 No-Build Conditions, the addition of traffic related to 
other local developments cause operations to reduce to LOS F in both peak hours. 
However, during the 2028 Build Conditions, delay does not increase by more than 
five seconds during either peak hour. The northeast-bound approach from 
Longwood Avenue tends to experience the highest levels of delay during both peak 
hours, especially for left-turning traffic.

A.13 Transportation Mitigation and Improvements 
A.13.1 
Enhanced Pedestrian/Bicycle Access 
The Project’s proposed pedestrian and bicycle-focused improvements are a central 
pillar of the Project’s public benefits commitment to the LMA neighborhood and the 
city as a whole, which in aggregate will dramatically improve the pedestrian 
experience throughout the Project Study Area and also the comfort and safety of 
cycling conditions along several of the key routes in the vicinity of the Project Site, 
improving conditions for both residents cycling within the neighborhood and also 
commuters cycling along major mobility corridors such as Brookline Avenue. 
As discussed in Section A.5.2., the Project will include the implementation of very 
significant pedestrian + bicyclist improvements that will be transformative to the 
LMA’s public realm. Potential enhancements include the following investments: 
• 
Short Street Improvements - The Project proposes access for all modes 
throughout Short Street between Riverway and Brookline Ave with the 
Project in place requiring that Short Street be integrated into the traffic 
signal at Brookline Ave at BIDMC Main Entrance. The change proposes the 
reconstruction of the existing brick pedestrian pathway between Pilgrim 
Road and Brookline Ave but replacing it with a proposed cross-section 
including an ADA-compliant grade-separated 12’ multi-use path with 2’ 
buffer on each side and two 11’ vehicle travel lanes to and from the 
proposed site driveway. All roadway improvements will be consistent with 
the objectives of BTD’s Complete Street Guidelines. This new driveway will 
be designed to provide access from Brookline Avenue (right-turn in only) 
and egress from the Project site via an adjacent garage portal and via 
Pilgrim Road. The inbound driveway will terminate at the garage entry, 
thereby restricting through traffic access to the Riverway. Similarly, Short 
Street Extension will remain one-way from Pilgrim Road to the Riverway, 
thereby eliminating any opportunity for unintended through traffic in either 
travel direction on Short Street between the Riverway and Brookline Avenue. 
At Brookline Avenue, the existing traffic signal will be reconstructed to 
support access and egress from Short Street. Note, however, that left turns 
into the site will be restricted due to the offset Short Street and Beth Israel 
Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC) East Campus driveways.

Brookline Ave Improvements - The Project will design and construct a 6’ 
grade-separated bicycle lane with 2’ buffer between Longwood Avenue and 
Fenway/Riverway on the north side of Brookline Avenue. Existing 
MBTA/LMA Shuttle bus stops adjacent to the Project on the north side of 
Brookline Avenue will also be reconstructed to be floating bus stops with 
shelters. The Project will implement a new mid-block driveway that will be 
signalized, providing primary access and egress for vehicles to and from the

the Colleges of the Fenway path connecting to Emmanuel College and onto

are comfortable for all ages and abilities including children (as noted in 
section A.9.1). 
A.13.2 
Transportation Demand Management Plan (TDM) 
The Project will be supported by a robust Transportation Demand Management 
(TDM) program intended to reduce dependence on vehicle travel, minimize single 
occupancy vehicle (SOV) drive-alone trips and enhance mobility by alternative 
transportation modes. This TDM program has been developed based upon the latest 
BTD TDM Point System model targeting a mobility score of 71-90 (based on the 
mobility score map for the projects’ location) which requires a target of 90 points. 
The BTD model checklist is included in the Appendix for reference.

Department Comments
Included here are Boston Public Works Department (PWD) comments for the Massachusetts College of Pharmacy
and Health Sciences IMPNF.
Project Coordination:
The developer should coordinate with the City of Boston if proposing any changes in use, dimensional, parking, or
loading elements.
Project Specific Scope Considerations:
The developer should coordinate with BTD and PWD to develop safety and accessibility improvements for
pedestrians and cyclists in the area.
Pedestrian Access:
The developer should consider extending the scope of sidewalk improvements along the site frontage.
Site Plan:
The developer must provide an engineer’s site plan at an appropriate engineering scale that shows curb
functionality on both sides of all streets that abut the property.
 
Construction Within The Public vs Private Right-of-Way:
Although the general comments below apply specifically to work associated with the project within the public
right-of-way, it is preferred and encouraged for construction in the private right-of-way to be consistent with City
standards for public ways, as well, to the extent possible. Should these streets ever become public ways, they must
conform to the City standards as outlined below.
All work within the public way shall conform to Boston Public Works Department (PWD) standards. Any
non-standard materials proposed within the public way will require approval through the Public
Improvement Commission (PIC) process and a fully executed License, Maintenance and Indemnification
(LM&I) Agreement with the PIC.
Sidewalks:
The developer is responsible for the reconstruction of the sidewalks abutting the project and, wherever possible, to
extend the limits to the nearest intersection to encourage and compliment pedestrian improvements and travel
along all sidewalks within the ROW within and beyond the project limits. The reconstruction effort also must meet
current American’s with Disabilities Act (ADA)/ Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (AAB) guidelines,
including the installation of new or reconstruction of existing pedestrian ramps at all corners of all intersections
abutting the project site if not already constructed to ADA/AAB compliance per Code of Massachusetts Regulations
Title 521, Section 21 (https://www.mass.gov/regulations/521-CMR-21-curb-cuts). This includes converting apex
ramps to perpendicular ramps at intersection corners and constructing or reconstructing reciprocal pedestrian
ramps where applicable. Plans showing the extents of the proposed sidewalk improvements associated with this
project must be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval. Changes to any curb geometry
will need to be reviewed and approved through the PIC.
Please note that at signalized intersections, any alteration to pedestrian ramps may also require upgrading the
traffic signal equipment to ensure that the signal post and pedestrian push button locations meet current ADA and
Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) requirements. Any changes to the traffic signal system must
be coordinated and approved by BTD.

All proposed sidewalk widths and cross-slopes must comply to both City of Boston and ADA/AAB standards.
The developer is encouraged to contact the City’s Disabilities Commission to confirm compliant accessibility within
the Public ROW.
Green Infrastructure:
The developer shall work with PWD, the Green Infrastructure Division, and the Boston Water and Sewer
Commission (BWSC) to determine appropriate methods of green infrastructure and stormwater management
systems within the Public ROW. The ongoing maintenance of such systems shall require an LM&I Agreement with
the PIC.
Driveway Curb Cuts
Any proposed driveway curb cuts within the Public ROW will need to be reviewed and approved by the PIC. All
existing curb cuts that will no longer be utilized shall be closed.
Discontinuances
Any discontinuances (sub-surface, surface or above surface) within the Public ROW must be processed through
the PIC.
Easements
Any easements within the Public ROW associated with this project must be processed through the PIC.
Landscaping
The developer must seek approval from the Chief Landscape Architect with the Parks and Recreation Department
for all landscape elements within the Public ROW. The landscaping program must accompany a LM&I with the
PIC.
Street Lighting
The developer must seek approval from the PWD Street Lighting Division, where needed, for all proposed street
lighting to be installed by the developer. All proposed lighting within the Public ROW must be compatible with the
area lighting to provide a consistent urban design. The developer should coordinate with the PWD Street Lighting
Division for an assessment of any additional street lighting upgrades that are to be considered in conjunction with
this project. All existing metal street light pull box covers within the limits of sidewalk construction to remain shall be
replaced with new composite covers per PWD Street Lighting standards. Metal covers should remain for pull box
covers in the roadway. For all sections of sidewalk that are to be reconstructed in the Public ROW that contain or
are proposed to contain a City-owned street light system with underground conduit, the developer shall be
responsible for installing shadow conduit adjacent to the street lighting system. Installation of shadow conduit and
limits should be coordinated through the BPDA Smart Utilities team.
Roadway
Based on the extent of construction activity, including utility connections and taps, the developer will be responsible
for the full restoration of the roadway sections that immediately abut the property and, in some cases, to extend the
limits of roadway restoration to the nearest intersection. A plan showing the extents and methods for roadway
restoration shall be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval.
Additional Project Coordination
All projects must be entered into the City of Boston Utility Coordination Software (COBUCS) to review for any
conflicts with other proposed projects within the Public ROW. The developer must coordinate with any existing
projects within the same limits and receive clearance from PWD before commencing work.

Resiliency:
Proposed designs should follow the Boston Public Works Climate Resilient Design Guidelines
(https://www.boston.gov/environment-and-energy/climate-resilient-design-guidelines) where applicable.
Please note that these are the general standard and somewhat specific PWD requirements. More detailed
comments may follow and will be addressed during the PIC review process. If you have any questions, please feel
free to contact me at jeffrey.alexis@boston.gov or at 617-635-4966.

IMPNF for Renewal dated July 24, 2024, pursuant to Sections 80D-5.2(e), 80D-6, and 
80D-8 of the Boston Zoning Code (the "Code"); and (2) authorize the Director to 
take all actions and execute any and all documents deemed necessary and 
appropriate relative to the IMPNF for Renewal. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That in connection with the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
for the renewal and extension of the NEC Institutional Master Plan, 
dated July 24, 2024 ("IMPNF for Renewal"), and after consideration of 
the IMPNF for Renewal, the BRA hereby finds that: (a) the NEC 
Institutional Master Plan and the IMPNF for Renewal (collectively, the 
“Amended IMP”), conforms to the provisions of Article 80D of the 
Boston Zoning Code (“the Code”); (b) the IMPNF for Renewal, conforms 
to the general plan for the City as a whole; and (c) on balance, nothing 
in the IMPNF for Renewal, will be injurious to the neighborhood or 
otherwise detrimental to the public welfare, weighing all the benefits 
and burdens; and 
 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the BRA waives further review of the IMPNF for Renewal pursuant 
to Sections 80D-5.2(e), 80D-6, and 80D-8 of the Code and approves the 
Amended IMP for a period of two (2) years from the date of approval 
of this renewal vote by the BRA, which date is September 12, 2026; and 
 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the BRA hereby authorizes the Director to take all actions and 
execute any and all documents deemed necessary and appropriate 
and in the best interest of the BRA by the Director in connection with 
the Amended IMP.

MEMORANDUM 
 
 
 
 
 
 
OCTOBER 10, 2024 
 
TO: 
 
BOSTON REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY 
D/B/A BOSTON PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT AGENCY (BPDA) 
AND DEVIN QUIRK, ACTING DIRECTOR 
 
FROM: 
CASEY HINES, SENIOR DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
NICK CARTER, DEVELOPMENT PORTFOLIO MANAGER 
ILANA HAIMES, ZONING COMPLIANCE PLANNER I 
JAMES FITZGERALD, DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF PLANNING REVIEW 
SAM VALENTINE, SITE DESIGN 
MEGHAN RICHARD, SENIOR URBAN DESIGNER 
JEONG-JUN JU, URBAN DESIGNER 
 
SUBJECT: 
726 SHAWMUT AVENUE, ROXBURY (“NEW MADINAH”) 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency ("BPDA") authorize the 
Director to: (1) issue a Certification of Approval for the proposed 
development located at 726 Shawmut Avenue in Roxbury (as defined 
below, the “Proposed Project”), in accordance with Article 80E, Small 
Project Review of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”); (2) enter 
into a Community Benefits Agreement in connection with the 
Proposed Project, and to take any other actions and to execute any 
other agreements and documents that the Director deems 
appropriate and necessary in connection with the Proposed Project. 
 
 
PROJECT SITE 
 
The Proposed Project is located on the corner of Shawmut Avenue, Williams Street 
and Gary Street and encompasses approximately 10,609 square feet of land (the 
“Project Site” or “Site”). Located along Shawmut Avenue in Roxbury, in the 
Boulevard Planning District Overlay, the Project Site is a significant gateway to 
Roxbury’s culturally rich neighborhoods. Occupying the length of Shawmut Avenue 
between Williams Street and Gary Street, the Site is long, relatively flat, and very 
narrow in several locations. It is comprised of 6 lots, totaling approximately 10,609 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
26 
 
sf, most of which is currently serving as paved parking for the existing structure. 
The Project Site currently consists of an existing mosque, and a parking lot. 
 
DEVELOPMENT TEAM 
 
The development team includes: 
 
Proponent: 
 
 
Society for Islamic Brotherhood Inc. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Imam Abdullah Faaruuq 
 
Article 80 Consultant: 
 
Highland Development Group, LLC. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Armindo Goncalves 
 
Architect: 
 
 
 
Monte French Design Studio 
 
 
 
 
Development Consultant: 
Mark Winkeller 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
The Proposed Project, “New Madinah,” seeks to provide expansion to the Society 
for Islamic Brotherhood and their religious and social services through the 
redevelopment of their current building and adjacent under-utilized land. 
 
The Proposed Project would raze the existing structure and surface parking to allow 
for the complete redevelopment of the Site. As a mixed-use development, the 
project proposes over 14,000 sf of new cultural, commercial, and services space, 
along with thirty-eight (38) new income-restricted residential rental units, a 
common roof deck, and a green roof (collectively, the “Proposed Project”). The 
residential rental units include approximately thirteen (13) studio units, eight (8) 
one-bedroom units, fifteen (15) two-bedroom units, and two (2) three-bedroom 
units, all of which will be made affordable to households earning not more than 
80% of the Area Median Income. 
 
The proposed ground floor will be generally dedicated to public, commercial, and 
cultural uses, including a multi-purpose event space, cultural cafe and bookstore, 
and access to the mosque and educational spaces above. 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
26 
 
 
Towards the southwest end of the site would be the proposed residential entry, 
bike storage access, and surface parking underneath the residential floors above. 
The frontages along both Shawmut Avenue and Williams Street would include a 
new colonnade of street trees and other amenities to align with the city’s Complete 
Streets Guidelines. 
 
The Proposed Project also includes the removal of two, existing, street trees. BPDA 
Board approval vote does not authorize tree removals in the adjacent rights-of-way, 
the proposed removal of existing trees located in the public way will be subject to 
Massachusetts General Law Chapter 87. The table below summarizes the 
Proposed Project’s key statistics:

ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On June 16, 2023, the Proponent filed an Application for Small Project Review with 
the Planning Department for the Proposed Project, pursuant to Article 80E of the 
Code (the “Code”). The Planning Department sponsored and held a virtual public 
meeting on September 9, 2023, via Zoom. The meeting was advertised in the local 
newspapers, posted on the Planning Department website and a notification was 
emailed to all subscribers of the Planning Department’s Roxbury neighborhood 
update list. The public comment period ended on September 23, 2023. 
 
The development team has discussed the project with Planning Department staff 
members prior to filing this application to identify issues, address concerns, and 
make preliminary design changes accordingly. Additionally, as part of the Article 80 
Review process, the development team has met with neighbors to obtain feedback 
and answer questions from community members. The team will continue to work 
with the Planning Department and other city agencies in accordance with Article 80 
and the Inspectional Services Department requirements. 
 
 
 
PLANNING AND ZONING CONTEXT 
The Proposed Project Site is located in the Roxbury Neighborhood, in Lower 
Roxbury, between the Frederick Douglass Square Historic District and Nubian 
Square. The Site is located within the study area of the Roxbury Strategic Master 
Plan, and more specifically under the area of PLAN: Nubian Square. The 
development proposal adheres to the planning goals of the Roxbury Strategic 
Master Plan, which advocates for both increased housing opportunities at different 
income levels and the enhancement of educational and cultural resources in the 
neighborhood through increased public involvement of community organizations 
(including faith-based agencies) in the Roxbury community. The Master Plan also 
highlights the preservation of historic public assets in the Roxbury neighborhood. 
 
While PLAN: Nubian Square focuses primarily on vacant and city-owned parcels, it 
also supports a primary goal of affordable housing preservation and development. 
The Proposed Project as submitted by the Proponent provides for the addition of 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
26 
 
38 affordable housing units to the neighborhood. The expansion of community 
space and education centers within the Mosque for the Praising of Allah & Islamic 
Multi-Service Organization also supports the Jobs and Economic Development section 
of PLAN: Nubian Square. 
 
The planning goals of Imagine Boston 2030, Go Boston 2030, and Housing Boston 
2030 are all supported by the intention of the proponent’s development proposal. 
The addition of housing and community support programs to the existing faith-
based neighborhood institution directly contribute to the enhancement of the 
neighborhood and encouragement of dense, mixed-use development identified in 
the Opportunity of Growth in Imagine Boston 2030. The proposed parking ratio, 
and creation of housing opportunities in proximity to the MBTA’s Nubian Square 
and Ruggles Stations, align well with the goals of Go Boston 2030. 
 
The Proposed Project is located in the Roxbury Neighborhood Zoning District, 
within a Multifamily Residential (MFR) subdistrict, governed by Article 50 of the 
Code. Community uses and places of worship are allowed uses, and restaurant and 
retail uses are conditional uses and an extension of current conditions in the area. 
The Proposed Project is also located in a Boulevard Planning District zoning overlay, 
which applies to developments within 100’ of specified city boulevards, in the case, 
Melnea Cass Boulevard. 
 
The Proposed Project supports the goals of increased affordable housing and 
housing near neighborhood centers as described in the City of Boston’s planning 
initiatives. Thus, relief is recommended for the proposed floor area ratio and height 
of the development. As noted above, the proposed transportation plan aligns with 
relevant city policy and merits zoning relief for minimum off-street parking and 
loading requirements. Due to the parcel’s unusual shape, including an access road 
along Dade Street, relief is recommended for minimum front, side, and rear yard 
setback requirements. Relief is also recommended for the proposed lot area per 
dwelling unit and usable open space, as the proposed dimensions represent a 
reasonable and contextually appropriate use of the land 
 
 
 
 
MITIGATION AND COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
26 
 
The Proposed Project will include mitigation measures and community benefits to 
the neighborhood and the City of Boston (the “City”), including: 
 
● In compliance with Boston’s Complete Streets policy, the Proponent will 
make much-needed sidewalk and streetscape improvements to Shawmut 
Avenue. PIC approvals for proposed improvements shall be completed 
before building permit issuance for the Proposed Project. The physical 
mitigation improvements must be completed upon Certificate of Occupancy. 
These proposed improvements are subject to design review and approval by 
the Boston Transportation Department (BTD), Public Works Department 
(PWD), PIC, and the Planning Department. 
o The Proposed Project will enhance the streetscapes and public realm 
by implementing the following at the Project Site: 
▪ 
Constructing ADA compliant ramps, including the ramps serving 
the Shawmut Ave and Williams Street crosswalk, sidewalks, the 
reciprocal ramps as required by code, and crosswalks where 
possible (5-foot minimum clear path of travel); 
▪ 
Ensuring minimal and code compliant gapping between the 
edge of the detectable warning panels and the edge of the curb; 
▪ 
To be determined through more detailed design review, these 
improvements will consider curb extensions at the Shawmut 
Ave and Williams Street corner to provide additional dimension; 
● 38 new units of affordable housing. 
● New community space in the building 
● Before issuance of the Certificate of Approval, the Proponent will make a 
one-time “bikeshare” contribution of $16,330 to the Boston Transportation 
Department (“BTD”) per the City of Boston Bike Parking Guidelines. 
● Revitalizing underutilized parcels to create additional housing units and 
worship space. 
● Creating a dedicated bike room for storage of bikes within the building to 
encourage bicycling as a mode of transportation. 
o Bike room to meet minimum dimensions required by the City of 
Boston Bike Parking Guidelines. 
● Adding revenue in the form of property taxes to the City of Boston. 
● Creating temporary construction and labor jobs. 
 
The community benefits described above will be set forth in the Community Benefit 
Agreement for the Proposed Project. Any required community benefit contribution 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
26 
 
payments shall be made to the BPDA or respective City of Boston department 
before issuance of the initial building permit by the City of Boston Inspectional 
Services Department (“ISD”) and will be distributed as outlined above. The Proposed 
Project and public realm improvements are subject to Planning Department Design 
Review. 
 
HOUSING PROGRAM AND INCLUSIONARY DEVELOPMENT POLICY 
 
Projects financed as one entity where at least 40% of the units are income-
restricted are exempt from the Inclusionary Development Policy dated December 
10, 2015 (the “IDP”). The Proposed Project is financed as one entity and contains 
thirty-eight (38) income-restricted rental units, or 100% of the total units, surpassing 
40% of the total units. As such, the Proposed Project is exempt from the IDP. 
 
As currently proposed, eight (8) units will be made affordable to households 
earning not more than 30% of the Area Median Income (“AMI”), as published by 
the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (“HUD”), twenty-
eight (28) units will be made affordable to households earning not more than 60% 
of the AMI, one (1) unit will be made affordable to households earning not more 
than 70% AMI, and the remaining one (1) unit will be made affordable to 
households earning not more than 80% of the AMI. The affordability of the 
Proposed Project will be finalized through the public funding process and the 
ongoing affordability will be monitored under a MassDocs Agreement. 
 
RECCOMENDATIONS 
 
The Proposed Project complies with the requirements set forth in Section 80E of 
the Code for Small Project Review. Therefore, Planning Department staff 
recommends that the Director be authorized to issue a Certification of Approval for 
the Proposed Project; and take any other action and execute any other agreements 
and documents that the Director deems appropriate and necessary in connection 
with the Proposed Project. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue a Certification 
of Approval pursuant to Section 80E-6 of the Boston Zoning Code (the 
"Code"), approving the development at 726 Shawmut Avenue in the 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
26 
 
Roxbury neighborhood, proposed by the Society for Islamic 
Brotherhood (the “Proponent”), for the construction of a new (6) six-
story, mixed-use building containing approximately 49,614 gross 
square feet of 38 residential rental units, worship space, and 4 off-
street parking spaces (the “Proposed Project”), in accordance with the 
requirements of Small Project Review, Article 80E, of the Code, subject 
to continuing design review by the BPDA; and 
 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to enter into a 
Community Benefits Agreement, and to take any other actions and to 
execute any other agreements and documents that the Director 
deems appropriate and necessary in connection with the Proposed 
Project.

MEMORANDUM 
 
 
 
 
 
September 15, 2022 
 
 
TO: 
BOSTON REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY 
 
D/B/A BOSTON PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT AGENCY (“BPDA”)1* 
 
AND JAMES ARTHUR JEMISON II, DIRECTOR 
 
FROM: 
MICHAEL CHRISTOPHER, DIRECTOR OF DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
 
CASEY HINES, DEPUTY DIRECTOR OF DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
 
QUINN VALCICH, PROJECT MANAGER 
 
SUBJECT: 
PUBLIC HEARING TO CONSIDER THE INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
NOTIFICATION FORM FOR THE FIFTH AMENDMENT TO 
NORTHEASTERN UNIVERSITY 2013-2023 INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
d/b/a the Boston Planning & Development Agency (the “BPDA”) Board 
authorize the Director to: (1) issue an Adequacy Determination 
approving the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form for the Fifth 
Amendment to Northeastern University 2013-2023 Institutional Master 
Plan ("IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment'') filed by Northeastern 
University on June 15, 2022, in connection with the Snell Library 
renovations and addition project ("Proposed Project") pursuant to 
Article 80D-5.4 and Section 80D-9.2 of the Boston Zoning Code (the 
"Code"); (2) petition the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the 
Proposed IMP Amendment; (3) issue a Certification of Consistency 
pursuant to Section 80D-10 of the Code in connection with the 
Proposed Project as described in the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment; 
(4) execute and deliver any and all other agreements and documents 
deemed necessary and appropriate by the Director, in connection with 
the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment. 
______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
 
1* Effective October 20, 2016, the BRA commenced doing business as BPDA. 

 
 
The Northeastern University (the “University”) Institutional Master Plan (“IMP”) was 
approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) Board in November 
2013, adopted by the Zoning Commission on March 24, 2014 and became effective 
on March 30, 2014, with subsequent amendments in 2016, 2017, and 2022 (“NEU 
IMP”). On February 10, 2021, the University submitted a Third Amendment to 
Northeastern University 2013-2023 Institutional Master Plan (the “Third IMP 
Amendment”) and associated Draft Project Impact Report. The proposed Third IMP 
Amendment includes a new mixed-use building, containing 810 beds above a five-
story podium of teaching and learning (the “Third IMP Amendment Proposed 
Project”). The Third IMP Amendment Proposed Project and Third IMP Amendment 
are still under review by the Boston Planning & Development Agency (the “BPDA”) 
and are not included in the project considered in this memo. 
 
Separately, on June 15, 2022, the University submitted to the BPDA the IMPNF for 
Fifth IMP Amendment, seeking to renovate approximately 138,000 square feet of 
interior space and add approximately 2,500 square feet of new space to the Snell 
Library. The interior work for the Proposed Project involves the renovation of 
portions of the building and the exterior work involves the enclosure of areas 
immediately adjacent to the building on the first floor that are mostly beneath an 
overhand created by the existing floors above. The Proposed Project will facilitate 
the rapidly evolving research and learning objectives of the University, allow library 
specialists to more effectively partner with faculty and scholars, and conceive how a 
21st century experiential research library works. The Proposed Project does not 
meet the threshold of a substantial renovation in accordance with Section 80B-2 
and 80D-9 of the Code, and therefore does not qualify for Large Project Review. 
 
 
PROJECT REVIEW 
 
The IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment, filed on June 15, 2022, is being reviewed 
under the Expedited Review Procedure of Section 80D-9.2 of the Code. Pursuant to 
Section 80D-9.2 of the Code, a proposed amendment to an IMP may be submitted 
under an expedited review procedure if: (1) such amendment proposes no changes 
to the IMP other that the addition of one of more Proposed Projects; and (2) each of 
such Proposed Projects meets the requirements of Section 80D-9.2(b), that such 
project does not meet the size thresholds of Large Project Review. The Proposed 
Project does not meet the threshold for Large Project Review. No other changes are 
proposed. The comment period for the IMPNF closed on July 29, 2022. A Task Force 
meeting was held on July 13, 2022. 

 
 
 
MITIGATION & COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
Northeastern University Library provides numerous community benefits including: 
● Easy access to Archives and Special Collections for Boston community 
members, either walk-in or by appointment 
● New event space to continue our long history of community-driven 
programming/workshops that highlight Archives and other material on local 
history, activism, and social change 
● Broad community engagement through the Boston Research Center initiative 
where the library works with local community organizations to identify needs 
and help make discoverable historic and contemporary data and resources 
about Boston 
● Strategic partnerships with Boston Public Schools to bring resources and 
programming into the classroom, with a focus on Teaching with Archives and 
leveraging the Library's relationships with publishers and information 
providers to integrate new STEM resources and offer expertise in STEM 
education to BPS 
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, staff recommends that the BPDA Board authorize the 
Director to: (1) issue an Adequacy Determination approving IMPNF for Fifth IMP 
Amendment filed by Northeastern University on June 15, 2022, in connection with 
the Proposed Project, pursuant to Article 80D-5.4 and Section 80D-9.2 of the Code; 
(2) petition the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the Proposed IMP 
Amendment; (3) issue a Certification of Consistency pursuant to Section 80D-10 of 
the Code in connection with the Proposed Project as described in the IMPNF for 
Fifth IMP Amendment; (4) execute and deliver any and all other agreements and 
documents deemed necessary and appropriate by the Director, in connection with 
the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That in connection with the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
for the Fifth Amendment to the Northeastern University 2013-2023 
Institutional Master Plan, filed by Northeastern University on June 15, 

 
 
2022 (the “IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment”), describing the Snell 
Library renovations and addition project (the “Proposed Project”) 
presented at a public hearing held at the offices of the Boston 
Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) on September 15, 2022, and after 
consideration of evidence presented in connection with the IMPNF for 
Fifth IMP Amendment, the BRA hereby finds that: (a) the IMPNF for 
Fifth IMP Amendment conforms to the provisions of Article 80D of the 
Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”); (b) the IMPNF for Fifth IMP 
Amendment conforms to the general plan for the City as a whole; and 
(c) on balance, nothing in the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment will be 
injurious to the neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public 
welfare, weighing all the benefits and burdens; 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That pursuant to Article 80D of the Code, the Director be authorized to 
petition the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the IMPNF for 
Fifth IMP Amendment in substantial accord with that presented to the 
BRA Board at the September 15, 2022 meeting; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue an Adequacy 
Determination pursuant to Article 80-D5.4(c) and 80D-9.2 of the Code 
approving the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment; and 
 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is authorized to issue a Certification 
of Consistency for the Proposed Project pursuant to Section 80D-10 of 
the Code when the Director finds that the Proposed Project is 
consistent with the IMPNF for Fifth IMP Amendment; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to execute and deliver 
any and all other agreements and documents deemed necessary and 
appropriate by the Director in connection with the foregoing, on such 
terms and conditions as the Director deems necessary and 
appropriate.

B-1 
MEMORANDUM 
SEPTEMBER 14, 2023 
 
 
TO: 
BOSTON REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY 
 
D/B/A BOSTON PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT AGENCY (BPDA) 
 
AND JAMES ARTHUR JEMISON II, DIRECTOR 
 
FROM: 
MICHAEL CHRISTOPHER, DIRECTOR FOR DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
CASEY HINES, DEPUTY DIRECTOR FOR DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
NICK CARTER, SENIOR PROJECT MANAGER 
 
SUBJECT: 
NUBIAN ASCENDS, ROXBURY 
 
 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(“BRA”) d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) 
authorize the Director to: (1) issue a Determination waiving the 
requirement of further review pursuant to Section 80A-6 of the Boston 
Zoning Code (the “Code”) in connection with the First Notice of Project 
Change submitted to the BPDA on July 26, 2023 (the “First NPC”) by 
Nubian Ascends Partners, LLC (the “Proponent”) for the Nubian Square 
Ascends mixed-use project (the "Proposed Project"); (2) issue a 
Certification of Compliance under Section 80B-6 for the Proposed 
Project, upon successful completion of the Article 80 review process; 
(3) execute and deliver a Cooperation Agreement, an Affordable 
Housing Agreement and Restriction, and any and all other agreements 
and documents that the Director deems appropriate and necessary in 
connection with the Proposed Project. 
 
PROJECT SITE 
 
The Project Site is a BPDA-owned site consisting of approximately 87,879 square 
feet of vacant land bounded by Washington Street to the north west, Harrison 
Avenue to the south east, Eustis Street to the north and Palmer Street to the south. 
Originally a parking lot for the long-shuttered grocery store Blair’s Foodland, the 
BPDA purchased the blighted Property from a private owner on December 23, 
1985. It is presently used for parking by local employees and visitors to Nubian 
Square. The Project Site, known as the Blair Lot, was the subject of an intensive 
 

 
 
community planning process through PLAN: Nubian Square. 
 
The Project Site is part of the Dudley Square Economic Development Area (”EDA”) as 
shown on Map 6A-6C of the Boston Zoning Maps in the Roxbury District, and 
therefore is principally governed by the provisions of Article 50 of the Boston 
Zoning Code (the “Code”). The Project Site is also located within a Boulevard 
Planning District ("BPD") with overlays to underlying sub-districts as noted in 
Section 50-37. Part of the Project Site is located in the Eustis Street Protection Area 
for the Eustis Street Architectural Conservation District. 
 
DEVELOPMENT TEAM 
 
Proponent: 
 
 
Nubian Ascend Partners LLC 
 
 
 
 
 
Richard Taylor 
 
Architect: 
 
 
 
Stantec Architecture Boston 
 
 
 
 
 
Tamara Roy 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Dream Collaborative 
 
 
 
 
 
Nick Brooks 
 
Landscape Architect: 
 
Ground Inc. 
 
 
 
 
 
Shauna Gillies-Smith 
 
Civil and Transportation Engineer: Bryant Associates 
 
 
 
 
 
Todd Brayton 
 
 
 
 
 
James Comeau 
 
Geotechnical Engineer: 
McPhail Associates LLC 
 
 
 
 
 
Scott Smith 
 
Environmental Consultant: 
GEI 
 
 
 
 
 
Ryan Hoffman 
 
Legal Counsel: 
 
 
Rubin and Rudman, LLP 
 
 
 
 
 
Andrew Kara, Esq. 
 
 
 
 
 
Michael Novaria, Esq. 
 
Permitting Consultant: 
Bevco Associates, Inc. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Beverley Johnson 
 
PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
Nubian Ascend Partners, LLC (the “Proponent”) proposes the redevelopment of the 
former Blair’s Foodland Site in the Nubian Square neighborhood of Roxbury. 
Previously Approved on December 16, 2021, the Proponent proposed to create 
approximately 365,475 gross square feet (“GSF”) of new residential use, including 15 
homeownership units with a preference for local artist, of which ten (10) would be 
income restricted, and will also include retail, which would include a culinary hall 
providing opportunities for local restauranteurs, commercial office/laboratory 
space, entertainment and artistic/cultural space, including a new performance hall, 
a publicly-accessible pedestrian corridor that would provide access to all project 
components, and a 300-space above-grade parking garage (the “Previously 
Approved Project”). 
 
The Previously Approved Project will also provide substantial public realm 
improvements, with approximately 25% of the Project Site dedicated to creating 
dynamic community gathering spaces, including the creation of Artist’s Way, a new 
pedestrian connection through the project site that will create access to the retail, 
cultural and office portions of the Proposed Project. 
 
The First NPC, filed July 26, 2023, seeks to change the income restriction mix of the 
residential component of the Previously Approved Project from 10 income 
restricted units to 15 income restricted units. The First NPC will also remove the 
artist preference for the housing. No other changes are contemplated through this 
First NPC.

the agency Research Department. 
 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On July 29, 2021, the Proponent filed a Project Notification Form ("PNF") with the 
BPDA pursuant to Article 80B of the Code. The BPDA published notice of the filing in 
the Boston Herald on July 28, 2021 and was sent to BPDA mailing lists. A Scoping 
Session for City and State officials was held on August 17, 2021. 
 
The BPDA hosted a virtual Impact Advisory Group (“IAG”) meeting on August 23, 
2021. A virtual public meeting was held on September 2, 2021. The public 
comment period in connection with the PNF concluded on September 10, 2021. A 
second virtual public meeting was held on November 8, 2021. A second IAG 
meeting was held on December 6, 2021. 
 
The public meetings were advertised in the Bay State Banner, El Mundo, and El 
Planeta newspapers, while both the public meeting and Roxbury Neighborhood 
Council Project Review Committee/IAG meeting were posted on the BPDA calendar 
and website, and email notifications were sent to all subscribers of the BPDA's 
Roxbury neighborhood email update list. Local elected officials and their staff were 

 
 
also notified of all meetings. 
 
The Proponent met with the Roxbury Neighborhood Council (“RNC”) to discuss the 
site zoning on two occasions: (1) A one-on-one meeting with the RNC on November 
3, 2021; and (2) The RNC Public Meeting on November 4, 2021. The Proponent also 
responded to a follow-up letter from the RNC on December 2, 2021. 
 
The Previously Approved Project and its mitigation package were approved on 
December 16, 2021. The First NPC does not change the previously approved 
mitigation package. 
 
On July 26, 2023, the Proponent filed the First NPC for the Proposed Project in 
accordance with section 80A-6 of the Code. The First NPC filing initiated a thirty-day 
(30) public comment period with a closing date of August 25, 2023. The comment 
period was subsequently extended to September 8, 2023. 
 
The BPDA subsequently sponsored and held a virtual combined IAG and 
community meeting by Zoom on August 28, 2023. The meeting was advertised on 
the BPDA website and notifications were sent out to the Roxbury neighborhood via 
the BPDA’s email lists. 
 
ZONING 
 
The Project Site is located within the Roxbury Neighborhood District in accordance 
with Article 50 of the Boston Zoning Code (the "Code"). The Project Site is further 
located within the Dudley Square EDA as shown on City of Boston Map 6A-6C. The 
majority of the Project Site, which is referred to as the "Blair Site", is located within 
an area in which Planned Development Areas (“PDA”) may be permitted. A portion 
of the Project Site is also located within a Boulevard Planning Overlay District 
pursuant to Article 50, Section 50-37 of the Code. Pursuant to Article 50, Section 50-
11 of the Code, within the Dudley Square EDA, the maximum allowed Building 
Height is fifty-five (55) feet and the maximum allowed Floor Area Ratio (“FAR”) is two 
(2) and the minimum allowed Lot Size, Lot Width, Lot Frontage, Front Yard, Side 
Yard, Rear Yard and Usable Open Space are set forth in Table C of Article 50. Article 
50 Section 50-14 of the Code allows for a maximum allowed Building Height of 65 
feet and Floor Area Ratio of 2.0 for PDAs within the Dudley Square EDA. The 
Proposed Project will reach a maximum building height of up to 128 feet and a 
maximum Floor Area Ratio of up to 3.50. The Proposed Project will seek zoning 
relief from the use regulations, dimensional regulations including but not limited to, 

 
 
maximum allowed Building Height maximum allowed Floor Area Ratio, and 
insufficient Rear Yard and other regulations and requirements of the Code through 
the Board of Appeal. 
 
 
INCLUSIONARY DEVELOPMENT POLICY 
 
Projects financed as one entity and where at least 40% of the units are income 
restricted are exempt from the Inclusionary Development Policy, dated December 
10, 2015. The Proposed Project is financed as one entity and contains fifteen (15) 
income restricted units (100% of total units) surpassing 40% of the total units. As 
such, the Proposed Project is exempt from the Inclusionary Development Policy. 
 
The housing affordability of the project will be finalized through the public funding 
process and if awarded, the ongoing housing affordability of the project will be 
monitored under a MassDocs agreement. 
 
If the project proceeds without public funding, the location of the IDP Units will be 
finalized in conjunction with BPDA staff and outlined in the Affordable Housing 
Agreement (“AHA”), and sales prices will be adjusted according to BPDA published 
maximum rents and income limits, as based on HUD AMIs, available at the time of 
the initial marketing of the IDP Units. 
 
The AHA must be executed along with, or prior to, the issuance of the Certification 
of Compliance for the Proposed Project. The Proponent must also register the 
Proposed Project with the Boston Fair Housing Commission (“BFHC”) upon issuance 
of the building permit. The IDP Units will not be marketed prior to the submission 
and approval of an Affirmative Marketing Plan to the BFHC and the BPDA. 
Preference will be given to applicants who meet the following criteria, weighted in 
the order below: 
(1) Boston resident; 
(2) Household size (a minimum of one (1) person per bedroom); and 
(3) First time homebuyer. 
 
Where a unit is built out for a specific disability (e.g., mobility or sensory), a 
preference will also be available to households with a person whose need matches 
the build out of the unit. The City of Boston Disabilities Commission may assist the 
BPDA in determining eligibility for such a preference. 
 

 
 
The IDP Units will not be marketed prior to the submission and approval of the 
Plan. A deed restriction will be placed on each of the IDP Units to maintain 
affordability for a total period of fifty (50) years (this includes thirty (30) years with a 
BPDA option to extend for an additional period of twenty (20) years). The 
household income of the buyer and sales price of any subsequent sale of the IDP 
Units during this fifty (50) year period must fall within the applicable income and 
sales price limits for each IDP Unit. IDP Units may not be rented out by the 
developer prior to sale to an income eligible buyer, and the BPDA or its assigns or 
successors will monitor the ongoing affordability of the IDP Units 
 
The Area Media Incomes (“AMI”) for the project will now be eight (8) units at 80% 
AMI and seven (7) units at 100% AMI. 
 
AFFIRMATIVELY FURTHERING FAIR HOUSING 
 
The Proposed Project has agreed to the following Affirmatively Furthering Fair 
Housing (AFFH) Interventions. 
 
Article 80 Interventions 
 
● Provide 10 units (approximately 67% of total units) as on-site, income-
restricted units 
 
 
Marketing and Housing Access Interventions 
 
● Use best practices in marketing the market-rate units that are inclusive and 
welcoming to members of protected classes 
 
Proponent must submit the marketing materials for its market rate units detailing 
best practices that will be used as well broker information to BPDA staff for review 
prior to marketing the market-rate housing units. 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Approvals have been requested of the BPDA for the issuance of a Director’s 
Determination pursuant to Section 80A-6 of the Code that the Proposed Project 
does not significantly increase the impacts of the Proposed Project that are within 
the scope of the required review or warrant further review, and for the issuance of 

 
 
a Certification of Compliance under Section 80B-6 upon successful completion of 
the Article 80 review process. BPDA staff believes that the First NPC meets the 
criteria for the issuance of the requested Determination by the Director. It is 
therefore recommended that the BPDA approve the Proposed Project and 
authorize the Director to: (1) issue a Determination waiving the requirement of 
further review pursuant to Section 80A-6 of the Code, in connection with the First 
NPC for the Proposed Project; (2) issue a Certification of Compliance for the 
Proposed Project, under Section 80B-6 upon successful completion of the Article 80 
review process; and (3) execute and deliver a Cooperation Agreement, an 
Affordable Housing Agreement and Restriction, and any and all other agreements 
and documents upon terms and conditions deemed to be in the best interest of the 
BPDA, in connection with the Proposed Project. Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue a Director’s 
Determination pursuant to Section 80A-6 of the Boston Zoning Code 
(the “Code”), which (i) finds that the program revisions described in the 
First Notice of Project Change submitted to the Boston Redevelopment 
Authority (the “BRA”) on July 26, 2023 (the “First NPC”) do not 
significantly increase the impacts of the proposed Nubian Square 
Ascends project (the "Proposed Project") that are within the scope of 
the required review and waives the requirement of further review of 
the Proposed Project, subject to continuing design review by the BRA; 
and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue a Certification 
of Compliance for the Proposed Project upon the successful 
completion of all Article 80 processes; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to execute a 
Cooperation Agreement, an Affordable Housing Agreement and 
Restriction, and any and all other agreements and documents which 
the Director deems appropriate and necessary in connection with the 
Proposed Project, all upon terms and conditions determined to be in 
the best interests of the BRA.

SUBJECT: 
PUBLIC HEARING TO CONSIDER THE FIFTH AMENDMENT TO THE 
DEVELOPMENT PLAN FOR PLANNED DEVELOPMENT AREA NO. 67, 
OLMSTED GREEN, IN THE DORCHESTER AND MATTAPAN 
NEIGHBORHOODS OF BOSTON. 
 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
("BRA") d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”): (1) 
approve the Fifth Amendment to the Development Plan for Planned 
Development Area No. 67, Olmsted Green in Mattapan, Boston, 
Massachusetts (the "Fifth Amendment to Development Plan”); (2) 
authorize the Director to petition the Boston Zoning Commission for 
approval of the Fifth Amendment to Development Plan, pursuant to 
Sections 3-1A.a and 80C of the Code; (3) authorize the Director to issue a 
Determination waiving the requirement of further review pursuant to 
Section 80A-6.2 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”) in connection 
with the Notice of Project Change for the Fifth Amendment to 
Development Plan filed by Brooke Charter Mattapan School (the 
“Proponent”), on May 6, 2022 (the “NPC”); (4) authorize the Director to 
issue a Certification of Consistency pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Code, 
upon successful completion of the Article 80C Planned Development Area 
review process; and (5) authorize the Director to take all actions and 
execute all documents deemed necessary and appropriate by the 
Director in connection with the foregoing, including, without limitation, 
amending an existing Cooperation Agreement or Development Impact 
Project Agreements, if required. 
 
 
1* Effective October 20, 2016, the BRA commenced doing business as BPDA. 

 
2 
 
PROJECT SITE 
The Development Plan for Planned Development Area No. 67, Olmsted Green (the 
“Development Plan”) encompasses an approximately 42.5-acre site in the Mattapan 
section of Boston, comprising three parcels of land (the “Site”). Two of the parcels 
are former Boston State Hospital campus parcels which abut the east and west 
sides of Morton Street, (designated as the “East Campus” and “West Campus,” 
respectively). The third parcel is an approximately four-acre parcel formerly owned 
by Lena Park Community Development Corporation (the “Lena Park Parcel”) and is 
adjacent to the East Campus. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The Olmsted Green Project is a mixed-use development, including residential, 
senior housing, community facilities, mental health program space, urban farming, 
retail, open space, accessory parking and recreational facilities known as the 
Olmsted Green Project. As set forth in the Development Plan, the Olmsted Green 
Project involved the development on the Site of multiple buildings and facilities 
containing a total combined Gross Floor Area of approximately 851,000 square 
feet. The Development Plan, which included the Olmsted Green Project was 
approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority in January 2006, for which the 
original Development Plan was adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission in 
February 2006. This current NPC proposes an addition to the Brooke Mattapan 
Charter School, the development of which was included in the Second Amendment 
to the Development Plan (the “Second Amendment”). The Second Amendment was 
approved by the BPDA on November 15, 2012, adopted by the Boston Zoning 
Commission on December 12, 2012, and approved by the Mayor on December 20, 
2012. 
 
The Brooke Mattapan Charter School serves almost 500 students, from 
kindergarten through grade seven. The proposed new addition would house a 
cafeteria, wellness and counseling supports, as well as other administrative offices. 
 
DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
 
This Fifth Amendment to the PDA Plan (“Fifth PDA Amendment”), as set forth below, 
amends the Development Plan only with respect to the allotted square footage for 
the Brook Charter School Project Component (already constructed) on the Lena 

 
3 
Park Parcel (the “Proposed Project”), and the total Gross Floor Area for the Olmsted 
Green Project. This Fifth PDA Amendment amends the provision that the school use 
on the Lena Park Parcel may be up to approximately 73,600 square feet from 
approximately 61,000 square feet (for a total increase in square footage of 
approximately 12,600 square feet). This Fifth PDA Amendment also revises the total 
Gross Floor Area for the Olmsted Green Project to approximately 853,600 square 
feet from approximately 841,049. 
 
The Proponent shall undergo subsequent design review with the BPDA. The design 
review process will require the proponent to provide alternative parking layouts for 
any proposed additional parking, so as to not negatively impact the vegetation and 
open space character along the greenbelt roadway - American Legion Highway; a 
robust green buffer shall be maintained along American Legion Highway. 
 
The Proponent agrees to complete the Boston Smart Utilities review in conjunction 
with the aforementioned design review process. The items to be reviewed include: 
● A basic Utility Site Plan showing any new utility infrastructure, stormwater 
management and /or low impact design strategies, as appropriate, to ensure 
there are no conflicts between proposed and existing conditions; 
● A Smart Utilities checklist denoting any of the above strategies; and 
● A COBUCS report, as-applicable. 
The Proponent is committed to supporting Boston’s resiliency, sustainability and 
carbon neutral 2050 goals. The Proposed Project will be designed and constructed 
to USGBC LEED BD+C New Construction v4.1 certifiability achieving 45 points. 
 
ZONING 
 
The Proposed Project is situated in the Enterprise Protection Subdistrict (“EPS”) of 
the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood District, Article 60 of the Code. The Project is 
also situated in the following overlay districts: (i) American Legion Highway 
Greenbelt Protection Overlay District (“GPOD”) pursuant to Section 29-7.3 of the 
BZC; (ii) Planned Development Area No. 67 established pursuant to Section 3-1A.a 
and 60-30 of the Code; and (iii) Olmsted Green Smart Growth Overlay District 
(“SGOD”) established pursuant to Article 87A of the Code. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW 
 

 
4 
On October 18, 2022, the Proponent filed a Notice of Project Change (“NPC”) and 
the Fifth Amendment to Development Plan with the BPDA, which initiated a public 
comment period concluding on December 2, 2022. 
 
The BPDA hosted a Public Meeting on November 10, 2022. This meeting was 
advertised in the local neighborhood newspapers, posted to the BPDA’s calendar, 
and email notification was sent to all subscribers of the BPDA’s Dorchester and 
Mattapan neighborhood updates. 
 
RECOMMENDATION 
 
Based on the foregoing, BPDA staff recommends that the BPDA Board : (1) approve 
the Fifth Amendment to Development Plan; (2) authorize the Director to petition 
the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the Fifth Amendment to 
Development Plan, pursuant to Sections 3-1A.a and 80C of the Boston Zoning Code (the 
“Code”); (3) authorize the Director to issue a Determination waiving the requirement of 
further review pursuant to Section 80A-6.2 of the Code in connection with the NPC for 
the Fifth Amendment to Development Plan; (4) authorize the Director to issue a 
Certification of Consistency pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Code, upon successful 
completion of the Article 80C Planned Development Area review process; and (5) 
authorize the Director to take all actions and execute all documents deemed 
necessary and appropriate by the Director in connection with the foregoing, 
including, without limitation, amending an existing Cooperation Agreement or 
Development Impact Project Agreements, if required. 
 
An appropriate vote follows: 
 
VOTED: 
That, in connection with the Fifth Amendment to Development Plan for 
Planned Development Area No. 67, Olmsted Green (the “Fifth 
Amendment to Development Plan”), in Mattapan, Boston, presented at 
a public hearing, duly held at the offices of the Boston Redevelopment 
Authority (“BRA”) on December 15, 2022, and after consideration of 
evidence presented at and in connection with the hearing, the BRA 
finds with respect to the Fifth Amendment to Development Plan that: 
(a) the Planned Development Area (“PDA”) Plan is not for a location or 
project for which PDAs are forbidden by the underlying zoning, as 
amended; (b) the portion of the Proposed Project in the Fifth 
Amendment to Development Plan complies with any provisions of the 
underlying zoning, as amended, that establish use, dimensional, 
design or other requirements for Proposed Projects in PDAs; (c) the 

 
5 
Fifth Amendment to Development Plan complies with any provisions 
of the underlying zoning that establish planning and development 
criteria, including public benefits, for PDAs; (d) the Fifth Amendment to 
Development Plan conforms to the plan for the district, subdistrict, or 
similar geographic area in which the PDA is located, and to the general 
plan for the City as a whole; and (e) such Fifth Amendment to 
Development Plan complies with, facilitates, and advances the City of 
Boston's obligations, responsibilities, goals and programs regarding 
Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing and Affirmatively Integrated 
Communities, with particular regard to concerns identified in an Analysis 
of Impediments, AFFH Assessment Component, and with regard for 
impacts that may trigger displacement; and (f) on balance nothing in the 
Fifth Amendment to Development Plan will be injurious to the 
neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public welfare, weighing 
all benefits and burdens; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the BRA approves, pursuant to Section 3-1.A and Section 80C of the 
Code, the Fifth Amendment to Development Plan in substantial accord 
with the same, as presented to the BRA Board at its public hearing on 
December 15, 2022; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to petition the Boston 
Zoning Commission for approval of the Fifth Amendment to Development 
Plan, pursuant to Section 3-1A. and Section 80C of the Code, in substantial 
accord with the same, as presented to the BRA at its public hearing on 
December 15, 2022; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue a 
Determination waiving the requirement of further review pursuant to 
Section 80A-6.2 of the Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”) in connection 
with the Notice of Project Change for the Fifth Amendment to 
Development Plan filed by Brooke Charter Mattapan School, on October 
18, 2022; 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue a Certification 
of Consistency for Planned Development Area Review for the Brook 

 
6 
Charter School addition project pursuant to Section 80C-8 of the Code 
when the Director finds that the Fifth Amendment to Development 
Plan has been approved by the BRA and the Boston Zoning

1A.a. and Article 80C of the Code; and

That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to take all actions and

FIFTH AMENDMENT TO DEVELOPMENT PLAN 
 
FOR 
 
PLANNED DEVELOPMENT AREA NO. 67 
 
OLMSTED GREEN 
 
American Legion Highway, Morton Street and Harvard Street 
 
BOSTON, MASSACHUSETTS 
 
Dated: November 28, 2022 
 
 
 
Pursuant to Section 3-1 A and Article 80, Section 80C of the Zoning Code of the City of Boston 
(“Code”), this amendment constitutes the Fifth Amendment to Development Plan for Planned 
Development Area No. 67, Olmsted Green (“Fifth PDA Amendment”). 
 
 On January 26, 2006, the Boston Planning & Development Authority, then known as the Boston 
Redevelopment Authority (the “BPDA”), approved a zoning Map Amendment Application to establish 
Planned Development Area No. 67 and a Development Plan for Planned Development Area No. 67, 
Olmsted Green (the “Original PDA Plan”). On February 15, 2006, the Boston Zoning Commission 
adopted said Map Amendment and approved the Original PDA Plan. 
 
The Original PDA Plan encompasses an approximately 42.5-acre site in the Mattapan section of 
Boston, comprising three parcels of land (the “Site”). Two of the parcels are former Boston State Hospital 
campus parcels which abut the east and west sides of Morton Street, (designated as the “East Campus” 
and “West Campus”, respectively). The third parcel is an approximately four-acre parcel formerly owned 
by Lena Park Community Development Corporation (the “Lena Park Parcel”) and is adjacent to the East 
Campus. The Original PDA Plan provided for the construction of a mixed-use development, including 
residential, senior housing, community facilities, mental health program space, urban farming, retail, open 
space, accessory parking and recreational facilities known as the Olmsted Green Project. As set forth in 
the Original PDA Plan, the Olmsted Green Project involved the development on the Site of multiple 
buildings and facilities containing a total combined Gross Floor Area of approximately 851,000 square 
feet. 
 
BOARD APPROVED	30
			DOCUMENTNO. 8023

KH 817360.5 
First Amendment to the Original PDA Plan 
 
A First Amendment to the Original PDA Plan (“First PDA Amendment”) amended the Original 
PDA Plan by reducing the Senior Housing Component on the East Campus from 83 Units and 
approximately 76,000 square feet of Gross Floor Area to 59 Units and approximately 59,049 square feet 
of Gross Floor Area. The First PDA Amendment also decreased the total Gross Floor Area for the 
Olmsted Green Project from approximately 851,000 square feet to approximately 834,000 square feet. 
The First PDA Amendment was approved by the BPDA on November 16, 2010, adopted by the Boston 
Zoning Commission on November 17, 2010, and approved by the Mayor on November 19, 2010. 
 
Second Amendment to PDA Plan 
 
A Second Amendment to the Original PDA Plan (“Second PDA Amendment”) further amended 
the Original PDA Plan by approving the permitted uses for the Lena Park Parcel to include a school and 
by reducing the Gross Floor Area for the Project Component on the Lena Park Parcel from 80,000 square 
feet to 61,000 square feet. The Second PDA Amendment also further decreased the total Gross Floor 
Area for the Olmsted Green Project from approximately 834,000 square feet to approximately 815,000 
square feet. The Second PDA Amendment was approved by the BPDA on November 15, 2012, adopted 
by the Boston Zoning Commission on December 12, 2012 and approved by the Mayor on December 20, 
2012. 
 
Third Amendment to PDA Plan 
 
The Third Amendment to the PDA Plan (“Third PDA Amendment”) further amended the 
Original PDA Plan with respect to the uses, dimensions and parking requirements for uses for the Vinfen 
and Heritage House parcels on the East Campus. The Third PDA Amendment amended the PDA Plan to 
change the intended development to delete the Heritage House and Vinfen Nursing and Rehab Facility 
uses on Parcels E2 and E3 of the East Campus and insert in their stead a new school use having a Gross 
Floor Area of approximately 95,000 square feet (the “High School Component”), and to allow the parking 
requirements for the High School Component to be determined through Large Project Review under 
Article 80 of the Code. The Third PDA Amendment was approved by the BPDA on March 16, 2017, 
adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission on April 12, 2017, and approved by the Mayor on April 20, 
2017. 
 
Fourth Amendment to PDA Plan 
 
 
The Fourth Amendment to the PDA Plan (“Fourth PDA Amendment”) further amended the 
Original PDA Plan with respect to the uses, dimensions and parking requirements for the urban farm and 
food retail components on the East Campus. The Fourth PDA Amendment amended the Original PDA 
Plan to allow for the development of an open space and active and passive recreational component in 

KH 817360.5 
place of the urban farm and food retail components. The Fourth PDA Amendment allowed for open 
space/recreational uses with an approximate gross floor area of 789,000 square feet. The Fourth PDA 
Amendment was approved by the BPDA on March 12, 2020, adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission 
on May 13, 2020, and approved by the Mayor on May 29, 2020. Collectively, the Original PDA Plan, the 
First PDA Amendment, the Second PDA Amendment, the Third PDA Amendment, and the Fourth PDA 
Amendment are hereinafter referred to as the “PDA Plan”. 
 
Fifth Amendment to PDA Plan 
 
 
This Fifth Amendment to the PDA Plan (“Fifth PDA Amendment”), as set forth below, amends 
the PDA Plan only with respect to the square footage for the Project Component on the Lena Park Parcel, 
and the total Gross Floor Area for the Olmsted Green Project. This Fifth PDA Amendment amends the 
provision that the school use on the Lena Park Parcel may be up to approximately 73,600 square feet from 
approximately 61,000 square feet. This Fifth PDA Amendment also revises the total Gross Floor Area 
for the Olmsted Green Project to approximately [853,600] square feet from approximately 841,049. 
Capitalized terms in this Fifth PDA Amendment, unless otherwise defined herein, shall have the meaning 
set forth in the PDA Plan and the Code.

MEMORANDUM
