INCLUSIONARY DEVELOPMENT POLICY 
 
The Overall Project contemplates the development of up to 2,511 total residential 
units, including both for sale and rental units. These 2,511 residential units include 
1,911 units already constructed (the “Completed Units”) plus the 600 units currently 
proposed under the 2022 NPC (the “NPC Units”). 
 
The first 2,500 units developed within the Overall Project (including units constructed 
on the developed Blocks) shall be subject to the Inclusionary Development Policy 
("IDP") in effect at the time of the BPDA's approval of the Original Project in 2010, 
which was the IDP as amended on September 27, 2007 (the "2007 IDP"). All units 
within the Proposed Project other than the first 2,500 units of the Overall Project shall 
be subject to the IDP dated December 10, 2015 (the "2015 IDP"). For the creation of 
on-site IDP units, the 2007 IDP required at least 15% of the market rate units (which 
is also approximately 13.04340% of the total units), and the 2015 IDP requires 13% 
of the total units. As currently proposed the 2007 IDP shall apply to 2,500 units and 
the 2015 IDP shall apply to 11 units. This results in a total required minimum IDP 
obligation of 328 IDP units. 
 
Should the Overall Project contain more than 2,500 residential units the 2015 IDP 
shall apply to all units over the first 2,500 developed. As currently proposed, the 
Overall Project consisting of up to 2,511 is required to produce a minimum of 328 
IDP units. Of these 231 units are Completed Units leaving 97 more IDP units to be 
constructed as NPC Units. 
 
With regard to the Proposed Project, the Proponent has agreed to provide up to 170 
IDP units exceeding the required 97 IDP units that remain to be constructed. This 
will bring the total IDP obligation for the Overall Project to 401 IDP units exceeding 
the required 328 IDP units that must be included in the Overall Project. Subject to 
the approval of the BPDA, the Proponent may satisfy the remaining IDP requirement 
(i.e. 170 IDP units) in whole or in part through the construction of income-restricted 
units reserved for City of Boston/BPDA-certified artists ("Artist IDP Units"). 
 
The location of the IDP units will be finalized in conjunction with BPDA staff and 
outlined in an Affordable Housing Agreement ("AHA") or an Affordable Rental 
Housing Agreement and Restriction (“ARHAR"), and sales prices, rents, and income 
limits will be adjusted according to BPDA published maximum sales prices, rents, and 

 
10 
 
 
 
income limits, as based on HUD AMIs, available at the time of the initial sale or rental 
of the IDP units. With the exception of Artist IDP Units whose size, features and 
distribution shall be approved by the BPDA in conjunction with the Mayor’s Office of 
Arts and Culture, IDP units must be comparable to or exceed the size, design, and 
quality of market rate units in the Proposed Project, cannot be stacked or 
concentrated on the same floors, and must be consistent with or exceed bedroom 
counts relative the market rate units in the Residential Block in which the units are 
being provided. 
 
An AHA or ARHAR must be executed along with, or prior to, the issuance of the Partial 
Certification of Consistency for a residential Block. The Proponent must also submit 
Affirmative Marketing Plan(s) (the "Plan") for the Affordable Housing Agreement(s) to 
the Boston Fair Housing Commission and the BPDA. Preference will be given to 
applicants who meet the following criteria, weighted in the order below: 
 
(1) Boston Resident 
(2) Household Size (a minimum of one (1) person per bedroom); 
(3) First time homebuyer (for home ownership units only) 
(4) Boston Certified Artist (for Artist IDP Units only) 
 
Where a unit is built out for a specific disability (e.g., mobility or sensory), a 
preference will also be available to households with a person whose need matches 
the build out of the unit. The City of Boston Disabilities Commission shall assist the 
BPDA in determining eligibility for such a preference. 
 
The IDP units will not be marketed prior to the submission and approval of the Plan. 
Homeownership units may not be rented prior to sale to an eligible buyer. 
A deed restriction or covenant will be placed on the IDP units to maintain affordability 
for a total period of fifty (50) years (this includes thirty (30) years with a BPDA option 
to extend for an additional period of twenty (20) years). The household income of 
any subsequent renter or buyer of the IDP units during this fifty (50) year period must 
fall within the applicable income for each IDP Unit. The BPDA or its assigns or 
successors will monitor the ongoing affordability of the IDP units, The Proponent 
shall satisfy the IDP requirements set forth above by providing the required IDP units 
on-site.

RESILIENCY & SUSTAINABILITY 
 
The 2022 NPC proposes multiple measures designed to increase the Proposed 
Project’s already significant commitment to environmental sustainability and 
resiliency: 
 
• Increase open space and remove pervious area on Block F to create a 
signature 1.4-acre public open space at the heart of the neighborhood. This 
newly expanded open space will yield significant climate change resiliency 
benefits, capturing additional stormwater and retaining it on site rather than 
discharging it immediately into the BWSC system. 
• Plant approximately 100 trees in connection with the Proposed Project to 
reduce the urban heat island effect, improve pedestrian comfort, and 
contribute to a robust urban tree canopy in the Seaport neighborhood. 
• Raise the target bar for LEED certification from Silver to Gold (v4.2) for the 
project described in the 2022 NPC. 
• Incorporate heat-recovery chiller plants in the Proposed Project to enhance 
overall building energy performance. 
• Comply with the then-current Article 37 requirements at the time each Block 
of the Proposed Project seeks BPDA Design Review approval. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
The Proponent filed the 2022 NPC on May 6, 2022. The BPDA sponsored Public 
Meetings to discuss the proposed 2022 NPC on July 11, 2022 and December 5, 2022 
and Impact Advisory Group (“IAG”) meetings on July 25, 2022 and November 3, 2022, 
all of which were held virtually. The meetings were advertised in the relevant 
neighborhood newspapers (South Boston Online and South Boston Today), email 
notification of the 2022 NPC submission and meeting was sent to all members of the 
IAG and local City and state elected officials and their staff members, the meeting 
was posted to the BPDA website and calendar, and notification was sent to all 
subscribers of the BPDA’s South Boston waterfront neighborhood updates. 
 
The public comment period in connection with the Proponent’s submission of the 
2022 NPC and the First Amendment to Development Plan concluded on July 29, 2022. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
 

 
12 
 
 
 
The Proposed Project is located within the Harbor Park Fort Point Waterfront District 
(Article 42E) of the Boston Zoning Code, Planned Development Area #78 and the 
planning boundaries of the 1999 Seaport Public Realm Plan. The Planning Division 
staff also considered district and citywide plans including the 100 Acres Master Plan, 
the Fan Pier PDA Development Plan, the South Boston Waterfront Gateways Study, 
the Crossroads Initiative, Imagine Boston 2030 and Go Boston 2030, and public 
feedback 
to 
review 
the 
Project. 
 
The Proposed Project aligns with citywide and district goals to increase affordable 
housing, job opportunities, public open space, environmental sustainability and 
climate change resiliency. The key considerations of the BPDA staff during the review 
of the Proposed Project were building programs, housing affordability, resilience to 
sea-level rise and coastal storms, green/efficient building construction, reducing 
carbon emissions through the reduction of parking spaces, and the creation of a 
larger public open space with a design informed by community input. 
 
PROJECT BENEFITS IN CONNECTION WITH 2022 NPC 
 
In connection with the 2022 NPC, the Proponent has committed to a number of 
additional public benefits, and has provided confirmation of several prior 
commitments associated with the 2017 NPC and the 2019 NPC, as follows: 
 
New Public Benefits Commitments: 
 
• The adjustment to the proposed use of Block G will result in payments of DIP 
funds in the amount of approximately $9 million in housing linkage funds and 
approximately $1.7 million in jobs training linkage funds. These amounts will 
help to further support the creation of affordable housing and job training 
programs. 
• The Proponent will fund the design and installation of protective measures for 
the currently paint-only bicycle lanes on the Evelyn Moakley Bridge to further 
extend the more than 1.5 miles of protected cycling infrastructure that the 
Proponent has either completed or will be constructing in connection with the 
Overall Project’s development. The design of this additional cycling 
infrastructure will proceed promptly upon approval of the 2022 NPC, and the 
construction will be completed prior to the completion of the first Block of the 
project described in the 2022 NPC, subject to applicable City approvals. 
• In furtherance of the City’s modern mobility goals, the Proponent will fund the 
design and implementation of additional Transportation Network Company 

 
13 
 
 
 
(TNC) pick-up/drop-off zones along Seaport Boulevard and Northern Avenue 
and will fund the installation of approximately 10 new public on-street EV 
charging stations available for public use within the Project area in 
consultation with key City agencies. 
• In furtherance of the goals set forth in the South Boston Seaport Strategic 
Transit Plan, the Proponent will commit $250,000, payable evenly over two (2) 
years commencing with the issuance of a full building permit for the first Block 
of the project described in the 2022 NPC to begin construction, to support a 
last-mile shuttle service serving the South Boston Waterfront area. 
• The Proponent’s design of the newly expanded Seaport Common will ensure 
that the open space considers the perspectives of a diverse group of 
stakeholders. The design for the newly expanded Seaport Common will be 
subject to BPDA Design Review in accordance with the PDA Plan, as well as 
Boston Civic Design Commission (“BCDC”) review. In addition, the Proponent 
will conduct a community-facing design process that will solicit stakeholder 
input at the outset of the design process, as well as in connection with key 
design milestones as plans are developed, in parallel with BPDA and BCDC 
review. 
 
Public Benefits Confirmations: 
 
• The Proponent will construct the Fort Point Community Theater (“FPCT”) on 
either Block L-3 or Block L-6 of the Seaport Square Project. The FPCT, as 
described in the PDA Plan, is a performing arts venue comprising 
approximately 150 seats in a state-of-the-art, flexible “black box” double-
height venue that will be suitable for a variety of performance types and 
audience configurations. The FPCT’s construction, which the Proponent has 
re-affirmed in the 2022 NPC, will contribute meaningfully to the landscape of 
performing arts venues available in Boston and significantly increase the 
performing arts venue inventory available to the Fort Point arts community.

1. 
PDA Development Plan Background. On November 16, 2017, the Boston 
Redevelopment Authority, d/b/a the Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) 
approved an amendment to the maps entitled “Zoning Districts City of Boston” to establish 
revised boundaries for Planned Development Area No. 78, and also approved an Amended and 
Restated Development Plan for Planned Development Area No. 78 (the “2017 Development 
Plan”). On December 13, 2017, the Boston Zoning Commission (the “Commission”) approved 
the map amendment and the 2017 Development Plan, which became effective on December 13, 
2017. The Development Plan provides for the redevelopment of an approximately 33.5 acre area 
of land (the “Site”) in the South Boston Waterfront District for a mixed-use project (the 
“Project”). Capitalized terms used but not defined herein shall have the meanings ascribed to 
such terms in the 2017 Development Plan. The 2017 Development Plan, as amended by this First 
Amendment, is referred to herein as the “Development Plan”. 
2. 
Purpose of First Amendment to Development Plan. This First Amendment 
amends the 2017 Development Plan to reflect the elimination of the approved but not yet 
constructed retail building on Block F, the potential construction of a free-standing structure of 
up to approximately 2,000 square feet of Gross Floor Area to accommodate Civic/Community 
Users and Cultural Facilities (expected to be programmed in conjunction with the Massachusetts 
Fallen Heroes Memorial on Block F), and the creation of additional open space on Block F 
pursuant to the Open Space Election described in Section X of the Original Plan. This First 
Amendment also revises certain details of the residential program for the Project, to reflect 
currently-proposed uses of Block G, Block L3, and Block L6, and adjusts the timing of 
transportation monitoring studies to be conducted by the Proponent to reflect impacts of the 
COVID-19 pandemic on transit usage and vehicle traffic. 
This First Amendment also address the permissibility of certain uses within the Project. 
Specifically, this First Amendment allows Clinic Use and related uses, including medical clinics, 
medical spas, cosmetic surgery clinics, offices of dentists and orthodontists, and similar uses, as 
well as animal hospitals, kennels, caterer’s establishments and bakeries.

NUPOOR MONANI, SENIOR INSTITUTIONAL PLANNER AND PROJECT 
MANAGER 
KATHLEEN ONUFER, SENIOR PLANNER 
SCOTT SLARSKY, SENIOR URBAN DESIGNER 
JOE BLANKENSHIP, SENIOR TRANSPORTATION PLANNER 
JILL ZICK, SENIOR LANDSCAPE ARCHITECT 
 
 
SUBJECT: 
PUBLIC HEARING FOR ST ELIZABETH’S MEDICAL CENTER (“SEMC”) 
2022-2026 INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN AND TO CONSIDER THE 
PROPOSED PARKING GARAGE PROJECT AS A DEVELOPMENT IMPACT 
PROJECT 
______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(“BRA”) d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency: (1) issue an 
Adequacy Determination pursuant to Section 80D-5.4 (c) of the Boston 
Zoning Code (“Code”) approving the St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center 
Institutional Master Plan 2022-2026 (the “Proposed IMP”); (2) petition 
the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the Proposed IMP for a 
term of four (4) years from the effective date of approval of the IMP; 
(3) authorize the Director to issue one or more Certifications of 
Consistency pursuant to Section 80D-10 of the Code in connection 
with the IMP Proposed Projects; (4) issue a Preliminary Adequacy 
Determination waiving the requirement of further review pursuant to 
Article 80B-5.4(c)(iv) of the Code for the proposed St. Elizabeth's 
Medical Center Parking Garage project (the ”Proposed Project”), 
approving the Draft Project Impact Report (“DPIR”) and the 
 
∗ Effective October 20, 2016, the BRA commenced doing business as BPDA. 

2 
 
Supplemental Filings of February 8, 2022 and April 19, 2022 and 
waiving the requirement for the filing and review of a Final Project 
Impact Report, subject to BPDA design review; (5) authorize the 
Director to issue one or more Certifications of Compliance for the 
Proposed Project pursuant to Section 80B-6 of the Code, upon 
successful completion of the Article 80 Large Project Review process; 
and (6) authorize the Director to execute and deliver a Cooperation 
Agreement, which will include a provision requiring compliance with 
the Boston Residents Jobs Policy and any and all other documents and 
agreements as the Director deems appropriate and necessary in 
connection with the Proposed Project and the Proposed IMP. 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The SEMC Institutional Master Plan, dated January 26, 2007 (the “2007 IMP”) was 
approved by the BRA on March 29, 2007 and by the Boston Zoning Commission 
("BZC") on April 25, 2007 with an effective date of April 25, 2007, as amended by the 
IMPNF for Minor Amendment and Project Change ("First Amendment") filed on June 
10, 2008 and approved by the BRA on July 17, 2008. The most recent filing related 
to the IMP was the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form/Notice of Project 
Change approved by the BRA on May 15, 2012 ("SEMC IMP"). 
 
On September 6, 2019, SEMC filed an Institutional Master Plan Notification Form for 
the proposed IMP (“IMPNF”) to initiate review of the proposed Institutional Master 
Plan (“Proposed IMP”) pursuant to Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code, and a 
Project Notification Form (“PNF”) to initiate review of the proposed parking garage 
project (“Proposed Project”). The Proposed IMP and Proposed Project are described 
in greater detail in sections below. The BPDA issued a Scoping Determination on 
January 6, 2020 in response to both these filings. 
 
On November 5, 2021, SEMC filed the Proposed IMP and Draft Project Impact 
Report (“DPIR”) related to the Proposed Project as well as a Supplemental 
Information Document (“SID”) on February 3, 2022. The BPDA has since issued a 
Request for Supplemental Information (“Request”) in response to which SEMC 
submitted a second Supplemental Information Document on April 19, 2022. 
 
The Proposed IMP and Proposed Project have been reviewed by the Boston Civic 
Design Commission (“BCDC”) and received a vote of approval at the monthly 
meeting on May 3, 2022. 

3 
 
 
 
 

4 
 
THE PROPOSED IMP 
 
The Proposed IMP provides an update on proposed and existing uses and facilities 
on the St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center (“SEMC”) Campus and community benefits. The 
Proposed Project is a proposed institutional project within the Proposed IMP. 
 
SITE OF PROPOSED PROJECT 
 
The Proposed Project is located in the Brighton neighborhood within an 
approximately 42,450 square-foot area of the SEMC Campus bounded by 
Washington Street on the southeast, the SEMC Campus on the north, and the 
Overlook site on the southwest, which is currently being redeveloped for residential 
use. The Project Site is currently occupied by a sloped grassy hill and an at-grade 
parking lot with 47 spaces. The Project Site is located within the boundaries of the 
Proposed IMP. 
 
DEVELOPMENT TEAM 
 
The development team includes: 
 
Proponent: 
Steward Health Care 
 
Harrison Bane 
 
Legal Counsel: 
Rubin and Rudman LLP 
 
James H. Greene 
 
Architect 
Cube 3 
 
Brian O’Connor 
 
Permitting 
Fort Point Associates, Inc. 
Consultant: 
Katie Moniz 
 
Landscape 
Deborah Myers Landscape Architecture 
Architect: 
Deborah Meyers 
 
Transportation 
MDM Transportation Consultants, Inc. 
Consultant: 
Robert Michaud 
 
 
 

5 
 
DESCRIPTION AND PROGRAM 
 
The Proposed Project includes construction of an approximately 203,000-square-
foot, six-floor parking garage at 253 Washington Street in Brighton, Massachusetts 
to consolidate existing parking accommodations currently spread throughout the 
neighborhood into a single location directly adjacent to critical care facilities. The 
Parking Garage will be served by an additional driveway from Washington Street 
and a driveway within the St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center campus. The Project will 
add approximately 610 parking spaces, a secure bicycle room with approximately 
32 spaces, 32 covered bicycle parking spaces, and a rooftop solar array. 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
 
On November 20, 2018, the Proponent filed a Letter of Intent (“LOI”) in accordance 
with the BPDA’s policy regarding Provision of Mitigation by Development Projects in 
Boston. The St Elizabeth’s Medical Center Task Force, a long-standing body 
appointed to advise the BPDA on the Institutional Master Plan and related 
development projects, serves as the Impact Advisory Group (“IAG”) for the 
Proposed Project. As the Task Force had been inactive for a period of time and has 
seen some attrition, on October 26, 2021, the BPDA reached out to existing 
members to confirm their interest and availability in continued participation. As 
memorialized in a BPDA Memorandum dated November 1, 2021, the Task Force 
was finalized with 6 members. 
 
The Proponent filed both an Expanded Project Notification Form (“PNF”) and an 
Institutional Master Plan Project Notification Form (“IMPNF”) on September 6, 2019, 
which initiated a public comment period that concluded on October 26, 2019. 
Notice of the receipt of the PNF and IMPNF by the BPDA was published in the 
Boston Herald on September 6, 2019. The notice, PNF, and the IMPNF were sent to 
the City’s public agencies/departments and elected officials pursuant to Section 
80A-2 of the Code. Additionally, copies of the PNF were sent to all Task Force 
members. 
 
Pursuant to Section 80B-5.3 of the Code, a Scoping Session related to the PNF and 
IMPNF was held with the City’s public agencies and elected officials to review and 
discuss the Proposed Project and the Proposed IMP. 
 

6 
 
On October 2, 2019, a Task Force Meeting was held. The Task Force Meeting was 
listed on the BPDA website. On October 15, 2019, a Public Meeting was held. The 
Public Meeting was advertised in the Boston Bulletin and listed on the BPDA 
website. 
 
On January 6, 2020, a Scoping Determination was submitted to the Development 
Team. In response to the Scoping Determination, on November 5, 2021, a Draft 
Project Impact Report (“DPIR”) was filed. The Proponent concurrently filed the 
Proposed IMP and the DPIR on November 5, 2021, which initiated a sixty (60) day 
public comment period. Both the DPIR and Proposed IMP comment periods were 
extended several times, ultimately concluding February 28, 2022. Notice of the 
receipt of the Proposed IMP by the BPDA was published in the Boston Herald on 
November 5, 2021. The notice, Proposed IMP, and DPIR were sent to the City’s 
public agencies/departments and elected officials pursuant to Section 80A-2 of the 
Code. Additionally, copies of the Proposed IMP and DPIR were sent to all of the Task 
Force members. The proposed IMP was dated November 5, 2021 and is described 
in Section 1.1 of the IMP as “SEMC Institutional Master Plan 2022-2026”. 
 
On December 9, 2021, a Virtual Task Force Meeting was held. The Virtual Task Force 
Meeting was listed on the BPDA website. On December 9, 2021, a Virtual Public 
Meeting was held. The Virtual Public Meeting was advertised in the Boston Bulletin 
and listed on the BPDA website. 
 
On February 8, 2022, a Supplemental Filing to the Proposed IMP providing details of 
a proposed Boston EMS Facility was filed by the Development Team. 
 
On February 17, 2022, a Virtual Task Force Meeting was held. The Virtual Task Force 
Meeting was listed on the BPDA website. On February 17, 2022, a Virtual Public 
Meeting was held. The Virtual Public Meeting was advertised in the Boston Bulletin 
and listed on the BPDA website. 
 
On March 21, 2022, a Request for Supplemental Information (“Request”) was 
submitted to the Development Team. In response to the Request, on April 19, 2022, 
a Supplemental Filing in response to the Request was filed. 
 
On May 3, 2022, the Proposed Project was approved by the Boston Civic Design 
Commission. 

7 
 
 
In addition to the above-mentioned meetings, the Proponent and BPDA also 
undertook community outreach efforts and participated in a series of meetings 
during the Article 80 Review process with local elected officials and the Allston Civic 
Association to discuss the Proposed IMP and Proposed Project and solicit feedback. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
 
The Proposed Project improves accessibility and pedestrian safety in support of 
pedestrian circulation goals identified in the 2022-2026 St. Elizabeth's Medical 
Center (SEMC) Institutional Master Plan. In support of Steward’s green building 
goals, Parksmart design practices are employed within the proposed parking 
garage to provide sustainable building and parking operations at SEMC, and the 
proposed photovoltaic system will serve as an energy security and resiliency critical 
resource for SEMC. The program of the proposed parking garage will consolidate 
staff parking occurring in short-term leased remote satellite parking lots, provide 
reliable parking accommodations and significantly reduce staff commute time. This 
program serves the SEMC guiding principles to provide accessible care to all who 
seek its services and its effort to be the best place to work in health care, in addition 
to their overall commitment to better patient care. 
 
The Proposed Project is located in the Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan area. The 
Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan provides a blueprint for improving how people move 
around Allston and Brighton by making it safer and more efficient for all modes of 
transportation—walking, biking, transit, and cars. The Plan will: improve the transit 
network, expand the bike network, improve walkability, enhance the main street 
and neighborhood experiences, and simplify intersections for all users. 
 
ZONING 
 
The Project Site is located in the Allston/Brighton Neighborhood District, Article 51 
of the Code, and also within an Institutional Master Plan Overlay District. In 
accordance with the provisions of Section 51.29.6, the term of the IMP is four (4) 
years in the Allston/Brighton Neighborhood District, and the four (4) year term of 
the IMP shall commence on the effective date of the approval of the IMP. 
 
 
 

8 
 
MITIGATION & COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
MITIGATION 
 
The Proposed Project will provide mitigation and community benefits for the 
Allston/Brighton neighborhood and the City of Boston as a whole, including: 
 
• Improved Street and Pedestrian Environment 
These proposed improvements shall be completed before Certificate of 
Occupancy issuance for the Proposed Project and/or IMP and are subject to 
review and approval by the Boston Transportation Department (BTD), Public 
Works Department (PWD), Public Improvement Commission (PIC), and the 
BPDA. 
 
 The Proposed Project will activate the Washington Street corridor with 
enhanced streetscapes that will include the construction of new 
sidewalks, increased pedestrian activity, an upgraded public realm along 
the project frontage in and around the Project Site, and will include a 
bocce court for community use, bicycle parking accommodations, site 
furniture, pedestrian lighting, landscaping, and street trees in compliance 
with City of Boston Complete Street Guidelines. 
 As part of the Proposed Project, the Proponent has committed to 
implementing an interim condition for Washington Street across the 
project frontage, which will allow for the transition of these streetscapes 
until the full extent of the transportation improvements associated with 
Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan can be implemented by the City. These 
interim conditions will include new sidewalks, street trees, and associated 
utilities and landscape plantings along the project frontage. The proposed 
improvements shall be coordinated with and approved by BPDA and BTD 
and completed before Certificate of Occupancy issuance for the Proposed 
Project. 
 The Proponent has committed to installing at least forty-three (43) new 
trees, including nine (9) street trees along Washington Street corridor, in 
and around the Project Site as part of the site plan improvements and 
mitigation associated with the Proposed IMP. The installation of the 
proposed street trees along Washington Street shall be completed before 
Certificate of Occupancy issuance for the Proposed Project. 
 
 
 

9 
 
• Sustainable Design/Green Building 
 The Proposed Project is committed to the advancement of sustainable 
and environmentally conscious design and construction. To that end, the 
Proposed Project is being designed to meet the requirements of Article 37 
of the Code and has committed to design and construct the parking 
garage to Silver Level certifiability standards under the Parksmart rating 
system. 
 The Proposed Project is committed to installation of a new 19,500 square 
foot solar array that will provide approximately 431,000 kilowatts of 
energy annually. 
 Improvements throughout the medical campus and the surrounding 
public realm include measures to minimize the impact of high-
temperature events, including the enhancement of more than 1.5 acres of 
green space and planting of additional shade trees and other 
improvements to pedestrian/bicycle amenities throughout the 
Washington, Cambridge, and Nevins Streets corridors. 
 
• Increased Employment 
 The Proposed Project will create approximately ten (10) permanent and 
one hundred and fifty (150) construction jobs. 
 
• Water and Sewage Infrastructure 
 The Proposed Project is anticipated to contribute to the Boston Water and 
Sewer Commission (BWSC) for infiltration/inflow mitigation fund at a rate 
of 4:1 for any new wastewater flows added to the BWSC system. 
 
• Transportation Improvements and Mitigation 
 The Proposed Project will provide several multi-modal transportation 
improvements and implement various mitigation measures, including: 
o Creating a robust Transportation Demand Management (TDM) 
strategy that encourages employee and visitor use of public transit 
to minimize single occupant vehicle trips, designating an on-site 
employee transportation coordinator, employee transit subsidies, 
dedicated car sharing spaces, and provides showers/changing 
rooms for staff that bicycles to work (TDM measures valued at over 
$125,000). 
 

10 
 
o Active participation in the Allston-Brighton Transportation 
Management Association (TMA), including maintaining a leadership 
participation role in the TMA by a senior SEMC staff member. 
 
o Funding new Bluebikes stations for a total of 36 bike share bikes in 
or around the Project Site. Subject to review and approval by BTD, 
PWD, PIC, and the BPDA, and other applicable 
agencies/departments, the proposed Bluebikes stations would be 
located at intersection of Washington/Cambridge Streets and 
Warren/Nevins Streets in coordination with planned public realm 
improvements associated with the Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan. 
Final location and financial contributions to support Bluebikes 
stations and operations will be approved by BTD. 
 
o Electric vehicle charging stations for 150 vehicles within the 
Proposed Project’s parking garage, consistent with the City’s 
Electric Vehicle (EV) Readiness Policy for New Developments. 
 
• Smart Utilities Policy 
 The Proponent shall complete the Smart Utilities review before obtaining 
a Certificate of Compliance. Based on the Proposed Project’s size and 
scope of work, the items to be reviewed and verified are listed below: 
o Stormwater retention of 1.25 inches over the impervious area; 
o Review the location of trees to ensure feasibility around other 
infrastructure (the review will be coordinated with BPDA’s Urban 
Design team); 
o An updated Utility Site Plan with the relevant utilities, including the 
items mentioned above as well as any other item included in 
previous comment letters; 
• Annual Property and Sales Tax Revenues 
 SEMC contributes more than $5,000,000 in property tax revenue annually 
to the City of Boston for SEMC facilities at 736 Cambridge Street, 45 
Nevins Street, and 253 Washington Street. 
 SEMC generates more $300,000 in sales tax revenue annually for the City 
of Boston. 
 
 
 

11 
 
• Charitable Care for the Community 
 SEMC provides approximately $200,000 annually in charitable care for 
under- and uninsured members of the Allston-Brighton neighborhood 
and surrounding communities. This charitable care provided by the 
Proponent combines with Health Safety Net (HSN) care through state 
reimbursements to total more than $2,000,000 annually in charitable care 
for the community. 
 
COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
In addition to the aforementioned mitigation, the Proposed Project includes the 
following community benefit commitments specific to the Proposed IMP and not 
included in other community benefit commitments to the Massachusetts 
Department of Public Health: 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to construct an approximately 2,300 square foot 
2-bay facility that can park two ambulance vehicles inside and has space for 
an office, lounge, locker & changing rooms with showers, full kitchen, toilet 
facilities and voice/data closet. This facility is estimated to be valued at more 
than $1,000,000 in construction costs and will be provided, as an additional 
community benefit, on a rent-free basis to EMS Boston subject to the terms 
of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between Steward Health Care 
and the Boston Public Health Commission dated June 8, 2022. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to maintain membership in the Allston-Brighton 
Transportation Management Association (TMA) with annual paid dues of 
appropriately $8,000 and contributions to key TMA initiatives for the 4-year 
term of the Proposed IMP. 
 
• 
The Proponent has agreed to work with BPDA, BTD, and MBTA staff to 
develop a preliminary conceptual design of a Bus Rapid Transit (“BRT”) lane 
from Parsons Street to Union Square. This work is valued at approximately 
$100,000. Scope of work will be determined by the time the TAPA is 
executed. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to make a snow emergency provision of 50 
parking spaces at 326 Washington Street (“the Elks Lot”) for use by Allston-
Brighton residents with valid City-issued Allston-Brighton neighborhood 
parking permits on a first-come-first-serve basis during City of Boston 

12 
 
declared snow emergencies. This parking provision is made for the 4-year 
term of the Proposed IMP. The Proponent is currently under lease 
agreement with the Elks Lot through 2026. Should the Proponent be unable 
to renew the parking lot lease at this location, provisions through end of the 
4-year term of the Proposed IMP for 50 snow emergency parking spaces will 
be made elsewhere on the SEMC campus. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to construct public realm streetscape 
improvements along Washington, Nevins, and Cambridge Streets along 
SEMC campus frontage to support future public right-of-way revitalization 
proposed through the Allston-Brighton Mobility Plan. Construction of these 
public realm streetscape improvements are valued at more than $100,000 
for pedestrian hardscape surfaces, curbing, planting of shade trees and 
other landscape plant materials, signage, and other public realm 
improvements. Specific improvements may include, but are not limited to, 
left turn markings and overhead signs on Cambridge Street, installation of 
larger stop signs, and installation of flex posts to reinforce existing striping. 
Improvements will be coordinated with BPDA and BTD prior to design and 
installation and should be completed no later than by issuance of Certificate 
of Occupancy. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to make a financial contribution of five thousand 
dollars ($5,000) annually throughout the 4-year term of the Proposed IMP to 
support elder care and community programming for seniors through the 
Veronica Smith Senior Center for the Allston-Brighton community. The five-
thousand-dollar financial contribution shall be made payable to the 
“Veronica Smith Senior Center” for their use in supporting and enhancing 
community health care programs. 
 
• The Proponent has agreed to make a financial contribution of fifty thousand 
dollars ($50,000) annually per year from 2024 to 2026to support community 
nutrition programming through the Allston Brighton Health Collaborative for 
the Allston-Brighton neighborhood. The fifty-thousand-dollar financial 
contribution shall be made payable to the “Allston Brighton Health 
Collaborative” in 2024, 2025, and 2026 for their use in supporting and 
enhancing community nutrition programs. 
 

13 
 
• The Proponent is committed to maintaining its annual scholarship program 
for Allston-Brighton residents pursuing a higher education degree in the 
health care field. This scholarship program is valued at $15,000 annually. 
 
• The Proponent is aware of a larger effort being undertaken by the City to 
improve pedestrian and bicycling conditions along Washington Street 
adjacent to the project site. No bus stop relocations, curb-changes, or other 
permanent improvements will be made on Washington Street by the project 
proponents prior to planning and design engagement with BPDA, the City of 
Boston, and MBTA service planning. However, to improve pedestrian safety 
along Washington Street adjacent to the project site prior to the City’s effort 
being implemented, the Proponent shall work with BPDA and BTD to design 
and install quick-build safety improvements along the corridor. The value of 
this is estimated to be approximately $25,000. 
 
The Proponent will provide the BPDA with evidence indicating that the above-
referenced mitigation and community benefits have been satisfied. BPDA approved 
construction signage must be installed at the Project construction site(s) before and 
during Project construction. The signage must be in the form of panels at highly 
visible locations at the construction site(s) or around the construction site 
perimeter and must be adjacent to each other. The BPDA will work with the 
Proponent to provide high-resolution graphics that must be printed at a large scale 
(minimum 8 feet by 12 feet). 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, the BPDA staff recommends that the BPDA Board: (1) 
approve the Proposed IMP, pursuant to Section 80D of the Code; (2) authorize the 
Director to petition the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the Proposed 
IMP for a term of four (4) years from the effective date of approval, pursuant to 
Article 80D of the Code; (3) issue a Preliminary Adequacy Determination waiving the 
requirement of further review pursuant to Article 80B-5.4(c)(iv) of the Code for the 
Proposed Project; (4) authorize the Director to issue a Certification of Compliance 
for the Proposed Project pursuant to Section 80B-6 of the Code and one or more 
Certifications of Consistency pursuant to Section 80D-10.1 (a) and (b) (i) and (ii) of 
the Code for the IMP Proposed Projects, upon successful completion of the Article 
80 Large Project Review process; and (5) authorize the Director to execute and 
deliver a Cooperation Agreement, which will include a provision requiring 
compliance with the Boston Residents Jobs Policy and any and all other documents 

14 
 
and agreements as the Director deems appropriate and necessary in connection 
with the Proposed Project and the Proposed IMP. 
 
Appropriate votes follow: 
 
VOTED: 
That, in connection with the St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center Institutional 
Master Plan 2022-2026 (the “Proposed IMP”) describing the St. 
Elizabeth's Medical Center Parking Garage project (the “Proposed 
Project”) presented at a public hearing duly held pursuant to Section 
80D-5.4(c)(ii) of the Boston Zone Code (“Code”) by the Boston 
Redevelopment Authority (the “BRA”) on May 12, 2022, and after 
consideration of evidence presented at, and in connection with, the 
hearing on the Proposed IMP and the Proposed Project, the BRA finds 
that, in accordance with Section 80D-4 of the Code, that: (a) the 
Proposed IMP complies with the Scoping Determination issued in 
connection with the Expanded Plan Notification Form (“PNF”) 
submitted on August 20, 2019; (b) the Proposed IMP conforms to the 
provisions of Article 80D of the Code; (c) the Proposed IMP conforms 
to the general plan for the City as a whole; and (d) on balance, nothing 
in the Proposed IMP will be injurious to the neighborhood or 
otherwise detrimental to the public welfare, weighing all the benefits 
and burdens; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue an Adequacy 
Determination pursuant to Article 80D-5.4(c) of the Code approving 
the Proposed IMP; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to petition the Boston 
Zoning Commission for approval of the Proposed IMP for a term of 
four (4) years from the effective date of the approval, in substantial 
accord with that presented to the BRA at its public hearing on May 12, 
2022; and 
 
 
 

15 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue one or more 
Certifications of Consistency pursuant to Article 80D-10 of the Code 
when the Director finds that: (a) a Proposed Project is described 
adequately in the Proposed IMP and is consistent with the Proposed 
IMP, including the requirement of the subsection of (d) of Section 80D-
10 concerning the location of High Impact Subuses and (b) the 
Proposed IMP has been approved by the BRA and the Boston Zoning 
Commission in accordance with the applicable provisions of Article 
80D, lnstitutional Master Plan Review; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That following a virtual presentation of the Proposed Project at a 
public hearing held pursuant to section 80B-5.4(c)(iv) of the Code on 
May 12, 2022, the BRA hereby finds that the Proposed Project, as 
described in the Draft Project Impact Report (“DPIR”) dated November 
5, 2021, conforms to the general plan for the City of Boston as a whole 
and that nothing in the Proposed Project will be injurious to the 
neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public welfare; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue a Preliminary 
Adequacy Determination Waiving Further Review regarding the 
Proposed Project pursuant to Section 808-5.4(c)(iv) of the Code 
approving the DPIR dated November 5, 2021, and the Supplemental 
Filings of February 8, 2022 and April 19, 2022, and waiving the 
requirement for the filing and review of a Final Project Impact Report, 
subject to BRA design review; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to issue one or more 
Certifications of Compliance for the Proposed Project pursuant to 
Section 80B-6 of the Code upon successful completion of all Article 80 
processes for the Proposed Project; and 
 
 
 

16 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the Director be, and hereby is, authorized to execute and deliver 
a Cooperation Agreement, which will include a provision requiring 
compliance with the Boston Residents Jobs Policy and any and all 
other agreements and documents that the Director deems 
appropriate and necessary in connection with the Proposed Project 
and the Proposed IMP, all upon terms and conditions determined to 
be in the best interests of the BRA.

CHAIR STATEMENT 
January 16th, 2025 
This is a public hearing before the Boston Redevelopment Authority doing 
business as the Boston Planning & Development Agency, being held in 
conformance with Article(s) 80A-2 and 80D-5 of the Boston Zoning Code to consider 
the proposed First Amendment to the Suffolk University 2020 Institutional Master 
Plan for the 101 Tremont Street Project. 
The hearing was duly advertised on December 24, 2024, in the Boston 
Herald. 
 
This is a BPDA hearing on a proposed petition by the Agency. Staff members 
will first present their case and are subject to questioning by members of the 
Agency. Thereafter, anyone who wishes to testify about the proposed project will 
be afforded an opportunity. We are taking support and opposition at the same 
time. 
If you are planning to testify via Zoom, please take the time now to verify that 
your computer microphone is active and click the hand icon on your Zoom control 
panel. This will signal to staff that you would like to speak. When your hand is 
raised, it will be blue. If you are calling in to the meeting and would like to testify, 
please dial *9 to raise your hand. When I call for all testimony, staff will announce 
your name and allow you to talk. You must unmute your microphone, your webcam 
will not be active. 
If you are planning to testify in person in the Boardroom, please line up 
behind the podium after the presentation has concluded, we will call on you. 

In an effort to accommodate all who would like to speak about this proposal, 
each person will be given up to two minutes to comment. BPDA staff will indicate 
when thirty seconds remain. At that time, please conclude your remarks so that the 
hearing may continue, and others may be heard. Finally, the proponents are 
allowed a period of five to ten minutes for rebuttal if they so desire. 
Scott, please begin the presentation.

MEMORANDUM 
 JANUARY 16, 2025 
 
 
TO: 
 
BOSTON REDEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY
 
 
D/B/A BOSTON PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT AGENCY (BPDA)
 
 
AND KAIROS SHEN, DIRECTOR 
 
FROM: 
NUPOOR MONANI, SENIOR DEPUTY DIRECTOR FOR DEVELOPMENT REVIEW 
SCOTT GREENHALGH, PROJECT MANAGER 
FORD DELVECCHIO, PLANNING REVIEW PLANNER 
JOHN DALZELL, SERIOR ARCHITECT FOR SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT 
 
SUBJECT: 
PUBLIC HEARING TO CONSIDER THE FIRST AMENDMENT TO 
THE SUFFOLK UNIVERSITY 2020 INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
(“BRA”) d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”) 
authorize the Director to: 1) issue an Adequacy Determination 
approving the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form filed with the 
BPDA on August 15, 2024 (the “IMPNF”) for the proposed First 
Amendment to the Suffolk University 2020 Institutional Master Plan 
(the “Proposed IMP Amendment”) in connection with the 101 Tremont 
Street Project (“Proposed Project”); (2) petition the Boston Zoning 
Commission (“BZC”) for approval of the Amendment to Suffolk IMP and 
associated map amendment (the “Zoning Map Amendment”); (3) issue 
a Scoping Determination waiving further review of the Proposed 
Project pursuant to Section 80B-5.3(d) of the Boston Zoning Code 
(“Code”); (4) issue a Certification of Compliance for the Proposed 
Project pursuant to Section 80B-6 of the Code, upon successful 
completion of the Article 80 Large Project review process; (5) issue a

INTRODUCTION 
 
Suffolk University (the “University” or “Suffolk”) seeks to amend the 
Suffolk University 2020 Institutional Master Plan (“Suffolk IMP”) to add the Proposed 
Project which involves the redevelopment of 101 Tremont Street to create 
approximately 280 units of housing for undergraduate students. 
 
The Suffolk IMP was approved by the BRA Board on May 14, 2020, adopted by the 
BZC on June 10, 2020 and approved by the Mayor on June 19, 2020, with an 
effective date of June 19, 2020. 
 
On August 15, 2024, Suffolk submitted the Institutional Master Plan Notification 
Form for Amendment to the Suffolk University 2020 Institutional Master Plan. On 
October 23, 2024, Suffolk submitted the Proposed IMP Amendment. 
 
The Proposed IMP Amendment includes the 101 Tremont Street Residence Hall 
Project, a conversion of the existing approximately 88,265 square foot office 
building into approximately 67,170 square feet of student housing with a second-
floor amenities space for various student activities and student lounge. The ground-
floor level consists of approximately 8,938 square feet of publicly accessible 
retail/restaurant space which will remain (the “Proposed Project”). 
 
Suffolk University regards student housing as a critical component of its 
institutional mission. In the earlier 2008 IMP, the University set a target of housing 
50 percent of FTE undergraduate student population by 2018. For the Suffolk 2020 
IMP, Suffolk renewed its commitment to the 50 percent target with the One Court 
Street Residence Hall project. The University currently houses 1,518, or 
approximately 34.3% of the FTE undergraduate student population. With the 
addition of 1 Court Street in 2020, and the Proposed Project, the University will 
have created approximately 550 on campus beds since the Suffolk 2020 IMP. As 
such, the Proposed Project represents the University’s latest effort to secure long-

 
BOARD APPROVED

3 
 
term student housing over 10 years through 2030. The amended Suffolk 2020 IMP 
will include a total of 14 institutional projects in the City of Boston.

DESCRIPTION OF AMENDMENT AND THE 101 TREMONT STREET PROJECT 
The Suffolk IMP was approved by the BRA Board on May 14, 2020, adopted by the 
BZC on June 10, 2020 and approved by the Mayor on June 19, 2020, with an 
effective date of June 19, 2020. 
 
The Proposed Project, as described in the IMPNF, proposes a mixed-use 
institutional project at 101 Tremont Street in Downtown (“Project Site”), which 
includes changes to the building and use program. The Proposed Project is a 

 
BOARD APPROVED 
20 
DOCUMENT NO. 8197

conversion of the existing approximately 88,265 square foot office building into 
approximately 67,170 square feet of student housing with a second-floor amenities 
space for various student activities and student lounge. The ground-floor level 
consists of 8,938-SF of publicly accessible retail/restaurant space which will remain. 
The Project will also include other supporting uses, including a student housing 
reception area, laundry room, student lounge space, and study rooms – all of which 
will be secure and accessible only to University students. 
 
 
The Proposed Project adds up to 280 student housing beds to the University’s 
permanent housing inventory. This helps relieve the burden on the existing 
multifamily housing stock in downtown neighborhoods and, notably, East Boston, 
which is currently the most popular off-campus housing neighborhood among the 
University’s undergraduate students. 
 
Moreover, the University continues its commitment to house 50 percent of full-time 
equivalent (“FTE”) students in University-managed housing within the ten-year term 
of the Suffolk IMP. The Proposed Project represents the next step in achieving this 
goal, which requires the University to continue identifying and securing long-term 
additional student housing capacity. This represents a significant increase from the 
current figure of FTE students housed on campus, which stands at approximately 
40 percent. The University’s goal contributes to the City’s established goal of 
reducing the number of undergraduates living off campus in Boston’s rental 
housing market by approximately 50 percent by the year 2030. 
 
 Existing trash removal equipment and containers located on Bosworth Street will 
be removed and all trash removal for the building will be handled by the utilization 
of the trash facility and compactor located at Suffolk’s neighboring building-Sargent 
Hall- at 120 Tremont Street, and Suffolk maintenance personnel will remove trash 
from the building on a daily basis. 
 
During ongoing design review with the urban design staff, the Proponent for the 
Project will study the articulation, constructability and energy impacts of 
maintaining the existing window profiles for all windows to be replaced. Where 
operable windows exist today, the Proponent will consider providing a replacement 
window with a horizontal mullion at the location of the existing meeting rail and 
offset the panes of glass to maintain the appearance of an operable window. The

PLANNING AND ZONING CONTEXT 
 
Launched in October 2023, the Downtown Residential Conversion Incentive Pilot 
Program “Downtown Conversion Program” aims to support the adaptive reuse of 
commercial office buildings into residential use. The Pilot Program was informed by 
both 1) the City of Boston’s October 2022 Downtown Revitalization Report which 
analyzed and made recommendations for downtown economic revitalization, as 
well as 2) the PLAN: Downtown planning process which recommended a downtown 
office conversion program as a key strategy for achieving the PLAN goals. While this 
project is not utilizing the tax credit offered by the Pilot program, the Proposed 
Project helps to further the goals outlined in the plan and help to reinforce the 
residential growth of Downtown. The Proposed Project and corresponding IMP 
amendment also the further goals of the Boston Housing Strategy 2025 which 
notes, “the City will work with Boston’s many colleges and universities through their 
Institutional Master Plan processes to reduce the number of students living in off-
campus housing.”

50,000 GSF within a Downtown District, and such use is classified as a High Impact 
Sub-use of an Institutional Use. Therefore, the Proposed Project is subject to review 
and approval from both the BRA and the BZC.

and the Proposed Project is subject to review under Section 80B of the Code. On 
August 15, 2024, Suffolk submitted the IMPNF and the Project Notification Form 
(“PNF”) for the Proposed Project. On October 23, 2024, Suffolk submitted the 
Proposed IMP Amendment. 
 
Suffolk presented the Proposed Project to the Suffolk Task Force and public in joint 
Task Force and Public Meetings held on September 17, 2024, and November 19,

PROJECT BENEFITS AND MITIGATION 
 
TRANSPORTATION 
The University will make much-needed sidewalk and streetscape improvements to 
Bromfield and Tremont Streets. All sidewalk improvements are subject to design 
review and may require approval for a Specific Repairs Action with the Public 
Improvement Commission (“PIC”) 
● The Proposed Project will include a complete restoration of the surrounding 
sidewalks on Bromfield, Tremont and Bosworth Streets, as well as an 
extension of the sidewalk on the corner of Tremont and Bromfield Street to 
provide additional pedestrian areas, construct ADA-compliant curb ramps, 
and improved crosswalks in a heavily pedestrian area of Boston. 
● The project will also remove the trash storage for 101 Tremont from the 
Bosworth Street right-of-way, and instead provide building trash storage in a 
neighboring Suffolk University building at 120 Tremont Street. 
● Within thirty (30) days of issuance of the Building Permit, the Proponent will 
make a one-time $75,000.00 contribution to the Boston Transportation 
Department (“BTD”) to support the bike share system.

(“TAPA”) with Boston Transportation Department (“BTD”) to articulate a

SUSTAINABILITY / ARTICLE 37 
 
Per Zoning Article 37, the Proposed Project will achieve LEED v4 New Construction 
Silver / 53 points and will pursue additional green building strategies and credits, if 
obtainable, to achieve LEED Gold / 60+ points. The existing building will be 
improved through a combination of exterior enclosure and mechanical system 
upgrades including all-efficient-electric space and DHW water heating systems. The 
Proposed Project has a modeled Building 2035 preliminary Carbon Emissions 
Intensity of 1.78 kg CO2e/sf-yr (Grid Elec. Emission without RPS). 
 
Within 60 days of Board approval, the Proposed Project will provide the following 
items for Interagency Green Building Committee review and approval: 
● Preliminary (updated) Building Performance Model - including annual carbon 
emissions, Building 2035 predictive Carbon Emissions Intensity, energy uses, 
and a summary of the Proposed Project building enclosure and system 
upgrades. 
● Climate Resiliency Checklist – to be completed via the Developer Portal with 
the resultant PDF submitted with these responses. 
● Embodied Carbon Life Cycle Assessment – to reduce embodied carbon 
related emissions prepare a whole building Life Cycle Assessment of building 
structure, enclosure and insulation components and materials including the 
benefits of existing building reuse. Identify and include lower embodied 
carbon solutions. 
 
SMART UTILITIES 
 
The project plan will comply with the Smart Utilities requirements found in Article 
80B of the Code. As proposed no new utilities will be needed, but any new utilities 
and/or lateral connections related to the project within any City right of way will be

telecom and fiber providers to ensure broadband equity and possible future

INCLUSIONARY DEVELOPMENT POLICY 
 
The Inclusionary Development Policy (“IDP”), dated December 10, 2015, exempts 
any Proposed Projects from IDP requirements if the Project is: (a) financed as one 
entity and provides 40% or more of units within the project as income-restricted, (b) 
a dormitory, or (c) an otherwise exempt site usage under the Zoning Code. As such, 
the Proposed Project, as a dormitory, is exempt from obligations under the IDP.

Suffolk University Institutional Master 
Plan Amendment 
In accordance with Article 80D-9 of the City of Boston Zoning Code (the “Code”), Suffolk University 
(“Suffolk” or the “University”) is submitting this Institutional Master Plan Amendment (“IMP 
Amendment”) to the Boston Planning and Development Agency (BPDA) to amend the 2020 Suffolk 
University Institutional Master Plan (the “2020 IMP”) to include the conversion of 101 Tremont Street, 
an existing approximately 88,265-square foot (SF) office building recently acquired by the University, 
into a residence hall for students consisting of up to 280 beds (the “Proposed Project”). The existing 
office building is located at 101 Tremont Street within the Downtown neighborhood of Boston (the 
“Project Site”). Refer to Figure 1 for the Campus Locus Map. 
Suffolk University regards student housing as a critical component of its institutional mission. In the 
2020 IMP, the University renewed the 2008 Institutional Master Plan (“2008 IMP”) commitment to the 
target of housing 50 percent of the full-time equivalent (“FTE”) undergraduate student population. In 
September 2019, Suffolk University submitted an Institutional Master Plan Notification Form (the 
“2020 IMPNF”) commencing the 2020 IMP, which considers the ten years of the University’s growth 
and development through 2030. The 2020 IMP was submitted to the BPDA in January 2020, and 
approved by the BPDA Board on May 14, 2020, and was then adopted by the Boston Zoning 
Commission (BZC) on June 10, 2020 for a ten (10) year term until June 19, 2030. An Institutional 
Master Plan Notification Form (IMPNF) and Project Notification Form (PNF) were submitted on 
August 15, 2024 for the Proposed Project. 
1.1 Suffolk University Mission and Objectives 
Since its inception, Suffolk University’s fundamental mission has been to respond to the evolving 
needs of society by providing an opportunity for motivated and capable students to obtain a quality 
education in a challenging yet supportive environment at an affordable cost. 
Suffolk University welcomes and remains accessible to people from a wide variety of backgrounds. It 
is the University's tradition, and remains its practice, to provide academic services for people of 
various levels of preparation and ability, and programs of sufficient depth and academic quality 
education at a reasonable cost. To respond to the evolving needs of today's world, Suffolk furnishes 
a variety of cross-cultural and international experiences in which diversity and excellence are 
inextricably interdependent.

Suffolk University places students at the center of its efforts and emphasizes academic excellence 
through teaching based on the application of theory, research to practice, and public service. In 
keeping with its historic mission of serving a broad constituency, the University offers day and 
evening programs at both the graduate and undergraduate levels. In addition, the University is 
strongly committed to continuing education. 
Suffolk University's location near the State House, government agencies, the courts, and New 
England's legal, medical, business, and financial centers allows it to utilize neighboring institutions to 
provide internships, cooperative education assignments, and other forms of experiential learning and 
research. Throughout its history, Suffolk University has established linkages with business, public 
administration, and legal communities for the purpose of providing financial support, research 
opportunities, adjunct faculty, professional advice, and placement for graduates. 
In its most recent strategic planning effort, the University updated the Mission Statement and Vision, 
respectively, as follows: 
Mission Statement 
At Suffolk University we are driven by the power of education, inclusion, and engagement to change 
lives and positively impact communities. Committed to excellence, we provide students with 
experiential and transformational learning opportunities that begin in the center of Boston, reach 
across the globe, and lead to extraordinary outcomes for our graduates. 
Vision 
Suffolk University will be a leader in experiential learning, known nationally and internationally for 
excellence in providing students access to real-world and global learning opportunities through 
outstanding academic and co-curricular programs and partnerships that take full advantage of our 
borderless, urban campuses in Boston and Madrid. We will advance our mission by ensuring that our 
students gain the core competencies needed to build successful careers in a rapidly changing world. 
A sharp focus on preparing students and alumni for lifelong career and community success will put 
Suffolk at the forefront of career education efforts at colleges and universities nationwide. 
1.1.1 University Objectives 
Suffolk’s development of competitive undergraduate and graduate programs in the arts and 
sciences, business, and law has been the foundation of its ongoing planning process. To continue to 
be a competitive institution, Suffolk has determined that it must enhance the academic, residential, 
student life, athletic, and cultural resources available to its current and prospective students. 
In summer 2019, the University issued the Suffolk 2025 Strategic Plan, stating the University’s Mission 
Statement and Vision and identifying a strategic framework for achieving them (the “Strategic Plan”). 
The Strategic Plan outlines specific goals to be met over the six-year period (2019-2025) and 
identifies six interrelated focus areas, including integrated education, community, reputation, 
infrastructure, resources, and finance, which are described further below in Section 1.1.3.

1.1.2 Major Programs and Initiatives 
Suffolk University prides itself on being a provider of high quality, practical, and experiential 
education designed to prepare graduates for careers. The University believes that the characteristics 
that distinguish it from competing institutions are: 
› A broad range of flexible class schedules that include day, night, and weekend sessions; 
› Affordable tuition; 
› Small class sizes; and 
› A convenient downtown location that is accessible to commuters and professionals. 
The University’s academic programs are offered through three schools: College of Arts and Sciences, 
Law School, and Sawyer Business School. 
College of Art and Sciences 
The College of Arts and Sciences has as its credo that liberal learning prepares students of all ages 
and backgrounds to live more fulfilling lives, to appreciate and contribute to the communities of 
which they are members, and to reach their ethical, personal, intellectual, and financial goals. To help 
its students maximize their potential, the college emphasizes critical and analytical thinking through 
a rigorous “success skills” undergraduate core program in written and oral communication, 
computing, analyzing, and integrating. Faculty scholarship supports diversified liberal arts 
concentrations available in the humanities, the natural sciences, and the social sciences, along with 
graduate programs in several fields, most offering career-related professional program tracks and 
practical experience on or off campus. 
The College of Art and Sciences goals are as follows: 
› 
To provide students with liberal learning that emphasizes a curriculum of inquiry, expanding 
perspectives and specialization. 
› 
To offer undergraduate, graduate and professional education that provides students with the 
means to explore and adapt their career and personal goals and objectives in a changing 
economic and technological environment. 
› 
To assure that undergraduate and graduate students develop an appropriate level of core 
competencies and their capacities for critical inquiry, creativity, research and analysis. 
› 
To create a diverse community of teachers and learners where students and faculty engage in 
the free expression of ideas, fostering independent thought and mutual respect. 
› 
To provide opportunities for students to enhance their aesthetic, intellectual and moral 
capabilities, and their sense of self-worth, self-confidence, and civic responsibility. 
› 
To attract and maintain an excellent faculty with a commitment to teaching, research, and 
service to the University and the greater community. 
› 
To attract and retain an increasingly competent student body consistent with the mission of 
the University. 
› 
To provide an educational environment, which includes appropriate classrooms, technologies, 
libraries, laboratories, recreation areas, and other facilities that enhance the process of student 
learning.

1.1.3 Strategic Plan 
In June 2019, the University issued the Suffolk 2025 Strategic Plan, which states the University’s 
Mission Statement and Vision, and identifies a strategic framework for achieving them. 
The Strategic Plan presents six interrelated focus areas, as follows: 
1. Integrated Education identifies targets relating to the University’s academic programming, 
highlighting a focus on experiential learning and career readiness. This section underscores the 
University’s commitment to lifelong learning, public engagement, civil discourse and service 
learning, and transformative co-curricular opportunities. 
2. Community establishes targets for the University’s workforce (focusing on diversity, inclusion, 
safety, health, and wellness) as well as alumni engagement and communications. The University 
plans to increase the number of faculty and staff from historically underrepresented groups and 
increase programming to support students from historically underrepresented groups as well. 
3. Reputation outlines the University’s strategy for strengthening its brand and promoting greater 
visibility. This will be achieved through hosting events, enhancing communications strategy, 
focusing on improving Suffolk’s rankings, and other key initiatives. 
4. Infrastructure identifies the University’s goals for developing campus infrastructure. This 
includes optimizing space usage in existing facilities, expanding the student housing portfolio, 
identifying and utilizing dedicated performance spaces, and exploring options for acquiring 
space to support new academic programs. This section emphasizes the University’s plans to 
develop and refine sophisticated Information Technology systems and policies. 
5. Resources identifies goals for developing the University’s resources with a focus on growing 
enrollment, retaining a greater percentage of students, decreasing admission rates, and 
enhancing campus diversity. This section describes the University’s plans for increasing 
philanthropic activity, improving corporate and foundation partnerships, optimizing resources 
for more efficient operation, and supporting new programs for institutional research. 
6. Finance identifies strategies for bolstering the University’s ability to respond nimbly to a 
changing marketplace. This section also establishes goals for improving bond ratings, 
generating an annual operating surplus of 3 percent to 5 percent, and revising the approach to 
managing the University’s endowment. 
1.1.4 Campus Master Plan 
Accommodating growth on an urban campus poses unique master planning challenges. In such a 
setting, institutional master planning requires the University to be clear about preferred areas of 
expansion and to maintain a proactive approach to opportunities as they arise. The 2020 IMP for the 
Suffolk University campus will build on the existing campus resources that include the University’s 
historic core, which is located on the edges of Beacon Hill. The vision of the 2020 IMP framework

represents a trajectory located along Cambridge and Tremont Streets that extends from the existing 
core of the campus in the direction of Downtown Crossing. This framework is best described as the 
Suffolk Crescent, which was originally conceptualized during the 2008 IMP process. 
The campus planning goals of the 2020 IMP are to: 
› 
Formalize an on-going effort to create a long-term strategic plan that will establish the 
University’s physical growth needs over the next ten years; 
› 
Establish a stronger sense of campus, particularly through the expansion of student housing in 
Downtown Boston; 
› 
Nurture the working relationship with surrounding communities; 
› 
Establish a trajectory for growth that builds on the University’s existing campus but sets forth new 
concentrated areas for development (these areas – four in total – are referred to as “growth 
clusters,” which, taken together with a fifth “academic central campus” cluster, form the Suffolk 
Crescent); 
› 
Seek opportunities for development where no one cluster must bear the burden of all of the 
University’s space needs; 
› 
Locate future uses near existing University assets without overwhelming any one cluster with a 
saturation of university-related uses; and 
› 
Identify sites where complementary programs can coexist and help bolster the existing context. 
1.2 Status of 2020 IMP Projects and Need for Amendment 
The most recent IMP renewal commenced in May 2018, when Suffolk filed for the renewal of the IMP 
and approval for a new student dormitory project at 1 Court Street. Approval of the 2020 IMP on 
May 14, 2020 was a continuation of the University’s institutional master planning efforts supported 
by the BPDA and BZC since 2002. 
Suffolk’s campus is integrated throughout Downtown Boston, loosely located along the spine of 
Tremont Street to Cambridge Street. The physical character of the campus is emblematic of how the 
University's students are integrated into the working environment of Boston; at a physical and 
human level, the University's campus is knitted into the urban fabric of the city. The 2020 IMP 
proposed to utilize thirteen buildings within Boston, in addition to one outdoor athletic facility in 
East Boston (Figure 1). 
The 2020 IMP aimed to build on existing campus resources, including the University's historic core 
located on the edges of Beacon Hill. Furthermore, the 2020 IMP sought to support the well-planned 
development of institutional facilities to enhance Suffolk's public service and economic development 
roles in surrounding neighborhoods. The 2020 IMP acknowledged that universities often need to 
expand and renovate their facilities more frequently than other types of establishments, and 
recognized that the cumulative impact of such expansions could be more significant than that of 
individual projects. 
Suffolk University regards student housing as a critical component of its institutional mission. In the 
2008 IMP, the University set a target of housing 50 percent of FTE undergraduate student population 
by 2018. For the 2020 IMP, Suffolk renewed its commitment to the 50 percent target. Figure 2, shows 
the existing property locations and building footprints within the City of Boston. To date, the

University continues its efforts to increase its student housing portfolio in order to meet this target. 
The University currently houses 1,518, or approximately 34.3% of the FTE undergraduate student 
population. With the addition of 1 Court Street in 2020, and the Proposed Project, as well as the 
termination of the temporary 1047 Commonwealth Avenue student housing facility, the University 
will have created approximately 550 on campus beds since the 2020 IMP. As such, the Proposed 
Project represents the University’s latest effort to secure long-term student housing over 10 years 
through 2030. The amended 2020 IMP will include a total of 14 institutional projects in the City of 
Boston. 
Over the past years, the University has experienced a greater demand by its students for guaranteed 
residential accommodation for the first and second years of enrollment. The Proposed Project aims 
to enhance the experience of its students by offering more on-campus student housing. With the 
campus located in the heart of Boston, the Proposed Project will provide student housing in an area 
with convenient access to Suffolk’s academic facilities and is in keeping with the objectives of the 
Suffolk 2020 IMP.

The Proposed Project, as described in this IMP amendment, will include the addition of a new 
institutional project at 101 Tremont Street, Boston, MA (Figure 2). This addition will expand the 
University’s student housing, echo the 2020 IMP to establish a strong sense of campus in Downtown 
Boston and SU growth clusters and provide students with convenient access to the University’s 
academic facilities. The new addition is located in growth cluster #2, as depicted in Figure 3. 
the Proposed Project is consistent with the goals of the approved 2020 IMP, proposing to convert the 
existing approximately 88,265-SF office building into approximately 67,170-SF of student housing 
with a second-floor amenities space for various student activities and student lounge. The ground-
floor level consists of 8,938-SF of publicly accessible retail/restaurant space which will remain.

last twenty years. Within the 2020 IMP, the University committed to continue efforts to secure long-

Suffolk University must provide separate estimates of peak and continuous maximum 
water demand for residential, commercial, industrial, irrigation of landscaped areas, and 
air-conditioning make-up water for the project with the site plan. Estimates should be 
based on full-site build-out of the proposed project. Suffolk University should also 
provide the methodology used to estimate water demand for the proposed project. 
2. 
Suffolk University should explore opportunities for implementing water conservation 
measures in addition to those required by the State Plumbing Code. Suffolk University 
should consider outdoor landscaping which requires minimal use of water to maintain. If 
Suffolk University plans to install in-ground sprinkler systems, the Commission 
3 

recommends that timers, soil moisture indicators and rainfall sensors be installed. The use 
of sensor-operated faucets and toilets in common areas of buildings should be considered. 
3. 
Suffolk University is required to obtain a Hydrant Pennit for use of any hydrant during 
the construction phase of this project. The water used from the hydrant must be metered. 
Suffolk University should contact the Commission's Meter Department for infonnation 
on and to obtain a Hydrant Petmit. 
4. 
Suffolk University will be required to install approved backflow prevention devices on 
the water services for fire protection, vehicle wash, mechanical and any iITigation 
systems. Suffolk University is advised to consult with Mr. Larry Healy, Manager of 
Engineering Code Enforcement, with regards to backflow prevention. 
5. 
The Commission is utilizing a Fixed Radio Meter Reading System to obtain water meter 
readings. For new water meters, the Commission will provide a Meter Transmitter Unit 
(MTU) and connect the device to the meter. For information regarding the installation of 
MTUs, Suffolk University should contact the Commission's Meter Deparhnent. 
Sewage I Drainage 
I. 
In conjunction with the Site Plan and the General Service Application Suffolk University 
will be required to submit a Stonnwater Pollution Prevention Plan. The plan must: 
• 
Identify specific best management measures for controlling erosion and preventing 
the discharge of sediment, contaminated stonnwater, or construction debris to the 
Commission's drainage system when construction is underway. 
• 
Include a site map which shows, at a minimum, existing drainage patterns and areas 
used for storage or treatment of contaminated soils, groundwater or stonnwater, and 
the location of major control structures or treatment structures to be utilized during 
the construction. 
• 
Specifically identify how the project will comply with the Department of 
Environmental Protection's Perfonnance Standards for Stormwater Management both 
during construction and after construction is complete. 
2. 
The Commission encourages Suffolk University to explore additional oppo1iunities for 
protecting stonnwater quality on site by minimizing sanding and the use of deicing 
chemicals, pesticides, and fe1iilizers. 
3. 
The discharge of dewatering drainage to a sanitaiy sewer is prohibited by the 
Commission. Suffolk University is advised that the discharge of any dewatering drainage 
to the stonn drainage system requires a Drainage Discharge Pennit from the 
Commission. If the dewatering drainage is contaminated with petroleum products, 
4 

Suffolk University will be required to obtain a Remediation General Pennit from the 
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for the discharge. 
4. 
Suffolk University must fully investigate methods for retaining stonnwater on-site before 
the Commission will consider a request to discharge stonnwater to the Commission's 
system. The site plan should indicate how stonn drainage from roof drains will be 
handled and the feasibility ofretaining their stonnwater discharge on-site. Under no 
circumstances will stonnwater be allowed to discharge to a sanitary sewer. 
5. 
The Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (MassDEP) established 
Stormwater Management Standards. The standards address water quality, water quantity 
and recharge. In addition to Commission standards, Suffolk University will be required to 
meet MassDEP Stonnwater Management Standards. 
6. 
Sanitary sewage must be kept separate from stonnwater and separate sanitmy sewer and 
storm drain service connections must be provided. The Commission requires that existing 
stonnwater and sanitmy sewer service connections, which are to be re-used by the 
proposed project, be dye tested to confinn they are connected to the appropriate system. 
7. 
The Commission requests that Suffolk University install a permanent casting stating 
"Don't Dump: Drains to Boston Harbor" next to any catch basin created or modified as 
part of this project. Suffolk University should contact the Commission's Operations 
Division for infonnation regarding the purchase of the castings. 
8. 
The food service facility built as part of this project, will be require grease traps in 
accordance with the Commission's Sewer Use Regulations Suffolk University is advised 
to consult with the Commission's Operations Department with regards to grease traps. 
Thank you for the oppmiunity to comment on this project.
