Included here are Boston Public Works Department (PWD) comments for the Suffolk University - 101 Tremont 
Street IMP. 
 
Project Coordination: 
The developer should coordinate with the City of Boston if proposing any changes in use, dimensional, parking, or 
loading elements. The developer should coordinate with William Moose regarding the downtown crossing 
reconstruction project. The developer should also coordinate with BDPA and BTD regarding any potential 
mitigation. 
 
Project Specific Scope Considerations: 
The developer should coordinate with BTD and PWD to develop safety and accessibility improvements for 
pedestrians and cyclists in the area.The developer shall coordinate with PWD in regards to the construction of the 
pedestrian ramps at the corner of Tremont St and Bosworth St and Tremont St. and Bromfield St according to 
current MAAB/ADA standards. 
 
Site Plan: 
Developer must provide an engineer’s site plan at an appropriate engineering scale that shows curb functionality on 
both sides of all streets that abut the property. 
 
Construction Within The Public vs Private Right-of- Way: 
Although the general comments below apply specifically to work associated with the project within the public 
right-of-way, it is preferred and encouraged for construction in the private right-of-way to be consistent with City 
standards for public ways, as well, to the extent possible. Should these streets ever become public ways, they must 
conform to the City standards as outlined below. 
 
All work within the public way shall conform to Boston Public Works Department (PWD) standards. Any 
non-standard materials proposed within the public way will require approval through the Public 
Improvement Commission (PIC) process and a fully executed License, Maintenance and Indemnification 
(LM&I) Agreement with the PIC. 
 
Sidewalks: 
The developer is responsible for the reconstruction of the sidewalks abutting the project and, wherever possible, to 
extend the limits to the nearest intersection to encourage and compliment pedestrian improvements and travel 
along all sidewalks within the ROW within and beyond the project limits. The reconstruction effort also must meet 
current American’s with Disabilities Act (ADA)/ Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (AAB) guidelines, 
including the installation of new or reconstruction of existing pedestrian ramps at all corners of all intersections 
abutting the project site if not already constructed to ADA/AAB compliance per Code of Massachusetts Regulations 
Title 521, Section 21 (https://www.mass.gov/regulations/521-CMR-21-curb-cuts). This includes converting apex 
ramps to perpendicular ramps at intersection corners and constructing or reconstructing reciprocal pedestrian 
ramps where applicable. Plans showing the extents of the proposed sidewalk improvements associated with this 
project must be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval. Changes to any curb geometry 
will need to be reviewed and approved through the PIC. 
 
Please note that at signalized intersections, any alteration to pedestrian ramps may also require upgrading the 
traffic signal equipment to ensure that the signal post and pedestrian push button locations meet current ADA and 
Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) requirements. Any changes to the traffic signal system must 
be coordinated and approved by BTD.

Commission (BWSC) to determine appropriate methods of green infrastructure and stormwater management 
systems within the Public ROW. The ongoing maintenance of such systems shall require an LM&I Agreement with

Discontinuances 
Any discontinuances (sub-surface, surface or above surface) within the Public ROW must be processed through 
the PIC. 
 
Easements

The developer must seek approval from the Chief Landscape Architect with the Parks and Recreation Department 
for all landscape elements within the Public ROW. The landscaping program must accompany a LM&I with the 
PIC.

The developer must seek approval from the PWD Street Lighting Division, where needed, for all proposed street 
lighting to be installed by the developer. All proposed lighting within the Public ROW must be compatible with the 
area lighting to provide a consistent urban design. The developer should coordinate with the PWD Street Lighting 
Division for an assessment of any additional street lighting upgrades that are to be considered in conjunction with 
this project. All existing metal street light pull box covers within the limits of sidewalk construction to remain shall be 
replaced with new composite covers per PWD Street Lighting standards. Metal covers should remain for pull box 
covers in the roadway. For all sections of sidewalk that are to be reconstructed in the Public ROW that contain or 
are proposed to contain a City-owned street light system with underground conduit, the developer shall be 
responsible for installing shadow conduit adjacent to the street lighting system. Installation of shadow conduit and 
limits should be coordinated through the BPDA Smart Utilities team. 
 
Roadway 
Based on the extent of construction activity, including utility connections and taps, the developer will be responsible 
for the full restoration of the roadway sections that immediately abut the property and, in some cases, to extend the

restoration shall be submitted to the PWD Engineering Division for review and approval.

conflicts with other proposed projects within the Public ROW. The developer must coordinate with any existing 
projects within the same limits and receive clearance from PWD before commencing work.

SUBJECT: 
REQUEST AUTHORIZATION AND APPROVALS REGARDING THE 
INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN NOTIFICATION FORM FOR THE 
RENEWAL OF THE TUFTS UNIVERSITY HEALTH SCIENCES CAMPUS 
INSTITUTIONAL MASTER PLAN 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
d/b/a the Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”): (1) 
approve the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form for renewal 
and extension of the Tufts University Health Sciences Campus 
Institutional Master Plan, dated October 13, 2023, ("IMPNF for 
Renewal") pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6, and Section 
80D-8 of the Boston Zoning Code (the "Code"); and (2) authorize the 
Director to take all actions and execute any and all documents 
deemed necessary and appropriate relative to the IMPNF for Renewal. 
_______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Tufts University’s most recent Institutional Master Plan for their Health Sciences 
Campus, based in the Chinatown, Mission Hill, and Fenway neighborhoods of 
Boston, was approved by the Boston Redevelopment Authority in December 1994, 
adopted by the Boston Zoning Commission in March 1995, updated May 3, 2004, 
amended in 2007, amended and renewed in 2009, and further amended and 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
18 
DOC No. 8087 
 
 
 
renewed in 2020. The term of the IMP expired on October 20, 2023 (collectively, the 
“Tufts IMP”). 
 
On October 13, 2023, Tufts submitted an IMPNF for Renewal to the Boston Planning 
& Development Agency (“BPDA”), signaling its intention to renew the Tufts IMP for a 
period of two years. Tufts is not proposing a new “Proposed Institutional Project”, 
as that term is understood in the Code; is not adding new land area to the Tufts 
IMP; is not proposing any changes to the Tufts IMP which would constitute a 
change in use, dimensional, parking or loading elements thereof (other than de 
minimus dimensional changes), and BPDA staff do not anticipate any greater 
impacts from the continuation of the implementation of the Tufts IMP than that 
which were originally evaluated. 
 
 
INSTITUTIONAL TEAM 
 
Proponent: 
Tufts University 
Liza Perry 
 
Legal Counsel: 
 
Krokidas & Bluestein LLP 
 
 
 
 
Kathy Cochrane Murphy 
 
Consultant: 
 
LSC Planning & Development, LLC 
 
 
 
 
Lauren Shurtleff 
 
 
 
 
ARTICLE 80 REVIEW 
 
The IMPNF for Renewal is subject to Institutional Master Plan Review and qualifies 
for a waiver of further review in accordance with Sections 80D-5.2(e), 80D-6, and 
80D-8 of the Code in that: (i) no new Proposed Institutional Projects are planned; (ii) 
no changes in the Institutional Master Plan are proposed that would constitute a 
change in the use, dimensional, parking or loading elements of the Institutional 
Master Plan (other than de minimus dimensional changes); and (iii) no significantly 
greater impacts would result from continued implementation of the approved 
Institutional Master Plan than were originally projected. Tufts seeks approval of the 
IMPNF for Renewal of Tufts IMP for a period of two years, until November 16, 2025. 

 
 
BOARD APPROVED 
18 
DOC No. 8087 
 
 
 
 
The submission of the IMPNF for Renewal on October 13, 2023, initiated a 30-day 
comment period that ended on November 15, 2023. Notice of submission was 
published in the Boston Herald on October 16, 2023. 
 
 
CONTINUED COMMUNITY BENEFITS 
 
All community benefits currently offered pursuant to the existing Tufts IMP will 
continue through the length of the renewed IMP. 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
Based on the foregoing, staff recommends that the BPDA Board: (1) approve the 
IMPNF for Renewal dated October 13, 2023, pursuant to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 
80D-6, and Section 80D-8 of the Boston Zoning Code (the "Code"); and (2) authorize 
the Director to take all actions and execute any and all documents deemed 
necessary and appropriate relative to the IMPNF for Renewal.

That in connection with the Institutional Master Plan Notification Form 
for the renewal and extension of the Tufts University Health Sciences 
Campus Institutional Master Plan, dated October 13, 2023, (the “IMPNF 
for Renewal”), and after consideration of the IMPNF for Renewal, the 
Boston Redevelopment Authority (“BRA”) hereby finds that: (a) the 
Tufts University Health Sciences Campus Institutional Master Plan and 
the IMPNF for Renewal (collectively, the “Renewed IMP”), conforms to 
the provisions of Article 80D of the Boston Zoning Code (“the Code”); 
(b) the Renewed IMP, conforms to the general plan for the City as a 
whole; and (c) on balance, nothing in the Renewed IMP, will be 
injurious to the neighborhood or otherwise detrimental to the public 
welfare, weighing all the benefits and burdens; and 
 
FURTHER 
VOTED: 
That the BRA waives further review of Tufts University Health Sciences 
Campus Institutional Master Plan and the IMPNF for Renewal pursuant

to Section 80D-5.2(e), Section 80D-6 and Section 80D-8 of the Code 
and approves the Renewed IMP as the renewed Institutional Master 
Plan for a period of two (2) years from the date of approval of this 
renewal vote by the BRA, that is November 16, 2025; and 
 
FURTHER

That the BRA hereby authorizes the Director to take all actions and 
execute any and all documents deemed necessary and appropriate 
and in the best interest of the BRA by the Director in connection with

CHAIR STATEMENT 
October 10, 2024 
This is a public hearing before the Boston Redevelopment Authority doing 
business as the Boston Planning & Development Agency, being held in 
conformance with Articles 80A-2 and 80D-5 of the Boston Zoning Code to consider 
the proposed 2024-2034 Institutional Master Plan for Wentworth Institute of 
Technology. 
The hearing was duly advertised on September 26 in the Boston Herald. 
This is a BPDA hearing on a proposed petition by the Agency. Staff members 
will first present their case and are subject to questioning by members of the 
Agency. Thereafter, anyone who wishes to testify about the proposed project will 
be afforded an opportunity. We are taking support and opposition at the same 
time. If you are planning to testify, please take the time now to verify that your 
computer microphone is active and click the hand icon on your Zoom control panel. 
This will signal to staff that you would like to speak. When your hand is raised, it will 
be blue. If you are calling in to the meeting and would like to testify, please dial *9 
to raise your hand. When I call for all testimony, staff will announce your name and 
allow you to talk. You must unmute your microphone, your webcam will not be 
active. 
In an effort to accommodate all who would like to speak about this proposal, 
each person will be given up to two minutes to comment. BPDA staff will indicate 
when thirty seconds remain. At that time, please conclude your remarks so that the 
hearing may continue, and others may be heard. Finally, the proponents are 
allowed a period of five to ten minutes for rebuttal if they so desire. 
 

Nick, please begin the presentation.

______________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
SUMMARY: This Memorandum requests that the Boston Redevelopment Authority 
d/b/a Boston Planning & Development Agency (“BPDA”): (1) issue an 
Adequacy Determination pursuant to Section 80D-5.4(c) of the Boston 
Zoning Code ("Code") approving the Wentworth Institute of 
Technology Institutional Master Plan ("Wentworth IMP") for a term of 
10 years from the effective date; (2) authorize the Director of the BPDA 
to petition the Boston Zoning Commission for approval of the 
Wentworth IMP and associated Map Amendment, pursuant to Section 
80D-6 of the Code; and (3) authorize the Director to execute and 
deliver any and all documents deemed necessary and appropriate in 
connection with the Wentworth IMP. 
 
 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31 
 DOCUMENT NO. 8178 
 
INTRODUCTION 
Wentworth Institute of Technology (the “Proponent” or the “University”) is seeking 
an Adequacy Determination approving its 2024-2034 Institutional Master Plan 
(“Wentworth IMP”). The Wentworth IMP describes the proposed institutional 
projects that Wentworth aims to complete over the next decade to realize strategic 
goals in both academic and community development. The Wentworth IMP includes 
six (6) proposed institutional projects totaling approximately 916,000 square feet, 
including the creation and improvement of four (4) significant open spaces. These 
proposed institutional projects include the following institutional uses: academic, 
student housing, student life, open space, parking, and accessory and support 
spaces. 
 
DEVELOPMENT TEAM 
Proponent: 
Wentworth Institute of Technology 
 
David Wahlstrom 
 
Master Planning 
Perkins & Will 
Architect: 
Gautam Sundaram 
Brad Rogers 
 
Legal Counsel: 
Nixon Peabody LLP 
 
Jennifer Schultz, Esq. 
 
Transportation: 
VHB 
Sean Manning 
 
Sustainability: 
Riverstone Sustainability 
Debra Shephard 
 
Government Relations: The Strategy Group 
 
Dave Newman 
 

BOARD APPROVED 
 
 
 
 31 
 DOCUMENT NO. 8178 
 
 
ZONING CONTEXT 
Wentworth’s Campus (the “Site”) is in the Mission Hill Neighborhood District, at the 
crossroads of the Fenway and Mission Hill neighborhoods, and is located in the 
Institutional Master Plan Area. The northern portion of the Site is located within (i) 
the Wentworth Institute IS subdistrict under the base provisions of the Code, (ii) the 
Groundwater Conservation Overlay District, which is governed principally by Article 
32 of the Code, and (iii) the Restricted Parking Overlay District. The southern 
portion of the Site is located within (i) the Local Industrial subdistrict under the base 
provisions of the Code, and (ii) the Special Study Overlay District. The entire Site is 
subject to an Institutional Master Plan pursuant to Article 80D of the Code. 
 
PLANNING CONTEXT 
The Wentworth Institute of Technology Institutional Master Plan (IMP) for 2024-
2034 contains six new Proposed Institutional Projects (PIPs) and identifies progress 
made since the implementation of the previous IMP. The IMP covers the university 
campus, comprising 31 acres in the Mission Hill and Longwood neighborhoods. The 
previous Institutional Master Plan was submitted in 2011, amended in 2017, and 
extended through March 2023. 
 
The previous IMP and its subsequent amendments provide the planning and zoning 
context for this IMP. The 2010 IMP included five PIPs, including the renovation and 
building addition for the Flanagan Campus Center at Beatty Hall, an addition to the 
Ira Allen Building, a new seven-story student residence hall, a new Center for 
Engineering and Innovation Sciences, and a New Sweeney Field athletic field. With 
the exception of the Field, presently under construction, all PIPs were completed as 
of the expiration of the prior IMP. 
 
The proposed IMP includes a series of Urban Design Guidelines that, in conjunction 
with the development proposals, align with existing citywide planning initiatives. 
These guidelines include the development of an open space framework, a strong

ARTICLE 80 REVIEW PROCESS 
The Wentworth IMP is subject to Institutional Master Plan Review pursuant to 
Section 80D of the Code. 
On March 10, 2023, the University filed an Institutional Master Plan Notification 
Form (“IMPNF”) proposing this IMP. Pursuant to Section 80D-5.3 of the Code, a 
Scoping Session was held on April 4, 2024, with the City’s public agencies to review 
and discuss the IMPNF. The Boston Planning and Development Authority (“BPDA”) 
then issued a Scoping Determination in response to staff and public comments on 
the IMPNF on December 5, 2023. On February 21, 2024, the Proponent filed the 
IMP in response to the BPDA’s Scoping Determination. 
Copies of submissions were sent to the Wentworth Institute of Technology Task 
Force. Community meetings to discuss the Wentworth IMP have been held on the 
following dates: 
• Task Force Meeting: April 3, 2024 
• Task Force Meeting: August 16, 2024 
• Public Meeting: May 13, 2024 
 
FUTURE PROJECT REVIEW 
At this time, BPDA Board approval is being sought only for approval of the 
Wentworth IMP. The future Article 80B Submissions for the PIPs will be reviewed by 
staff, be subject to all applicable regulations at the time of submission and be 
considered by BCDC before any further BPDA Board action on such submissions.

B. Student Housing 
The PIPS in total add approximately 1,324 net new student housing beds to the 
University’s permanent housing inventory. This significant increase is intended to 
help relieve the burden on the existing multifamily housing stock in nearby 
neighborhoods such as Fenway and Mission Hill by freeing up space in the local 
rental market. As of School Year 2023-24, Wentworth housed approximately 55% of 
its students on campus; with the completion of the three Residential Life dormitory 
PIPs described in the IMP, Wentworth will be able to house approximately 80% of 
its students on campus. 
 
C. Improved Street and Multimodal Networks 
 
The PIPs intend to create clear student life and academic clusters on campus, 
fostering a vibrant campus that consolidates much of Wentworth’s surface parking 
to two underground garages, thus freeing up more open space for improved 
circulation around and through the campus by walking, biking, and taking transit. 
Enhanced landscaping will further beautify the street edge and enhance the 
pedestrian experience along Ruggles Street, Huntington Avenue, Parker Street, and 
Annunciation Road.

Improvements to the existing pedestrian Pike, framing the south edge of the 
Campus, will better facilitate east-west neighborhood access in and through the 
campus for people walking and biking. The Proponent shall ensure the Pike is open 
to the public 24 hours per day, seven days per week, and will be limited to walking, 
dismounted biking, and placemaking activities. The Pike shall not be used for motor 
vehicle access for parking, loading, or services. The Pike must be a minimum of 12 
feet in width, free and clear of obstructions and open to the sky, with a typical 
minimum width of 20 feet clear of obstructions and open to sky. It will be 
constructed of an accessible surface in coordination with the Disabilities 
Commission. The Pike enhancements will be connected with the PIPs located in the 
existing West Lot and will be completed with the final building completing the new 
West Quad. A pedestrian path will remain open through construction.

coordination with PIPs:

Huntington Avenue will serve as an enabling element of the first PIP of the 
West Quad PIPs to eliminate conflicts between pedestrians and left-turning 
vehicles and create an accessible, multimodal gateway for the campus. 
Anticipated changes will include, at minimum, a wider sidewalk and 
furnishing zone; a narrowed Ruggles Street driveway with a continuous,

D. Historic Preservation 
Wentworth has committed to immediate repairs needed to stabilize designated 
landmark buildings referred to as the “Vienna Brewery Complex” located at 47 and 
133 Station Street, Boston. The objectives of the immediate repair and shoring work 
are to stabilize, replace, and/or repair deteriorated masonry at the facades of the 
two buildings and shore portions of the deteriorated framing and reduce water 
infiltration. These repairs are associated with the Certificate of Occupancy needed 
for the New Sweeney Field project. In a memo to the Boston Landmarks 
Commission on August 26, 2024, Wentworth stated that the “re-use, of the Brewery 
Complex cannot be incorporated into Wentworth’s future planning; it is therefore 
apparent that Wentworth must find another organization with a community-based 
mission that has the resources and vision to rehabilitate and transform this site in a 
manner that furthers Wentworth’s and that organization’s mission while also 
honoring its historic status.”

The PIPs have been informed by strategies to encourage development along 
important corridors and framing open spaces. Buildings along Huntington Avenue 
intend to locate active student, public, and community-oriented programs along 
these perimeter edges to foster a rich and active public realm and strengthen 
connections to surrounding neighborhoods and commercial nodes. The PIPs will 
also attractively frame existing and new campus quadrangles and provide vibrant 
new spaces that will attract both students and members of the public. The PIPs will 
also create greater usable open space by replacing many current surface parking 
lot areas with new landscaped and hardscape areas and accessible connections 
through the campus, thus providing significant aesthetic and physical

Planning Department Development Review process for each PIPs and associated 
public realm improvements, the University will work closely with Planning 
Department Urban Design Staff and other stakeholders through the full design 
review process. 
F. Green Building & Environmental Planning 
The University endeavors to prioritize increasing energy performance for its PIPs, 
and intends to seek strategies that support low-carbon building operations, 
integration of renewable energy resources, embodied carbon reduction, and LEED 
points that may be achieved with each PIP without significantly adding cost to the 
PIPs. Through the increase in open spaces set forth in the Wentworth IMP, the 
University also intends to follow strategies that expand the tree canopy, mitigate 
stormwater, promote biodiversity, and enhance the resiliency of Wentworth’s 
landscape features by planting a mix of native and adaptive species, and creating 
microhabitats and other design features appropriate to the campus context.

CHAPTER 1 
INTRODUCTION 
Wentworth Institute of Technology, Inc. (“Wentworth” or the “University”) is a technology university 
with five schools focused on engineering, computing, design, science, and management. The 
University consists of 31 acres of land between the Southwest Corridor and the Back Bay Fens. 
Wentworth previously filed its Institutional Master Plan approved by the Boston Planning and 
Development Agency (“BPDA”) in 2011, as amended in 2017 and extended in 2021 for two years 
(“Prior IMP”). Upon expiration of the Prior IMP, in March 2023, Wentworth filed its Institutional 
Master Plan Notification Form (“IMPNF”) on March 10, 2023. Wentworth is pleased to submit this 
Institutional Master Plan (“IMP”) to the BPDA to commence the review process pursuant to Section 
80D-8 and 80D-5(2) of the Boston Zoning Code, 1956 Mass. Acts c. 665 (“Code”). 
With this IMP, Wentworth seeks to modernize and evolve into an institution that educates the 
leaders of tomorrow while continuing its tradition for more than a century of contributing to the 
local community. Modernizing means creating a sustainable, resilient, and accessible campus that 
reflects the University’s values, ensuring that Wentworth continues to attract students who will 
become future industry leaders in Boston and beyond. It also means strengthening the Wentworth 
community by providing more permanent long-term housing on campus to create a cohesive on-
campus experience for our students and to help alleviate the housing affordability crisis in Boston. 
Through the goals set forth here, Wentworth is setting the stage for the continued pursuit of 
educational excellence as the University seeks to train students in industries with the most in-
demand jobs and provide them with the real-life experience that makes Wentworth students and 
alumni so effective and sought after. 
Lastly, this IMP is also about remaining consistent and stable, and ensuring that as the University 
continues to modernize and evolve, it also remains on strong footing. Therefore, while Wentworth 
is seeking to increase enrollment during the term of the IMP, its enrollment goal is to return to pre-
pandemic levels; not above and beyond that. Moreover, despite consistent increased demand for 
more parking and vehicles even after the pandemic, and despite Wentworth’s plans to bring more 
students back to campus housing, the number of parking spaces is intended to remain consistent 
with the current campus supply. And, as always, this IMP has its roots firmly in Wentworth’s long-
standing dedication to a collaborative and iterative relationship with its neighbors and fellow 
community members, who the University continues to enjoy working closely with to create a more 
vibrant and diverse community within the Mission Hill neighborhood. 
1.1 
History and Background of Wentworth 
For more than a century, Wentworth has delivered a first-rate highly relevant education to prepare 
students for rewarding careers. Along with close faculty mentorship, Wentworth has prepared 
students to work with industry-standard technology by employing one of the most effective 
practices in education: you learn best by doing it. Wentworth is a nationally recognized, private, 
coeducational university offering master’s, bachelor's, and associate degrees, in addition to 
certificate programs, to over 3,500 full-time students annually. More than 50,000 alumni—who have

assumed leadership roles in a multitude of professions in industry, education, non-profits, and 
government—have graduated from Wentworth since it first opened its doors in 1911. 
Wentworth has been a university committed to training the technical workforce of greater Boston 
and continues to evolve its courses, programs, and degrees, making the City a beacon of scientific 
and technical development. Employers seek out Wentworth co-op students and graduates for their 
demonstrated abilities to quickly become productive members of the workforce, technical problem-
solving skills, and educational preparation that allows them to adapt to continuously changing 
technologies. More than 58% of Wentworth students are offered post-graduate, full-time 
employment by their co-op employers. 
The University is proud of its role in the surrounding neighborhood and community. In partnership 
with Mission Main Apartments and Alice Heyward Taylor Apartments, Wentworth has worked with 
the community to maintain the safety, development, and overall well-being of the neighborhood. 
Through the STRIVE Program, Wentworth has provided vocational opportunities for Boston Public 
School students who receive special education services (see Chapter 8). Wentworth has also 
successfully maintained public spaces, such as the Evans Way Park, and other open space on 
campus. Additionally, it continues to open its private facilities to community organizations free of 
charge. 
1.2 
History of IMP 
Wentworth filed its first Institutional Master Plan (the “Initial IMP”) in 1999. The Initial IMP covered 
2000 through 2008 and included one proposed project for the development of a new residence 
hall as an addition to Baker Hall located at 610 Huntington Avenue. Subsequently, the Initial IMP 
was amended twice. The first amendment, filed in April of 2003, allowed for the development of a 
second new student residence at 555 Huntington Avenue and the incorporation of an existing 12-
person residence hall located at 66 Louis Prang Street. The second amendment, filed in June of 
2007, approved the addition of a property located at 525 and 634 Huntington Avenue as interim 
open green space. During the term of the Initial IMP, Wentworth made significant progress towards 
Boston’s goal of expanding the University’s capacity to house students on campus, increasing the 
total number of student bed spaces from 1,033 to 1,936. 
Wentworth filed its second Institutional Master Plan (the “Prior IMP”) in 2010. The Prior IMP covered 
2010 through 2020 and included five institutional projects. Those projects were: (1) the renovation 
and building addition for the Flanagan Campus Center at Beatty Hall; (2) an 18,000 square foot 
addition to the Ira Allen Building at 540 Parker Street; (3) a new 7-story student residence at 525 
Huntington Avenue to house 305 students; (4) a 45,000 square foot Center for Engineering and 
Technology; and (5) a new soccer field on a single level deck above a parking garage (“New Sweeney 
Field”). The Prior IMP was amended once in 2017 to amend the fourth project—the 45,000 square 
foot Center for Engineering and Technology—to an approximately 69,000 square foot Multipurpose 
Academic Building (the “Center for Engineering, Innovation and Science” or “CEIS”). In January 2021, 
Wentworth filed a two-year renewal of the Prior IMP to the extend the expiration date to 2023. All

2.1 
Introduction 
This chapter describes Wentworth’s history, mission, vision, objectives, diversity, equity, and 
inclusion initiatives, academic programs, student enrollment, and Campus Master Plan. 
2.2 
History of Wentworth 
Wentworth is a nationally recognized private coeducational institution of higher education that 
offers cooperative baccalaureate programs, master’s degrees, and certificate programs in the 
disciplines of engineering, computing, design, science, and management. Founded in 1904, through 
a bequest from Arioch Wentworth, a Boston merchant and real estate investor, the University 
opened its doors in 1911. 
For over 100 years, Wentworth has been proud to call the Mission Hill neighborhood of Boston its 
home. Just as Boston has grown and changed over that time, Wentworth has evolved from a 
technical school into a higher education institution granting both undergraduate and graduate 
degrees. 
Wentworth has graduated approximately 50,000 students who have assumed leadership roles in 
industry, education, and government. Wentworth graduates and cooperative education (“co-op”) 
students are sought after for their demonstrated abilities to quickly become productive members 
in the workplace, for their technical problem-solving skills, and for their educational preparation 
that allows them to adapt to continuously changing technologies. 
The University maintains that providing quality teaching is its most important function and that 
scholarly and applied research enhances teaching. These principles have driven Wentworth to 
becoming the university it is today. Wentworth’s programs are practical and rigorous, designed to 
achieve a unity of theory and practice through a “hands-on” approach. Communication skills, team 
building, and analytical thinking are central to the educational process. The programs are supported 
by full- and part-time faculty who are active in their disciplines. They bring professional experience 
into the classroom and laboratory, provide needed direction and discipline for the development of 
technical skills, and motivate and counsel for confidence building. In turn, both faculty and students 
are supported by laboratories, a library, a learning center, and students are provided with a full 
array of student services expected at a private institution of higher education. The Massachusetts 
Department of Higher Education approved Wentworth’s university designation in July 2017. The 
designation followed Wentworth’s establishment of graduate programs in four distinct professional 
fields of study and is a confirmation that Wentworth has faculty, facilities, and resources necessary 
to support sound graduate programs. 
2.3 
Mission Statement 
Wentworth Institute of Technology, the university of opportunity, provides our diverse community 
of learners with access to educational programs responsive to evolving market needs. Through a

uniquely effective, hands-on, experiential, and cooperative education approach, Wentworth 
prepares graduates who are future-focused and career-ready. 
2.4 
Vision 
Placing the student at the center of what we do, our vibrant and diverse campus community of 
faculty, staff, and students, helps each member reach their greatest potential. We seek to maximize 
the value of our graduates’ contributions to global society and their effectiveness as future leaders. 
2.5 
Wentworth’s Strategic Pillars and Objectives 
Inclusive Excellence 
We commit to the continuous development of a campus culture that is increasingly diverse, 
equitable, and inclusive. We strive to develop a campus where everyone feels valued and 
meaningfully supported toward reaching their full potential. 
High Value Learning 
We commit to offering a high return on investment by providing an education that equips our 
graduates with knowledge that is coupled with a highly valued skillset. We accomplish this through 
opportunities to address real-world challenges, applied research, social impact projects, 
cooperative education, collaborative experiences, cross-cultural exchange, and the effective use of 
advanced technologies. 
Transformative Student Experience 
We commit to prioritizing the health and well-being of our students and providing opportunities 
in support of their growth and transformation. Our holistic approach includes an interconnection 
of high-value learning, with high-quality services, activities, programs, and opportunities that align 
with student needs, interests, goals, and aspirations. 
Next Generation Partnerships 
We commit to maximizing the mutual benefits of partnerships with industry, alumni, and various 
communities. Through these partnerships, we enhance the quality of learning for our students and 
provide industry with a resource of skilled graduates. Through mutually beneficial forms of 
engagement, we support the lifelong learning needs of our alumni. We promote economic and 
social development in communities that include Boston and beyond. 
2.6 
Building a Sustainable Future 
Wentworth recognizes the need for urgent action to address the environmental challenges facing 
Boston and society at large. Wentworth sees a natural fit between sustainability and its core values 
of putting students first, using the world as our classroom, and thinking outside the box. 
Wentworth’s students will be the leaders of sustainable change by bringing multidisciplinary skills, 

Wentworth Institute of Technology

2-3 
Mission & Objectives 
real-world experience, and a deep understanding of environmental and social issues to whatever 
career they pursue. 
Wentworth is consistently recognized among the top green colleges by the Princeton Review. From 
green buildings to hands-on learning and engagements with diverse community stakeholders, 
Wentworth’s bold leadership on sustainability is evident in its commitment to treating the campus 
as a living laboratory and training tomorrow’s leaders in sustainable innovation. 
Campus as a Living Laboratory for Sustainability 
Since 2005, Wentworth has committed to green building standards for all major construction 
projects, transforming the campus with spaces that are healthy, energy-efficient, environmentally 
responsible, and high performance. 
For example, as early as 2005, Wentworth’s 555 Huntington Avenue Residence Hall was constructed 
to LEED standards and features a roof-top rainwater harvesting system used to irrigate the 
surrounding landscape. Most recently, Wentworth’s New Sweeney Field Project, which is currently 
underway, will be constructed to Parksmart standards, a green rating system for parking garages. 
Sustainable transportation features will include Wentworth’s first installation of EV charging stations 
and a secure bicycle cage to store both bikes and motorized scooters. 
Overall, this means that Wentworth's new construction and major renovation projects have 
achieved the LEED Silver certifiable target, resulting in more than 25% of campus buildings (by gross 
square feet) being built or renovated to high-performance building standards. Furthermore, despite 
the University’s urban setting, more than 200,000 square feet of the campus grounds have been 
designed to manage stormwater and promote groundwater recharge. 
Training Tomorrow’s Leaders in Sustainability 
Wentworth’s academic programs include undergraduate degrees in Climate Resilience and Building 
Sciences, more than 20 courses that focus exclusively on sustainability concepts, and more than 70 
additional courses related to sustainability. In these courses, students can study topics ranging from 
energy systems to green infrastructure and environmental justice. As is a hallmark of Wentworth’s 
educational model, students build foundational knowledge of environmental issues in their courses, 
which then allows them to make meaningful community connections in service-learning projects, 
and in their co-ops at innovative organizations tackling real-world challenges like climate change. 
Most recently, Wentworth’s Bachelor of Science in Architecture program was one of only fourteen 
programs in the U.S. to earn a Department of Energy “Zero Energy Design Designation.” 
Detailed information regarding Wentworth’s commitment to sustainability is set forth below in 
Chapter 7. 
2.7 
Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion

Mission & Objectives 
As part of Wentworth’s strategic planning around “Inclusive Excellence,” the Division of Diversity, 
Equity, and Inclusion was formed in 2020 to ensure that DEI is the top priority for the University. Its 
offices work independently and collaboratively with each other and other departments to ensure 
DEI practices are implemented at Wentworth through learning and development, equity training 
and workshops, community and industry partnerships, student engagement and initiatives, college 
access and pipeline programs, and recruitment, retention, and success efforts. 
Wentworth is committed to fostering an accessible campus environment and connecting 
individuals with the resources needed to be successful. This objective is accomplished through a 
myriad of initiatives and programs designed to “expand the local college access and success 
pipeline” to recruit and matriculate underserved learners in the community and cultivate internal 
and external campus partnerships that contribute to the growth and development of students, staff, 
and faculty. Integral to Wentworth’s central DEI mission is acknowledging the diversity of our 
student and employee identities, celebrating their success, and amplifying their voices to create an 
engaged, receptive, inclusive campus and surrounding community. Wentworth ensures this diverse 
pool of voices and identities are supported institutionally by establishing and implementing 
policies, procedures, and related educational opportunities that promote equity while creating 
accountability among all community members. 
In 2020, the University appointed and hired a Vice President for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion, 
whose role is to lead development of a comprehensive framework in order to further the 
University’s goal of creating a welcoming and inclusive learning and working environment. 
Wentworth’s Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion division is currently composed of four offices: the 
Center for Cultural and Global Engagement, the Center for Community and Learning Partnerships 
(“CLP”), Office of Institutional Equity, and the Industry Corps. 
Center for Diversity and Global Engagement 
These programs promote cross-cultural perspectives, inclusivity, leadership, development, and 
personal growth within the Wentworth community, and fosters a welcoming and safe environment 
for all students with a specific focus on underserved populations and their allies. A few of these 
initiatives include: 
• 
Beloved Community Social Justice Retreat, encouraging students to participate in 
self-reflection exercises that examine power and privilege through an overnight 
retreat. 
• 
Umoja Cultural Graduation Ceremony, acknowledging and embracing the rich 
culture of graduating students of color while celebrating their achievements and 
contributions to the Wentworth community. 
• 
Equity Leadership Series, addressing equity and change through a series of 
workshops.

Center for Community and Learning Partnerships 
Since 2000, the CLP has been Wentworth’s neighborhood engagement arm and the hub for college 
access and success of Boston residents. With a rich history of engaging its neighbors in the local 
community, Wentworth strengthens local relationships and creates long-term partnerships with the 
community. The University offers the expertise of its students, faculty, and staff to support the needs 
of Boston residents, through programs including:

Alternative Spring Break, providing students the opportunity to apply what they are

Office of Institutional Equity 
The Office of Institutional Equity supports the University in cultivating and maintaining a campus 
environment that is equitable, inclusive, and accessible. Among its many responsibilities are 
managing compliance with state and federal non-discrimination laws, providing educational 
programming to the community, coordinating prompt, thorough, and impartial resolutions to 
allegations of discrimination, establishing meaningful non-discrimination policies, and identifying 
and eliminating obstacles to accessibility for students, faculty, and staff. 
Industry Corps 
The Industry Corps aims to deliver education-to-career pathways driven by the needs of the local 
economy. Participants can earn stacked credentials that will build their portfolio of skills, which 
allows them the opportunity to either join the workforce immediately after completion or continue 
with additional education at Wentworth.

(“IPAC”). Through IPAC, corporate/academic communication is maintained to assist the faculty with 
the development of a technological education that is responsive to the needs of, and the latest 
trends in, the industry.

3.1 
Summary of Campus Properties 
The campus of Wentworth is located at the crossroads of the Mission Hill and the Fenway 
neighborhoods of Boston. It is a true urban campus with a rich diversity of neighbors, including the 
Massachusetts College of Art and Design (“MassArt”), the Mission Main and Alice Heywood Taylor 
housing developments, the Greek Orthodox Cathedral of the Annunciation, the Museum of Fine 
Arts, Northeastern University, the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority Ward Street 
headworks, and the Engine 37 and Ladder 26 firehouse of the Boston Fire Department, along with 
private residential properties along Huntington Avenue, Louis Prang and Vancouver Streets. Both 
programmatically and physically, Wentworth is an institution closely knit into its urban environment. 
The campus is well served by public transit. Wentworth lies within steps of both the Longwood and 
Museum of Fine Arts MBTA Green Line trolley stops. Roxbury Crossing and Ruggles Stations on the 
MBTA’s Orange Line are also close to campus, providing access to both commuter rail and subway 
service. Ten major MBTA bus routes and several shuttles operated by the Longwood Collective 
serve the campus. In addition, Wentworth is just a block away from the Southwest Corridor Park’s 
commuter bike path. 
Wentworth’s campus consists of 37 buildings set on 31 acres. Its facilities include: 14 residence halls 
housing approximately 1,787 students; 14 academic and administrative buildings; one building and 
three ancillary structures devoted to athletics; and four buildings associated with the Facilities 
Department/services. In addition, two currently vacant structures that were once part of a brewery 
complex and designated as a historic landmark by the Boston Landmarks Commission are also 
owned by Wentworth. The location, size, and uses of each of Wentworth’s facilities are presented 
in Tables 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4 included in this section. Broadly speaking, Wentworth’s campus has 
a straightforward organization with academic, administrative, and student life functions clustered 
in the center of campus around the “Quad” and residence halls clustered along both edges of 
Huntington Avenue. 
3.2 
Summary of Open Space 
Currently, Wentworth’s campus consists of ample open space, much of which is surrounded by 
campus buildings, spanning the length of the campus from the Southwest Corridor to the Colleges 
of the Fenway. The major existing open spaces are depicted in Figure 3.1. As a result of community 
feedback, one of the goals of the University over the term of this IMP—and in the longer-range 
Campus Master Plan—is to create an inclusive urban-scale connection between public outdoor 
spaces spanning across the Colleges of the Fenway from the Back Bay Fens to the Southwest Corridor 
Park. The improvements will not only activate the open space to better serve students, but the 
improvements will also more strongly connect Wentworth’s campus to the surrounding 
neighborhood. The open space improvements proposed over the term of this IMP will be described 
in Chapters 4, 5 and 7.

3.5 
Campus Infrastructure 
Wentworth is comprised of 37 buildings, 13 of which make up the “main” campus and are serviced 
from the central plant. As well, there are seven brownstones located at Louis Prang and Vancouver 
Streets. Over time, other properties and buildings have been added to the campus. The result is 
that utility feeds are a compilation of systems. 
During the Prior IMP term, Wentworth experienced a modest amount of physical growth with the 
acquisition of two former gas station properties on Huntington Avenue and a residential property 
on Louis Prang. The residential property on Louis Prang was renovated and put into service as a 
residence hall, and construction of two new residence halls at 555 Huntington Avenue and 610 
Huntington Avenue required the demolition of three existing buildings. The gas stations originally

at 525 Huntington Avenue were demolished and a new residence hall was built at that location. 
During this period, many systems (electrical, steam, water, drain, and sewer) have been upgraded. 
Fuel oil is no longer used for heating on campus. Drains in the main parking lot recharge the 
groundwater; water from some roofs along with a 1,500-foot well are used for landscape irrigation. 
Approximately 30% of the campus electricity is from co-generation. 
The following is a brief description of the infrastructure servicing the Wentworth campus: 
3.5.1 
Electrical Service 
The campus is served by Eversource for all of its electrical power requirements. Referring to Figure 
3.2, the main campus (Buildings 1-10, 15, and 19) is serviced by Eversource and consists of two 
13.8kV feeds terminating in Building 1. From this point, the electrical service is distributed by 
conduits which run in service tunnels or underground duct bank systems. A 570kW natural gas fired 
co-generation plant provides steam for heating and electrical generation. Electric energy can be 
resold to Eversource depending on main campus demand. All other buildings are fed from 
Eversource with standalone systems. 
The Ira Allen Building and most of the Annex Complex, formerly known as Boston Trade High 
School, (Buildings 18, 20, 21, 22, and 23) are fed from a 4,160 volt-1200amp service from the front 
of the Annex at 550 Parker Street. Annex East (Building 24) is fed from a 4,160 volt-1600amp service 
off Annunciation Road. 
The residence halls along Evans Way and the north side of Huntington Avenue (Buildings 11, 12, 
and 13) are fed from a 13.8kV service from Evans Way. 610 and 620 Huntington Avenue residence 
halls (Buildings 14 and 16) are together fed from a 13.8kV service off Ward Street. Building 14 has 
two 75kW co-generators that provide electricity and both domestic and heating hot water. 525 
Huntington Avenue is fed from a 13.8kV service from Louis Prang Street. Emergency power and 
lighting are provided by diesel or natural gas fired generator sets strategically located throughout 
the campus. 
Residence halls (Building 27) located at 60, 62, 66, and 68 Louis Prang Street and 7, 9, and 15 
Vancouver Street have separate single phase distribution in each dwelling. Here, emergency 
lighting is provided by battery packs. 
3.5.2 
Heating and Cooling 
Wentworth’s Power Plant (Building 1) provides low pressure steam (12 psi) for heating to the main 
campus (Buildings 1-10, 15, and 19). The steam is produced from three boilers and the gas fired 
co-generator which together can deliver 23,000 lbs. of steam per hour. The steam heating system 
also incorporates a vacuum return system. 
Two 600-ton electric chillers provide cooling for Williston, Wentworth, Dobbs, Watson, Kingman, 
Willson, Beatty, and the Center for Engineering, Innovation and Sciences (Buildings 2-8, 10, and 19).

University’s facilities are outdated, inefficient, and in need of upgrades. The primary needs of 
Wentworth during this IMP period include the expansion and modernization of instructional 
facilities to keep Wentworth’s academic programs at the forefront of technology; the addition of 
quality residences to house more students on-campus; improvements to increase accessibility in 
buildings and open spaces; and moving parking below grade to physically open up land for more 
strategic development (as set forth in this IMP) and useable green space for students and the 
neighborhood. 
4.1.2 
Academic Facilities 
A space utilization and demand analysis was conducted as part of Wentworth’s Campus Master 
Plan to determine the number, size, and type of instructional and support spaces needed to meet 
the current program demand. The analysis found that several of the institution’s existing classroom, 
laboratory, workshop spaces, and studios are either lacking or outdated, and therefore new 
academic buildings are needed to improve the spaces utilized in Wentworth’s experiential “hands-
on” approach to education pedagogy. The proposed new academic buildings—the West Quad 
Academic Building and the Annex Academic Complex—is described in more detail in the following 
chapter. The new academic buildings will provide active learning spaces focused on creating 
collaborative and experiential spaces compared to traditional methods used for spaces in the past. 
4.1.3 
Student Life Services and Recreation 
A demand analysis was conducted as part of Wentworth’s Campus Master Plan on the student life 
and recreational spaces to examine the different types and varying needs for student spaces. This 
process was grounded in a demand-based programming analysis, based on findings from student 
and faculty/staff surveys and feedback on dining and recreation preferences. The demand analysis 
found that both the existing cafeteria and fitness center are significantly undersized to serve 
Wentworth’s current and expected future enrollment including accommodating some from our 
Colleges of the Fenway partnership. As a result, a proposed project for this IMP term is the Pike 
Residence Hall, which features a much-needed dining hall, fitness center, and retail at street level. 
The demand analysis also found that year-round, indoor-outdoor gathering spaces, such as a 
temporary tent pitched in the quad during COVID, were highly utilized by students and are missing 
on campus. As a result, projects such as the New Campus Front Door, are proposed by Wentworth 
over this IMP term to improve access and public space.

4.1.5 
Housing 
Wentworth is committed to meeting Boston’s goals for housing students on campus and has 
determined its need for student housing based on both the City’s goals and its own goals. Given 
the current condition of some of its buildings that house students, Wentworth is at a competitive 
disadvantage when recruiting prospective students. Wentworth has conducted a residential space 
demand analysis as part of the Campus Master Plan, which considered factors such as building 
suitability, enrollment projections, and the City’s goals as noted above. The analysis revealed that 
Edwards/Rodgers Hall, among other residences, need replacing due to facility age, usability, and 
suitability. As a result, Wentworth proposes to replace the currently outdated Edwards/Rodgers Hall 
with a new residential building that can house approximately 651 net new students, as further 
described in Chapter 5 (Huntington Residence Hall). 
Furthermore, analysis revealed that student engagement, likelihood of academic success, and 
overall student experience improve when undergraduate students, especially underclassmen, live 
on campus. This is, in part, because students that live on campus can build community and bond 
with peers in a manner that allows for academic success. Therefore, one of the goals of this IMP is 
to add residential capacity that would allow all freshmen to live on-campus in one or two central 
locations. For example, Wentworth is envisioning that the Huntington Residence Hall project 
proposed in Chapter 5 be dedicated to housing the entire freshmen class, thereby creating a sense 
of belonging, fostering collaboration, creativity and innovation by allowing spaces for organic and 
intentional meetups and creating a cohesive freshman class community to help bolster students 
through their academic career.

gatherings, such as commencement ceremonies, student activities, movie nights, summer BBQs,

public assembly require a mix of thoughtfully designed landscaped and hardscaped areas, which

4.1.8 
Parking 
In order to remain competitive in the highly competitive landscape of higher education in and 
around the Boston area, and to continue to serve its student body and greater community’s needs, 
Wentworth must continue to provide on-campus parking. For the numerous on- and off-campus 
factors and others set forth below and in Chapter 6, the demand for on-campus parking spaces 
will remain the same—or become greater than—the demand during the Prior IMP. Still, despite this 
possibility of increased demand, unlike many other nearby institutions that have increased their 
parking counts, Wentworth is not seeking additional parking spaces from its current inventory. 
Instead, through this IMP, Wentworth is seeking to maintain the same number of spaces that 
currently exist and have existed for the last 20+ years, and to reduce their impact on the 
surrounding community by placing a significant number of these parking spaces underground. 
The majority of Wentworth’s faculty and staff commute by car, on average, from over 10 miles away 
from the University and Wentworth’s co-op model increases the need for many students to 
commute by car. Wentworth has historically had approximately 28.7% of its undergraduate and 
graduate students living at home in various surrounding cities and town thus requiring many to 
commute into the City for school by car. In addition, for over 50 years, students have been choosing 
Wentworth because of its focus on hands-on technical and practical training through its co-op 
programs. These programs are located at the business office of the participating employers and 
can be located all throughout the Commonwealth or even beyond and therefore, often require that 
students drive to off-campus locations not easily accessible by public transportation. Finally, the 
COVID pandemic caused a seismic reduction in public transit usage everywhere including 
Wentworth and this behavior has largely become permanent with an increased demand for parking 
passes on campus since 2021. 
On top of Wentworth’s own need for and utilization of parking on its campus, the Mission Hill and 
Longwood Medical and Academic Area (“LMA”) communities have long relied on the University’s 
willingness to host parking for community events, because of the extremely limited parking 
availability in these neighborhoods. There has thus been a long-standing practice of neighbors, 
community organizations, and city departments depending on Wentworth to provide one-time as 
well as re-occurring relief for their parking needs during the hours when Wentworth students or 
faculty use them less. Wentworth also has parking needs which include providing parking for 
visitors and guest, and parking for events such as commencement, career fairs, conferences and 
symposiums, family/alumni weekend, accepted student day, open houses, and student sports 
events. To serve members of Wentworth’s community, the University has historically provided 
approximately 1,000 parking spaces on its campus; of these spaces, approximately 250 are for 
students, with the remainder for faculty and staff. This change will also enable a sizeable shift toward 
electric vehicles as EV charging station infrastructure will be included with the new parking areas.

Open Space and Public Realm - Urban Design Guidelines 
A series of linked open spaces and quads form the organizational framework of the future campus, 
and the following urban design principles and strategies help further the Three Big Ideas: 
• 
The “Pike”: The “Pike”—stretching from Evans Way Park to Annunciation Road—is 
reinforced as the primary east-west pedestrian spine of the campus that unites and 
organizes an expanded open space network. Development along its edges should 
frame this corridor and activate this space with high levels of transparency at the 
ground level where applicable. Landscape infiltration strategies such as rain gardens 
and other features along its length should echo the historic Stony Brook’s trajectory 
through campus. The Pike will be open 24 hours a day to pedestrian access, which will 
promote a welcoming atmosphere bustling with activity for not only members of the 
Wentworth community, but also for others in the greater community to enjoy including 
Colleges of the Fenway students, neighbors, and abutters. The current state of the Pike, 
which is as narrow as five feet wide, will be transformed into a beautiful and spacious 
central corridor that connects to the essential pedestrian circulation routes of the 
Southwest Corridor and Emerald Necklace, enshrines the robust and dynamic energy 
of the local community on campus, and provides an inviting social gathering space for 
all. 
 
• 
Campus Edges: Campus edges should be thoughtfully designed to balance the desire 
for a clear institutional identity with fostering an open, welcoming, and accessible 
campus for students, neighbors, and visitors of all ages and levels of mobility. 
Development should avoid unnecessary fencing, dense hedges, blank building walls,

4.3 
Pedestrian Guidelines and Objectives 
Wentworth’s guiding principles for pedestrian circulation are to: 
• 
build strong pedestrian connections into and through the Wentworth campus; 
• 
link to surrounding neighborhoods, institutions, open spaces and public pedestrian 
pathways; and 
• 
enhance pedestrian experience, safety, and accessibility. 
 
Wentworth is a compact campus with all of its facilities located within a five-to-seven-minute walk 
of each other and a five-to-ten-minute walk to two MBTA Green Line stops (Longwood and 
Museum of Arts) and two MBTA Orange Line Stations (Ruggles and Roxbury Crossing). For students, 
faculty, staff, neighbors, and visitors, the primary mode of transportation while on campus is 
walking. 
Wentworth is positioned at a critical geographic point in Boston between Olmsted’s Emerald 
Necklace and the Southwest Corridor Park. The Campus Master Plan envisions the campus as the 
missing connective tissue between these urban-scale landscape systems, unifying them through a 
robust, performative open space framework. The formerly insular and fragmented campus is united 
by twin pedestrian spines linking together a series of unique outdoor gathering spaces. A 
reinvigorated “front lawn” becomes a welcoming front door, softening boundaries between the 
school and surrounding community. As people move through the campus, they experience the 
innovative and transformational learning happening throughout Wentworth. 
Front Lawn and Ruggles Street 
The proposed redevelopment of Wentworth’s front lawn will greatly improve the pedestrian 
experience on Ruggles Street. Today, tall privet hedges wall off Wentworth’s formal lawn from the 
public, separating the public from the University’s front door and creating a narrow sidewalk with 
a suboptimal pedestrian experience. The proposed improvements remove the hedges to allow for 
a wider sidewalk—compliant with the Boston Complete Streets Guidelines—with an amenity zone 
and invites pedestrians into the campus to experience a reimagined and activated open space. The 
proposed redevelopment will nevertheless respect and maintain the Annunciation Greek 
Cathedral’s view corridor to and from Huntington Avenue, which is a community and neighborhood 
benefit that Wentworth desires to maintain. 
A mid-block crossing to the new development at 500 Huntington Avenue links Wentworth’s 
campus to the new complex both functionally and visually. This will create a vibrant public realm 
and a safe experience for pedestrians that will utilize extended pedestrian paths across campus and 
improved crosswalks to create inclusive circulation routes throughout the neighborhood.

4-13 
Planning Framework 
At Wentworth’s main entrance on Ruggles Street, Wentworth Hall will be renovated to allow for 
direct access to the Quad from the front lawn through the building. Currently, navigating from 
Wentworth’s main entrance to the Quad requires traveling a winding, multi-floor route through 
several adjoining buildings. Pedestrian access to the heart of the campus will be greatly enhanced 
with the development of this new entry point and the related wayfinding signage that will be 
installed at the time of the renovation. The driveway serving Wentworth’s main entrance on Ruggles 
Street will also consider safety elements relating to its connection to public transit and traffic flow. 
Huntington Avenue 
Wentworth’s proposed new development along Huntington Avenue will enhance the pedestrian 
experience and will, where appropriate, incorporate new ground-floor retail or other activated 
streetscape uses fronting the street. New development along Huntington will improve the existing 
narrow sidewalks and incorporate concepts from the Boston Complete Streets Guidelines. Building 
setbacks will be informed by the Avenue of the Arts guidelines, allowing for a gracious sidewalk 
and a vibrant public experience. 
The Pike and East-West Connections 
The “Pike” is Wentworth’s—and the Colleges of the Fenway’s—primary pedestrian spine, and is a 
path heavily traveled each day by those making their way through the campus. It was envisioned 
as a link between Wentworth’s academic core campus and its residential buildings along 
Huntington Avenue. It currently runs through the campus in an east to west direction beginning at 
the Wentworth Annex on Parker Street, crossing Parker Street via a mid-block crosswalk, and 
extending through the central campus along the Quad and West Parking Lot to the crosswalk at 
Leopard Plaza where it crosses Huntington Avenue to MassArt Park adjacent to Wentworth’s 
residences on Huntington Avenue and Evans Way. This pedestrian way then continues from the 
MassArt Park in a westerly direction as a part of a route connecting the five Colleges of the Fenway. 
The proposed plan enhances this east-west experience by transforming the West Lot into a vibrant 
usable space through the construction of Pike Residence Hall, as well as by providing opportunities 
for aesthetically pleasant screening such as a series of mural walls along the southern edge of the 
Pike to frame and activate this important pedestrian thoroughfare. 
The proposed plan also expands on the Pike concept, creating a second parallel pathway mirroring 
the Pike on the north side of the Quad, thus strengthening the network of pedestrian paths through 
the campus. 
West Campus Pedestrian Network 
Currently, pedestrians are forced to walk through the West Lot to access the Quad and academic 
buildings. Pedestrians often walk north-south along the side of the Power Plant and Kingman and 
Willson Hall, traversing an active vehicular zone with no sidewalk.

The transformation of the West Lot into usable space and a new residence hall will significantly 
improve the pedestrian experience for the large population currently walking through the parking 
lot to access the campus. 
East Campus Pedestrian Connectivity 
Wentworth hopes to strengthen the pedestrian connection across Parker Street from the core 
campus through the redeveloped Annex site. Currently the Annex acts as a barrier between the 
campus and the surrounding community. The proposed plan opens a new walkable corridor of 
green space through the Annex site, providing a new point of access to the campus from the east. 
With the completion of the proposed projects, Wentworth’s campus will serve as a key connection 
point for pedestrians connecting the Back Bay Fens, Longwood Medical Area, Colleges of the 
Fenway, and Southwest Corridor through an engaging pedestrian experience.

Multimodal Framework

one of the main planning frameworks of this IMP is considering its existing multimodal framework 
and determining how its proposed institutional projects could strengthen or enhance its 
multimodal framework, including its pedestrian connectivity, bicycle connectivity, public transit 
connectivity, and motor vehicle connectivity. A more detailed discussion of each of these is 
contained in Chapter 6: Transportation. A plan showing the campus’s proposed multimodal

new student residential hall with up to 400 student beds and associated spaces. This PIP provides

of this surface parking area with a building that helps to both frame the Pedestrian Pike and to 
alleviate the Boston’s housing crisis by bringing students back on campus and thereby opening up 
more apartments within the surrounding community. 
This PIP will also have no negative impact on the surrounding area as it is replacing a surface parking 
area with student housing and usable open space in an area of campus that does not directly abut 
the residential neighborhood. The height of the PIP will fit into its surrounding context and new

5.1.3 
West Quad Academic Building 
Wentworth is proposing a new academic building (“West Quad Academic Building”) to replace 
existing instructional spaces that lack accessibility and are in dire need of updates. The West Quad 
Academic Building will provide new academic space utilized in the experiential, “hands-on” 
approach to educational pedagogy that is at the heart of Wentworth’s mission. The West Quad 
Academic Building will be up to approximately 150 feet tall, containing up to 140,000 GSF, and is 
intended to provide academic spaces such as new modernized classrooms, workshop space, and 
design studios, as well as administrative spaces such as offices, galleries, and student collaboration 
spaces. 
Construction of the West Quad Academic Building requires the demolition of the existing, outdated 
Kingman (12,176 GSF) and Willson (8,135 GSF) Halls, which are located west of the Quad—in the 
heart of Wentworth’s campus—and east of the “West Lot” parking lot off Huntington Avenue (see 
Figure 5.4 for the location of the proposed academic building). The construction of the West Quad 
Academic Building will also free up space within the Annex Complex so that these outdated 
buildings can be taken down and rebuilt in a modern manner that meets current and acceptable 
building and accessibility standards. 
Wentworth envisions that the West Quad Academic Building will frame a new western gateway into 
the core campus from the intersection of Ruggles Street and Huntington Avenue and connect to 
future open space. 
This PIP will have minimal negative impact on the surrounding area as it is replacing 
Willson/Kingman Halls, which are currently academic buildings. The new academic building is 
located near the center of campus, away from public streets, and will not result in an increase in 
traffic. This PIP, which is in the center of campus and away from neighboring properties, will not 
cast additional shadows in the surrounding neighborhood. In fact, this PIP will be a major 
improvement from the existing, underutilized Willson/Kingman Halls, which have little transparency 
and connection to the overall campus on the ground floor, an inaccessible second floor, and 
outdated amenities.

5.5 
Zoning 
Wentworth’s entire campus is located within the Mission Hill Neighborhood District of the City of 
Boston, as defined in Boston Zoning Code Map 6D. All institutional use parcels are identified with 
the designation of “Institutional Master Plan Area.” Most of the institutional use parcels are located 
within the Wentworth Institute Institutional Subdistrict, while a small portion is located southeast 
outside of the main campus, and another east of Parker Street is located within the Local Industrial 
Subdistrict. Most of campus north of Ward Street is located within the Groundwater Conversation 
Overlay District, and most of the campus located west of Parker Street is located within the 
Restricted Parking Overlay District. 
This 2024–2034 IMP is the framework for the zoning controls for Wentworth’s institutional uses. 
While there are underlying zoning districts and overlay districts that include Wentworth’s 
institutional properties, the IMP is the controlling document for zoning approvals. The institutional 
uses include “college and university use,” which is defined in Article 2 of the Boston Zoning Code 
to include “subuses such as classrooms, residences, student housing, eating facilities, research 
laboratories, athletic facilities, libraries, faculty and other offices, museums, auditoria and other 
facilities of public assembly, parking, and other similar uses.” Under the provisions of the Mission 
Hill Neighborhood District, Table D of Article 59, college or university use is allowed as of right in 
the Wentworth Institute Institutional Subdistrict. Outside of the main campus, in the Local Industrial 
Subdistrict, such use shall also be deemed to comply pursuant to the IMP. The PIPs listed in the 
sections above include a description of the maximum dimensional limits of proposed projects as 
they are anticipated at the time of the IMP. Minor deviations from the descriptions provided herein 
may occur as specific project design progress. PIPs may be constructed in multiple phases, in 
approximately the order listed above, and may also be constructed to less than the approved 
maximum build-out. All projects that exceed the applicable thresholds shall also be subject to 
review under Article 80B Large Project Review and Article 80E Small Project Review, as applicable.

80E, as applicable, these changes are also deemed to be consistent with the IMP. 
The following addresses the relationship between the IMP and other zoning districts and ordinances 
that cover Wentworth’s campus. 
Groundwater Conservation Overlay District 
The Groundwater Conservation Overlay District (“GCOD”) was established under Article 32 of the 
Boston Zoning Code to protect and restore groundwater levels within the City of Boston and, by 
doing so, to protect and enhance the City’s historic neighborhoods and structures. GCOD generally 
covers the main Wentworth campus north of Ward Street and Prentiss Street. 
Activities subject to GCOD include new construction, substantial rehabilitation, excavation, and 
paving. Projects subject to GCOD generally need to demonstrate that they will not adversely affect 
groundwater levels and recharge a volume of stormwater equal to a one-inch rainstorm where 
feasible. 
As further discussed in this IMP, Wentworth has been careful to ensure that new construction 
projects within and near the GCOD do not adversely affect groundwater levels. For projects within 
GCOD, the University will document compliance with GCOD standards through the BPDA Certificate 
of Consistency with the IMP. 
Restricted Parking Overlay District 
The Restricted Parking Overlay District (“RPOD”) is a Special Purpose Overlay District established 
under the provisions of Section 3-1A of the Boston Zoning Code. The RPOD requires that off-street 
parking facilities, including parking lots, parking garages, and ancillary or accessory parking for 
nonresidential uses to obtain a conditional use permit. Portions of the main campus west of Parker 
Street are located within the RPOD. 
Wentworth manages its parking supply on a campus-wide basis. It manages the transportation 
needs of its students, faculty, and staff via a Transportation Demand Management (“TDM”) plan, 
which is set forth in Chapter 6 of this IMP. Chapter 6 details the measures Wentworth has taken to 
promote alternative transportation modes and discourage single occupancy vehicles. Through the 
TDM plan, Wentworth will properly manage the parking supply and will document the compliance 
with the RPOD standards through the BPDA Certificate of Consistency on the IMP.

6.1 
Introduction 
This chapter includes analyses of the effects of the IMP Projects on transportation systems within 
and surrounding the Wentworth campus. The transportation systems analyzed include pedestrian, 
transit, bicycle, loading/service, vehicle traffic, and parking, and the analyses included herein 
address the comments in the Request for Additional Information dated November 29, 2023. 
The focus of this chapter is to be responsive to transportation-related comments from city 
departments, as well as the Wentworth Task Force and other involved community members and 
organizations. Representatives of the Wentworth consultant team met with representatives of the 
Boston Planning and Development Authority (“BPDA”) and the Boston Transportation Department 
(“BTD”) on multiple occasions over the course of 2022 and 2023 to help further define and evolve 
the City’s expectations and refine IMP Project elements related to transportation. An emphasis on 
pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure improvements to the Wentworth campus is a main focus of 
our analysis and future planning. 
The purpose of these analyses is to: 
• 
Define and quantify existing transportation conditions in the Project Study Area; 
• 
Estimate the transportation impacts that will be generated under future conditions 
based on the anticipated program for the IMP Projects; 
• 
Develop a set of mitigation strategies and improvement measures which will help 
lessen the transportation demand effects of the IMP Projects; and 
• 
Illustrate the Project’s prioritization of pedestrian and bicycle modes as part of the 
overall Transportation Demand Management (“TDM”) strategy and commitment 
to modern mobility. 
 
The analyses presented in this chapter cover the existing conditions and forecast future conditions 
with and without the proposed IMP Projects and quantify and describe their potential impacts on 
the transportation system serving Wentworth. In consultation with City staff, the potential impacts 
identified in these analyses have been used to inform the site circulation plan and the mitigation 
strategies that will help reduce the impacts of IMP Projects on the transportation system serving 
the Wentworth campus and surrounding neighborhood in this part of the Longwood Medical and 
Academic Area (“LMA”).

6.1.2 
Study Methodology 
The transportation analysis was conducted in three stages: (1) Existing Conditions, (2) Future 
Conditions, and (3) Mitigation. The first stage evaluated Existing Conditions; it involved collecting 
pedestrian, bicycle and vehicular volume data, and quantifying and describing existing 
transportation conditions near Wentworth’s campuses. This included the transportation 
infrastructure, pedestrian and bicycle facilities, transit operations, on-campus loading, traffic 
operations, parking, and Wentworth’s transportation demand management programs. 
The second stage of the study evaluated Future Conditions; it involved projecting and comparing 
future transportation conditions with and without the IMP Projects. Trips generated by the IMP 
Projects were estimated by mode, and vehicle trips were distributed to the roadway network. 
Parking demands for the IMP Projects were estimated and impacts on other transportation services 
are described. 
For the traffic impact analyses, morning and evening peak hour operations have been examined for 
the following conditions: 
• 
2023 Existing Condition – The traffic analysis uses traffic volume data from May 
2023 and existing geometric conditions on study area roadways and intersections 
to evaluate traffic operations. 
• 
2030 No-Build Condition – The forecast of future traffic volumes without the IMP 
Projects has been determined by increasing the existing traffic volumes by 
including expected traffic growth from other nearby city-approved projects in the 
area; per the City’s guidance, no annual growth percentage is applied to the 
existing volumes. Planned infrastructure improvements were also considered and 
included in the 2030 No-Build Condition. 
• 
2030 Build Condition – The build traffic forecast was determined by adding the 
IMP Projects-related traffic and infrastructure modifications to the 2030 No-Build 
Condition. Impacts of the IMP Projects on the study area are also described.
